The doctor of the nations also saw, who said: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who take hold of the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14)?
39.5: Therefore, the bride, supported by angelic ministries and thronged about by the heavenly host as she walks, is like the horsemen of the Lord; to those, surely, which once in the chariots of Pharaoh triumphed by so stupendous a miracle of divine help. For if you attend diligently, all things that you admire magnificently performed there, you will find here likewise to be admired. Except that it is now triumphed more magnificently, in that the things which there went before corporally are here fulfilled spiritually. Does it not, indeed, seem to you much stronger and far more glorious to prostrate the devil than Pharaoh; and to subdue the aerial powers than to overthrow the chariots of Pharaoh? There, finally, it was fought against flesh and blood; here, against princes and powers, against the rulers of the world of these darknesses, against spiritual wickedness in the heavens (Eph. 6:12). And follow now with me the individual members of the proportion. There a people is led out of Egypt, here a man out of the world; there Pharaoh is prostrated, here the devil; there the chariots of Pharaoh are overthrown, here the carnal and worldly desires which fight against the soul are cast down; those in the waves, these in tears; those of the sea, these bitter. I think that the demons even now cry aloud, if perhaps it happens to fall in upon such a soul: Let us flee from Israel, because the Lord fights for him (Exod. 14:25). Do you wish that I even designate to you some of the princes of Pharaoh by their proper names, and describe them concerning their chariots, after the likeness of which you also may be able to find others, if there are any, by yourself? Truly a great prince of the spiritual and invisible king of Egypt is Malice, great is Lust, great is Avarice. And these indeed possess their own territories under their king, just as their own are assigned to each. For Malice holds dominion in every region of evil deeds and crimes; Lust presides over all the uncleanness and baseness of the flesh; Avarice has obtained by lot the principality in the parts of rapine and fraud.
39.6: Now also receive what sort of chariots Pharaoh has prepared for these his princes to pursue the people of God. For Malice has her chariot standing on four wheels: Ferocity, Impatience, Boldness, Shamelessness. For that chariot is very swift to shed blood, which is neither stopped by innocence, nor retarded by patience, nor bridled by fear, nor held back by shame. It is drawn, moreover, by two exceedingly swift horses, and most ready for every destruction: earthly Power and worldly Pomp. For then that chariot of malice runs very swiftly, when on the one hand the effect of power is at hand to fulfill its malicious attempts; on the other the applause of pomp smiles upon the crimes committed, so that the word may be fulfilled which is written: Since the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed (Ps. 10:3); and again another Scripture: This, he says, is your hour, and the power of darkness (Luke 22:52). Further, two charioteers preside over these two horses: Haughtiness and Envy; and haughtiness indeed drives the pomp, but envy the power. For he is borne away by the swift love of diabolical pomps, whose heart first swelled within himself. For that which stands firmly in itself, compressed by fear, modest by gravity, solid by humility, sound by purity, will by no means be lightly swept away by the breeze of this vanity. Likewise, is not the beast of earthly power driven by envy, and urged on this side and that with certain spurs of envy — the suspicion, namely, of failing, and the fear of giving way? For one thing is that the successor is suspected, and another that the invader is feared. With these goads, therefore, earthly power is continually driven. And this, indeed, is how the chariot of malice stands.
39.7: But the chariot of Lust is likewise whirled by a four-horse team of vices: namely, Gluttony of the belly, Lust of intercourse, Softness of garments, and the Slackness of ease and sleep. It is drawn by two horses equally: Prosperity of life, and Abundance of things; and the two who preside over these are the Torpor of idleness and faithless Security: because plenty loosens idleness, and, according to the Scripture: The prosperity of fools shall destroy them (Prov. 1:32); not indeed for any other reason, but that it makes them wrongly secure: But when they shall have said, Peace and security; then sudden destruction shall come upon them (1 Thess. 5:3). These have no spurs at all, nor whips, nor anything of the sort, but in place of these they use a canopy to make shade, and a fan to draw up wind. Further, the canopy is Dissimulation, making shade, and protecting from the heat of cares. For it is proper to a soft and delicate soul to dissemble even necessary cares, and, lest it feel the burning anxieties, to hide under the hiding-place of dissimulation. But the fan is Profusion, bringing the wind of adulation. For the luxurious are lavish, buying with gold the wind from the mouth of flatterers. And of this enough.
39.8: But now Avarice likewise is borne on four wheels of vices, which are Pusillanimity, Inhumanity, Contempt of God, and Forgetfulness of death. Further, the beasts that draw are Tenacity and Rapacity; and one charioteer presides over both of these: the Ardor of possessing. For Avarice alone, since it does not allow many to be hired, is content with one servant. But he himself, the very prompt and indefatigable executor of the work enjoined, in urging on the straining beasts, uses the sharpest whips: the Lust of acquiring and the Fear of losing.
39.9: There are also other princes of the king of Egypt who themselves likewise have their chariots in the expedition of their lord, such as Pride, which is one of the greater princes; such as Impiety, the enemy of the faith, holding itself also a great place in the house and kingdom of Pharaoh; and there are still many other satraps and horsemen of a lower order, whose number is not in the army of Pharaoh; whose names and offices, and likewise their arms and their equipment, I leave to your studies to be sought out, that you may be exercised in these. In the strength, therefore, of these princes and of their chariots, the invisible Pharaoh, running about everywhere, rages in tyrannical fashion with whatever forces he can against all the household of the Lord, and in these very days pursues Israel going out of Egypt. But he, neither borne on chariots nor protected by arms; nonetheless strengthened by the hand of the Lord alone, sings securely: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; the horse and his rider he has cast into the sea (Exod. 15:1); likewise: These in chariots and these in horses; but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God (Ps. 20:8). And let these things have been said for the similitude adduced concerning the horsemen of the Lord and the chariots of Pharaoh.
39.10: After these things she is called the beloved. For he indeed was a friend even before the deliverance, otherwise he would not have delivered her whom he had not loved; but she, by the benefit of the deliverance, was led to be his beloved. Hear, finally, one who confesses. Not because we loved him, he says, but because he first loved us (1 John 4:10). Recall now to me Moses and the Ethiopian woman, and recognize already then prefigured the marriage of the Word and of the sinful soul; and discern, if you can, what tastes sweeter to you in the consideration of that most sweet sacrament: whether the all-too-kind condescension of the Word, or the inestimable glory of the soul, or the unlooked-for confidence of the sinner. But Moses could not change the skin of the Ethiopian woman; Christ could. For it follows: Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of the turtle-dove. But let this be reserved for another sermon; so that, ever taking with eagerness the things that are set before us on the table of the Bridegroom, we may bring them forth to his praise and glory, even of Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
39.title: Concerning the chariots of Pharaoh, that is, of the devil, and concerning the princes of the army, who are malice, luxury, and avarice.

40.1: Your cheeks are beautiful, like the turtledove's cheeks (Song 1:9). Tender is the bride's modesty; and at the rebuke of the bridegroom, I think, her face was suffused with a blush, and, appearing more beautiful from this, she immediately hears: Your cheeks are beautiful, like the turtledove's cheeks. But take care that you think not carnally of the colored corruption of the flesh, and the matter of the yellow or bloody humor, suffusing the surface of the glassy skin superficially and evenly: from which, moderately mixed with one another, a pale-red blush is tempered into a working of bodily beauty, to make comely the appearance of the cheeks. Otherwise that incorporeal and invisible substance of the soul exists neither distinguished by bodily members, nor painted with visible colors. But do you, with a spiritual gaze, if you can, reach that spiritual essence; and, to fit the pattern of the proposed likeness, think of the face of the soul, the intention of the mind; from which, to be sure, the uprightness of the work is estimated, just as from the face the beauty of the body. Further, understand modesty, as it were a color in the face, because this virtue especially both brings in comeliness and increases grace. Your cheeks, therefore, are beautiful, like the turtledove's cheeks. He could more customarily put 'face' and describe [her] as beautiful, as is the custom for one whose beauty is praised, saying 'with a beautiful face' or 'with a comely face': but I know not what he willed to himself, that he thought it better to say 'cheeks' in the plural, unless that I would by no means believe that to be idle. For the Spirit of wisdom speaks, to whom it is not lawful to ascribe anything at all as idle, or as spoken otherwise than it ought to have been. There is, therefore, without doubt a cause, whatever it may be, why he preferred to say 'cheeks' in the plural, rather than 'face' in the singular. And if you have nothing better, I will open that which seems [right] to me.
40.2: Two things are necessarily required in the intention, which we said to be the face of the soul, namely the matter and the cause; that is, what you intend, and for the sake of what. And from these two, to be sure, the beauty or the deformity of the soul is judged; so that, for example, the soul which has held both these things upright and chaste, to it is deservedly and truly said: Your cheeks are beautiful, like the turtledove's cheeks. But she who shall lack one of these two, of her it cannot be said that her cheeks are beautiful like the turtledove's, on account of that deformity which will yet be in part. But much less will this be able to suit her, who is found to have neither of these as praiseworthy. But all this will be made plainer in examples. If, for example, one directs his mind to inquiring after truth, and that from the love of truth alone; does he not seem to you to have both the matter and the cause honorable, and deservedly to claim for himself that which is said: Your cheeks are beautiful, like the turtledove's? seeing that in neither of his cheeks any blemish of reproach appears. But if he has directed himself to truth not at all from a desire of truth, but under the pretext of vainglory, or of some other temporal advantage whatsoever: now, even if he seems to have one of his cheeks beautiful, you will not nevertheless, as I judge, hesitate to judge him deformed even in part, whose other face the foulness of the cause has defiled. But if you have seen a man not intent upon any honorable pursuits, but ensnared by the allurements of the flesh, given over to the belly and to luxury, such as are those whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things (Phil. 3:19): what of that man? will you not judge him most foul on both sides, in whose intention, to be sure, both the matter and the cause are found reprobate?
40.3: To intend, therefore, not toward God, but toward the world, is of a worldly soul, and one having not any one of its cheeks beautiful at all. But to intend as it were toward God, yet not for the sake of God, is plainly of a hypocritical soul: whose face, although one part seems comely, in that it looks toward God with some intention or other; yet that very simulation destroys all that is comely in it, and rather everywhere brings in foulness. But if one has turned his intention toward God, whether solely, or chiefly, for the necessities of the present life; we say that it is not, indeed, foul with the dregs of hypocrisy, yet somewhat darkened through the vice of pusillanimity, and less acceptable. Further, on the contrary, to intend toward something other than God, yet for the sake of God; this is not the leisure of Mary, but the business of Martha. But far be it that I should say that one of this sort has anything deformed! Nor yet would I affirm that she has attained to the perfection of beauty: since she is still anxious and troubled about many things, and cannot but be sprinkled even with the thin dust of earthly actions. Yet a chaste intention, and the reference of a good conscience toward God, wipe this off quickly and easily, even in the hour of holy repose. To seek God alone, therefore, for his own sake alone, this plainly is to have both faces of the bipartite intention most beautiful; and this is proper and special to the bride, to whom it befits to hear, deservedly, by a singular prerogative: Your cheeks are beautiful, like the turtledove's cheeks.
40.4: But why, like the turtledove? It is a modest little bird, and its way of life is said to be passed not with many, but content with a single companion, so that if it has lost him, it does not seek another, but thereafter lives alone. You, therefore, who hear these things, so that you may indeed not hear idly those things which are written for your sake, and now are turned about and debated for your sake: you, I say, if you are moved by incitements of the Holy Spirit of this kind, and burn to give heed how you may make your soul the bride of God; strive to have both these cheeks of your intention beautiful, that, an imitator of that most chaste bird, you may sit, according to the prophet, solitary, since you have lifted yourself above yourself (Lam. 3:28). It is altogether above you, to be betrothed to the Lord of angels. Is it not above you, to cleave to God and to be one spirit with him? Sit, therefore, solitary, like the turtledove. Let nothing be [common] to you and the crowds, nothing with the multitude of the rest; and even forget your own people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty (Ps. 45:11-12). O holy soul, be alone, that you may keep yourself for him alone of all, whom you have chosen for yourself out of all. Flee the public, flee even your own household; withdraw from friends and intimates, even from him who ministers to you. Or do you not know that you have a modest bridegroom, and one who would by no means grant you his presence while others are present? Withdraw, therefore, but in mind, not in body; but in intention, in devotion, in spirit. For the Spirit before your face is Christ the Lord, and he requires the solitude of the spirit, not of the body, although at times you separate yourself even in body, not without profit, when you can do so opportunely, especially in the time of prayer. You hold also in this both the commandment of the bridegroom and the pattern: You, he says, when you pray, enter into your room, and having shut the door, pray (Matt. 6:6). And what he said, he did. He used to spend the whole night alone in prayer, not only hiding himself from the crowds, but not admitting even any of the disciples, nor any of the household (Luke 6:12-13). Finally, he had brought three of his intimates with him, when he hastened willingly to death; and he withdrew even from them, wishing to pray (Matt. 26:37-39). Therefore do you also likewise, when you shall wish to pray.
40.5: For the rest, only the solitude of the mind and of the spirit is enjoined upon you. You are alone, if you think not of common things, if you desire not things present, if you despise what many look up to, if you loathe what all desire, if you avoid quarrels, if you feel not losses, if you remember not injuries. Otherwise, not even if you are alone in body are you alone. Do you see that you can be both alone, when among many; and among many, when you are alone? You are alone in whatever great throng of men you may mix: only take heed not to be either a curious explorer, or a rash judge, of another's manner of life. Even if you detect anything wrongly done, do not on that account judge your neighbor, but rather excuse [him]. Excuse the intention, if you cannot [excuse] the deed; suppose ignorance, suppose surprise, suppose chance. But if the certainty of the matter altogether refuses every dissembling, persuade nonetheless yourself, and say within yourself: The temptation was too violent; what would it have done of me, if it had likewise received power over me? And remember that I now address the bride, and not instruct the friend of the bridegroom, whose office is more diligently to observe that no one sin, and to examine whether he sins, and to correct [him] if there has been a sin. From which necessity, to be sure, the bride is free, living alone to herself, and to him whom she loves, her bridegroom and likewise her Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
40.title: That intention is the face of the soul: what is its beauty or deformity; what are its solitude and boldness.

41.1: Your neck is like chains (Song 1:10). A neck is wont to be adorned with chains, not to be compared to them. But let those women do this, in whom because there is not comeliness of their own, it is necessary that they beg it from elsewhere, whence they may feign themselves to be beautiful. For the bride's neck is so comely in itself, and so becomingly as it were formed by nature, that it does not require external adornment. For what need is there to apply the dyes of foreign colors to one for whom a beauty that is her own, and as it were innate, suffices, to such a degree that she can even equal the splendor of those very chains which are sought for ornament? This indeed he wished to be understood, who said that chains hang not at all from the neck, as is customary, but rather that the neck itself is like chains. The Holy Spirit must not now be invoked by us, that just as He deigned to grant us to find the spiritual cheeks of the bride, so also He may deign to show her spiritual neck. And to my understanding indeed (since it lies upon me to speak what I feel) nothing for the present shines forth more probable or more likely, than that the understanding itself of the soul is signified by the name of the neck. You also, I think, will approve the same thing, if you attend to the reason of the likeness. Does it not indeed seem to you that the understanding, in some way, performs the office of the neck, through which your soul conveys into itself the vital nourishment of the spirit, and pours it into certain inward parts of its manners and affections? This neck, then, of the bride, that is, the pure and simple understanding, since it shines forth enough by itself with naked and open truth, does not need ornament; but rather adorns the soul becomingly, as a precious chain, and therefore is described as like the very chains. Truth is a good chain, purity or simplicity is good, to be wise unto sobriety is plainly a good chain. The understanding of the philosophers or heretics does not have in itself this splendor of purity and truth: and therefore they take great care to color it and paint it over with the trappings of words, and the wiles of syllogisms, lest, if it appear naked, the foulness of the false should also appear.
41.2: It follows: 'We will make you little chains of gold, inlaid with silver.' If he had said faciam, in the singular, and not faciemus, in the plural, I would have pronounced that the bridegroom spoke this too absolutely and undoubtingly. But now see that we perhaps more fittingly assign it to her companions, consoling the bride as it were by such a promise, that until she attains to the vision of him, for whose sake she so burns with desire, they will make for her beautiful and precious little chains, which are ornaments of the ears. And this for this reason, I think, because faith is from hearing; and as long as one walks by faith and not by sight, labor is rather to be given to instructing the hearing, than to exercising the sight. For in vain is the eye directed which has not been cleansed by faith, since the power of seeing is promised to those only who are clean of heart (Matt. 5:8). But it is written: 'Cleansing their hearts by faith' (Acts 15:9). Since, therefore, faith is from hearing, and from it is the cleansing of sight, deservedly they attended to adorning the ears, while hearing, as reason taught, is a preparation for sight. 'You,' they say, 'O bride, gasp for the brightness of the beloved to be beheld; but this belongs to another time.' But we give in the present ornaments to your ears, which will be for you in the meantime a consolation, and will be a preparation for this very thing which you demand, as if they say to her that saying of the prophet: 'Hear, O daughter, and see' (Ps. 45:11). You desire to see, but hear first. Hearing is a step to sight. Therefore hear, and incline your ear to the ornaments which we make for you, that through the obedience of hearing you may attain to the glory of vision. We give to your hearing joy and gladness. For it is not ours to give to your sight (in which is the fullness of joy and the fulfillment of your desire), but his whom your soul loves. He himself, that your joy may be full, will show himself to you; he himself will fill you with gladness with his countenance. You in the meantime receive for consolation these little chains from our hand; for the rest, delights are in his right hand even to the end.
41.3: It must be observed of what sort of little chains they offer her: 'Golden,' he says, 'and inlaid with silver.' Gold is the splendor of divinity, gold is the wisdom which is from above. Shining with this gold, as certain seals as it were of truth, these — to whom that is the ministry, the heavenly goldsmiths — promise that they will fashion, and will insert into the inner ears of the soul. Which I do not think to be anything other, than to weave certain spiritual likenesses, and in them to bring the purest perceptions of divine wisdom into the beholding sight of the contemplating soul, that it may see, at least through a mirror and in an enigma, that which as yet it cannot in any way behold face to face. Divine are the things we speak, and utterly unknown except to those who have experience: how, to wit, in this mortal body, faith as yet holding its state, and the substance of clear light not yet laid open, the contemplation of pure truth nevertheless sometimes presumes to play its parts within us, even in part; so that it may be lawful even for any of us, to whom this has been given from above, to take up that saying of the Apostle: 'Now I know in part'; and again, 'We know in part, and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor. 13:12, 9). But when something more divine flashes briefly upon the mind exceeding itself, and as it were in the swiftness of a flashing light, whether for the tempering of excessive splendor, or for the use of teaching, immediately — I know not whence — certain imaginative likenesses of lower things are at hand, conveniently accommodated to the perceptions divinely infused, by which that purest and most splendid ray of truth, being in some manner shaded, may become both more tolerable to the soul itself, and more capable for those to whom it shall will to communicate it; yet I judge that they themselves are formed in us by the suggestions of the holy angels, just as, on the contrary, it is not doubtful that contrary and evil suggestions are thrust in through the evil angels.
41.4: And perhaps hence is that mirror and enigma, as I have said, through which the Apostle saw (1 Cor. 13:12), fabricated as it were by the hands of angels out of pure and beautiful imaginations of this kind: to the end that we may perceive that that which is beheld pure and without every fantasy of bodily images is of God; and that we may assign to the angelic ministry whatever elegant likeness, by which it shall appear worthily clothed. Which another interpretation seems to have signified more expressly, saying: 'We will make you likenesses of the goldsmith, with distinctions of silver' (Song 1:11, according to the LXX). It is the same thing, 'with distinctions of silver,' and 'inlaid with silver.' In which he seems to me to signify not only that likenesses are suggested within through the angels, but also that the splendor of eloquence is ministered outwardly through them, by which, adorned fitly and becomingly, they are both more easily and more delightfully grasped by hearers. But if you say: 'What have eloquence and silver in common!' the prophet says to you: 'The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in fire' (Ps. 12:7). Thus, then, those heavenly ministering spirits make for the bride wandering on earth little chains of gold, inlaid with silver.
41.5: But see how she desires one thing, and receives another: and on her striving for the quiet of contemplation the labor of preaching is imposed; and to her thirsting for the presence of the bridegroom, the care of bearing and nourishing the bridegroom's children is enjoined. Nor does this happen to her now only; but also at another time, as I remember, when she sighed for the embraces and kisses of the bridegroom, it was answered to her: 'How much better are your breasts than wine' (Song 1:2); that from this she might understand herself to be a mother, and to be called back to giving milk to the little ones, and to nourishing her children. Perhaps also in other places of this Song you too, unless you are slow to inquire, will be able to perceive this very thing by yourself. Was not this thing once prefigured in the holy patriarch Jacob, when, frustrated of the longed-for and long-awaited embraces of Rachel, against his will and unknowingly he received instead of the barren and beautiful one the fruitful and blear-eyed one? (Gen. 29:23.) Thus, then, now the bride, desiring and inquiring to know where in the midday hours the beloved feeds and lies down, carries back instead of him chains of gold, inlaid with silver; that is, wisdom with eloquence; without doubt for the work of preaching.
41.6: We are surely taught from this, that sweet kisses are often to be interrupted because of breasts giving suck; and that one must live not for oneself, but for all. Woe to those who have received both to think rightly of God and to speak rightly, if they esteem piety a gain; if they turn to empty glory that which they had received to be laid out for the gains of God; if, being wise on high things, they do not consent to lowly things. Let them fear what is read in the prophet, the Lord saying: 'I gave them my gold and my silver; but they made Baal of my silver and my gold' (Hos. 2:8). You, then, hear what the bride answered, having received indeed a rebuke on the one hand, but on the other a promise. For she is neither lifted up by the promises, nor does she grow angry for the repulse; but, as it is written: 'Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you' (Prov. 9:8); and again, as to what pertains to the gifts and promises: 'The greater you are, humble yourself in all things' (Sir. 3:20); which both will appear better from her answer. But the discussion itself, if it pleases, let it be deferred to another beginning of a sermon, and concerning those things which have been said, let us glorify the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
41.title: In what way the bride meanwhile receives great consolation from the contemplation of the divine brightness, before she arrives at her clear vision.

42.1: While the king was at his table, my spikenard gave forth its fragrance (Song 1:12). These are the words of the bride, which we have put off until this present day; this is the answer which she gave when she was rebuked by the bridegroom — not, however, to the bridegroom, but to his companions: which may easily be observed from the words themselves. For since she does not say, as it were, to a second person: 'When you were king at your table,' but: 'When he was at his table,' it is clear that she does not speak to him, but concerning him. Suppose then that the bridegroom, when he had either rebuked or repressed her (as far as it seemed fit), having discovered her modesty from the blushing of her cheeks, departed from the place, that she, he being absent, might speak the more freely the things that she felt; and that even if she had grown more fearful than was fitting, as usually happens, and more dejected in mind, the consolations of her companions would raise her up. Yet he himself did not neglect to do that too, as much as he judged fitting for the time. For to leave clear how greatly that rebuke pleased him, inasmuch as he perceived that it was accepted worthily and as it ought to be, he assuredly did not withdraw himself before, from the abundance of the heart (as there is no doubt), he broke forth into her praises, and commended the beauty of her cheeks and of her neck. Therefore they also who remain with her speak kindly to her, and offer gifts, knowing the will of the Lord. To them, therefore, is her answer. And the literal construction of the figure, indeed, is thus.
42.2: But before we begin to draw out the kernel of the spirit from this shell, I say one thing briefly. Happy is he to whom his own reproof so answers, as we have the pattern of the present passage. Would that there were rather need to rebuke no one; for that is better. But since we all offend in many things, I am not allowed to be silent, to whom it lies by office to reprove sinners, and charity urges me the more. But if I shall reprove and do what is mine to do, and that reproof going forth does by no means do what is hers, nor attain that for which I sent it, but returns to me empty, like a dart striking and rebounding: what state of mind do you think I then have, brethren? Do I not grieve, am I not tormented? And that I may usurp for myself something from the words of the Master, since I cannot from wisdom, I am utterly straitened between two things, and I know not what I should choose (Phil. 1:22-23): whether to please myself in what I have spoken, because I have done what I ought; or to do penance for my word, because I have not received what I willed? I willed, indeed, to slay the enemy, and to rescue the brother; and I did not so, but rather the contrary happened: for I wounded the soul, and increased the fault, since contempt also was added. 'They are unwilling to hear you,' he says, 'because they are unwilling to hear me' (Ezek. 3:7). You see what majesty is despised. Do not think that you have spurned me alone. The Lord has spoken; and what he said to the prophet, he said also to the apostles: 'He who despises you,' he says, 'despises me' (Luke 10:16). I am not a prophet, I am not an apostle; and yet I serve, I dare to say, in the place of prophets and apostles: and with those whose merits I do not equal, I am entangled in their cares; though, to my great confusion, though to my great peril, I sit upon the chair of Moses, whose life, however, I do not claim for myself, nor do I experience its grace. What then? is honor not therefore to be paid to the chair, because it is occupied by one unworthy? Even if the Scribes and Pharisees sit upon it, he says: 'Do what they say' (Matt. 23:2-3).
42.3: Often, too, impatience is joined to contempt, so that someone, when rebuked, not only does not care to be corrected, but is, moreover, angry with the one who rebukes him, after the manner of a madman repelling the hand of the physician. Wonderful perversity! He is angry with the one who heals, who is not angry with the one who shoots! For there is one who shoots in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps. 11:3), who has now shot even you yourself unto death; and are you not stirred against him? Are you indignant at me, who desire that you be made whole? 'Be angry,' he says, 'and sin not' (Ps. 4:5). If you are angry with sin, not only do you by no means sin, but you even blot out what you had sinned. But now you both retain the sin by spurning the remedy, and you add sin by being irrationally angry; and it is a sin sinning beyond measure.
42.4: Sometimes shamelessness is also added, so that he not only bears impatiently that he is rebuked, but even shamelessly defends that for which he is reproved. This is plainly despair. 'The forehead of an adulterous woman,' he says, 'has been made to you; you have refused to blush' (Jer. 3:3): and he says: 'My zeal has departed from you; I will not be angry with you any more' (Ezek. 16:42). At the mere hearing I tremble. Do you not perceive of how great peril, and of how great horror and trembling, a thing the defense of sin is? He says again: 'Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise' (Rev. 3:19). If, then, zeal has deserted you, so has love: nor will you be worthy of love, who are judged unworthy of chastisement. You see that God is then the more angry, while he is not angry. 'Let us have mercy on the impious,' he says, 'and he will not learn to do justice' (Isa. 26:10). This mercy I do not want. This compassion is above every anger, hedging in for me the ways of justice. Surely it is better for me, according to the counsel of the Prophet, to lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord at any time be angry, and I perish from the just way (Ps. 2:12). I would have you be angry with me, Father of mercies; but with that anger by which you correct the wanderer, not that by which you cast out from the way. Your benign correction, indeed, produces that for us; your dreadful dissimulation nourishes this. For not when I know not, but when I feel that you are angry, do I trust you most to be merciful: for when you have been angry, you will remember mercy. 'God,' he says, 'you wast propitious to them, and avenging upon all their devices' (Ps. 99:8). He speaks of Moses and Aaron, and Samuel, whom he had just sent on before; and this he calls propitiation, namely, that which was theirs. God did not spare their excesses. Go now then, you, and shut this out for yourself forever, by defending error, and by accusing correction. Is not this to call evil good, and good evil? Will not impenitence, the mother of despair, soon sprout forth from this hateful shamelessness? For who would repent of the good which he thinks it to be? 'Woe to those,' he says (Isa. 5:20). That woe is eternal. It is one thing for each one to be tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence; and another to seek of his own accord evil as though it were good, to hasten to death as though to life, wickedly secure. For such persons, I say, I would rather at times have been silent, and have dissembled what I perceived to be wrongly done, than to have rebuked to so great a ruin.
42.5: You may perhaps say to me, that my good may return to me, and that I have freed my soul, and am clean from the blood of the man to whom I announced and spoke, that he might turn from his evil way, and live. But even if you add countless things of this sort, they will yet by no means console me, beholding the death of a son. As though truly by that reproof I sought my own deliverance, and not rather his! For what mother, even if she knows that she has brought all the care and diligence she could to a sick son, if at length she sees herself frustrated, and all her labors to be wholly ineffectual, he nevertheless dying, has she ever on that account refrained from tears? And she, indeed, this for a temporal death; how much more does there await me, for the eternal death of my son, assuredly much weeping and wailing, even though I am conscious of nothing in myself whereby I have failed to announce it to him? You see, moreover, from how great evils on the other side it frees both him and us, he who, when rebuked, answers gently, acquiesces with reverence, complies modestly, confesses humbly. To this soul I would profess myself a debtor in all things, to this one my minister and servant, as to the most worthy bride of my Lord, and to one who could truly say: 'While the king was at his table, my spikenard gave forth its fragrance.'
42.6: Good is the odor of humility, which, ascending from this valley of weeping, having perfused the neighboring regions round about, sprinkles even the royal table itself with a grateful sweetness. Nard is a lowly herb, which they who have more curiously explored the powers of herbs report to be also of a hot nature. And therefore through it I seem to myself not unsuitably to take in this place the virtue of humility, but one which burns with the vapors of holy love. Which I say, forsooth, for this reason, because there is a humility which truth brings forth for us, and it has no heat: and there is a humility which charity forms and inflames. And this one, indeed, consists in affection, that one in knowledge. For you, if you should look within at yourself by the light of truth and without dissimulation, and should judge yourself without flattery, I do not doubt that you also will be humbled in your own eyes, made the viler to yourself from this true knowledge of yourself, although perhaps you would not yet suffer even that to be in the eyes of others. You will therefore be humble, but for the present from the work of truth, and by no means yet from the infusion of love. For if, of that very truth which has veraciously and salubriously shown you to yourself, as you had been illuminated by its splendor, so you had been affected with its love, you would beyond doubt have wished, as far as in you lies, that all hold concerning you the same judgment which you know the truth itself holds concerning you. Truly, 'as far as in you lies' I would say; since often it is not expedient that all things which we know of ourselves become known to all, and by the very charity of truth, and the truth of charity, we are forbidden to wish that to be made public which would harm the one learning it. Otherwise, if, held by a private love of yourself, you likewise keep within you shut up the judgment of truth, to whom would it be doubtful that you love truth the less, you who prefer to it either your own advantage or honor?
42.7: You see, therefore, that it is not the same thing — that a man, convicted by the light of truth, no longer savors high things of himself, and that he freely consent to humble persons, aided by the gift of charity. For that is of necessity, this of will. 'He emptied himself,' he says, 'taking the form of a servant' (Phil. 2:7), and giving the form of humility. He himself emptied himself, he himself humbled himself, not by necessity of judgment, but by love of us. He could, indeed, show himself vile and contemptible, but plainly not so esteem himself, because he knew himself. Therefore he was humble by will, and not by judgment, who offered himself as being such as he knew not himself to be; rather, he who did not ignore that he himself was the highest, chose to be esteemed the least. Finally he says: 'Learn of me, that I am meek and humble of heart' (Matt. 11:29). He said 'of heart' — by the affection of the heart, that is, by will. Thus he excluded necessity, who confessed the will. For not in the way in which I or you find ourselves in truth worthy of dishonor and contempt, worthy of every extremity and inferiority, worthy even of punishments, worthy of blows; not so, I say, did he: which things, however, he experienced all of them, because he willed it, as humble of heart; humble, namely, with that humility which the affection of the heart persuaded, not that which the examination of truth extorted.
42.8: Therefore I said that this appearance of voluntary humility is created in us, not by the reproof of truth, but by the infusion of charity, because it is of the heart, because of affection, because of the will: but whether rightly, do you judge. And likewise let this also be equally examined by your judgment, whether I have worthily assigned the same humility to the Lord, whom it is established that by charity he was emptied, by charity made less than the angels, by charity made subject to his parents, by charity bowed to the Baptist's hands, by charity suffered the weaknesses of the flesh, by charity, finally, was subject to death, and inglorious on the cross. But let this one thing also still be for your consideration, whether rightly I have thought this very humility, so warm with charity, to be signified by a lowly and hot herb, that is, by nard. And if you shall so approve all things (for you will approve them, acquiescing to manifest reason), then, if you are already humbled in yourself with that necessary humility which Truth, searching hearts and reins, instills into the senses of the watchful soul, add the will, and make of necessity a virtue, since there is no virtue without the agreement of the will. Thus, however, will this be done, if you are not willing to appear other abroad than you find yourself within. Otherwise fear, lest you read concerning yourself: 'For he dealt deceitfully in his sight, that his iniquity might be found unto hatred' (Ps. 36:3). 'A weight,' he says, 'and a weight is an abomination before God' (Prov. 20:10). For what? do you depreciate yourself in secret with yourself, weighed on the balance of truth; and abroad, lying as of another price, do you sell yourself to us for a greater weight than you received from truth itself? Fear God, and be not willing to do this most evil thing, that whom truth humbles, the will exalt: for this is to resist truth, this is to fight against God. But rather acquiesce to God, and let the will be subject to truth; and not only subject, but also devoted. 'Will not my soul,' he says, 'be subject to God?' (Ps. 62:2).
42.9: But it is little to be subject to God, unless you are also subject to every human creature for God's sake; whether to an abbot, as to one excelling; or to the priors, as to those appointed by him. I say more: to be subject to equals, to be subject also to inferiors. 'For so,' he says, 'it becomes us to fulfill all justice' (Matt. 3:15). Go you also to the lesser, if you wish to be perfect in justice; yield to the inferior, bowing yourself to the junior. For doing this, you also will draw to yourself that word of the bride which she spoke: 'For my spikenard gave forth its fragrance.' The odor is devotion, the odor is good report, which reaches to all, that you may be the good odor of Christ in every place, conspicuous to all, lovely to all. He who is that humble one, compelled to humility by truth, cannot do this; since he keeps it for himself, and does not suffer it to go forth, so that, spread abroad, it may smell sweet outside. Rather, he does not have the odor, because he does not have devotion, inasmuch as he humbles himself not spontaneously, nor willingly. But the humility of the bride, like nard, scatters its odor, warm with love, vigorous with devotion, redolent in good report. The humility of the bride is voluntary, it is perpetual, it is fruitful. Her odor is neither exterminated by reproof, nor by praise. She had heard: 'Your cheeks are beautiful like the turtledove's, and your neck like chains' (Song 1:10). She had received also the promise of golden ornament, and nevertheless she still answers with humility: and the greater she hears herself to be, the more she humbles herself in all things. She does not glory in merits, nor amid her praises does she forget humility, which she also humbly confesses under the name of nard; as if with the voice of the virgin Mary she said: 'I am conscious of no merit in myself for so great a condescension, save that God has regarded the humility of his handmaid' (Luke 1:48). For what else is, 'My spikenard gave forth its fragrance,' than: 'My humility has pleased'? 'Not my wisdom,' she says, 'not my nobility, not my beauty, which were nothing to me, but the humility which alone was in me gave forth its fragrance' — that is, its wonted one. Humility pleases God as of custom; of custom, plainly, and out of habit, the exalted Lord regards the lowly: and therefore, when he was king at his table, that is, in his lofty habitation, thither also the odor of humility ascended. 'He dwells in the heights,' he says, 'and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth' (Ps. 113:5-6).
42.10: Therefore, when the king was at his table, the spikenard of the bride gave forth its fragrance. The table of the king is the bosom of the Father; because the Son is always in the Father. Nor doubt that this king is clement, to whom the perpetual table is the lodging of paternal benignity. Deservedly does the cry of the humble ascend to him, whose dwelling is the fountain of piety, to whom is familiar sweetness, to whom is substantial, or rather consubstantial, goodness: to whom, therefore, all that he is is of the Father, so that the trembling of the humble may suspect nothing at all in his royal majesty but what is paternal. Finally: 'For the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now will I arise,' says the Lord (Ps. 12:6). The bride, therefore, conscious of these things, as one of the household and most beloved, does not think that she is to be kept away from the grace of the bridegroom by the want of merits, presuming upon humility alone. Finally she names him king, for, terrified by the rebuke, she does not for the present dare to call him bridegroom; and she confesses that he dwells on high, yet even so humility does not distrust.
42.11: You can fit this speech to the primitive Church without incongruity, if you recall those days in which, the Lord having been taken up to where he was before, and sitting at the right hand of the Father, at that his ancient, noble and glorious table, the disciples were gathered together in one place, persevering with one accord in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brethren (Acts 1:13-14). Does it not seem to you that then indeed, at that time, the spikenard of the little and trembling bride gave forth its fragrance? Finally, when there was made suddenly a sound from heaven, as of a mighty spirit coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts 2:2), could not the poor little one then deservedly say: 'While the king was at his table, my spikenard gave forth its fragrance'? It was made manifest for certain to all remaining in that place, how grateful a humility, and how well-pleasing an odor had ascended, to which there was soon answered so copious and glorious a recompense. But she was not ungrateful for the benefit. For hear how, soon filled with devotion, she prepares herself to bear all evils for his name: for it follows: 'My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he will abide between my breasts.' My weakness, which you know, does not permit me to go further. This only I say, that under the name of myrrh she says herself ready to undergo the bitternesses of tribulations for the love of the beloved. The remainder of the chapter we shall pursue at another time, if, however, the Holy Spirit, entreated by you, shall be present, who may make us understand the words of the bride, which he himself, inspiring, formed, as he knows how to suit the praises of that one whose Spirit he himself is, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God, blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
42.title: Concerning the twofold humility: one, namely, which truth brings forth; and the other, which charity enkindles.

43.1: A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall abide between my breasts (Song 1:13). Before, a king; now, the beloved: before, in royal reclining; now, between the bride's breasts. Great is the virtue of humility, to which even the majesty of the Godhead so easily inclines itself. Quickly has the name of reverence been changed into the word of friendship: and he who was far off has in a short time been made near. A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me. Myrrh, a bitter thing, hard and rough, signifies tribulations. Foreseeing that they impend upon her for the sake of the Beloved, she speaks this rejoicing, confident that she will undergo all things manfully. They went, he says, rejoicing, the disciples, from the sight of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). On this account, finally, she calls the beloved not a bundle, but a little bundle, because she counts light, out of love for him, whatever of labor and of pain impends. Well is it a little bundle, because a little child is born to us (Isa. 9:6). Well is it a bundle, because the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared to the future glory which will be revealed in us (Rom. 8:18). For that which is at present momentary and light in our tribulation works in us, beyond measure, an eternal weight of glory in sublimity (2 Cor. 4:17). There will therefore be for us at some time a huge mass of glory, which now is a bundle of myrrh. Is it not a bundle, whose yoke is sweet, and whose burden is light (Matt. 11:30)? Not because it is light in itself (for the harshness of passion, the bitterness of death, is not light), but light nevertheless to the lover. And therefore she does not say only: A bundle of myrrh is my beloved; but: To me, she says, who love, he is a bundle. Whence she also names him Beloved, showing that the power of love overcomes the annoyance of all bitternesses, and that love is strong as death (Song 8:6). And that you may know that she does not glory in herself, but in the Lord, nor presume strength from her own virtue, but from the help of the Lord, she says that he will abide between her breasts, to whom, secure, she may sing: Even though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because you are with me (Ps. 23:4).
43.2: I remember that in one of the earlier sermons (Sermon 10, n. 1) I defined the two breasts of the bride as congratulation and compassion, according to the doctrine of Paul, saying: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). But because, moving among adversities and prosperities, she knows that perils are not lacking on either side, she wishes to have her Beloved in the midst of breasts of this kind, so that, fortified against both by his continual protection, neither may joys lift her up, nor sorrows cast her down. You also, if you are wise, will imitate the prudence of the bride, and will not suffer this so dear bundle of myrrh to be torn away from the chief place of your breast even for an hour, always keeping in memory those bitter things which he bore for you, and turning them over in assiduous meditation, that you too may be able to say: A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall abide between my breasts.
43.3: And I, brethren, from the beginning of my conversion, in place of a heap of merits, which I knew to be lacking to me, have taken care to bind together this bundle for myself and to place it between my breasts, gathered from all the anxieties and bitternesses of my Lord: first, namely, those infantile necessities; then, the labors which he bore in preaching, the fatigues in journeying, the watchings in praying, the temptations in fasting, the tears in sympathizing, the snares in conversing; lastly, the perils among false brethren, the reproaches, the spittings, the blows, the scoffs, the upbraidings, the nails, and others like these, which the evangelical forest is very abundantly known to have brought forth for the salvation of our race. Where truly, among so many little branches of this fragrant myrrh, I thought not even that myrrh to be omitted with which he was given to drink on the cross; nor even that, with which he was anointed in the tomb. Of these, in the first he applied to himself the bitterness of my sins; in the second he consecrated the future incorruption of my body. I will bring forth the memory of the abundance of the sweetness of these as long as I live; I will not to eternity forget these mercies, because in them I have been quickened.
43.4: These, once, holy David sought with tears, saying: Let your mercies come to me, and I will live (Ps. 119:77). These also a certain other of the saints recalled with a groan, saying: Many are the mercies of the Lord. How many kings and prophets wished to see, and did not see! They labored, and I have entered into their labors; I have reaped the myrrh which they planted; for me this salutary bundle has been kept; no one will take it from me; it shall abide between my breasts. I have said that to meditate on these is wisdom; in these I have established for myself the perfection of righteousness, in these the fullness of knowledge, in these the riches of salvation, in these the abundance of merits. From these there is to me at times a salutary drink of bitterness, from these again a sweet anointing of consolation. These raise me up in adversities, restrain me in prosperities, and, to one walking in the royal way amid the joys and sorrows of this present life, they afford a safe guidance on either side, thrusting back the evils threatening from here and from there. These reconcile to me the Judge of the world, while they portray him, who is tremendous to the powers, as gentle and humble; while they present him, who is inaccessible to principalities, terrible among the kings of the earth, as not only placable but also imitable. On this account these are frequent in my mouth, as you know; these always in my heart, as God knows; these most familiar to my pen, as appears; this is my higher philosophy for the present: to know Jesus, and him crucified. I do not ask, like the bride, where he lies down at midday (Song 1:7), whom, touched, I embrace abiding between my breasts. I do not ask where he feeds at midday, whom I behold as Savior on the cross. That is more sublime, this is sweeter; that is bread, this is milk; this refreshes the bowels of little ones, this fills the breasts of mothers; and therefore he shall abide between my breasts.
43.5: Do you also, most beloved, gather for yourselves this so dear bundle, insert it into the marrows of your heart, fortify with it the approach of your breast, that he may abide between your breasts also. Have him always not behind on your shoulders, but before your eyes, lest, carrying and not smelling him, both the burden oppress you and the odor not lift you up. Remember that Simeon received him in his arms (Luke 2:28); Mary carried him in her womb, cherished him in her lap; the bride placed him for herself between her breasts. And, that I may omit nothing, the word was made in the hand of the prophet Zechariah, and also of certain others. I think that Joseph also, the husband of Mary, often smiled upon him on his knees. All these had him before themselves, and not one behind. Let them therefore be an example to you, that you also may do likewise. For if you have before your eyes him whom you carry, surely seeing the straits of the Lord, you will carry your own more lightly, he himself helping — the Spouse of the Church, who is above all things God, blessed for ever. Amen.
43.title: In what way the consideration of the passion and labors of Christ makes the bride, that is, the soul, to go unharmed among the prosperities and adversities of this world.

44.1: A cluster of Cyprus, my beloved, [is] to me in the vineyards of Engaddi (Song 1:14). If the beloved [is] in myrrh, much more in the sweetness of the cluster. Therefore my Lord Jesus was to me myrrh in death, a cluster in the resurrection, who tempered himself for me into a most wholesome drink, unto tears in measure. He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification (Rom. 4:25), that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness (1 Pet. 2:24). Therefore you, if you have bewailed sins, have drunk bitterness; but if you have already breathed again into the hope of life with a holier life, the bitterness of myrrh has been changed for you into wine, which gladdens the heart of man. And perhaps it is this which signified that myrrhed [draught] which was offered to the Savior on the cross, and therefore he would not drink, because he was thirsting for that. You therefore, experiencing the wine of gladness after the bitternesses of myrrh, as I have said, will by no means rashly be able even you to say: My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me in the vineyards of Engaddi. Engaddi has a double interpretation, and both serve one understanding. For it is called 'the fountain of a kid,' and the baptism of the nations; and it openly designates the tears of those who sin. It is also called the eye of trial, which likewise pours forth tears; and let it look ahead to the temptations, which are by no means ever lacking to the life of man upon the earth. But also the people of the nations, who walked in darkness, could never by themselves come to know the snares of temptations, and through this could not escape [them] either, until through the grace of him who enlightens the blind, it received the eyes of faith, until it came to the Church, which has the eye of trial; until it delivered itself to spiritual men to be instructed, who, enlightened by the spirit of wisdom, taught by their own experience, can truly say that we are not ignorant of the wiles of the devil, and of his thoughts (2 Cor. 2:11).
44.2: They report that little shrubs of balsam grow in Engaddi, which are cultivated by the natives in the manner of vineyards: and hence perhaps he called them vineyards. Otherwise, what would a cluster of Cyprus do in the vineyards of Engaddi? who ever carried clusters from vines into vineyards? for wine is wont to be carried from elsewhere where it is lacking, not where it is present. Therefore he calls the vineyards of Engaddi the people of the Church, which has the liquor of balsam, the spirit of meekness, in which the tenderness of the little ones, still [young] in Christ, is gently cherished, and the sorrows of the penitents are consoled. But also, if any brother shall have been overtaken in some offense, the ecclesiastical man, who has already received this spirit, will take care to instruct such a one in the same spirit of gentleness, considering himself, lest he also be tempted (Gal. 6:1). In this type, as many as are to be baptized, the Church has been accustomed to anoint even corporally with material oil.
44.3: But because the wounds of him who fell among robbers, and was carried on the beast of the body of the pious Samaritan into the stable of the Church, receive healing not in oil alone, but in wine and oil together (Luke 10:30-34): the spiritual physician has need also of the wine of fervent zeal together with the oil of meekness, to whom indeed it befits not only to console the fainthearted, but also to rebuke the restless. For if he shall see him who was wounded, that is, who sinned, amended not at all by the bland and gentle exhortations which have been spent upon him, but rather even abusing his meekness, and through [his] patience becoming more negligent, and even sleeping more securely in his own sin: the oil of so sweet admonitions having been frustrated, it will be fitting indeed to use more biting remedies, and to pour in the wine of compunction; namely, to deal with him with harsh rebukes and invectives, and, if the cause requires it, and the hardness is so great, even to strike down the despiser with the rod of ecclesiastical censure. But whence has he this wine? For wine is not found in the vineyards of Engaddi, but oil. Let him seek therefore in Cyprus: for that island is fruitful of wine, and of the best wine; and taking from there for himself a huge cluster, which the spies of Israel of old carried on a staff (Num. 13:24), figuring in a beautiful figure the prophetic chorus going before, and the apostolic following, and Jesus in the middle: taking therefore this cluster for himself, let him say: My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus.
44.4: We have seen the cluster; let us see in what manner the wine of zeal is pressed out of it. For indeed if a man who is a sinner is not at all indignant against a sinning man, but rather, as it were sweating out over him a certain dew of sweetest balsam, shows a pious affection of compassion; this we know whence it comes, and you have already heard, but perhaps you have not noticed. For it has been said that from the consideration of himself, it comes to everyone to be meek toward all, while a man, by the counsel of the most wise Paul, that he may know how to condescend piously to those overtaken in sin, considers himself, lest he also be tempted? (Gal. 6:1). Is it not indeed hence that the love of the neighbor draws its root, concerning which it is commanded in the law: You shall love your neighbor as yourself? (Luke 10:27). From the inmost human affections, fraternal love surely draws the beginnings of its origin, and from a certain natural sweetness implanted in man toward himself, as from earthly moisture, it surely takes its vegetation and force, by which, while grace indeed breathes from above, it brings forth the fruit of piety: so that what the soul naturally desires for itself, it may not judge that it should be denied to the sharer of its nature, that is, to another man, by a certain right of humanity, where it can and ought, but may impart it spontaneously and willingly. There is therefore present in nature, if it does not become obsolete through sin, a liquor of this kind, of a pleasing and distinguished, as it were, sweetness, that it feels and shows itself more soft to have compassion on the sinning, than harsher [to be] indignant.
44.5: But because, according to the sentence of the Wise Man, dying flies destroy this ointment of sweetness (Eccl. 10:1), and nature has in itself nothing from which to repair for itself what has once been lost, it feels itself, by a lamentable change, to fall into that which Scripture truly says: The senses of man and his thoughts are prone to evil from adolescence (Gen. 8:21). Not a good adolescence, in which the younger son demands that a portion of the paternal substance be set apart for himself, and begins to wish to divide the good, which is possessed more sweetly in common; and to hold alone what is not lessened by participation, [but] is lost by partition. Finally: He squandered, he says, all his goods, living luxuriously with harlots (Luke 15:11, 13). Who are these harlots? See whether they are not those which destroy the ointment of sweetness, namely the carnal concupiscences, concerning which Scripture, most salutarily admonishing you, [says]: Go not, it says, after your concupiscences (Sir. 18:30). And deservedly does the Wise Man describe them as destined to die; since both the world passes away, and its concupiscence (1 John 2:17). Therefore, while we wish to make satisfaction to these severally, we deprive ourselves of the singular sweetness of the social and common good. These are altogether the foul and stinging flies, which in us defile the comeliness of nature, tear the mind with cares and anxieties, and destroy the sweetness of social grace. Hence man is called the younger son, because nature, corrupted by the slipperiness of a certain senseless adolescence, has lost all the juice of virile maturity and of wisdom; and, turned into roughness, with a dried-up mind despises all others besides itself, made without affection.
44.6: Therefore, from the very beginning of adolescence, the senses of man and his thoughts are prone to evil, that worst and most wretched [thing], and nature is readier to be indignant than to have compassion. Hence man, as though wholly divested of [his] humanity, in that he wills that help be brought to himself by men when he has need, does not will to bring help himself to men who have need. But rather does the man judge, despise, deride men, when they are delinquent, a sinner, not considering himself, lest he also be tempted. From which evil nature will by no means of itself rise again, as I have said, nor will it recover the oil of its inborn meekness, which has once been destroyed in it. Nevertheless, what nature cannot [do], grace can. Whom, therefore, the anointing of the Spirit, having pitied, shall deign to pour over again with its kindness, he will immediately return into a man, and moreover will receive something better from grace than from nature. In faith and lenity it will make him holy, and will give him not oil, but balsam in the vineyards of Engaddi.
44.7: For there is no doubt that the better gifts flow from the fountain of the kid, whose anointing indeed turns kids into lambs, and transfers sinners from the left to the right hand, those certainly previously more abundantly poured over with the anointing of mercy, that where sins have abounded, grace may also superabound (Rom. 5:20). Does it not indeed truly seem to you that that man has, in a manner, returned into a man, who, the ferocity of the worldly soul having been laid aside, and having recovered, even with the usury of grace, the anointing of human meekness, which the flies of carnal desires had utterly destroyed in him; from that man whom he bears, nay who he himself is, takes both the matter and the form of showing mercy to other men, so that, as though a wild gaping, he abhors not only to do to any of men what he himself would be unwilling to suffer, but even not to do to all men all things whatsoever he would wish to be done to himself?
44.8: Behold whence the oil. Whence the wine? Doubtless from the cluster of Cyprus. For if you love the Lord Jesus with [your] whole heart, whole soul, whole strength; if you shall see his injuries and contempt, will you be able to bear [them] in any way with an even mind? By no means: but soon seized by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of ardor, and, like a mighty one drunk with wine (Ps. 78:65), filled with the zeal of Phinehas, you will say with David: My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words (Ps. 119:139); and with the Lord: The zeal of your house has consumed me (Ps. 69:10; John 2:17). This most fervent zeal is therefore wine, pressed from the cluster of Cyprus, and the inebriating cup [is] the love of Christ. Finally, our God is a consuming fire (Deut. 4:24), and the prophet said that fire was sent from on high into his bones (Lam. 1:13), for this reason, that he was burning with divine love. Having therefore the oil of meekness from the fraternal, and the wine of emulation from divine love, approach securely to heal the wounds of him who fell among robbers, the best imitator of the most pious Samaritan. Say also securely, you too, with the bride: My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi: that is, the zeal of justice, the love of my beloved [is] to me in the affections of piety. And of this enough. For my weakness also dictates that I pause, as it often does; so that I am generally compelled to leave the discussions unfinished, as you yourselves know, and to reserve the remains of the chapters for another day. But what? I am prepared for the scourges (Ps. 34:18), knowing that I am still to receive things far unequal to my merits. Truly let me be beaten, let me be beaten as one working evil, if perchance the blows be reckoned unto merits: perhaps he will have mercy on the one beaten, who finds nothing good in me to reward, the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
44.title: Concerning the rebuke to be moderated according to the disposition of sinners, so that the humble and tractable are corrected gently, the hard and obstinate severely.

45.1: Behold, you are beautiful, my friend, behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are [like those] of doves (Song 1:15). Beautifully, most excellently: from love, the presumption of the bride; from love, the indignation of the bridegroom. The outcome of the matter proves this. For indeed a rebuke followed the presumption, an amendment followed the rebuke, a reward followed the amendment. The Beloved is present, the master is removed, the king disappears, dignity is put off, reverence is laid aside. For haughtiness gives way where affection grows strong. And just as once Moses spoke as a friend to a friend (Exod. 33:11), and the Lord answered: so also now between the Word and the soul, as between two neighbors, a friendship quite familiar is carried on in converse. Nor is it a wonder. From one fountain of love it flows into both to love one another, to be cherished together alike. Therefore words sweeter than honey fly to and fro, mutual glances of all sweetness are carried to one another, the holy tokens of love. Finally, he calls her friend, proclaims her beautiful, repeats beautiful, receiving in turn the same from her. Nor is the repetition idle, which is the confirmation of love, and perhaps intimates that something is to be sought.
45.2: Let us seek the twofold beauty of the soul: for this it seems to me to intimate. The loveliness of the soul is humility. I do not say this from myself, since the prophet said it before me: 'You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed' (Ps. 51:9), signifying humility by a lowly herb and one that purges the breast. By this the king and prophet trusts that he is washed after his grievous fall, and so to recover a certain snowy whiteness of innocence. But in him who has sinned grievously, humility, even if it is to be loved, is yet not to be admired. But if anyone keeps his innocence, and nevertheless joins to it humility, does he not seem to you to possess the twofold beauty of the soul? Blessed Mary did not lose her holiness, and she did not lack humility: and therefore the King desired her beauty, because she joined humility to innocence; finally: 'He has regarded the humility of his handmaid,' she says (Luke 1:48). Therefore blessed are they who keep their garments clean, namely those of simplicity and innocence, if only they add also to put on the beauty of humility. Verily, she who is found such will hear: 'Behold, you are beautiful, my friend, behold, you are beautiful.' Would that you might say even once to my soul, Lord Jesus: 'Behold, you are beautiful.' Would that you might keep humility for me! for I have kept the first garment badly. I am your servant. For I do not dare to profess myself a friend, I who do not hear the testimony of my beauty with its repetition. It suffices me if I hear it once. But what, if this also is in question? I know what I shall do: being a servant, I shall reverence the friend; being a deformed little man, I shall admire the beauty heaped up in her; I shall rejoice at the voice of the bridegroom, admiring notwithstanding so great a beauty. Who knows whether at least from this I shall find grace in the eyes of the friend, so that by her grace I also may be found among the friends? Finally, the friend of the bridegroom stands, and rejoices with joy because of the voice of the bridegroom. Behold, his voice [is] in the ears of the beloved: let us hear, and let us rejoice. They are present to one another, they speak together; let us stand together: let no care of the world, no allurement of the body draw us away from this conversation.
45.3: 'Behold,' he says, 'you are beautiful, my friend, behold, you are beautiful.' 'Behold' is the voice of admiration; the rest is of praise. Rightly to be admired is she, to whom lost holiness did not bring humility, but preserved holiness admitted it. Rightly is she found beautiful, to whom neither of the beauties was lacking. It is a rare bird on the earth, either not to lose holiness, or not to have humility excluded by sanctity: and therefore blessed is she who kept both. Finally it has been proved: she is conscious of nothing against herself, and she does not refuse correction. We, even when we sin greatly, scarcely bear to be reproved; but she, sinning nothing, hears with an even mind the bitter things [spoken] against her. For if she desires to see the brightness of the bridegroom, what evil is it? rather it is also of praise. And yet, rebuked, she does penance, and says: 'A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me, he shall abide between my breasts' (Song 1:13): that is: 'It suffices me, I wish now to know nothing but Jesus, and him crucified.' Great humility! Innocent in deed, she takes up the affection of one doing penance; and she who has not that from which she may repent, yet has that for which she may repent. Why then, you ask, was she rebuked, if she did nothing evil? But now hear the dispensation and the prudence of the bridegroom. As the obedience of Abraham was once surely tried, so also now the humility of the bride. And as he, obedience being fulfilled, then heard: 'Now I know that you fear God' (Gen. 22:12): so also to this one is now said, as it were under other words: 'Now I know that you are humble'; for this is what he says: 'Behold, you are beautiful.' And therefore he repeats the praise, that he may mark the beauty of humility added to the glory of holiness. 'Behold, you are beautiful, my friend, behold, you are beautiful.' 'Now I know that you are beautiful, not only from my love, but also from your humility.' I do not now say [you are] beautiful among women, nor beautiful in the cheeks, nor in the neck, as I used to say before: but I confess you beautiful simply, not indeed beautiful by comparison, not with distinction, not in part.
45.4: And he adds: 'Your eyes are [like those] of doves.' Openly is humility still commended. For to this it looks, that she, reproved for her high inquiry, did not delay at once to descend to more simple things, so as to say: 'A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me.' Verily, there is much distance between the face of glory and a bundle of myrrh: and therefore it is a great sign of humility, to acquiesce in being recalled from the one to the other. Therefore your eyes [are] [like those] of doves. 'Now,' he says, 'you do not walk in great things, nor in wonderful things above you: but, after the manner of a most simple bird, you are content with more simple things, nesting in the holes of the rock, dwelling in my wounds, and with a dove's eye willingly gazing upon those things which are of me alone, the incarnate and suffering one.'
45.5: Or certainly, because in the form of this bird the Holy Spirit appeared (Matt. 3:16), a spiritual rather than a simple gaze in her is commended under the name of the dove. And if this pleases you, you must refer the present passage to that which a little before the companions promised to make her golden earrings (Song 1:11), not intending, as I then taught, to adorn the ears of the body, but to form the hearing of the heart (above, Sermon 41, nn. 2-4). It could therefore come about that, by faith, which is from hearing, her heart being more cleansed, she should be rendered better instructed to see that which before she could not. And since from the earrings received she has appeared to have profited into a keener sight for spiritual understanding; it has pleased the bridegroom — to whom always, as far as in him is, it pleases to be seen rather in the spirit; and counting this also among her praises, he says: 'Your eyes [are] [like those] of doves.' 'Now,' he says, 'behold me in spirit, because the spirit before your face is Christ the Lord' (Lam. 4:20). And you have whence you may be able to do this, because your eyes are [those] of doves. Before you did not have [it], and therefore you were to be restrained: but now have abundance of living, because your eyes are [those] of doves, that is, spiritual. Not, indeed, the abundance which you asked: for not even now are you yet able [to attain] to that, but [that abundance] which can nevertheless suffice in the meantime. Truly, you are to be led from brightness to brightness: and therefore see now, as you are able; and when you shall be able more, you shall see more.
45.6: I do not think, brethren, I do not think this vision to be mediocre, nor common to all, although it be inferior to that by which he is to be seen in the future. Finally, take notice from those things which follow. For it follows: 'Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, behold, you are beautiful.' You see on how high [a height] she stands, and to how sublime a summit of mind she has raised [herself], she who claims for herself, with a certain property, the Lord of the universe as [her] beloved. For attend how she does not say simply, 'Beloved'; but, 'my beloved,' she says, that she might designate [him as] her own. It is a great vision indeed, from which she has grown into so much confidence and authority, that she knows not the Lord of all as Lord, but as beloved. For I think that on this occasion there were by no means brought to her senses images of the flesh, or of the cross, or any other likenesses whatsoever of bodily infirmities. For in these, according to the prophet, there was not in him form nor beauty (Isa. 53:2). But she, having looked upon him, now proclaims him beautiful and comely, signifying that he has appeared to her in a better vision. For mouth to mouth, as once with holy Moses (Exod. 33:11), he speaks with the bride; and openly, not through riddles and figures, she sees God. Finally, she proclaims with her mouth such [a one] as she also beholds with her mind, with a vision plainly sublime and sweet. Her eyes have seen the King in his beauty, yet not as king, but as beloved. Let one indeed have seen him upon a throne high and lifted up; and another also have testified that he appeared to him face to face: yet it seems to me that the eminence in this part is with the bride, because there he is read [as] seen [as] Lord, here [as] beloved. For so you have: 'I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up' (Isa. 6:1); and likewise: 'I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was made safe' (Gen. 32:30). But 'if I [am] the Lord,' he says, 'where is my fear?' (Mal. 1:6.) And if to those a revelation was made with fear; because where [there is] the Lord, there [is] fear: I verily, if the choice were given, would so much the more willingly, and so much the more dearly, embrace for the bride the vision, as I perceive it made in the better affection, which is love. For fear has punishment, but perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 4:18). Verily, there is much difference between appearing terrible in his counsels over the sons of men (Ps. 66:15), and appearing beautiful in form above the sons of men (Ps. 45:5). 'Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.' These words plainly resound of love, not of fear.
