45.7: But perhaps thoughts rise up in your heart, and, doubting with yourself, you ask, saying: By what reason are the words of the Word made to the soul referred, and again [those] of the soul to the Word, so that she has heard the voice of one speaking to her and declaring that she is beautiful, and in her turn has forthwith returned the same praise to her own praiser? How can these things come to pass? For we speak by a word; the Word does not speak. And likewise the soul has not whence to speak, unless the mouth of the body forms words for itself for speaking. You ask well: but attend that the spirit speaks, and that the things which are said ought to be understood spiritually. Whenever, therefore, you hear or read that the Word and the soul converse together, and behold one another; do not imagine for yourself that, as it were, bodily voices pass between [them], just as neither do bodily images of the speakers appear. Hear rather what you should think in matters of this kind. The Word is spirit, and the soul is spirit, and they have their own tongues, by which they speak to one another, and declare themselves present. And of the Word indeed the tongue is the favor of his condescension: but of the soul, the fervor of devotion. The soul is speechless and infant which does not have this [tongue], and there can be no converse at all for it with the Word. Therefore, when the Word moves its tongue of this kind, willing to speak to the soul, the soul cannot but feel [it]. For the word of God is living and effectual, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4:12). And again, when the soul moves its own [tongue], the Word will be able to be hidden much less; not only because he is present everywhere, but the more for this, that unless he himself is stirring it, the tongue of devotion is by no means moved to speak.
45.8: To say to the soul by his Word, 'you are beautiful,' and to call her friend, is to pour in [that] whence she may both love, and presume herself to be loved. But for the soul in turn to name the Word beloved, and to confess him beautiful; to ascribe to him, without feigning and fraud, that he loves and is loved, and to admire his condescension, and to be amazed at his grace. Since his beauty is his love; and therefore the greater, because it goes before. Therefore, with the marrow of her heart and with the voices of her inmost affections, she cries that he is to be loved by her so much the more amply and ardently, as she, loving, felt this earlier than [being] loved. And so the speech of the Word is the infusion of a gift; the response of the soul, with thanksgiving, is admiration. And therefore the more she loves, because she feels herself overcome in loving: and therefore the more she admires, because she knows herself anticipated. Whence she is not content to say [him] beautiful once, unless she repeats also [him] comely, marking by that repetition the eminence of his beauty.
45.9: Or certainly, in the twofold substance of Christ she expressed a beauty worthy of all admiration, in the one of nature, in the other of grace. How beautiful you are to your angels, Lord Jesus, in the form of God, in the day of your eternity, in the splendors of the saints, begotten before the day-star, the splendor and figure of the substance of the Father, and indeed a perpetual and by no means painted whiteness of eternal life! How comely you are to me! My Lord, in this very laying aside of this beauty of yours! For where you emptied yourself, where you put off the unfailing light with its natural rays; there piety shone forth more, there charity shone more brightly, there grace radiated more amply. How bright for me arise you, the Star out of Jacob (Num. 24:17), how luminous you come forth, the Flower from the root of Jesse (Isa. 11:1), how pleasant a light you have visited me in the darkness, O Dayspring from on high! (Luke 1:78.) How wondrous and stupendous even to the supernal Virtues [are you] in [your] conception by the Spirit, in [your] birth from the Virgin, in the innocence of [your] life, in the streams of [your] teaching, in the flashes of [your] miracles, in the revelations of [your] sacraments! How ruddy, finally, after your setting, O Sun of justice, you rise again from the heart of the earth! how beautiful in your stole at last (Isa. 63:1), O King of glory, you receive yourself into the heights of the heavens! How shall not all my bones say for all these things: 'O Lord, who is like you' (Ps. 35:10)?
45.10: Think, therefore, that the bride, looking upon these and like things in her Beloved, took note [of them], when she said: 'Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.' Nor these alone, but besides, without doubt, something of the beauty of the higher nature, which wholly flies past our gaze, and escapes all experience. Therefore the repetition marked the beauty of each substance. Hear then how she dances for joy at the sight and discourse of her Beloved, and before him, with a nuptial song, rejoicing, sings the things which are of love. For it follows: 'Our little bed is flowery, the beams of our houses are of cedar, our ceilings are of cypress.' But let us keep the song of the bride for a new beginning, that we also, made more cheerful from the rest, may more freely exult and rejoice in it, to the praise and glory of the Bridegroom himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God, blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
45.title: Concerning the twofold beauty of the soul; and in what way the soul speaks to the Word of God, and the Word to the soul: and what their tongues are.

46.1: Our little bed is flourishing, the beams of our houses are of cedar, our ceilings are of cypress (Song 1:16-17). He sings an epithalamium, describing the couch and the bridal chambers in a beautiful discourse. He invites the Bridegroom to rest. For this is better, to rest and to be with Christ. But it is necessary to go out to the gains because of those who are to be saved. But now, having found, as he thinks, the opportunity, he announces the adorned bridal chamber, and pointing out the little bed as it were with his finger, he invites the beloved, as I said, to rest, and, not enduring the ardor of heart with those going to Emmaus, draws him to the lodging of the mind, compels him to spend the night with himself (Luke 24:29, 32), and speaks with Peter: 'Lord, it is good for us to be here (Matt. 17:4).'
46.2: Now let us inquire what these things contain spiritually. And in the Church indeed I think that the bed in which one rests is the cloisters and monasteries, in which one lives in quiet from the cares of the world and the anxieties of life. And that bed is shown to be flourishing, when, sprinkled with the examples and institutions of the fathers as with certain sweet-smelling flowers, the conversation and life of the brethren shines forth. Moreover, understand the popular houses to be the assemblies of Christians: whom those who are placed in a high position, namely the Christian princes of each order, like beams [binding] walls, bind strongly by the just laws imposed, lest each one, living by his own law or will, like leaning walls and cast-down fences, dissent from themselves, and so the whole structure of the building, collapsing, be scattered. But the ceilings, which hang firmly from the beams and adorn the houses remarkably, I think to designate the gentle and disciplined manners of a well-instituted clergy, and the offices administered rightly. For how will the orders of clerics and their administrations stand, if they are not sustained by the benefit and munificence of the princes, like that of beams, and protected by their power?
46.3: But that the beams are described as of cedar and the ceilings of cypress, nature without doubt has in these kinds of wood that which befits the aforementioned orders. And cedar indeed, since it is a wood that does not rot, and likewise fragrant, and of great height, sufficiently indicates what sort of men ought to be taken into the place of the beams. Therefore it is necessary that those who are ordained over others be strong and constant, and likewise long-suffering in hope, and lifting up to the height of the supernal mind, who also, scattering everywhere the good odor of their faith and manner of life, may be able to say with the Apostle: 'For we are the good odor of Christ to God in every place (2 Cor. 2:15).' Likewise the cypress, a wood equally of good odor and likewise incorruptible, shows that whoever of the clergy ought also to be of incorrupt life and faith, so that he may deservedly be assigned to the beauty of the house and the adornment of the ceilings. For it is written: 'Holiness becomes your house, O Lord, unto length of days (Ps. 93:5).' Where plainly there is both the glory of holiness and the expressed perseverance of unfailing grace. Therefore it behooves the man who is taken for the ornament and beauty of the house to be adorned with good manners; and although he himself is always within, to have nevertheless a good testimony also from those who are outside. There are also other things fitting in the nature of these woods to those things which are spiritually discussed: but for the sake of brevity I pass them over.
46.4: But it is to be noted that the whole state of the Church is beautifully comprehended in one brief little verse; namely, the authority of the prelates, the beauty of the clergy, the discipline of the people, the quiet of the monks. In the consideration of these things, when all are rightly [ordered], holy mother Church rejoices, and then she also offers them to the beloved to be beheld, when she refers all things to his goodness, as the author of all, attributing nothing to herself of all things. For that he says 'ours' and 'of ours' is not a sign of usurpation, but of love: because evidently, by the confidence of excessive charity, she judges nothing of him whom she greatly loves to be alien from herself. For she does not think that she is to be kept away from the fellowship of the Bridegroom, or from the sharing of his rest, she who has always been accustomed to seek not the things which are her own, but those which are his: and this is the cause why she has dared to pronounce both the little bed and the houses common to herself and the Bridegroom together. For she said: 'Our little bed'; and, 'the beams of our houses'; and, 'our ceilings': boldly associating herself in possession with him, to whom she does not doubt she is joined in love. Not so she who has not yet renounced her own will, but lies by herself, dwells by herself: rather she does not [live] by herself, but, living luxuriously, consorts with harlots — I speak of the lusts of the flesh — with whom she wastes her goods, and the portion of substance which she demanded to be divided to herself (Luke 15:12-13).
46.5: But do you who hear or read these voices of the Holy Spirit think that you are able to apply to yourself some of these things which are said, and to recognize in yourself something of the happiness of the bride, which is sung by the Spirit himself in this song of love, lest it be said also to you, that you hear his voice, and do not know whence it comes or whither it goes? Behold, perhaps you too seek the quiet of contemplation, and you do well: only do not forget the flowers with which you read the little bed of the bride to be sprinkled. Therefore take care, you too, likewise to surround your own [bed] with the flowers of good works, and by the exercise of virtues, as with a flower, to forestall the holy fruit of leisure. Otherwise you will wish to slumber in a quite delicate leisure, if, not exercised, you seek to rest, and, the fruitfulness of Leah neglected, you desire to be delighted only by the embraces of Rachel. But it is also a preposterous order to demand the reward before the merit, and to take food before the labor, since the Apostle says: 'He who does not labor, let him not eat (2 Thess. 3:10).' 'From your commandments I have understood,' he says (Ps. 119:104): that you may know that the taste of contemplation is by no means due except to the obedience of the commandments. Therefore do not think that, for the love of your own quiet, any prejudice is on any account to be made against the acts of holy obedience or the traditions of the elders. Otherwise the Bridegroom will not sleep with you in one bed, especially in that one which you have sprinkled for yourself, in place of the flowers of obedience, with the hemlocks and nettles of disobedience. For which reason he will not hear your prayers, and being called he will not come: for so great a lover of obedience will not give himself to the disobedient, he who preferred to die rather than not to obey. But he does not approve the vain leisure of your contemplation, he who says through the prophet: 'I have labored, sustaining (Jer. 6:11)'; signifying the time in which, an exile from heaven and from the homeland of the highest quiet, he worked out salvation in the midst of the earth. But I fear rather lest that dreadful sentence also envelop you, thus thundering against the perfidy of the Jews: 'Your new moons, and sabbaths, and other festival days I will not bear'; again: 'My soul hates your calends and your solemnities, they have become burdensome to me (Isa. 1:13-14).' And the prophet will mourn over you, and will say: 'The enemies have seen her, and have derided her sabbaths (Lam. 1:7).' For why should the enemy not deride that which the beloved rejects?
46.6: I greatly marvel at the shamelessness of some who are among us, who, when they have disturbed all of us by their singularity, irritated us by their impatience, and despised us by their contumacy and rebellion, nevertheless dare to invite the Lord, with all the earnestness of prayers, to the bed of their conscience, so foul and so entirely lacking in purity. But when you shall have stretched out your hands, he says, I will turn away my eyes, and when you shall have multiplied your prayer, I will not hear (Isa. 1:15). For what? the little bed is not flourishing, but rather it is even fetid; and do you drag the King of glory there? Do you do this for resting, or for quarreling? The centurion forbids him to enter under his roof on account of his own unworthiness, whose faith nevertheless is fragrant in all Israel (Matt. 8:8, 10): and do you compel him to enter to you, defiled with the filth of so many vices? The prince of the apostles cries: 'Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man (Luke 5:8)'; and you say: 'Enter to me, Lord, since I am holy?' 'Be all,' he says, 'of one mind in prayer, love the brotherhood (1 Pet. 2:17).' And the vessel of election: 'Lifting up pure hands,' he says, 'without anger and disputing (1 Tim. 2:8).' Do you see how they agree with one another, and speak with the same spirit concerning the peace and tranquility of the soul, which he who prays ought to have, the prince of the apostles and the doctor of the gentiles? Go on, therefore, you, to stretch out your hands to God all day long, who trouble your brethren all day long, fight against unanimity, and separate yourself from unity.
46.7: And what do you wish me to do, you say? Truly, that first indeed you cleanse your conscience from every defilement of anger and disputing, and of murmuring and envy; and that you hasten to drive out from the dwelling of the heart whatever is known entirely to be opposed either to the peace of the brethren or to the obedience of the elders. Then also surround yourself with the flowers of whatever good deeds and praiseworthy studies, and with the perfumes of virtues; that is, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are modest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are holy, whatsoever things are lovable, whatsoever things are of good report, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline; take care to think on these things (Phil. 4:8), and to exercise yourself in them. To [a bed] of this kind you will securely call the Bridegroom: since when you shall have brought him in, you too will be able truly to say that our little bed is flourishing, your conscience truly smelling of piety, but of peace, but of gentleness, but of justice, but of obedience, but of cheerfulness, but of humility. And thus far concerning the little bed.
46.8: But let each one recognize himself to be the spiritual house of God, he who now walks not in the flesh, but in the spirit: 'For the temple of God,' he says, 'is holy, which you are (1 Cor. 3:17).' Take care, therefore, brethren, for this spiritual building, which you are, lest when it shall have begun to advance to things higher, it waver and fall, if it shall not have been supported and bound together with strong wood: take care, I say, to give to it incorruptible and immovable beams; namely, the chaste fear of the Lord, that which remains forever and ever (Ps. 19:10); patience, of which it is written that the patience of the poor shall not perish forever (Ps. 9:19); also long-suffering, which, persisting inflexible under whatever weight of the structure, is extended into the infinite ages of the blessed life, the Savior speaking in the Gospel: 'He who shall have persevered to the end, this one shall be saved (Matt. 10:22)'; but rather above all charity, which never falls away, because 'strong as death is love,' he says, 'hard as hell is jealousy (Song 8:6).' Then be diligent to lay under and bind to these beams other woods equally precious and beautiful, when however those shall have been at hand to you for the work of the ceilings for the beauty of the house; namely, the word of wisdom or of knowledge, prophecy, the grace of healings, the interpretation of words, and other such things, which are known plainly to be more fitting for adornment than necessary for salvation. Concerning these I have no precept, but I give counsel: since indeed it is established that woods of this kind are both laboriously sought, and difficult to find, and perilously worked (for our land is found to produce them rarely, especially in these times), I counsel, and I admonish, that these not be sought after overmuch; but rather that the ceilings be prepared from other woods, which, although they appear less splendid, are proven nevertheless to be not less strong, and besides are possessed more easily and more safely.
46.9: Would that there were available to me also the abundance of those woods with which the garden of the Bridegroom, the Church, is copiously dense: peace, goodness, kindness, joy in the Holy Spirit, to show mercy in cheerfulness, to give in simplicity, to rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:8, 15). Would you not judge that house, as far as concerns the ceilings, to be sufficiently and abundantly adorned, which you should have seen floored sufficiently and neatly with such woods? 'Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house (Ps. 26:8).' Always give me these woods, I pray, with which I may always show you the adorned bridal chamber of conscience: of conscience, I say, both of my own and of another. With these I will be content. There will also be those who will wish to acquiesce in my counsel in this matter, because I think that you too will be content: the rest I leave to the holy apostles, and to apostolic men. But do you also, most beloved, although you do not have those woods; nevertheless, if you have these, trust; nevertheless with all confidence draw near to the chief, corner, elect, precious stone; nevertheless upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets be you also built up as living stones, spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God, through Jesus Christ (Eph. 2:19-22; 1 Pet. 2:4-9, the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages). Amen.
46.title: Concerning the state and composition of the whole Church. Likewise, in what way by the active life, which is led under obedience, one arrives at the contemplative.

47.1: I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys (Song 2:1). I think this looks to the fact that the bride had commended the couch sprinkled with flowers. For lest she ascribe to herself those flowers with which the couch seemed adorned and the bridal chamber made fair, the bridegroom inserts that he himself is the flower of the field; and that the flowers come forth, surely, not from the bridal chamber, but from the field; and that by his gift and by participation in himself it comes about that it shines, and that it is fragrant. Lest anyone, therefore, should be able to reproach her, and to say: What do you have that you did not receive? But if you did receive it, why do you glory as if you had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7)? he himself, to his beloved, as an eager lover, so also a kindly instructor, piously and graciously shows her to whom she ought to assign the brightness in which she was glorying, and the sweet fragrance of the couch. I am the flower of the field, he says: from me is that in which you glory. Most wholesomely are we admonished from this place also, that one ought by no means to glory: and if anyone glories, let him glory in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17). And that according to the letter: now let us search out, with his help of whom it speaks, the spiritual understanding which is hidden in it.
47.2: And first, mark now with me a certain threefold state of the flower; in the field, in the garden, in the bridal chamber: so that after this it may also more easily become clear why he chose above all to call himself the flower of the field. And in the field indeed, and in the garden, a flower springs up, but in the bridal chamber not at all. It is fragrant and shines in it, yet not upright and standing, as in the garden or the field; but plainly lying, as one that has been brought in, not born there. For this reason it is also necessary, surely, to renew them frequently, and always to set on fresher flowers, because they by no means keep their odor for long, nor their beauty. But if, as I said beforehand in another sermon, the couch sprinkled with flowers is the conscience filled with good works (preceding sermon, no. 7); you surely see that, so the likeness may be kept, it by no means suffices to work what is good once or a second time, unless you unceasingly add new things to the former, inasmuch as, sowing in blessings, you may also reap of blessings. Otherwise the flower of a good work lies and withers, and in a short time every brightness is destroyed out of it, and every vigor, unless it is continually repaired by other and still other acts of piety laid upon it. This in the bridal chamber.
47.3: But in the garden it is not so: nor likewise in the field. For from the flowers once brought forth from themselves they continually supply that whereby the inborn comeliness may long persevere in them. Yet they themselves also differ among themselves, in that the garden indeed, in order that it may flower, is cultivated by the hand and the art of men: but the field of itself naturally produces flowers, and without any aid of human diligence. Do you think you already seem to yourself to perceive what that field is, neither furrowed by the plowshare, nor dug by the hoe, nor enriched with dung, nor sown by the hand of man; yet nonetheless graced with that noble flower, upon whom it is established that the Spirit of the Lord rested? Behold, he says, the odor of my son is as the odor of a full field, which the Lord has blessed (Gen. 27:27). Not yet had that flower of the field put on his appearance, and already he was giving forth his odor, when the holy and aged Patriarch, wasting in body, dim of sight but keen of smell, perceived him beforehand in the spirit, so as to cry this out for joy. He ought not, therefore, to have professed himself the flower of the bridal chamber, he who is a flower ever vigorous: nor likewise of the garden, lest he should seem begotten by human work. But beautifully and most fittingly, I am the flower of the field, he says, who both came forth without human industry, and, once he had come forth, no corruption thereafter held sway, that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke: You will not give your Holy One to see corruption (Ps. 16:10).
47.4: But, if it pleases, receive also another reason of this matter, not, as I judge, to be despised. For not without cause, surely, is the spirit described by the Wise Man as manifold, save that under one rind of the letter he is wont for the most part to cover diverse understandings of wisdom. And so, according to the aforesaid division concerning the state of the flower, virginity is a flower, martyrdom is a flower, a good action is a flower. Virginity in the garden, martyrdom in the field, a good work in the bridal chamber. And well is virginity in the garden, to which modesty is familiar, fleeing the public, rejoicing in hiding-places, patient of discipline. Finally, in the garden the flower is enclosed, which in the field is set out, and in the bridal chamber is scattered. And you have: A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed (Song 4:12). Which surely signifies the enclosure of modesty in a virgin, and the keeping of holiness inviolate: if, however, she be such as is holy in body and in spirit. Well likewise is martyrdom in the field, while the martyrs are exposed to the mockery of all, made a spectacle both to angels and to men. Is theirs not the pitiable voice in the psalm: We have been made a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and a derision to those who are round about us? (Ps. 79:4.) Well also is a good action in the bridal chamber, which makes the conscience both quiet and safe. After a good work, finally, one sleeps more securely in contemplation, and one sets about to look upon and to search out the things on high with so much the more confidence, as he is conscious to himself that he has by no means, from love of his own quiet, failed the works of charity.
47.5: And all these things, in some respect, are the Lord Jesus. He himself is the flower of the garden, a virgin begotten by the rod of a virgin. The same is the flower of the field, a martyr, the crown of martyrs, the pattern of martyrdom. Finally he was led forth outside the city, he suffered outside the camp, he was lifted up upon the tree, to be gazed upon by men, to be mocked by all. He himself likewise is the flower of the bridal chamber, the mirror and example of every kindness, even as he himself protested to the Jews, saying: Many good works have I shown you from my Father (John 10:32); and likewise the Scripture concerning him: Who went about, it says, doing good and healing all (Acts 10:38). If, then, the Lord is these three, what was the cause that of the three he preferred to call himself the flower of the field? Surely, that he might rouse to endurance her upon whom he knew that, if indeed she willed to live piously in Christ, the suffering of persecution would be let loose. This, therefore, he professes of himself the more gladly, that to which above all he wills to have a follower; and this is what I have said elsewhere, that always she both seeks quiet, and he stirs her on to labor, declaring to her that through many tribulations one must enter into the kingdom of heaven (Acts 14:22). Whence, when the Church, new upon the earth and newly espoused to himself, was disposing to return to the Father, he was saying to her: The hour comes, that everyone who kills you may think that he is offering a service to God (John 16:2); likewise: If they have persecuted me, he says, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). You also can gather in the Gospel many things like this declaration of evils that must be borne.
47.6: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. She, therefore, pointing out the couch, he calls to the field, he summons to the exercise. He thinks nothing will be more persuasive to her for entering the contest than if he set himself forth either as the example of the one contending, or as the prize. I am the flower of the field. Surely either is given to be understood in this discourse, either, namely, that he is the pattern of the one fighting, or that he is the glory of the one triumphing. Both you are to me, Lord Jesus, both the mirror of suffering and the reward of the one who suffers. Both strongly provoke and vehemently kindle. You teach my hands unto battle by the example of your power, you crown my head after the victory by the presence of your majesty; whether because I look upon you fighting, or because I look for you not only as the one who crowns, but also as the crown: in either you wonderfully draw me to yourself; either cord is most violent for the drawing. Draw me after you: gladly do I follow you, more gladly do I enjoy you. If you are so good, Lord, to those who follow you, of what sort will you be to those who lay hold of you? I am the flower of the field. He who loves me, let him come into the field, let him not shrink from entering the contest with me and for me, that he may be able to say: I have fought the good fight (2 Tim. 4:7).
47.7: And since not the proud or the arrogant, but rather the humble, who know not how to presume of themselves, are fit for martyrdom; he adds that he is also the lily of the valleys, that is, the crown of the humble, designating by the eminence of this flower the special glory of their future exaltation. For it will be, when every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low (Isa. 40:4): and then that brightness of eternal life, plainly a lily not of the hills but of the valleys, will appear. The just man shall blossom as the lily, he says (Hos. 14:5). Who is just, if not the humble? Finally, when the Lord was bowing himself to the hands of his servant the Baptist, and the latter was shrinking in dread from the majesty, Suffer it, he says; for thus it becomes us to fulfill all justice (Matt. 3:15), setting the consummation of justice, surely, in the perfection of humility. The just man, therefore, is humble; the just man is a valley. And if we shall have been found humble, we also shall blossom as the lily, and we shall flourish forever before the Lord. Will he not truly, and then most of all, prove himself the lily of the valleys, when he shall refashion the body of our lowliness, configured to the body of his brightness? (Phil. 3:21.) He does not say, our body, but, the body of our lowliness: that by the wonderful and everlasting whiteness of this lily he may signify that the humble alone are to be made bright. And let these things have been said for this, that the bridegroom professed himself to be the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.
47.8: Now also it would be good to hear what he next professes concerning his most dear one: but the hour does not allow it. For by our Rule nothing is permitted to be set before the work of God (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 43). By which name, indeed, Father Benedict therefore willed the solemnities of the praises, which are paid daily to God in the oratory, to be called, that from this he might more clearly show how intent he wished us to be upon that work. Whence I admonish you, most beloved, always to be present at the divine praises purely and strenuously. Strenuously indeed, that as reverently, so also eagerly, you stand before the Lord: not sluggish, not sleepy, not yawning, not sparing your voices, not cutting words off half-way, not skipping whole ones, not sounding with broken and slack voices some womanish stammer out of the nose; but bringing forth the words of the Holy Spirit with a manly sound, as is worthy, and with a manly affection. But purely, that while you sing the psalms you think of nothing other than that which you sing. Nor do I say that vain and idle thoughts alone are to be avoided: those also are to be avoided, at that hour at least, and in that place, which the brothers who hold office, for the common necessity, as though of necessity, are often compelled to admit. But I would surely not then counsel you to take in even those things which perhaps a little before, sitting in the cloister, you had read in the books, of the sort which even now, while I discuss them with a living voice, you carry away fresh from this audience of the Holy Spirit. They are wholesome, but you by no means turn them over wholesomely while singing the psalms. For the Holy Spirit at that hour does not receive as pleasing whatever else than you ought, the thing you ought having been neglected, you shall have offered. Whose will to do, according to his will, himself inspiring, may we always be able, by the grace and mercy of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
47.title: Concerning the threefold flower, namely, of virginity, of martyrdom, and of good works — and concerning the devotion to be had around the divine office.

48.1: As the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters (Song 2:2). They are not good daughters, who prick. Mark the worst growth of that which was cursed, our earth. When you cultivate it, he says, it will sprout thorns and thistles for you (Gen. 3:18). As long, therefore, as the soul is in the flesh, it surely moves among thorns; and it must suffer the disquietings of temptations and the stings of tribulations. But if she herself is a lily, according to the word of the bridegroom, let her see how watchful and solicitous she ought to be over the keeping of herself, hedged on every side with thorns, aiming their stings this way and that. For the tenderness of the flower does not in any way endure even the lightest prick of a thorn, but as soon as it is pressed even a little, it is pierced. Do you perceive how deservedly and how necessarily the prophet exhorts us to serve the Lord in fear (Ps. 2:11); and likewise the Apostle, to work out our own salvation with fear no less, and with trembling? (Phil. 2:12.) They held, surely, by their own experience, the truth of this sentence, inasmuch as they were friends of the bridegroom, who would not at all doubt that what is said pertains also to their own souls: As the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters. Finally one of them: I was turned, he says, in my distress, while the thorn is fastened in (Ps. 32:4). Well pierced is he who was turned from that. Well are you pricked, if you are pricked to the heart. Many, when they feel the punishment, correct the fault; and such a one can say: I was turned in my distress, while the thorn is fastened in. The thorn is guilt, the thorn is punishment, the thorn is a false brother, the thorn is an evil neighbor.
48.2: As the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters. O shining lily! o tender and delicate flower! unbelievers and subverters are with you: see how cautiously you walk among the thorns. The world is full of thorns: they are on the earth, they are in the air, they are in your flesh. To move among these and not be hurt at all is of the divine power, not of your virtue. But be of good courage, he says, for I have overcome the world (John 16:33). If, therefore, you look about and see the stings of tribulations, as of thorns, aimed at you on every side; let not your heart be troubled, nor let it fear, knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience probation, and probation hope, but hope does not confound (Rom. 5:3-5). Consider the lilies of the field, how they thrive and shine among the thorns. If God so keeps the grass, which today is and tomorrow is cast into the oven (Matt. 6:28-30), how much more his love and his most dear bride? Finally, the Lord keeps all those who love him (Ps. 145:20). As the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters. It is surely no mean title of virtue to live as a good man among the depraved, and among those who do evil to keep the brightness of innocence and the gentleness of manners: but more, if to those who hate peace you show yourself peaceful, and a friend to those very enemies. That, plainly, will claim for you by a certain right of its own the likeness given of the lily, which surely does not cease to brighten and to beautify, with its own brightness, the very thorns that prick it. Or does the lily not therefore seem to you to fulfill, in a certain manner, the perfection of the Gospel, by which we are bidden to pray for those who calumniate and persecute us, and to do good to those who hate us? (Luke 6:27, 28.) Do you, therefore, also do likewise, and your soul will be the beloved of the Lord, and he will praise you out of yourself, saying that as the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters.
48.3: There follows: As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. The bride returns the exchange of praise to the bridegroom who commends her, by whom to be praised is to be made praiseworthy, and whom to praise is to understand and to admire one who is praiseworthy. And just as her praise, figured by the bridegroom, is taken from an eminent flower, so in her turn, and from an excellent tree, she shows his singular glory and eminence. Yet I am moved concerning this tree, that it does not seem to be of so great an excellence as some of the rest: and therefore to be taken up less worthily into the work of a likeness, inasmuch as it does not suffice to fulfill the return of praise. As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Finally, neither does the bride seem to have thought much of it, she who took care to exalt this only among the trees of the woods, surely barren ones, and bearing no fruits fit for human food. Why, then, better and nobler trees having been passed over, has the mediocrity of this tree been brought forward to form the praise of the bridegroom? Was he, then, to receive praise by measure, he who did not receive the Spirit by measure? This, surely, the likeness given from that tree does: that he seems to have a superior, he who has no peer. What shall we say to these things? I confess, a small praise, since it is the praise of a little one. For not in this place is the great Lord preached, and to be praised exceedingly (Ps. 145:3), but the little Lord, and to be loved exceedingly, the little child, surely, who is born to us (Isa. 9:6).
48.4: Not majesty, therefore, is lifted up here, but humility is commended; and worthily and reasonably that which is weak and foolish of God is preferred to the strength and the wisdom of men. For they themselves are the woodland and fruitless trees, since, according to the Prophet, they have all turned aside, together they have been made useless; there is none who does good, there is not so much as one (Ps. 14:3). As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. The Lord Jesus is the one tree among the trees of the woods that makes fruit, according to the man, surely, and though set before men, yet made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:5). For in a wonderful manner he both, having been made flesh, subjected himself to the angels, and, remaining God, kept the angels subject to himself. Finally: You shall see, he says, the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man (John 1:51): which is, that in one and the same man, Christ Jesus, they both cherish the weakness and stand amazed at the majesty. Because, therefore, that tastes sweeter to the bride which lessens him, she more gladly exalts the grace, prefers the mercy, and stands amazed at the condescension. It pleased her, therefore, to admire the man among men, not God among the angels, just as the apple tree excels among the trees of the woods, and plainly not among the plantings of gardens. Nor does she think the praises lessened where, from the consideration of weakness, the goodness of loving-kindness is exalted. For by as much as in one respect she moderates the praises, by so much again in another respect she praises the more, pursuing less the glory of dignity, that the grace of condescension may stand forth. Just as, therefore, the Apostle says that what is foolish and weak of God is wiser and stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:25), but not than the angels; and just as the Prophet preaches him beautiful of form above the sons of men (Ps. 45:2), and not above the angels; so she surely, speaking in the same spirit, willed in this place, under the figure of the fruitful tree and of the woodland trees, to exalt the Man who is God above every grace of men, but not above the excellence of the angels.
48.5: As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. And well, among the sons; because, though he was the only son of his Father, he was eager to acquire for him many sons, and that without envy, whom he is not ashamed to call brothers, that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers. But rightly is he set before all who are adopted by grace, he who is son by nature. As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Rightly as an apple tree, which, after the likeness of a fruitful tree, both has the shade of refreshment and bears the best fruit. Or is he not truly a fruitful tree, whose flowers are the fruit of honor and of uprightness? (Sir. 24:23.) Finally, he is a tree of life to those who lay hold of him (Prov. 3:18). All the trees of the woods shall not be compared to this one, because, even if there be trees fair and great, which seem to bring help by praying, by ministering, by teaching, by aiding with examples, yet Christ alone, the Wisdom of God, is the tree of life, alone the living bread who descended from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:41, 33).
48.6: Therefore she says: Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat, and his fruit is sweet to my throat (Song 2:3). Rightly had she desired the shadow of him from whom she was to receive alike both refreshment and refection. For the other trees of the woods, indeed, even if they have the shade of comfort, yet have not the refection of life, not the lasting fruits of salvation. For there is one author of life, one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), who says to his bride: I myself am your salvation (Ps. 35:3). Not Moses, he says, gave you this bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven (John 6:32). For this reason, therefore, she had desired above all the shadow of Christ, because he alone is the one who not only cools from the heat of the vices, but also fills with the delight of the virtues. Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat. His shadow is his flesh; his shadow is faith. The flesh of her own Son overshadowed Mary; the faith of the Lord, me. And yet how does the flesh not overshadow me also, who eat it in the mystery? And the holy Virgin no less herself also had experience of the shadow of faith, she to whom it was said: And blessed is she who has believed (Luke 1:45). Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat. And the prophet: The breath, he says, before our face is Christ the Lord; under his shadow we shall live among the nations (Lam. 4:20). In the shadow among the nations, in the light with the angels. We are in the shadow so long as we walk by faith, and not by sight; and therefore the just man is in the shadow, who lives by faith. But he who lives by understanding is blessed; because no longer in the shadow, but in the light. David was just, and was living by faith, when he was saying to God: Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments, and I shall live (Ps. 119:73, 144); knowing that understanding would succeed to faith, that the light of life was to be revealed to understanding, and life to the light. First it is to come to the shadow, and so to pass over to that whose shadow it is, since, unless you believe, he says, you will not understand (Isa. 7:9, according to the LXX).
48.7: You see that faith is both life, and the shadow of life. For on the other side, a life led in pleasures, since it is not of faith, is both death and the shadow of death. For she who is a widow, he says, and lives in pleasures, is dead while she lives (1 Tim. 5:6). Finally, the wisdom of the flesh is death. (Rom. 8:6). But it is also the shadow of death, of that, namely, which torments forever. We also once sat in the dark places and in the shadow of death, conducting ourselves according to the flesh, and not living by faith; already dead indeed to justice, but a little short of being swallowed up by the second death. For as near as the shadow is to the body whose shadow it is, so near for certain did that life of ours draw to hell. Finally: Unless the Lord had helped me, he says, my soul had a little less dwelt in hell (Ps. 94:17). But now we have passed from the shadow of death to the shadow of life; or rather, we have been translated from death to life (1 John 3:14), living in the shadow of Christ, if indeed living, and not dead. For I do not think that, as soon as someone is in his shadow, he therefore lives in it, because plainly not everyone who has faith lives by faith. For faith without works is dead; nor can it give a life which it has not itself at all possessed. Therefore the prophet, when he had said: The breath before our face is Christ the Lord, was not content to go on and say: We are in his shadow; but: in his shadow, he says, we live among the nations. See you also, therefore, that you live, after the prophet's example, in his shadow, that at some time you may also reign in his light. For he does not have the shadow only; he has the light also. He himself, through the flesh, is the shadow for faith; he himself, through the Spirit, is the light for understanding. For he is both flesh and spirit. Flesh, for those who remain in the flesh; spirit, before our face, that is, in what is to come; if, however, forgetting the things that are behind, we stretch ourselves forward to the things that are before, so that, arriving there, we may learn by experience concerning the word which he spoke: The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life (John 6:63). Nor am I ignorant that someone, still remaining in the flesh, has said: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer (2 Cor. 5:16). But that is he: we, however, who have not yet merited to be caught up into paradise, nor yet to the third heaven, let us meanwhile feed on the flesh of Christ, let us venerate the mysteries, let us follow the examples, let us keep the faith; and we surely live in the shadow.
48.8: In the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat. Perhaps she glories that she has experienced something happier in this, that she says that in the shadow she did not, as the prophet, live, but sat. For to sit is to be at rest. But it is more to be at rest in the shadow than to live, just as to live is more than only to be in it. Therefore the prophet, taking up for himself what is common to the many, says: In his shadow we live; but the bride, having the prerogative, glories also that she has singularly sat beneath it. For not as he, in the plural, We live, so did she also say, We sat; but in the singular, I sat, that you may recognize the prerogative. Where, therefore, we live with labor, we who, conscious of our sins, serve under fear, there she, devout and loving, sweetly rests. Finally, fear has torment, love has sweetness. Whence she says: And his fruit is sweet to my throat; signifying the taste of contemplation, which she had obtained, sweetly lifted up by love. But that is in the shadow, because through a mirror and in a riddle. It will be, when the shadows decline as the light increases, or rather disappear altogether, and a vision as clear as it is lasting comes in beneath; and there will be not only sweetness for the throat, but also fullness for the belly; yet without loathing. Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat, and his fruit is sweet to my throat. Let us also, where the bride pauses, pause with her, glorifying, for the taste that has been taken, the master of the house who has invited us to such a feast, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
48.title: Concerning the mutual praise which is made between the bridegroom and the bride, and in what way by the shadow of Christ are understood his body and his faith.

49.1: The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity in me (Song 2:4). As indeed the letter of the chapter set before us seems to sound, a conversation sweet enough and familiar having been had with the beloved, according to her desire, he departing, the bride returns to the young maidens, so refreshed and kindled by the sight of him and by his speech that she appeared like a woman drunk. And as though they were astonished at the strangeness, and were seeking the cause, she answered that it was by no means wonderful if she were heated with wine, she who had gone into the wine cellar. And according to the letter, so. According to the spirit also she does not deny that she is drunk, but with love, not with wine, except that love is wine. The king brought me into the wine cellar. When the bridegroom is present, and the bride directs her speech to him, then the bridegroom is called either beloved, or, he whom my soul loves, she says; but speaking of him to the young maidens, she names the king. Why this? For this reason, I believe: both that it suits the bride who loves and is beloved to use more familiarly, so far as it concerns herself, the names of love, and that the young maidens, as needing discipline, have need to be pressed by the reverend name of majesty.
49.2: The king brought me into the wine cellar. What this wine cellar is, I pass over saying, because I recall that I have said it. Yet if the discourse is referred to the Church, when the disciples, filled with the Holy Spirit, were thought by the people to be drunk with new wine; then Peter, as the friend of the bridegroom, standing for the bride in the midst of them: These men, he says, are not drunk, as you suppose. Mark, meanwhile, that he denied not that they were altogether drunk, but that they were drunk as they had been reckoned by those men. For they were drunk, but with the Holy Spirit, not with new wine. And as though they were bearing witness to the people that they had truly been brought into the wine cellar, Peter again, for them all: But this is, he says, that which was spoken through the prophet Joel: And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord; I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy: your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. Or does that house not seem to you to have been a wine cellar, in which the disciples were gathered together alike, when suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts 2:13-17, 2), and fulfilled the prophecy of Joel! and could not each one of them, going out drunk from the abundance of that house, and given to drink of so great a torrent of pleasure, rightly have said: For the king has brought me into the wine cellar?
49.3: But you also, if, with your spirit gathered, with a mind sober and empty of cares, you enter alone the house of prayer, and, standing before God at some one of the altars, you touch the gate of heaven with the hand of holy desire, and, presented to the choirs of the saints, your devotion making its way through (since the prayer of the just makes its way through the heavens), in their presence, as one to be pitied, you bewail the miseries and calamities which you suffer; with frequent sighs and groanings that cannot be uttered you disclose your need, you beg for pity; if, I say, you do this, I trust in him who said; Ask, and you shall receive (Matt. 7:7), that, if you persevere in knocking, you will not go out empty. But when you have given yourself back to us full of grace and charity, and, fervent in spirit, you will not be able to hide the gift received, which you will share without envy; and you will be, to all, in the grace which has been given you, not only welcome, but perhaps even to be wondered at; you yourself also will be able truly to declare, that the king brought me into the wine cellar; only be careful to glory, not in yourself, but in the Lord. Nor would I say that every gift, though spiritual, comes forth from the wine cellar, since the bridegroom has other cells also, or storehouses, having hidden in them diverse gifts and graces, according to the riches of his glory: concerning which cells I remember that I have disputed more at large elsewhere (above, sermon 23). Are not these things laid up, he says, with me, and sealed in my treasuries? (Deut. 32:34.) Therefore, according to the diversity of the cells, there are differences of graces, and to each one the Spirit is manifested unto profit. And although to one indeed is given the word of wisdom, but to another the word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another the grace of healings, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of speeches, and to others other things like these (1 Cor. 12:7-11), yet none of them, on account of a thing of this sort, will be able to say that he has been brought into the wine cellar. For these things are taken from the other cells, or treasuries.
49.4: But if anyone, by praying, obtains to pass out of his mind into that secret thing of God, whence he soon returns burning most vehemently with the divine love, and hot with zeal for justice, and also exceedingly fervent in all spiritual studies and duties, so that he can say: My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire flames out (Ps. 39:3): he plainly, when from the abundance of charity he begins to belch forth a good and saving excess of the wine of gladness, will not unfittingly be said to have entered the wine cellar. For since the transports of blessed contemplation are two, one in the understanding and the other in the affection; one in light, the other in fervor; one in knowledge, the other in devotion: a pious affection, surely, and a breast warm with love, and an inpouring of holy devotion, and also a vehement spirit filled with zeal, are plainly brought back from nowhere but the wine cellar: and whoever is granted to rise from prayer with a wealth of these can say in truth, that the king brought me into the wine cellar.
49.5: There follows: He ordered charity in me. Altogether of necessity. For zeal without knowledge is not to be borne. Where, therefore, the emulation is vehement, there discretion is most necessary, and discretion is the ordering of charity. Zeal without knowledge is indeed always found less effective, and less useful; but very often it is also felt to be exceedingly harmful. The more fervid, therefore, the zeal, and the more vehement the spirit, and the more lavish the charity, the more watchful a knowledge is needed, which may hold the zeal in, temper the spirit, and order charity. Fittingly, therefore, lest the bride be feared, as though too much and not to be borne, for the impulse of the spirit which she seems to have brought back from the wine cellar, especially by the young maidens; she joins to this that she has likewise received that which belongs to discretion, that is, the order of charity. For discretion sets an order upon every virtue; order bestows measure and comeliness, and also continuance. Finally he says: By your ordering the day continues (Ps. 119:91); calling a virtue the day. Discretion, therefore, is not so much a virtue as a certain guide and charioteer of the virtues, an orderer of the affections, and a teacher of conduct. Take this away, and virtue will be a vice, and natural affection itself will rather be turned into a disturbance, and into the ruin of nature. He ordered charity in me. But this was done when, in the Church, he gave some to be apostles, and some prophets, and others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints (Eph. 4:11, 12). But it is needful that one charity bind all these, and temper them together into the unity of the body of Christ: which it will not be able to do at all, if it has not itself been ordered. For if each is borne along by his own impulse, according to the spirit which he has received, and rushes off indifferently to whatever he wills, according as he is moved, and not by the judgment of reason; while no one will be content with the office assigned to him, but all alike will attempt all things with an undiscerning administration, there will plainly be not unity, but rather confusion.
49.6: He ordered charity in me. Would that the Lord Jesus might order in me also the little of charity which he has given; so that all the things which are his may be my care, in such a way, however, that I care before all else for that which shall have stood as most of all my own purpose or office: but surely that first, in such a way that I am nonetheless moved the more toward many things which do not specially belong to me. For that which is to be cared for first will not always also be that which is to be loved more: since often what is first as to solicitude is less as to usefulness, and therefore ought also to be less in the affection. Frequently, therefore, what is put first because it has been laid upon one is put after by judgment: and what truth judges ought to be put first, the order of charity demands ought to be embraced more dearly. Does there not, for example, lie upon me, from what has been laid upon me, the care of you all? Whatever, now, I shall perhaps have preferred to this work, so that I watch over it the less, carrying it out worthily and usefully according to my strength; even if I perhaps seem to do it out of charity, the account of order does not consent. But if, before all things indeed, as I ought, I attend to this care, and yet I do not rejoice more at the greater gains of God which I shall perhaps have found are made through another, it is plain that I keep the order of charity in part, and in part not at all. But if I show myself both more solicitous toward that which lies upon me more specially, and nonetheless more affected toward that which is greater; on both sides I am surely found to have reached the order of charity, and there is no cause why I myself also cannot say, that he ordered charity in me.
49.7: But if you say that it is hard for anyone to rejoice more in another's great good than in his own small one, you will surely see, even from this, the excellence of grace in the bride, and that it is not for any soul you please to say, that he ordered charity in me. Why have the faces of some of you fallen just now at this discourse? For deep sighs bear witness to sadness of mind and to the casting down of conscience. Surely, measuring ourselves by ourselves, some of us feel, from the experience of our own imperfection, how rare a virtue it is not to envy another's virtue, much less to rejoice at it, much less still for each to congratulate himself so much the more than at his own, as he perceives himself outdone in virtue. There is still a little light in us, brethren, as many of us as feel in this way. Let us walk while we have the light, lest the darkness lay hold of us (John 12:35). To walk is to make progress. The Apostle was walking, who said: I do not consider that I have laid hold; and he adds: But one thing, forgetting the things which are behind, I stretch myself forward to the things which are before (Phil. 3:13). What is it, but one thing? But one thing, he says, has as it were remained to me, for a remedy, for a hope, for a consolation. What is that? Forgetting, namely, the things which are behind, I stretch myself forward to the things which are before. Great confidence! that the great Vessel of election, refusing to be called perfect, confesses that he is making progress. For me, if I am not walking but sitting, there is danger of being seized by the darkness of death. And who is sitting, except he who does not care to make progress? Beware of that: and if you are overtaken by death, you will be in refreshment. You will say to God: Your eyes saw my imperfect being, and in your book nonetheless, he says, they shall all be written. Who, all? Surely those who are found in the desire of making progress. For there follows: The days shall be formed, and no one in them (Ps. 139:16); you are to supply: shall perish; understand the days as those who are making progress, who, if they are overtaken by death, are to be made perfect in that which they lack. They shall be formed, and no one in them shall be left unformed.
49.8: And how, you say, can I make progress, I who envy a brother who is making progress? If you grieve that you envy, you feel it, but you do not consent to it. It is a passion, to be healed in time, not an action to be condemned. Only do not settle down there, meditating iniquity upon your bed, namely, how you may nurse the disease, gratify the plague, persecute the innocent, by slandering, by putting down, by twisting the things he has done well, and by hindering the things that are to be done. Otherwise it does no harm to one who is walking and stretching himself forward to better things, that it is no longer he who does it, but the sin that dwells in him (Rom. 7:20). There is, therefore, no condemnation for him who does not give his members as weapons to iniquity, not his tongue for speaking ill, not anything of the rest of the body for hurting or harming in any way; but is rather ashamed to be so ill affected: and by confessing, by weeping, by praying, tries to drive out the vice grown in from long habit; and when he does not prevail, he is found from this the milder toward all, and the humbler in his own eyes. What man, sound of mind, would condemn a man who has learned from the Lord to be meek and lowly of heart? (Matt. 11:29.) Far be it that an imitator of the Savior should be found shut out from salvation, of the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages! Amen.
49.title: In what way by discretion charity is ordered, so that all the members of the Church, that is, the elect, are bound together mutually.

50.1: You perhaps expect the sequel to be treated, thinking the verse finished which was last treated. But I am attempting something else: for I have what I may still set before you from the fragments of yesterday's feast, which I had gathered for myself lest they perish. But they will perish, if I set them before no one: for if I wish to have them alone, I myself shall perish. I am unwilling therefore to defraud your appetite, which I well know, of them: especially since they are from the dish of charity, the sweeter the subtler; the more savory the smaller. Otherwise it is altogether against charity to defraud concerning charity itself. And so here I am: He has ordered charity in me (Song 2:4).
50.2: There is charity in act, and there is also in affection. And concerning that which is of work, I think a law was given to men, and a commandment formed: for in affection who so has it as it is commanded? Therefore that is commanded unto merit, this is given unto reward. Whose beginning indeed, and progress, and even present life we do not deny can be experienced by divine grace; but we firmly maintain the consummation for future happiness. How then was that to be commanded which was in no way to be fulfilled? Or if it pleases you more that the commandment was given concerning the affective, I do not contend therefrom, provided that you too agree with me, that it can least of all in this life be fulfilled by any man, or could have been. For who would dare arrogate to himself that which Paul himself confesses he has not comprehended? (Phil. 3:13.) Nor was it hidden from the teacher that the weight of the precept exceeds the strength of men; but he judged it useful that from this very thing they be admonished of their own insufficiency, and that they might know clearly to what end of justice they ought to strive according to their strength. Therefore by commanding impossibilities he did not make men transgressors, but humble, that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world become subject to God; because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him (Rom. 3:19, 20). For receiving the commandment, and feeling the offense, we shall cry to heaven, and God will have mercy on us: and we shall know in that day that not by works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy he has saved us (Tit. 3:5).
50.3: And this I would have said, if indeed we have agreed that the affective law was commanded. But that it rather suits the actual seems to appear thence especially, that when the Lord had said: Love your enemies, he presently draws a conclusion from works: Do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27). Likewise Scripture: If your enemy hungers, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink (Rom. 12:20). And here you have concerning act, not concerning affection. But hear likewise the Lord commanding also concerning love of himself: If you love me, he says, keep my words (John 14:15). And here too we are sent to works through the enjoined observance of the commandments. But he would have warned superfluously concerning work, if love were already in the affection. So then you must needs also take that in this way, that you are commanded to love your neighbor as yourself (Matt. 22:39), even if it is not so openly expressed. Or do you not finally judge it enough for you to fulfill that commandment concerning love of neighbor, if you perfectly observe that in which it is rightly prescribed to every man from the law of nature: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not to another? (Tob. 4:16.) And likewise that: Whatever you wish that men do to you, do you also to others (Matt. 7:12).
50.4: Nor do I say this, that we should be without affection, and with a dry heart move only our hands to works. I have read among other things which the Apostle writes as great and grave evils of men, this also numbered, namely to be without affection (Rom. 1:31). But there is an affection which the flesh begets; and there is one which reason rules, and there is one which wisdom seasons. The first is that which the Apostle says is not subject to the law of God, nor can be (Rom. 8:7); the second, which he reports from the opposite side as consenting to the law of God, because it is good (Rom. 7:16); nor is there doubt that the contentious and the consenting differ from each other. But far indeed the third differs from both, which both tastes and savors that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 34:8), eliminating the first, rewarding the second. For the first indeed is sweet, but base; the second dry, but strong; the last is rich, and sweet. Therefore through the second works are done, and in it charity sits, not that affective which, seasoned with the salt of wisdom and growing rich, brings into the mind a great multitude of the sweetness of the Lord; but rather a certain actual, which although it does not yet sweetly refresh with that sweet love, yet vehemently kindles with love of that love itself. Let us not love, he says, in word, nor with the tongue, but in work and in truth (1 John 3:18).
50.5: Do you see how cautiously he walks in the middle between vicious and affectionate love, distinguishing equally from both this actual and saving charity? Neither does he receive in this love the fiction of a lying tongue, nor again does he exact the taste of affecting wisdom. Let us love, he says, in work and in truth: namely that we be moved to do well rather by a certain impulse of vivid truth, than by the affection of that savory charity. He has ordered charity in me. Which of these do you think? Both, but in opposite order. For the actual prefers the lower things, the affective the higher. For in a well-affected mind there is no doubt, for example, that the love of God is preferred to the love of man, and among men themselves the more perfect to the weaker, heaven to earth, eternity to time, the soul to the flesh. Yet in well-ordered action often, or even always, the opposite order is found. For both concerning the care of the neighbor we are more urged, and more often occupied; and we assist weaker brethren with more diligent assiduity; and by the right of humanity and by necessity itself we attend more to the peace of earth than to the glory of heaven; and by the disquiet of temporal cares we are scarcely permitted to feel anything of eternal things; and to the weaknesses of our body, the care of the soul being postponed, we almost continually minister; and finally to our weaker members themselves we surround with more abundant honor, according to the saying of the Apostle (1 Cor. 12:23): thereby in a certain way doing the word of the Lord, of which you have: The last shall be first, and the first last (Matt. 20:16). Finally who doubts that a man praying speaks with God? How often nevertheless thence, charity commanding, are we led away and torn away, for the sake of those who need our work or speech? how often does pious quiet piously yield to the tumults of affairs? how often is the book set aside by a good conscience, that one may sweat at the work of the hands? how often for administering earthly things do we most justly forgo the very celebrating of the solemnities of masses? An inverted order: but necessity has no law. Therefore actual charity works its own order according to the command of the householder, beginning from the last (ibid., 8). Pious surely and just, which is not a respecter of persons; nor considers the values of things, but the necessities of men.
50.6: But not so the affective: for it itself draws order from the first. For it is wisdom, through which assuredly each thing tastes according as it is: so that, for example, what by nature has more worth, the affection itself also feels as more worth, lesser things less, least things least. And that order of charity indeed truth makes; but this order of truth charity claims for itself. For both true charity is in this, that those who need more receive first: and again in this beloved truth appears, if we hold in affection the order which that holds by reason. You therefore if you love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength (Matt. 22:37); and leaping beyond that love of love with which actual charity is content, with a more fervent affection, and having received in fullness of spirit that near divine love itself, to which that is a step, you wholly kindle: God surely tastes to you, even if not entirely worthily according as he is (which assuredly is impossible to every creature), yet certainly according as your tasting is. Then you yourself will also taste to yourself according as you are, when you feel that you have nothing at all for which you may love yourself, except inasmuch as you are of God: since indeed you have poured wholly into him that whence you love. You will taste, I say, to yourself according as you are, when by the very experience of your love, and of the affection which you will have toward yourself, you find nothing in yourself worthy to be loved even by yourself, except for his sake, without whom you yourself are nothing.
50.7: Now indeed the neighbor, whom you truly ought to love as yourself, that he too may taste to you according as he is, will surely taste to you nothing other than you to yourself, who is this which you are: for he is a man. He therefore who does not love yourself, except because you love God; consequently loves all who likewise love him, as yourself. Further an enemy man, since he is nothing, for that he does not love God; cannot indeed be loved as yourself, who love God; yet you will love that he may love. But it is not the same thing, to love that he may love, and to love because he loves. Therefore that he too may taste to you according as he is, he will taste to you, not indeed what he is, who assuredly is nothing; but what he perhaps will be, which is near to nothing, since it still hangs under doubt. For of him of whom it is certain that he will not thereafter return to the love of God, he must taste to you, not now near to nothing, but nothing entirely, inasmuch as he is nothing forever. That one therefore excepted, who is not only now not to be loved, but moreover to be held in hatred, according to that: Did I not hate them that hate you, O Lord, and pine away over your enemies? (Ps. 139:21.) For the rest, charity ambitious in this part permits that not even the least affection be denied to any man, even the most hostile. Who is wise, and will understand these things?
50.8: Give me a man who before all things indeed loves God from his whole self; but himself and his neighbor, inasmuch as they love him; but the enemy, as one who will perhaps sometime love; further his parents of the flesh more nearly, because of nature; but his spiritual instructors more abundantly, because of grace; and in this manner attends to all the rest of God with ordered love, despising earth, looking up to heaven, using this world as not using it, and between things to be used and things to be enjoyed discerning with a certain inward savor of the mind, so that he cares for transitory things transitorily, and only for that which is needful, and as it is needful, and embraces eternal things with eternal desire: such a man, I say, give me, and I boldly pronounce him wise, to whom assuredly each thing truly tastes according as it is, and to whom in truth and security it belongs to glory, and to say that he has ordered charity in me. But where is he, or when are these things? Which I say weeping, how long do we smell, and not taste, looking toward the homeland, and not apprehending, sighing, and saluting from afar? O truth, homeland of exiles, end of exile? there I see you, but am not allowed to enter, held back by the flesh, but nor worthy to be admitted, filthy with sins. O Wisdom, who reach from end to end mightily in establishing and containing things; and dispose all things sweetly in blessing and ordering affections! direct our acts, according as our temporal necessity demands; and dispose our affections, according as your eternal truth requires, that each one of us may securely glory in you and say that he has ordered charity in me. For you are the power of God and the wisdom of God, Christ the bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, God blessed above all forever. Amen.
50.title: Concerning the twofold charity, namely, actual and affective; and concerning its ordering.

51.1: Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love (Song 2:5). Love has grown, because the incentives of love have proceeded more than usual. For you see how great this time was the abundance not only of seeing, but also of conversing. The vision itself also appears granted with a more serene countenance, and the speech more pleasant, and the discourse longer and more drawn out. And she has been not only delighted by conversation, but also gloried in praise. Besides this, she has been refreshed by the shade of him whom she had desired, fed with fruit, given to drink from the cup. For she is not to be thought to have gone forth thirsty from the wine cellar, into which she just now lately glories that she was brought; nay rather thirsty, because he who drinks me, he says, will still thirst (Sir. 24:21). After all these things, the bridegroom withdrawing after his custom, she declares that she languishes with love, that is, for love. For the more welcome she had experienced his presence, the more troublesome afterward she felt his absence. For the withdrawal of a thing which you love is an increase of desire; and what you desire more ardently you lack more painfully. She asks therefore meanwhile to be cherished with the fragrances of flowers and fruits, until he returns again, whose delaying she bears most grievously. And this is the order of the words.
51.2: Now already let us attempt, with the Spirit of truth guiding, to draw out the spiritual fruit which is in them. And if the common Church of the saints is here received as speaking, we are designated in the flowers and fruits; but also all who have been converted from the world in the whole world. In the flowers indeed the new and still tender conversation of beginners is shown, but in the fruits the fortitude of those progressing and the maturity of the perfect. Surrounded by these the mother, sojourning and bearing fruit, to whom to live is Christ, and to die gain; surely bears more evenly the trouble of her delay, because, according to Scripture, she is given of the fruit of her hands, as from the firstfruits of the spirit, and her works praise her in the gates (Prov. 31:31). But if according to the moral sense you wish both these to be assigned in one soul, namely both flowers and fruits; understand faith as the flower, the act as the fruit. Nor incongruously, as I think, will this seem to you, if you notice how, like a flower necessarily preceding the fruit, a good work also ought to be preceded by faith. Otherwise without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6), Paul attesting, or rather equally himself teaching: Everything that is not of faith is even sin (Rom. 14:23). And so neither without flower fruit, nor without faith a good work. But faith also without works is dead (James 2:20); just as a flower also appears uselessly, where fruit does not follow. Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love. Therefore from good works rooted in unfeigned faith the mind accustomed to quiet receives consolation, as often as, as is usual, the light of contemplation is withdrawn from it. For who, I do not say continually, but even for some time, while he remains in this body, enjoys the light of contemplation? But as often as, as I have said, she falls from the contemplative, so often she takes herself into the active, thence assuredly as from nearby to return more familiarly into the same; for these two are messmates of one another, and dwell together; for Martha is the sister of Mary. For even if she falls from the light of contemplation, yet she suffers herself in no way to fall into the darkness of sin, or the sloth of idleness, keeping herself indeed in the light of good operation. And that you may know that works also are light: Let your light shine, he says, before men (Matt. 5:16): which there is no doubt was said of works, which men could behold.
51.3: Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love. When that which is loved is present, love thrives; it languishes, when it is absent. Which is nothing other than a certain weariness of impatient desire, by which it is necessary that the mind of one vehemently loving be affected when he whom she loves is absent, while wholly in expectation she reckons any haste whatsoever as lateness. And therefore she asks that the fruits of good works with the fragrances of faith be heaped up for her, in which meanwhile she may rest while the bridegroom makes delay. I speak to you my experience which I have experienced. If ever indeed I have found that some of you have progressed from my admonitions, then I have not been reluctant, I confess, to prefer the care of speech to my own leisure and quiet.
