For when, for example after a sermon some angry man is found changed into a mild, the proud into a humble, the fainthearted into a strong: further the mild, the humble, the strong each in his own grace is recognized to have grown, and to have been made better than himself: but also those who perhaps had grown lukewarm and were languishing about spiritual study, torpid and drowsy, seem to have grown hot again and awakened at the fiery eloquence of the Lord; and those who, having deserted the fountain of wisdom, had dug for themselves cisterns of their own will not able to hold waters, and therefore at every command murmured with a dry heart, having in themselves no moisture of devotion: these, I say, when from the dew of the word, and the voluntary rain, which he has set apart. God for his inheritance, are proved to have flowered again into works of obedience, made in all things willing and devout; there is not, I tell you, whence sadness should come upon the mind, as for interrupted study of pleasant contemplation, when I shall have been surrounded with such flowers and fruits of piety. Patiently I am torn from the embraces of barren Rachel, that from Leah the fruits of your progress may abound for me. Least of all will I regret interrupted quiet for the care of speech, when I see my seed germinating in you, and from it the increase of the fruits of your justice growing. For charity which does not seek the things that are its own (1 Cor. 13:5), has long since easily persuaded me of this, namely to prefer none of my desirables to your advantages. To pray, to read, to write, to meditate, and if there are any other gains of spiritual study, these I have judged losses for your sake.
51.4: Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love. This therefore the bride has spoken to the young women in the absence of the bridegroom, admonishing them to progress in faith and good works until he comes, sensing that in this will be both the good pleasure of the bridegroom, and the salvation of the daughters, and her own consolation. I know that I have explained this place more fully in the book On the Love of God, and under another understanding: whether better or worse let the reader judge if it please anyone to see both. I shall not indeed be judged by a prudent man for diversity of senses, provided that truth patronize us on both sides; and charity, which the Scriptures ought to serve, may edify the more, the more true understandings she has drawn from them for her work. For when does that displease in the senses of the Scriptures, which we continually experience in the uses of things? Into how many uses, for example, is water alone taken up for our bodies? So any one divine word will not be beside the point, if it brings forth diverse understandings, to be accommodated to the diverse necessities and uses of souls.
51.5: There follows: His left hand under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. And moreover I remember that this also was more abundantly discussed in the aforesaid little work; but let us mark the order of the sermon. It is clear that the bridegroom is present again, I believe, that by his presence he may raise up her who languishes. For how should she not recover in his presence, whom absence had cast down? Therefore he does not endure the trouble of the beloved: he is present, nor can he make delay when summoned by such great desires. And because he had found her, while he was absent, faithful to works, and solicitous for gains, in this assuredly, that she had commanded flowers and fruits to be gathered for herself; he has also returned this time with a more ready remuneration of grace. Finally with one of his arms he supports the head of her who lies, preparing the other for embracing, that he may cherish her in his bosom. Happy the soul that reclines on the breast of Christ, and rests between the arms of the Word. His left hand under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. She does not say: He embraces; but, he shall embrace me, that you may know her so not ungrateful for the former grace, that she has anticipated the second by thanksgiving.
51.6: Learn in returning thanks not to be slow or sluggish, learn to give thanks for each gift. Carefully, he says, consider what is set before you (Prov. 23:1), that namely no gifts of God may be frustrated of due thanksgiving; not great, not middling, not small. Finally we are commanded to gather the fragments lest they perish (John 6:12); that is, not to forget even the least benefits. Does not that perish which is given to an ungrateful one? Ingratitude is an enemy of the soul, an emptying of merits, a scattering of virtues, a perdition of benefits. Ingratitude is a burning wind, drying up for itself the fountain of piety, the dew of mercy, the streams of grace. For this reason finally the bride, as soon as she felt the grace of the left hand, gave thanks, not waiting for the fullness which is in the right. For when it was mentioned that the left was already under her head, there did not also follow that she was likewise embraced by the right; but, he shall embrace me, she says.
51.7: But what do we think is the left hand of the Word the bridegroom, or the right? Does that which is called the word of man have such bodily parts divided in itself, and distinct lineaments, and distinguishing between left and right? How much more he, who is of God and is God, the Word admits no variety at all, but is who is (Exod. 3:14), in his own nature so simple that he has no parts, so one that he has no numbers. For he is the wisdom of God, of which it is written: And of his wisdom there is no number (Ps. 147:5). But if what is invariable must needs be incomprehensible, and for this reason also ineffable; where, I ask, do you find words by which you may worthily assign that majesty, or properly utter it, or fittingly define it? Yet let us speak somehow, what somehow we feel of it by the revealing of the Holy Spirit. We are taught by the authority of the Fathers, and by the custom of the Scriptures, that it is permitted to use fitting likenesses from known things; but also not to invent new words, but to borrow known ones, with which those same likenesses may be worthily and fittingly clothed. Otherwise you will ridiculously attempt to teach unknown things through unknown.
51.8: Therefore because by right and left adversities and prosperities are wont to be designated: it seems to me that in this place there can be understood by the left of the Word indeed the threat of punishment; but by the right the promise of the kingdom. But there is a time when our mind is pressed servilely by fear of punishment: and then the left is by no means to be said under the head, but over the head; nor can a soul so affected altogether say that his left hand is under my head. But if progressing from this spirit of servitude she has passed into a certain more worthy affection of free obedience, inasmuch namely as she is rather provoked by rewards than constrained by punishments, or rather if she is driven by love of the good itself; then she will be able to say without doubt that his left hand is under my head: since indeed she has overcome that servile fear, which is on the left, by a better and more excellent habit of mind, and by worthy desires has even drawn near to the right, in which are all the promises, the Prophet saying to the Lord: Delights are in your right hand forever (Ps. 16:11). Whence also with certain hope conceived she speaks with confidence: And his right hand shall embrace me.
51.9: You may already see with me, whether to one so affected and having attained this place of such great sweetness, that also from the psalm suits to be used, that she herself also may say: In peace in the selfsame I will sleep, and I will rest; especially since the cause which follows is at hand: Because you, O Lord, have singularly established me in hope (Ps. 4:8, 9). Which indeed is of this sort. As long as one is pressed by the spirit of servitude, and has little of hope, much of fear; there is for him neither peace nor rest, the conscience assuredly fluctuating between hope and fear, and especially because he is more abundantly tormented by the exceeding fear: for fear has punishment. And therefore it is not for him to say: In peace in the selfsame I will sleep and rest, when he cannot yet say that he has been singularly established in hope. But if little by little through increase of grace fear has begun to fail, and hope to progress; when at last it has come to this that charity rising with all her strength to the help of hope casts out fear: will not such a soul seem singularly established in hope, and therefore also already sleep in peace in the selfsame and rest?
51.10: If you sleep, he says, among the midst of lots, the wings of a dove silvered (Ps. 68:13). Which I think was said for this reason, because there is a place between fear and security, as between left and right, namely middle hope, in which the mind and conscience, a soft bed of charity assuredly being laid beneath, rests most sweetly. And perhaps in what follows of this same canticle this place will have been designated, where in the description of Solomon's litter among other things you have: He paved the midst with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem (Song 3:10). For he who feels himself singularly established in hope, no longer serves in fear, but rests in charity. Finally the bride rests and sleeps, for whom it is said: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you stir not up nor make the beloved to awake, until she herself will. Great and wonderful condescension, that he makes the contemplating soul rest in his bosom, and moreover guards her from troublesome cares, and protects her from the disquiets of actions, and the troubles of affairs; nor suffers her at all to be stirred up, except indeed at her own will. But that is not to be attempted in the straits of a sermon already ending, but rather another should be begun from this, that the delightful place may not be defrauded of due diligence in treating. Not that even then we are sufficient to think anything as of ourselves as from ourselves, especially in so worthy, and so excellent and altogether preeminent a matter; but our sufficiency is from God, the bridegroom of the Church Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all forever. Amen.
51.title: In what way the bride asks for herself fruits of good works to be heaped up together with the flowers and perfumes of faith; likewise concerning hope and fear.

52.1: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you stir not up nor make the beloved to awake, until she herself will (Song 2:7). The young women are forbidden: for these he calls daughters of Jerusalem, because, although delicate and soft, and as yet weak with feminine affections and acts, yet they cling to the bride in hope of progressing and of setting out for Jerusalem: they are therefore forbidden from troubling the sleeping bride, namely that they presume not at all to stir her up beyond her own will. For for this reason the sweetest bridegroom has placed his left hand under her head, according to those things which have been set forth, that in his bosom he might make her rest and sleep. And now as Scripture presently continues, he himself her guardian most graciously and most kindly watches over her, lest disturbed by the frequent and minute necessities of the young women she be compelled to awake. This is the literal coherence of the text. But indeed that adjuration made by the roes and the harts of the fields seems to have nothing at all according to the letter of reasonable consequence; so completely does the spiritual understanding claim it all for itself. But however that may stand, meanwhile it is good for us to be here, and to look for a little upon the goodness, sweetness, condescension of the divine nature. For what, O man, have you ever experienced in human affections sweeter than what is now expressed to you from the heart of the Most High? And it is expressed by him who searches the deep things of God, and cannot be ignorant of the things that are in him, because it is his Spirit; nor speak anything other than what he has seen with him, because he is the Spirit of truth.
52.2: Finally there is not wanting in our kind one who happy with this gift has deserved to be gladdened, and so has had experience of this sweetest secret in himself; unless however we altogether disbelieve the place of Scripture which is at hand, where the heavenly bridegroom is manifestly introduced most vehemently zealous for the quiet of a certain beloved of his, solicitous to keep her sleeping between his own arms, lest by any trouble or disquiet she be cast down from the sweetest sleep. I cannot contain myself for joy, that that majesty does not at all disdain to incline itself to our infirmity with so familiar and sweet companionship, and the heavenly Godhead does not despise to enter marriage with an exiled soul, and to show her the affection of a bridegroom seized with most ardent love. So, so I do not doubt it is in heaven, as I read on earth, and the soul will certainly feel what the page contains, except that this does not at all suffice to express how much that will then be able to receive, nor even how much it already can. What, do you think, will she receive there, who here is gifted with such great familiarity, that she feels herself embraced by the arms of God, cherished in the bosom of God, guarded by the care and zeal of God, lest while sleeping she perhaps be stirred up by anyone, until she of her own accord awakes?
52.3: Come then therefore, let us say if we can, what that sleep is, in which the bridegroom wishes his beloved to fall asleep, and suffers her not at all to be stirred up, except at her own judgment, lest perhaps when someone has read in the Apostle: It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep (Rom. 13:11), or in the Prophet that God is entreated by him, to enlighten his eyes lest he ever fall asleep in death (Ps. 13:3), he be disturbed by the equivocation of names, and find altogether nothing that he can worthily feel concerning the sleeping of the bride which is mentioned in this place. For not even that is like to this, which the Lord says of Lazarus in the Gospel: Lazarus our friend sleeps, let us go and awake him from sleep (John 11:11). For he was saying this of the death of his body, when the disciples thought it said of the sleeping of sleep. But this sleep of the bride is not a sleeping of the body, either peaceful, which sweetly lulls the senses of the flesh for a time, or horrible, which is wont to take away life utterly. But much more also it is alien from that by which one falls asleep in death, when namely one irrevocably perseveres in the sin which is unto death. But rather such a vital and wakeful slumber illuminates the interior sense, and death being driven away bestows everlasting life. For truly it is a sleeping, which yet does not lull the sense, but leads it away. It is also a death, which I would say without doubt, because the Apostle, if he speaks commendably of certain still living in the flesh: You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).
52.4: Therefore I also not absurdly would call the ecstasy of the bride a death, which yet snatches away not from life, but from the snares of life, that she may be able to say: Our soul as a sparrow has been delivered from the snare of the hunters (Ps. 124:7). For among the midst of snares one walks in this life, which assuredly are so often not feared, as often as by some holy and vehement thought the soul is snatched away from herself; if yet she so far withdraws and flies away in mind, that she also transcends this common use and custom of thinking: for in vain is the net cast before the eyes of them that have wings (Prov. 1:17). For what should luxury be feared, where not even life is felt? For when the soul exceeds, if not life, at least the sense of life, it is necessary that neither the temptation of life be felt. Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I will fly, and I will rest? (Ps. 55:6.) Would that by this death I may frequently fall, that I may escape the snares of death, that I may not feel the deadly blandishments of a luxurious life, that I may be stupefied to the sense of lust, to the heat of avarice, to the goads of anger and impatience, to the anguishes of solicitudes, and the troubles of cares! Let my soul die the death of the just, that no fraud may ensnare her, no iniquity delight her. A good death, which does not take away life, but transfers it into something better, good, by which the body does not fall, but the soul is lifted up.
52.5: But this is of men. But let my soul die also the death, if it can be said, of angels, that exceeding the memory of present things, she may strip herself not only of the desires of inferior and bodily things, but also of their likenesses, and may have pure conversation with those with whom there is likeness of purity. Such excess, as I think, is called either only, or chiefly, contemplation. For not to be held in living by the desires of things is of human virtue, but not to be involved in contemplating by the likenesses of bodies is of angelic purity. Yet both are of divine gift, both to exceed, both to transcend yourself is, but the one far, the other not far. Blessed is he who can say: Behold I have gone far fleeing, and I have remained in solitude (ibid., 7). He was not content to go out, unless he also made himself far, that he might be able to rest. You have leaped over the delights of the flesh, so that you no longer obey its concupiscences, nor are held by its allurements: you have progressed, you have separated yourself, but you have not yet gone far, unless you also prevail by purity of mind to fly over the phantasms of bodily likenesses rushing in from every side. Thus far do not promise yourself rest. You err, if short of this you think you find a place of rest, the secret of solitude, the serene of light, the dwelling of peace. But give me one who has arrived there, and I unhesitatingly confess him resting, who deservedly may say: Return, my soul, into your rest; because the Lord has dealt kindly with you (Ps. 116:7). And here truly is a place in solitude and a habitation in light, altogether according to the prophet, a tabernacle for a shade by day from the heat, for security and a hiding place from the whirlwind and from the rain (Isa. 4:6); of which also holy David: He has hidden me, he says, in his tabernacle in the day of evils, he has protected me in the secret of his tabernacle (Ps. 27:5).
52.6: Think therefore that the bride has withdrawn into this solitude, and there for the pleasantness of the place has sweetly fallen asleep among the embraces of the bridegroom, that is has exceeded in spirit, when the young women were forbidden to awaken her, until she herself should will. But how is that? For they were not forbidden simply, nor by a light admonition, as is usual; but by an altogether new and unwonted adjuration, namely by the roes and the harts of the fields. By which kind of wild beasts there seem to me to be expressed fittingly enough holy souls stripped of bodies, and at the same time the angels who are with God, assuredly because of sharpness of sight, and swiftness of leaping. For we know that both these things suit both spirits: for easily they both seek the heights, and penetrate the inmost things. Whose conversation also designated in the fields clearly signifies free and unencumbered discursions in contemplation. What then does the adjuration made by these mean? Assuredly that the restless young women may not dare for a light cause to call the beloved away from so reverend a company, with which without doubt she is mingled as often as she exceeds in contemplating. Beautifully therefore they are terrified by the authority of those, from whose society it is clear that she is torn away by their importunity. Let the young women attend whom they offend, equally when they disquiet the mother; and let them least so trust in maternal charity, that they do not fear to rush upon that heavenly assembly without great necessity. For let them think that they do this, as often as they are more troublesome than is just to her resting in contemplation. It is indeed placed in her own will, both to be free for herself, and to attend to their care as she shall have judged fitting, since she is forbidden to be stirred up by them, until she herself will. The bridegroom knows with how great love the bride burns even toward neighbors, and that the mother is sufficiently solicitous by her own charity for the progress of the daughters, nor will she in any way withdraw or deny herself to them as much and as often as there shall be need: and therefore he has judged that this dispensation may securely be entrusted to her discretion. For she is not such as many we see marked with the prophetic branding, who taking what is fat and strong, cast away what is weak (Ezek. 34:3, 4). Does a physician seek the healthy, and not rather the sick? If it happens, he perhaps acts as a friend, but not as a physician. Whom will you teach, good Master, if you drive away all the untaught? To whom, I ask, will you apply the diligence of discipline, if you either put to flight all the undisciplined, or flee them? In whom, I beseech, will you prove your patience, if you admit only the meek, and exclude the restless?
52.7: Yet there are of those sitting here, who would that they more attentively observed the present chapter. They would certainly think how great reverence is due to superiors, whom by rashly disquieting they also render themselves hostile to the citizens of heaven: and perhaps they would at last begin to spare us a little more than usual, nor so irreverently and lightly thrust themselves upon us when we are free. Rare enough for me, as they well know, is an hour granted for taking holiday from those who come upon me, even when they themselves will bear with me in all patience. But I raise this kind of complaint more scrupulously, lest perhaps some fainthearted one beyond the strength of his own patience dissemble from his necessities, while he fears to disquiet me. I forbear therefore, and lest I seem rather to give an example of impatience to the weak. The little ones of the Lord are those who believe in him; I do not suffer that they suffer scandal from me (Matt. 18:6). I do not use this power; but rather let them use me as they please: only that they may be saved. They will spare me if they have not spared, and in that rather I shall rest, if they have not feared to disquiet me for their necessities. I will comply with them as far as I can, and in them I will serve my God, as long as I shall be, in unfeigned charity. I will not seek the things that are mine; nor what is useful to me, but what is to many, that I will judge useful to me. This alone I pray, that my ministry may be acceptable and fruitful to them, if perhaps even from this I may find in the evil day mercy in the eyes of their Father and at the same time of the bridegroom of the Church Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him is God blessed above all forever. Amen.
52.title: Concerning the going out, which is called contemplation, in which the bridegroom makes the holy soul rest, being zealous for its rest.

53.1: The voice of my beloved (Song 2:8). Seeing the new modesty of the young women, and modest fear, namely that they had newly begun not to dare to thrust themselves upon her holy leisure, nor as yesterday and the day before to presume to be troublesome to her resting in contemplation: she recognizes that this has come to her by the care and work of the bridegroom; and exulting in spirit, whether for their progress, who are restrained from excessive and superfluous disquiet; or for her own freer quiet thereafter to come, or also for the condescension and favor of the bridegroom, so zealous for this very quiet of hers, and with such zeal defending her sweetest leisures, nay her most fervent studies, she says that the voice of her beloved does this, made for this reason to them. For he who is set over others in solicitude, scarcely ever, or rarely, is securely free for himself, while he always fears to make a want of himself to those subject, and not to please God, that he prefers his own quiet and the sweetness of contemplation to the common utility. But no little joy and security sometimes comes to one sweetly taking holiday, when from a certain fear and reverence toward himself divinely sent into the hearts of those subject, he understands that his quiet pleases God, who makes that they bear their necessities with a more even mind, than that they dare rashly to disturb the welcome leisures of their spiritual father. For the just trembling of the little ones manifestly signifies that they have heard within as it were the threatening and rebuking voice of him without doubt, who speaks in the prophet: I who speak justice (Isa. 63:1). His voice is his inspiration, and the striking of just fear.
53.2: Having therefore perceived this voice, the bride rejoicing and exulting: The voice, she says, of my beloved. She is a friend, and rejoices with joy because of the voice of the bridegroom. And she adds: Behold he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. Having perceived from the hearing of the voice the presence of the beloved, she unhesitatingly directs well-curious eyes to see him whom she had heard. Hearing leads to sight, because faith is from hearing (Rom. 10:17), by which hearts are cleansed, that God may be able to be seen: for so you have: Cleansing their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9). She sees therefore him coming, whom she had heard speaking, the Holy Spirit observing here also that order which is described in the Prophet thus: Hear, daughter, and see (Ps. 45:10). And that you may more certainly notice, not by chance, nor fortuitously, but rather by design and industry, for that reason namely which we have set forth, hearing in this place put before sight; see whether this order of words is not found observed also by holy Job, where he thus speaks to God: With the hearing of the ear I have heard you, and now my eye sees you (Job 42:5). But also where the Holy Spirit is remembered to have descended upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, is not hearing described as having preceded sight? For he says: Suddenly there was made from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind coming; and below: And there appeared to them parted tongues as of fire (Acts 2:2, 3). And here therefore the coming of the Holy Spirit is reported to have been perceived first by hearing, thereafter by sight. But of this enough; because you also, if you care to give attention to this kind of inquiry, will perhaps yourself also be able to find some similar things in other places of Scripture.
53.3: Now already let us consider that which needs more diligent inquiry, and has more difficult approaches, for which assuredly I confess that I altogether need the help of the Holy Spirit, that I may be able to bring into light who those mountains or hills are, upon which leaping, and skipping over them, the Church beheld the bridegroom with joyful gazes, I believe when he was hastening to her redemption, whose beauty she had desired. For that indeed for this reason I have so felt and not doubtfully, because something similar from the Prophet occurs to me, evidently foreseeing in spirit and expressing the coming of the Savior: In the sun he has set his tabernacle, and he himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber. He has exulted as a giant to run the way: from the highest heaven is his going forth, and his meeting even to the height thereof (Ps. 19:5, 6). This course and recourse is most known; from which, and to what it was begun and consummated, most known. What then? shall we paint for ourselves, whether reading these things in the psalms, or in the present canticle, a giant man of tall stature, seized with love of some absent little woman, and, while he hastens to the desired embraces, leaping over these mountains and hills, which we see with bodily mass rising above the level of the earth with such height, that even above the clouds some of them are perceived to have lifted their summit? But it does not befit to imagine such bodily phantasms, especially treating this spiritual canticle: but nor is it altogether permitted us, who remember to have read in the Gospel, that God is a spirit, and those who adore him ought to adore in spirit (John 4:24).
53.4: Who then are these spiritual mountains and hills, that afterward we may consequently recognize of what sort and of what kind the bridegroom (who is God, and for this reason also is spirit) was giving leaps in them, or upon them? If we think those in which the Gospel reports that once ninety-nine sheep were left, when their pious shepherd came to seek one on earth which had perished (Matt. 18:12); nonetheless the matter is still in obscurity, and the understanding sticks: while it is difficult to find what or what sort of other spiritual mountains or hills likewise those spiritual and supercelestial beatitudes (for they themselves without doubt are the sheep there mentioned) have for dwelling, or for feeding in them. Yet if there were not some in truth, Truth would not have said this. But nor would the Prophet long before have brought forth concerning the heavenly city Jerusalem, that her foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps. 87:1), if there were not truly holy mountains there. Finally that that heavenly habitation truly has, not only spiritual, but also living and rational mountains and hills, hear Isaiah: The mountains and the hills shall sing praises before God (Isa. 55:12).
53.5: Who then are these unless the same very spirit-inhabitants of heaven, whom we have said by the Lord's voice to be called sheep, so that they themselves are the mountains who are the sheep? Unless perhaps it seems absurd to you, either mountains to be fed in mountains, or sheep in sheep. And according to the letter indeed it sounds hard; but according to the spiritual understanding it tastes sweet, if we subtly notice how the shepherd of both flocks, namely the wisdom of God Christ, administers one and the same food of truth otherwise to his flocks on earth, otherwise in the heavens. For we indeed mortal men meanwhile in the place of our pilgrimage must needs eat our bread in the sweat of our face, begging it without in labor and hardship; that is, either from learned men, or from sacred books, or certainly through the things that have been made, beholding the invisible things of God understood. But the angels in all fullness, although not from themselves, yet in themselves, with as great facility as also happiness receive, whence also they live blessedly. For they are all teachable of God: which indeed the elect of men are sometime to attain is promised with certain truth, and is not yet granted to experience with secure happiness.
53.6: Therefore mountains are fed in mountains, or sheep in sheep, when indeed those heavenly spiritual substances within themselves abundantly find of the Word of life, whence they may perpetuate their blessed life, they themselves the same both mountains and sheep: mountains, because of fullness or loftiness; sheep, because of meekness. For full of God, lofty in merits, heaped with virtues, nonetheless yet with all and humble obedience they submit and incline their raised tops to the command of that far preeminent majesty, as most meek sheep walking in all things at the nod of their shepherd, and following him whithersoever he goes. And in these, according to the prophet David, truly holy mountains, as the first of all created wisdom, the foundations of the city of the Lord from the beginning firmly established stand (Ps. 87:1); which assuredly is one in heaven and on earth, although in part sojourning, and in part reigning. And from these nonetheless, according to Isaiah, as from certain vital well-sounding cymbals, continual thanksgiving resounds, and the voice of praise (Isa. 51:3), filling with sweet and unceasing voice what a little before we have mentioned from the same Prophet, that the mountains and the hills shall sing praises before God: and likewise what that other speaking to the Lord God: Blessed, he says, are they who dwell in your house, O Lord: forever and ever they shall praise you (Ps. 84:4).
53.7: These therefore: that we may return to that from which we have digressed a little, but, as I think, necessarily: those are the mountains and hills, in which the Church saw the heavenly bridegroom leaping with wonderful alacrity, when he was hastening to her embraces; and not only leaping, but also skipping over them. Do you wish that I show you these leaps from the writings of the prophets and of the apostles? Not that I now begin to repeat all the testimonies which concerning this matter can be found among them by the leisured (for this is long, and there is no need); but I set down only those which briefly and openly seem to establish what is said of the leaps of the bridegroom. David says of him that he has set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber: he has exulted as a giant to run the way, from the highest heaven is his going forth (Ps. 19:5, 6). Behold how great a leap he has given, from the highest heaven to the lands. For indeed I find nowhere else where he has set his tabernacle in the sun, that is, has deigned to show his presence in light and in the open, he himself the inhabitant of inaccessible light, unless assuredly on earth. Finally: He was seen on earth, and conversed with men (Bar. 3:38). On earth, I say, openly, which is in the sun, he has set his tabernacle, namely the body, which from the body of the Virgin he deigned to fashion for himself for this, that in it he who is invisible in himself might be seen; and so all flesh might see the salvation of God, when he had come in the flesh.
53.8: He leaped therefore upon the mountains, that is upon those highest spirits, when he descended even to them, opening to them graciously the sacrament hidden from ages, and the great mystery of piety. But skipping over these higher and more eminent mountains, namely the cherubim and seraphim, and also the dominions, principalities and powers, and the virtues too, he deigned to descend even to the lower order of angels, as to hills. But did he remain even in them? He skipped over the hills also. For he did not, he says, take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham (Heb. 2:16), which assuredly is lower than angels, that the word might be fulfilled which the mentioned Prophet spoke, speaking thus to the Father of the Son: You have made him a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:5). Although this indeed can be understood as said for the commendation of human nature, that man created to the image and likeness of God, and endowed with reason after the likeness of an angel, yet differs a little from an angel because of a body from earth. But hear the apostle Paul openly pronouncing of him: Who when he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man (Phil. 2:6, 7); and again: When, he says, the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4, 5). He therefore who was made of a woman, and made under the law, without doubt not only leaped over the mountains descending, that is the greater and higher beatitudes, but also the lesser angels, who indeed in comparison with the higher are deservedly designated by the name of hills. But he who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than any bearing flesh upon earth, even if that one be the great John the Baptist (Luke 7:28). For although indeed we confess God man, even in man to preeminently far incomparably above every principality and power; yet it is certain that although he goes before in majesty, yet he has succumbed in infirmity. So therefore he leaped upon the mountains, and skipped over the hills, when he most graciously showed himself lower not only to the higher, but also to the lower spirits. Nor only to those heavenly spirits, but also to those themselves who inhabit houses of clay, he showed himself subject, leaping over and conquering by humility even the humility of men. Finally he was subject to Mary and Joseph, when he was twelve years old, in Nazareth (Luke 2:51, 42): and at the Jordan already a youth he inclined himself to the hands of John (Matt. 3:13). But the day also is declined, nor yet do I altogether wish to descend from these mountains.
53.9: But if this time we wish to explore all the pleasant places of these, as it delights, to search the hidden things; it is to be feared lest either the sermon lack welcome brevity, or the large and excellent matter be defrauded of due diligence by haste. Let us pause therefore today already, if it please, upon these mountains; because it is good for us to be here, where placed by the shepherd Christ together with the holy angels in a place of pasture, we are both more pleasantly fed, and more abundantly. And we too are sheep of his pasture. Let us therefore ruminate, as clean animals of the good shepherd, what with all avidity we have swallowed in today's sermon; in another sermon more attentively to perceive the remainder of the same chapter, by the gift of the bridegroom of the Church Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all forever. Amen.
53.title: That by the mountains and hills are signified the heavenly spirits, whom the bridegroom passes over by his coming into the lands, or by the mystery of his Incarnation.

54.1: Upon the same chapter, which was treated in yesterday's sermon, I am about to say also another understanding which I have reserved for today: you prove, and choose the better things. There is no need to repeat the former things which I do not think have slipped away in so brief a space. If nevertheless otherwise, they have been written as they were spoken, and taken down by the pen, as also the other sermons, that what perhaps has slipped away may easily be recovered. Wherefore receive other things. Behold he comes, she says, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills (Song 2:8). She speaks of the bridegroom: who assuredly then leaped upon the mountains, when sent by the Father to evangelize to the poor, he did not disdain to perform the office of Angels, made the Angel of great counsel, who was Lord. He himself descended to the lands, who was wont to delegate others: the Lord himself made known his salvation, himself in the sight of the nations revealed his justice (Ps. 98:2). When therefore all, according to the saying of Paul, are ministering spirits, sent for ministry because of those who receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14); he who was above them was made among them as one of them, dissembling the injury, heaping up grace. But hear himself. I came not, he says, to be ministered to, but to minister, and to give my soul for many (Matt. 20:28). Which indeed none of the others is found to have done, so that as many as have seemed to have ministered, he himself has surpassed by devoted and faithful obsequies. A good minister, who has ministered his flesh for food, his blood for drink, his soul for a price. Good plainly, who lively in spirit, fervent in charity, devoted in piety, not only leaps upon the mountains, but also skips over the hills, that is surpasses and conquers in alacrity of ministering, inasmuch as God his God has anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows (Ps. 45:7): in which assuredly he singularly exulted as a giant to run the way. Finally he skipped over Gabriel, and came before to the Virgin, the same archangel attesting, when he says: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). What? Whom you just now left in heaven, you now find in the womb. In what manner? He has flown and flown before upon the wings of the winds. You are overcome, O archangel: he has skipped over you who sent you before.
54.2: Or certainly he was leaping upon the mountains, when of old he appeared to the fathers in angels: which assuredly seems to suit the property of the letter more. For he does not say, leaping upon the mountains; but, upon the mountains, so that he himself seems to leap in them, who makes and gives that they leap; just as he speaks in the prophets, works in the just, when he bestows words on those, and works on these. Add that some of them bore his person, so that each of them spoke, not as an angel, but as the Lord. For example, that angel who spoke with Moses, said, not, I am of the Lord, but, I am the Lord, and that he repeated more frequently. He was leaping therefore upon the mountains, that is in the angels, in whom he both spoke, and showed his presence to men. For he was leaping to men, but in angels, not in himself; not in his own nature, but in a subject creature. For he who leaps, goes from place to place: which does not fall upon God. Therefore upon the mountains, that is in the angels, he was leaping, who could not in himself; and he was leaping even to the hills, that is the patriarchs and prophets, and the other spiritual men of earth. But he was also skipping over the hills, when not only to great and spiritual men, but also to some of the people, and even to some women equally he deigned to speak and appear in angels. Or he calls hills the aerial powers, which indeed are by no means now numbered among the mountains, for that by pride they have flowed down from the loftiness of virtues; yet neither do they swell down by penitence even to the lowly of the valleys, or to the valleys of the humble. Of these I think that was said in the psalms: The mountains, like wax, have melted from the face of the Lord (Ps. 97:5). These therefore swelling and barren hills, as placed in the middle between the mountains of the perfect and the valleys of penitents, he without doubt skipped over, who leaps upon the mountains; and these being passed by and despised he descended to the valleys, that the valleys may abound with grain. Further those from the opposite side are condemned to eternal aridity and barrenness, as you have the prophet's imprecation upon them: Neither dew, he says, nor rain descend upon you. And that you may know that he speaks this to the angels who have transgressed under the figure of the mountains of Gilboa, Where, he says, many wounded have fallen (2 Sam. 1:21). How many in these cursed mountains of the army of Israel have fallen from the beginning, and daily fall! Of whom also you have in the same prophet, when he says to the Lord: As the wounded sleeping in the sepulchers, of whom you are no more mindful, and they themselves have been cast off from your hand (Ps. 88:5).
54.3: It is not therefore wonderful, if these remain barren and unfruitful, not heavenly mountains, but aerial hills, upon which neither dew nor rain descends; since the author of grace and bestower of blessings skips over them, and descends to the valleys, that he may water with heavenly shower the humble who are upon the earth, and they may bring forth fruit in patience, fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (Matt. 13:8, 23; Luke 8:15). Finally he has visited the earth, and has inebriated it: he has multiplied to enrich it (Ps. 65:9). He has visited the earth, not the air because the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord (Ps. 33:5). Finally, He has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 74:12); has he also in the midst of the air? This against Origen, who in the air again impudently crucifies the Lord of glory for the demons with a lie, when Paul conscious of this mystery affirms that rising from the dead he dies no more, death shall no more have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9).
54.4: But he has not only visited the earth, who has skipped over the air, but also heaven, Scripture saying: O Lord, in heaven is your mercy, and your truth even unto the clouds (Ps. 36:5). For even unto the clouds is the heaven which the holy angels inhabit, whom the Bridegroom has not skipped over, but leaps in them, so that he imprints upon them two certain footprints of his feet, mercy and truth: concerning which footprints of the Lord I remember that I have more fully discussed in former sermons (serm. 6). But from the clouds and below is the habitation of demons in this lowest and misty air; in whom the bridegroom does not leap, but skips over them and passes by nor do they retain in themselves any footprint of God passing. For how is there truth in the devil, of whom in the Gospels the sentence of Truth stands, that he has not stood in the truth, but has been a liar from the beginning? But nor would anyone call him merciful, who nonetheless from the beginning is convicted by that same truth of the Gospel to have been a murderer (John 8:44). Further however as the householder, such also his household. Beautifully therefore the Church singing of the Bridegroom, that he dwells on high, and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth (Ps. 113:5, 6), makes no mention at all of those proud spirits who move in the air, because God resists the proud, and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).
54.5: She sees therefore him leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills, according to the imprecation of David saying: Let the Lord visit all the mountains which are round about it, that is round about Gilboa; but from Gilboa let him pass (2 Sam. 1:21). For to the devil, who is designated by Gilboa, on this side and that are mountains which the Lord visits; above angels, below men. For for his own punishment falling from heaven he has obtained a place in this air, middle between heaven and earth, that he may see and envy, and by envy itself be tormented, Scripture saying: The sinner shall see and be angry, he shall gnash with his teeth, and pine away (Ps. 112:10). How wretched, when he looks up to the heavens, in which he beholds innumerable mountains shining with divine brightness, resounding with divine praises, sublime in glory, abounding in grace! How more wretched, when he looks upon the earth, having nonetheless very many mountains of the people of acquisition, solid in faith, lofty in hope, spacious in charity, cultivated with virtues, filled with the fruits of good works, receiving from the dew of heaven as from the leap of the bridegroom a daily blessing! With how great pain and rancor do we think that most greedy of glory looks upon these so glorious mountains round about him, when he despises himself and his from the opposite side uncultivated, dark, barren of all goods, so that he feels himself to be the reproach of men and of angels, who reproached all, according to that in the Psalms: This dragon which you have formed to sport with him? (Ps. 104:26.)
54.6: And this, because for their pride the Bridegroom skips over them, leaping upon the mountains which are round about him, as a fountain ascending from the midst of paradise, watering all things, and filling every living thing with blessing. Blessed are they who drunk with the torrent of this pleasure sometimes or rarely are deserving, in whom although it does not flow continually, at least by hours the water of wisdom and the fountain of life leaps, that there may be made in them also a fountain of water leaping unto eternal life. And indeed the stream of this river gladdens the city of God, truly continually and abundantly. But upon our mountains which are on earth, would that sometimes having made as it were an inundation he may not disdain to give some leaps, by which sufficiently watered, they may be able to drip even rare little drops also upon us, who are valleys, lest we remain altogether dry and barren! Misery, and want, and altogether a strong famine in that region, which is never moistened by any such leaps, or distillations, the fountain of wisdom flowing past and skipping over it: And because they had not wisdom, he says, they have perished for their foolishness (Bar. 3:28).
54.7: Behold he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. To this he leaps that he may skip over, who does not wish to reach all; for neither is God well pleased in all. Brethren, if, according to the wisdom of Paul, these things have been written for our correction (1 Cor. 10:11), let us observe the discrete and circumspect leaps of the Bridegroom, how namely both among Angels and among us, he leaps upon the humble, and skips over the proud: since indeed the Lord is high and looks upon the lowly, and knows the high from afar (Ps. 138:6). These things, I say, let us attend to, that we may be cautious to prepare ourselves for the saving leaps of the Bridegroom, lest as from the mountains of Gilboa he perhaps pass also from us, if he has beheld us unworthy of his visitation. Why do you pride yourself, earth and ashes? Even from Angels the Lord skips over, abhorring their pride. Therefore let the rejection of Angels be the amendment of men: for it has been written for their correction. Let even the evil of the devil work together with me unto good, and let me wash my hands in the blood of the sinner. How, you say? Hear. Upon the proud devil assuredly a horrible and fearful curse is hurled, the prophet David in spirit saying of him under the type of Gilboa, as has been mentioned above: The mountains, he says, which are round about it, let the Lord visit, but from Gilboa let him pass.
54.8: Indeed I reading this, and turning my eyes upon myself, and looking diligently, find myself infected with that very pestilence, which in the angel the Lord so greatly abhorred, that for that reason he would turn aside from him, when he deigned all the mountains round about him, whether of Angels, or of men, with the grace of his visitation; and fearing and trembling I say to myself: If thus it has been done with an angel, what will become of me earth and ashes? He swelled in heaven, I on a dunghill. Who would not reckon pride more tolerable in a rich man, than in a poor? Woe to me! if so harshly it has been punished in that powerful one because his heart was lifted up, nor did it profit him that pride is known to be akin to the powerful; what is to be exacted of me both wretched, and proud? Finally already I pay the penalties, already I am most bitterly scourged. Not without cause indeed from yesterday and the day before this languor of mind has invaded me, and dullness of mind, a certain unwonted inertia of spirit. I was running well: but behold a stone of stumbling in the way; I have struck, and fallen. Pride has been found in me, and the Lord has turned aside in anger from his servant. Hence that barrenness of my soul, and want of devotion which I suffer. How has my heart so dried up, it has been curdled like milk, it has been made like earth without water? Nor can I be pricked to tears; so great is the hardness of heart. The psalm does not taste, it does not please to read, it does not delight to pray, I do not find the wonted meditations. Where is that inebriation of spirit? where the serenity of mind, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit? Therefore sluggish to the work of the hands, sleepy at vigils, hasty to anger, stubborn in hatred, more indulgent to tongue and throat, slower and duller to preaching. Alas! the Lord visits all the mountains round about me, but to me he does not draw near. Am I not a hill of those whom the bridegroom skips over? For one indeed I behold of singular abstinence, another of admirable patience, another of highest humility and meekness, another of much mercy and piety; that one frequently exceeding in contemplation, this one striking and penetrating the heavens by insistence of prayers, and others preeminent in other virtues. These, I say, I consider all fervent, all devout, all unanimous in Christ, all abounding in heavenly gifts and grace, as truly spiritual mountains who are visited by the Lord, and frequently receive the bridegroom leaping in them. But I, who find nothing of these in myself, what else should I think myself than one of the mountains of Gilboa, whom that most benign visitor of all the others passes by in his anger and indignation?
54.9: Little children, this thought takes away the lifting up of the eyes, conciliates grace, prepares for the leaps of the bridegroom. These things I have transfigured in myself for your sake, that you also may do so. Be imitators of me. Which I do not say now of the exercise of virtues, or the discipline of manners, or the glory of holiness (for neither would I rashly arrogate to myself anything of this kind worthy of imitation); but I wish you not to spare yourselves, but to accuse yourselves, as often as perhaps in yourselves, even to a little, you detect grace growing lukewarm, virtue languishing, just as I also accuse myself for such things. This is to do of a man, who is a curious inspector of himself, and a searcher of his ways and studies, and in all things always holds suspect the vice of arrogance lest it creep in. In truth I have learned that nothing is equally efficacious for meriting, retaining, recovering grace, than if at every time before God you are found not to savor high things, but to fear. Blessed is the man who is always fearful (Prov. 28:14). Fear therefore when grace has smiled, fear when it has gone away, fear when it will return again; and this is to be always fearful. Let these three fears succeed one another by turns in the mind, according as grace either deigns to be present, or offended to withdraw, or again returning appeased is felt. When it is present, fear lest you do not work worthily from it: for this the Apostle warns: See, saying, that you receive not the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6:1); and to the disciple: Do not, he says, neglect the grace which is in you (1 Tim. 4:14); and of himself he said: That the grace of God in me was not void (1 Cor. 15:10). The man knew, having the counsel of God, that to neglect the gift redounds to the contempt of the giver, nor to expend it for that for which it was given; and he judged that to be intolerable pride: and therefore most carefully he himself also avoided this evil, and taught that it was to be avoided. But again a pit lies hidden here, which I do not wish to be hidden from you, from which that very spirit of pride so much more dangerously, as more secretly, as you have in the psalm, lies in wait as a lion in his den (Ps. 10:9). For if he cannot prevail to hinder the action, he attempts the intention, suggesting and persuading, that you arrogate to yourself the effect of grace. Which kind of pride indeed you should not doubt is far more intolerable than that former. For what is more hateful than that voice, by which certain ones said: Our hand is high, and not the Lord, has done all these things? (Deut. 32:27.)
54.10: If therefore it is to be feared while grace remains; what, if it has withdrawn? is it not then much more to be feared? Plainly much more; because where grace fails you, you fail. Hear for indeed what the giver of grace says. Without me, he says, you can do nothing (John 15:5). Fear therefore when grace is withdrawn, as one about to fall presently; fear and tremble, God being angry with you, as you feel; fear, because your custody has left you. Nor doubt that pride is in the cause, even if it does not appear, even if you are conscious of nothing to yourself. For what you do not know, God knows; and he who judges you, he himself is. But neither is he who commends himself approved, but whom God commends (2 Cor. 10:18). Does God commend you, when he deprives of grace? Or does he who gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), take away from the humble what was given? Therefore the privation of grace is an argument of pride. Although nevertheless sometimes grace is withdrawn, or drawn back, not for pride which already is, but which will be, unless it be withdrawn. You have an evident document of this matter from the Apostle, who unwillingly bore the goads of his flesh, not because he was exalted, but lest he be exalted (2 Cor. 12:7). But whether already existing, or not yet, pride nonetheless will always be the cause of withdrawn grace.
54.11: Now if grace repropitiated has returned, then much more is it to be feared, lest perhaps it happen to suffer a relapse, according to that from the Gospel. Behold you have been made whole, go and now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you (John 5:14). You hear that to relapse is worse than to fall into. Therefore as the danger grows strong, let fear also grow strong. Blessed are you, if you have filled your heart with this threefold fear, that you fear indeed for grace received, more for grace lost, far more for grace recovered. Do this, and you will be a water-jar at Christ's feast, filled even to the brim, containing namely measures, not only twos, but also threes, that you may deserve the blessing of Christ, which may convert your waters into the wine of joy, and perfect charity may cast out fear (1 John 4:18).
54.12: What I say is of this sort. Water is fear, because it cools from the heat of carnal desires. The beginning, he says, of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Ps. 111:10); and you have: The water of saving wisdom has given him to drink (Sir. 15:3). If fear is wisdom, and wisdom water; fear is water; finally: The fear of the Lord, he says, is a fountain of life (Prov. 14:27). Further the water-jar is your mind. Holding, he says, each two or three measures. Three measures, three fears. And they filled them, he says, even to the brim (John 2:6, 7). Not one fear, not two also, but all three together fill even to the brim. At every time fear God, and from all your heart, and you have filled your water-jar even to the brim. God loves an entire gift, a full affection, a perfect sacrifice. Take care therefore to bring a full water-jar to the heavenly nuptials, that of you also it may be said: That he has filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:3). He who so fears, neglects nothing. For whence should negligence enter into fullness? Otherwise what can still take something in, is not full. By the same reason indeed one cannot at once both so fear, and savor high things. For there is not where you may admit pride, filled with the fear of the Lord. And so of the other vices it is to be felt, because it is necessary that all be excluded by the fullness of fear. Then at last if you have feared fully, if perfectly, charity will give savor to your waters at the Lord's blessing. For without charity fear has punishment. And indeed charity is wine, which gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15). But perfect charity casts out fear, that where water had been, wine may begin to be unto the praise and glory of the bridegroom of the Church Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all forever. Amen.
54.title: In what way again by the mountains are signified angels and men, and by the hills demons. Likewise concerning the threefold fear, by which each one ought to fear lest he lose the grace of doing well received from God.

55.1: My beloved is like a roe and a young hart (Song 2:9). It hangs upon the preceding verse. For him whom it had just described as leaping and hastening, it consequently compares to a roe and a young hart. Aptly indeed, because this kind of animal is swift in running and agile in leaping. Moreover the discourse is of the bridegroom, and the Word is the bridegroom. And the Prophet says of God that his word runs swiftly (Ps. 147:15); surely fitting for this place, where the bridegroom, who is the Word of God, is described as leaping and passing over, made like therefore to a roe and a young hart. And this is the reason of the likeness. Add yet, lest no little proportion of the likeness itself should be wanting even for the soul, that the roe indeed excels not only by swiftness of course, but also by sharpness of sight. Which assuredly regards properly that part of the narration wherein the bridegroom is reported to appear not only leaping but also passing over; because unless with a sharp and piercing glance he could not at all, especially while running, discern upon whom he ought to leap, and whom he ought to pass over. Otherwise a comparison from the young hart alone could have sufficed to designate the swiftness of one hastening; for he is known to bear himself with a more rapid course. But now, since this bridegroom, though ardently loving, seems to rush in running into the embraces of the beloved, nevertheless knows how to direct his steps, or rather his leaps, by prudent consideration, cautious where he ought to fix his foot: it was needful indeed that with the young hart a likeness also of the roe should be given, so that both through that the desire of the one who saves, and through this the judgment of the one who chooses, might be expressed. Christ surely is just and merciful, savior and judge: and because he loves, he wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4); and because he judges, he knows who are his (2 Tim. 2:19), and he himself knows whom he has chosen from the beginning (John 13:18).
55.2: Therefore let us meanwhile feel these two goods of the bridegroom, namely mercy and judgment, recommended to us by the Holy Spirit in these two animals, that in testimony of the integrity and perfection of our faith we also, imitating the Prophet, may sing mercy and judgment unto the Lord (Ps. 101:1). But I do not doubt that other things also concerning the nature of these can be shown by those who are curious and skilled in such matters, which can usefully and fittingly be applied to the bridegroom: but these, as I judge, can suffice to give the reason of the likeness brought forward. Beautifully, however, the Holy Spirit gave the likeness not of a stag, but of a young hart of the stags, in which he both made mention of the Fathers, from whom Christ is according to the flesh, and recalled the infancy of the Savior. For as a young hart appeared the little one who is born to us (Isa. 9:6). But you who desire the coming of the Savior, fear the scrutiny of the judge, fear the eyes of the roe, fear him who says through the prophet: And it shall be in that day, and I will search Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph. 1:12). He is of sharp sight; his eye will leave nothing unsearched. He will search the reins and hearts (Ps. 7:9), and the very thought of man shall confess to him (Ps. 76:10). What is safe in Babylon, if Jerusalem awaits scrutiny? For I think that in this place the prophet by the name Jerusalem designated those who in this world lead a religious life, imitating as far as they can the manners of that heavenly Jerusalem by an honest and ordered way of life; and not like those who are of Babylon, wasting life in the disturbance of vices and the confusion of crimes. Finally their sins are manifest, going before unto judgment, and they need not scrutiny but punishment. But mine, who seem a monk and a Jerusalemite, my sins certainly are hidden, overshadowed by the name and habit of a monk: and therefore it will be necessary that they be investigated by a subtle discussion, and as if with lamps brought near be brought forth from darkness into light.
55.3: We can bring forward something also from the psalm to confirm that which is said of Jerusalem to be searched. For he says under the person of the Lord: When I shall take a time, I will judge justices (Ps. 75:2). The ways of the just, unless I am mistaken, and their acts he says he will discuss and examine. It is greatly to be feared when it shall come to this, lest under so subtle an examination many of our justices, as they are thought, appear sins. Yet there is one thing: if we have judged ourselves, we shall not be judged (1 Cor. 11:31). A good judgment, which withdraws me and hides me from that strict and divine judgment. Utterly I dread to fall into the hands of the living God; with desire I wish, judged, to be presented to the face of wrath, not as one yet to be judged. The spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15). I will therefore judge my evils, I will judge my goods also. Evils I will take care to correct by better acts, to wash away with tears, to punish with fasts, and with the other labors of holy discipline. In goods I will think humbly of myself, and, according to the Lord's precept, I will reckon myself an unprofitable servant, who have only done that which I ought to do (Luke 17:10). I will take care to offer neither tares for grain, nor chaff with grain. I will search my ways and my pursuits, that he who is about to search Jerusalem with lamps may find nothing in me unsearched or undiscussed. For he will not judge twice for the same thing.
55.4: Who will grant me so clearly to pursue and prosecute all my faults, that I need fear the eyes of the roe in nothing, that in nothing I may come to blush at the light of the lamps? And now I am seen, but I do not see: the eye is present to which all things are open, though he himself is not open. There will be a time when I shall know, even as I also am known: but now indeed I know in part, yet I am not known in part, but wholly. I fear the look of that explorer who stands behind the wall. For this Scripture adds of him whom for sharpness of sight it likened to a roe: Behold he himself stands, it says, behind the wall, looking through the windows, looking through the lattices. Of which in its place we shall see. This hidden explorer of hidden things, therefore, I fear. The bride fears nothing, because she is conscious of nothing to herself. What finally should she fear, the friend, the dove, the beautiful one? For presently you have: Behold my beloved, she says, speaks to me. He speaks nothing; and therefore I dread the look, because I have not the testimony. What do you hear of yourself, O bride? What does your beloved say to you? Arise, he says, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one (Song 2:10). But this also I will reserve for another beginning, nor will I constrain by brevity those things which desire diligence; lest perhaps I also be found guilty in this, if you be found less built up in this part unto the understanding and love of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.
55.title: In what way a man by true penance can escape the judgment of God.

56.1: Behold he himself stands behind the wall, looking through the windows, looking through the lattices (Song 2:9). According to the letter indeed he seems to say that he who was seen approaching with leaps had drawn near even to the dwelling of the bride, and standing behind the wall would look in more curiously through the windows and cracks, and from modesty would not presume to thrust himself in. But according to the spirit it is understood that he has drawn near nonetheless, yet otherwise, just as it was fitting both to be done by the heavenly bridegroom, and to be said by the Holy Spirit. For a true and spiritual understanding admits nothing that would become either the author or the narrator ill. Therefore he drew near to the wall when he cleaved to the flesh. The flesh is the wall, and the approach of the Bridegroom is the incarnation of the Word. Moreover the lattices and windows through which he is said to look are, as I think, the senses of the flesh and human affections, through which he took experience of all human necessities. Finally he himself bore our languors, and he himself carried our sorrows (Isa. 53:4). Therefore by human affections and bodily senses he used openings and windows, that made man he might know the miseries of men by experience, and become merciful. He knew also before, but otherwise. Finally the Lord of virtues himself knew the virtue of obeying, and yet, as the Apostle witnesses, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered (Heb. 5:8). In this manner he learned mercy also, although the mercy of the Lord is from eternity. The same Doctor of the Gentiles teaches this also, where he asserts that he was tempted in all things according to likeness without sin, that he might become merciful (Heb. 4:15). Do you see that he was made what he was, and learned what he knew, and sought for himself with us cracks and windows through which he might more diligently explore our calamities? But so many openings did he find in our ruinous wall full of cracks, as he felt in his own body experiments of our infirmity and corruption.
56.2: Thus therefore the bridegroom was standing behind the wall, and looking through the windows and lattices. And well standing, because he alone truly stood in the flesh, who did not feel the sin of the flesh. We can also faithfully understand this, that he stood by the power of divinity, who by the infirmity of the flesh fell, saying himself: The spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak (Matt. 26:41). But I think that also favors this sentence which holy David in this mystery, as a prophet of the Lord and prophesying, was speaking of the Lord; and indeed speaking of Moses, but looking to the Lord. For he himself is the true Moses, who truly came through water, and not in water only, but in water and blood. Therefore the aforesaid prophet says: He said that he would destroy them (for he was speaking of the Father), if Moses his chosen had not stood in the breach in his sight, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them (Ps. 106:23). In what manner, I ask, did Moses stand in the breach? how, I say, either did he stand, if he was broken: or if he stood, how was he broken? But I will show you, if you will, who truly stood in the breach. I know no other who could have done this, except my Lord Jesus, who certainly was living in death, who broken in body on the cross was standing in divinity with the Father; in the one beseeching with us, in the other propitiating with the Father. And he was standing behind the wall, while that by which he lay in him was manifest in the flesh, and that by which he stood in him was as it were hidden behind the flesh; surely one and the same man manifest, and God hidden.
56.3: But also to each of us who desire his coming, I think that he nonetheless stands behind the wall, while this body of ours, which certainly is of sin, meanwhile hides his face from us, and shuts out his presence. Finally: While we are in this body, he says, we are pilgrims from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6). Not because in the body, but because in this body, which assuredly is of sin, and is not without sin. And that you may know that not bodies but sins obstruct, hear Scripture: Our sins, it says, separate between us and God (Isa. 59:2). And would that only one wall of the body stood against me, and I suffered only that obstacle which is sin in the flesh, and that many walls of vices were not between. For I fear that even besides that which is in nature, I have added very many from my own iniquity, by whose interposition I have elongated the Bridegroom too far from me; so that, if I would speak the truth, I would confess that he stands behind walls for me, not behind a wall.
56.4: But I say this more plainly. The bridegroom indeed is equally and indifferently present everywhere, by the presence surely of the divine majesty, and by the greatness of his power. Yet by the showing or withholding of grace he is said to be far from some, near to some, of angels at least and of men, that is of rational creatures. Finally salvation is far from sinners (Ps. 119:155). And holy David nonetheless says: Why, O Lord, hast thou withdrawn far off? (Ps. 10:1.) But from the saints by a pious dispensation for a time and not wholly, but according to something, he sometimes makes himself far. But from sinners of whom it is said: The pride of them that hate thee ascends always (Ps. 74:23); and again: Their ways are defiled at all times (Ps. 10:5); he is always, and very far, and this in wrath, and not in mercy. Wherefore the saint prays to God, and says: Decline not in wrath from thy servant (Ps. 27:9); knowing that he could also decline in mercy. Therefore the Lord is near to his saints and elect, even when he seems to be far; and not equally to all, but to some more, to some less, according to the diversity of merits. For although the Lord is near to all that call upon him in truth, and is nigh to them that are of a troubled heart; yet perhaps not to all, so that they can say that he himself stands behind the wall. But how near is he to the bride, who is divided by only one wall. Therefore she desires to be dissolved, and the middle wall being broken to be with him whom she trusts to be behind the wall.
56.5: But I, since I am a sinner, do not desire to be dissolved, but I fear, knowing that the death of sinners is very evil (Ps. 34:21). How is death not very evil, where Life does not come to help? I fear to go out, and I tremble at the very entrance of the harbor, while I do not trust that he stands near who may receive me going out. For what? do I go out securely, if the Lord does not keep my going out? Alas, I shall be the sport of demons intercepting me: he not standing by who may redeem, nor who may make me safe. No such thing was to be feared for the soul of Paul, for whom from the sight and embrace of the Beloved only one wall stood in the way, namely the law of sin, which he found in his members. That itself is the concupiscence of the flesh, which he could not wholly lack, while he was in the flesh. With this one wall indeed interposed he was not far a pilgrim from the Lord; whence also he was wishing, crying: Who shall deliver me from the body of this death? (Rom. 7:24.) Knowing that by the short cut of death he would immediately arrive at life. By this one law therefore Paul confessed himself to be held, namely by concupiscence, which planted immovably in his flesh he bore unwillingly; for the rest: I am conscious to myself of nothing, he says (1 Cor. 4:4).
56.6: But who is like Paul, who namely does not sometimes consent to this concupiscence unto obeying sin? Let him know therefore who has consented to sin, that he has set up against himself also another wall, that very wicked and illicit consent: nor can he who is of this sort glory that the Bridegroom stands for him behind the wall, when already walls are between, not a wall. Much less if consent has come to affection, when a third wall also now bars and impedes the approach of the bridegroom, namely the act itself of sin. What, if habit also chance to have brought sin into use, or use even into contempt? as it is written: When the wicked has come into the depth of evils, he despises (Prov. 18:3). If you go out thus, will you not be able a thousand times to be devoured by roaring ones prepared for food, before you arrive at the Bridegroom, shut off from you now not by one, but by so great a number of walls? First, concupiscence; second, consent; third, act; fourth, habit; fifth, contempt. Take care therefore with all your strength to resist the first concupiscence, that it may not drag you into consent; and every fabric of malice thereafter vanishes: nor is there anything at all that prohibits the Bridegroom from drawing near to you, except only the wall of the body, so that you also may be able to glory saying of him, that behold he himself stands behind the wall.
56.7: But this also must be provided for you with all vigilance, that he may always find open the windows and certain lattices of your confessions, through which he may look upon you kindly within, because his regard is your progress. They say that lattices are narrower than windows, such as those who write books are wont to fit for themselves for receiving light upon the pages. Whence also I think that those are called cancellarii who are deputed by office to writing charts. Since therefore there are two kinds of compunction, one in sorrow for our excesses, the other in exultation for divine gifts, as often as I make that confession which is by no means made without anguish of heart, namely of my sins; I seem to myself to open a lattice, that is, a narrower window. Nor is it doubtful that through that one he gladly looks, the pious explorer who stands behind the wall, because a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise (Ps. 51:17). Finally he also exhorts to this very thing: Tell you, he says, your iniquities first, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:26). But if sometimes with a heart dilated in charity, for the consideration of the divine condescension and compassion, it pleases to relax the mind into a voice of praise and thanksgiving, I think that I open for the Bridegroom standing behind the wall not now a narrow, but a most ample window, through which, unless I am mistaken, he looks the more gladly, the more the sacrifice of praise honors him. At hand from the Scriptures is to approve both these confessions; but I speak these things to those who know them, and you are not to be burdened with superfluities, who scarcely suffice for searching out necessities. So great indeed are the sacraments of this epithalamium, and the praises and proclamations which are sung in it of the Church and of her bridegroom Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.
56.title: That sins and vices are like walls standing between God and the sinner.

57.1: Behold my beloved speaks to me (Song 2:10). See the advances of grace, and mark the steps of the divine condescension. Attend to the bride's devotion and skill, how with watchful eye she observes the bridegroom's coming, and thereafter more diligently looks upon all things of him. He comes, he hastens, he draws near, he is present, he looks, he addresses; and none of these moments escapes the bride's industry, anticipates her notice. He comes in the angels, hastens in the patriarchs, draws near in the prophets, is present in the flesh, looks in miracles, addresses in the apostles. Or thus: He comes by the affection and zeal of pitying, hastens by the zeal of helping, draws near by humbling himself, is present to those present, looks ahead to those to come, speaks teaching and persuading concerning the kingdom of God. Such therefore is the coming of the bridegroom. Blessings and the riches of salvation are with him, and all things that are of him abound with delights, overflowing surely with joyful and saving sacraments. Moreover she who loves watches and observes. And blessed is she whom the Lord shall find watching. He will not pass her by, nor go beyond her, but will stand and speak to her, and will speak loving things: for he will speak as a beloved. For so you have: Behold my beloved speaks to me. Well beloved, who comes to speak loving things, not however rebuking things.
57.2: For she is not of those who are deservedly reproved by the Lord, that they knew how to judge the face of the sky, but had not known at all the time of his coming (Matt. 16:3). For this one so skillful, and prudent, and well watching, both foresaw him coming from afar, and marked him leaping for haste, and most watchfully observed him passing over the proud, that by humility he might draw near to her who was humble; and at last when he was already standing, and was hiding himself behind the wall, nonetheless she recognized him present, and also perceived him looking through the windows and lattices; and now for the reward of so great devotion and religious solicitude she hears him speaking.
