For indeed if he had looked, and had not spoken at all, that look could have been suspect, lest perhaps it were more of indignation than of love. Finally he looked upon Peter, and made him no word: and therefore perhaps that one wept (Luke 22:61-62), because looking upon him, he was silent. But this one, since after the look she merited also the address, not only does not weep, but also glories for joy crying, Behold my beloved speaks to me. You see that the Lord's glance, though in itself it always remains the same, is yet not always of the same efficacy; but is conformed to the merits of each whom he looks upon, and upon some indeed strikes fear, but upon others rather brings consolation and security. Finally he looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble, while on the other hand he looked upon Mary, and poured in grace. He has regarded, she says, the humility of his handmaid; for behold from this all generations shall call me blessed (Luke 1:48). These are not the words of one weeping or trembling, but of one rejoicing. He looked likewise in this place upon the bride, and she neither trembled, nor wept after the manner of Peter, because she did not savor the earth, as he did; but he gave joy in her heart, testifying by address with what affection he looked upon her.
57.3: Finally hear how the words which he speaks are not of one indignant, but of one loving. There follows: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one. Happy the conscience that merits to hear these things of itself! Who, think you, among us is so watchful and observing the time of his visitation, and so carefully exploring the bridegroom approaching through each of his moments, that when he has come and knocked, he may open to him at once? For these things are not so related of the Church that we individually, who together are the Church, ought not to share in these her blessings. For in this we have all been called generally and without distinction, that we may possess the blessings by inheritance. Whence also he dared to say to the Lord indeed: I have acquired thy testimonies by inheritance forever, because they are the exultation of my heart (Ps. 119:111); by that inheritance, I think, by which he presumed himself to be a son of his Father who is in heaven. Moreover if a son, then an heir; an heir of God, and coheir of Christ. But a great thing he glories that he has acquired by that inheritance, the testimonies of the Lord. Would that I had merited to hold even one testimony of the Lord concerning myself! because that one exults not in one, but in many testimonies. Finally he says again: In the way of thy testimonies I have been delighted, as in all riches (Ps. 119:14). And truly what are the riches of salvation, what the delights of the heart, what the true and cautious security of the soul, except the attestations of the Lord? For not he, he says, who commends himself is approved, but whom God commends (2 Cor. 10:18).
57.4: Why are we until now still cheated of these divine commendations or attestations, and deprived of the paternal inheritance? As if he had not also begotten us willingly by the word of truth, so we remember ourselves in nothing so commended by him, nor to have obtained any testimonies of him concerning us. Where is that which the Apostle says, that the Spirit of God himself bears witness to our spirit, that we are sons of God (Rom. 8:16). How sons, if without share in the inheritance? Our very want certainly reproves us of negligence and carelessness. For if any of us wholly and perfectly, according to the word of the Wise Man, give his heart to watching early unto the Lord who made him, and pray in the sight of the Most High (Sir. 39:5), and at the same time with all desires study according to the prophet Isaiah to prepare the ways of the Lord, to make straight the paths of his God (Isa. 40:3), to whom with the Prophet it is to say: My eyes are always toward the Lord (Ps. 25:15); and because I was providing the Lord always in my sight (Ps. 16:8): shall not this one receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his salvation? (Ps. 24:5.) He will surely be visited frequently, nor will he ever be ignorant of the time of his visitation, however much he who visits in the spirit come clandestine and stealthy, as being a modest lover. Therefore while he is still acting afar, a soul well watching with sober mind will foresee him, and thereafter will discover all things which in the coming of the beloved we have shown the bride to have marked as skillfully as significantly, because he himself says: They who have watched for me early shall find me (Prov. 8:17). For she will also recognize the desire of him hastening: and when he is near, and when he will already be at hand, she will perceive at once; and also with blessed eye she will discern the eye of him looking upon her, like a ray of the sun entering through the windows and cracks of the wall: and at last she will hear voices of exultation and love, called friend, dove, beautiful.
57.5: Who is wise and will understand these things, so as to be able also worthily to distinguish them from one another, and to designate each, and to define them unto the understanding of others? If that is hoped from me, I would rather hear them from one experienced, and who is accustomed and exercised in such things. But since whoever is of this sort chooses rather modestly to hide by silence what he perceives by silence, and to keep his secret to himself, judging that safer for himself: I say, to whom it is of office to speak, nor is it permitted to be silent, whatever that is which I hold of such things either by my own or by another's experience, and which many can easily experience, leaving surely the higher things to those able to grasp them. If therefore I shall have been admonished, either outwardly by a man or inwardly by the Spirit, concerning keeping justice and preserving equity; a saving persuasion of this sort will be for me surely a forerunner of the bridegroom's imminent coming, and a certain preparation for worthily receiving the heavenly visitor, the Prophet indicating this to me, by saying that justice will walk before him (Ps. 85:13); and again he speaks to God thus: Justice and judgment, he says, are the preparation of thy seat (Ps. 89:14) Nonetheless the same hope will smile, if a word has sounded concerning humility or patience, or also concerning fraternal charity and obedience to be rendered to prelates; but most of all concerning pursuing holiness and peace, and seeking purity of heart, since indeed Scripture says: Holiness becomes the house of the Lord (Ps. 93:5); and: His place is made in peace (Ps. 76:2); and: The clean of heart shall see God (Matt. 5:8). Whatever therefore either of these, or of any other virtues whatever, shall have been suggested to the mind, will be for me, as I have said, a signification that the visitation of the Lord of virtues is imminent upon my soul.
57.6: But if also a just man shall have corrected me in mercy, and rebuked me, I shall feel the same, knowing that the zeal of the just and benevolence make a way for him who ascends above the setting (Ps. 68:4). A good setting, when at the correction of the just a man stands, and vice falls, and the Lord ascends upon it, trampling it with his feet, and crushing it that it may not rise again. Therefore the rebuke of the just is not to be despised, which is the ruin of sin, the health of the heart, and also God's way to the soul. But nor is any word at all that builds unto piety, unto virtues, unto the best manners, to be heard negligently; because there also is the way by which the salvation of God is shown (Ps. 50:23). But if a pleasing and acceptable word comes, so that with fastidiousness driven away it is heard with desire, already the Bridegroom is to be believed not only to come, but also to hasten, that is to come with desire. For his desire creates yours; and that you hasten to admit his word, thence it is that he himself hastens to enter; for not we him, but he, he says, first loved us (1 John 4:10). Now if you also feel a fiery utterance, and from it the conscience burned in the recollection of sin; remember then of whom Scripture says, that fire shall go before him (Ps. 96:3), and doubt not that he himself is near. Finally the Lord is nigh unto them that are of a troubled heart (Ps. 34:18).
57.7: But if you are not only pricked in that word, but also wholly converted to the Lord, swearing and establishing to keep the judgments of his justice, know already that he himself is present, especially if you feel yourself to burn with love of him. For you read both of him, both that fire namely goes before him, and that he himself nonetheless is fire. For Moses says of him that he is a consuming fire (Deut. 4:24). But they differ, in that that fire which is sent before has ardor, but not love: cooking, but not refining, moving, and not promoting. It is sent before only for exciting and preparing, and at the same time for reminding what you are of yourself, that afterward what you will soon be of God may taste the sweeter. But the fire which is God consumes indeed, but does not afflict, burns sweetly, lays waste happily. For it is truly a desolating coal, but which so exercises the force of fire upon vices, that in the soul it exhibits the office of unction. Therefore in the virtue by which you are changed, and in the love by which you are inflamed, understand the Lord present. For the right hand of the Lord does virtue (Ps. 118:16). But this change of the right hand of the Most High is not made (Ps. 77:10), except in fervor of spirit, and in charity unfeigned, so that he who is of this sort may say: My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire burns (Ps. 39:3).
57.8: Moreover when by this fire every stain of sin and rust of vices has been consumed, if now with cleansed and cleared conscience there follows a certain sudden and unwonted breadth of mind, and an infusion of light illuminating the intellect either unto knowledge of the Scriptures, or unto acquaintance with mysteries, of which the one I think is given for our delighting, the other for building up neighbors; the eye of him who looks is without doubt this, bringing forth your justice as light, and your judgment as noonday, according to that of the prophet Isaiah: Thy light, he says, shall arise as the sun (Isa. 58:10), etc. But surely not through open doors, but through narrow openings will so great a ray of brightness pour itself in, this ruinous wall of the body still standing at least. You err if you hope otherwise, to whatever purity of heart you advance, since that chief contemplator says: We see now through a glass and in a riddle, but then face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).
57.9: After this regard of so great condescension and compassion, there follows a voice blandly and gently insinuating the divine will, which is nothing other than love itself, which cannot be idle, soliciting and persuading concerning the things that are of God. Finally the bride hears that she should arise and make haste, without doubt unto the gains of souls. For this true and chaste contemplation has, that the mind which it has vehemently kindled with divine fire, it sometimes so fills with zeal and desire of acquiring for God those who may likewise love him, that it most gladly interrupts the leisure of contemplation for the zeal of preaching: and again having obtained its wishes, to some extent in this part it returns the more ardently to the same, the more fruitfully it remembers that it interrupted; and again having taken the taste of contemplation, it recurs more strongly to seeking the accustomed gains with eagerness. But amid these alternations the mind often fluctuates, fearing, and vehemently seething, lest perhaps to one of these, while it is distracted hither and thither by its affections, it cling more than is just; and so in either deviate even a little from the divine will. And perhaps holy Job was suffering something of this sort, when he said: If I sleep, I say, when shall I arise? and again I will await the evening (Job 7:4): that is: Both when quiet, I accuse myself of neglected work; and when occupied, likewise of disturbed quiet. You see a holy man heavily seething between the fruit of work and the sleep of contemplation: and though always occupied in goods, yet always as it were doing penance for evils, and with a groan seeking the will of God at each moment. For the only remedy or refuge in such things is prayer, and frequent groaning to God; that what, when, and how far he wills us to do, he may continually deign to show us. You have, as I think, these three, that is preaching, prayer, contemplation, recommended and designated in three words. For deservedly she is called friend, who studiously and faithfully seeks the bridegroom's gains by preaching, counseling, ministering. Deservedly dove, who nonetheless for her own faults groaning and entreating in prayer does not cease to win divine mercy for herself. Deservedly also beautiful, who shining with heavenly desire clothes herself with the beauty of heavenly contemplation, only in those hours in which she can conveniently and opportunely do so.
57.10: But see also whether that can be fitted to this threefold good of one soul; namely of those three persons dwelling together in one house, friends surely of the Savior, and quite familiar to him. I speak of Martha ministering, and Mary at leisure, and Lazarus as it were groaning under the stone, and begging the grace of resurrection (Luke 10:38-42; John 11). These things have been said because the bride is described as so skillful and watchful in observing the paths of the bridegroom, that it cannot at all escape her when, and in how great haste, he comes to her but also when he is far, and when near, and when present, she cannot be preoccupied by any suddenness so as to be ignorant: and because therefore she has merited not only to be looked upon mercifully, but also worthily to be gladdened by voices of love, and to rejoice with joy because of the voice of the bridegroom. 11, We too have added to these things, though boldly, that any soul also of us, if it likewise watches, will likewise also be greeted as friend, consoled as dove, embraced as beautiful. Everyone will be reputed perfect, in whose soul these three shall be seen to concur fittingly and opportunely, so that he knows both to groan for himself, and to exult in God, and at the same time is able to help the utilities of neighbors; pleasing to God, cautious for himself, useful to his own. But who is sufficient for these things? Would that this itself in all of us, even if not whole in each, at least the several in different ones, as they seem to be had today, may be reserved for long times! For we have Martha, as the Savior's friend, in those who faithfully administer exterior things. We have also Lazarus, as a groaning dove, namely the novices, who lately dead to sins, for wounds still recent labor in their groaning under fear of judgment; and like the wounded sleeping in the tombs, of whom no one is remembered longer, so they think themselves not to be reputed, until at Christ's command, the weight of fear removed, as the mass of a pressing stone, they can breathe again unto hope of pardon. We have also Mary contemplating in those who by the progress of longer time, with the grace of God cooperating, have been able to advance unto something better and more joyful; when already presuming on indulgence, they are not so much careful to turn within themselves the sad image of sins, as certainly they delight insatiably to meditate in the law of God day and night; sometimes also with unveiled face beholding the glory of the bridegroom with ineffable joy, they are transformed into the same image from brightness to brightness, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). Now to what he who a little before seemed to defend her lest she sleeping should be awakened exhorts the bride to arise and make haste, we shall see in another sermon. May he himself be present, that he may deign to open to us also the reason of this sacrament, the bridegroom of the Church Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.
57.title: Concerning the visitations of the Lord to be observed; by what marks or signs they may be perceived.

58.1: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come (Song 2:10). Who says this? Without doubt the bridegroom. And is it not he who a little before so greatly forbade the beloved to be awakened? By what pact therefore does he now command not only that she arise, but that she also hasten? Something similar from the Gospel comes to mind. For on that night on which the Lord was betrayed, when he had at last commanded the disciples who were with him, wearied by longer watches, to sleep and rest, in that very hour: Arise, let us go, he says, behold he has drawn near who will betray me (Matt. 26:46). Now also similarly in almost one moment he both forbids the bride to be awakened, and awakens her: Arise, saying, and come. What then does so sudden a change of will or counsel mean for itself? Do we think the bridegroom used levity, and wished something before which he soon did not wish? By no means. But recognize those alternations which I recommended to you above, if you remember, and not once, namely of holy quiet and of necessary action; and that in this life there is not abundance of contemplating, nor lasting leisure, where the more compelling and more urgent utility of office and work presses. Therefore after his manner the bridegroom, when he perceives that the beloved has rested a little in his own bosom, does not delay to draw her again to those things which have seemed more useful. Yet not as if unwilling: for neither would he himself at all do what he forbade to be done; but for the bride to be drawn by the bridegroom is to receive from him himself the desire by which she is drawn, the desire of good works, the desire of bearing fruit for the bridegroom; for whom to live is the bridegroom, and to die gain.
58.2: And it is a vehement desire, which solicits her not only to arise, but also to arise hastily: for so you have: Arise, make haste, and come. Nor does it little comfort that she hears, come, and not: Go: by this understanding herself not so much to be sent as to be led, and that the bridegroom will come together with her. For what does she reckon difficult for herself with him as companion? Set me, he says, beside thee, and let anyone's hand fight against me (Job 17:3); again: If I shall walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, for thou art with me (Ps. 23:4). Therefore she is not awakened beyond what she wills, when first it is brought about that she wills: which is nothing other than an implanted avidity for holy gain. She is also animated to the enjoined work, and is rendered more eager from the opportuneness of the time. It is a time for doing, he says, O bride, because winter has passed, when no one could work. The rain also, which by the flood made covered the earth, was impeding cultivations, and either was killing the sown, or forbidding to be sown; that rain, I say, has run out, has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared in our land, signifying surely that the vernal temper is present, the convenience of working, the nearness of crops and of fruits. Then he adds where and what first it is needful to work: The time, saying, of pruning has come (Song 2:12). She is led therefore to cultivating the vineyards: which that they may be able to answer the husbandmen with more abundant fruits, before all things it is necessary that sterile branches be cast away, harmful ones cut down, superfluous ones pruned. These according to the letter.
58.3: Now already let us see what of this sort, as by a historical scheme, is spiritually hinted to us to be understood. And that vineyards indeed are souls or Churches, and at the same time what the reason of this thing is, I have already said to you, and you have heard, nor do you need to hear it again. To these therefore to be revisited, corrected, instructed, saved, a more perfect soul is invited, which yet has obtained that ministry not by its own ambition, but called by God as Aaron. Moreover what is the invitation itself, except a certain inward stimulation of charity piously soliciting us to emulate fraternal salvation, to emulate the beauty of the house of the Lord, the increases of his gains, the increases of the fruits of his justice, the praise and glory of his name? Therefore as often as he who has to rule souls, or to intend by office to the zeal of preaching, has felt his interior man to be moved by religious affections of this sort concerning God; so often let him understand for certain that the bridegroom is present, so often that he is invited by him to the vineyards. To what, except that he may pluck up and destroy, and build and plant?
58.4: But since for this work, as for every thing under heaven, not every time is available and apt, he who invites adds that the time of pruning has come. He knew this to be present who was saying: Behold now is the acceptable time, behold now is the day of salvation; giving no offense to any, that our ministry be not blamed (2 Cor. 6:2-3). Without doubt he was warning already to prune and cut away the vicious and superfluous, and everything finally that could give offense and impede the fruit of salvation, knowing that the time of pruning had come. Therefore also he was saying to a certain faithful cultivator of the vineyards: Reprove, rebuke, entreat (2 Tim. 4:2); in the first and second of these enjoining pruning or uprooting, in the last planting. And these things indeed the bridegroom through the mouth of Paul concerning the time of working. But hear what through his own mouth concerning the consideration of times, under another scheme and name of things indeed, he spoke with the new bride. Do you not say, he says, that there are four months, and the harvest comes? Behold I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, that they are white already unto harvest (John 4:35); again: The harvest indeed is great, the laborers few: ask the Lord of the harvest, that he send laborers into his harvest (Matt. 9:37-38). As therefore there he was showing that the time of reaping the crops of souls was present, so also here he announces that the time of pruning equally intelligible vineyards, that is souls or Churches, has come; wishing perhaps by the diversity of words to distinguish between both things, that we understand harvests as peoples, vineyards as congregations of saints dwelling together.
58.5: Moreover the winter time, which he signifies to have passed, seems to me to designate that when the Lord Jesus was no longer walking openly among the Jews, because they had conspired against him, wishing to kill him. Whence also he was saying to certain ones: My time has not yet come; but your time is always ready; and again: Go you up to this feast day, I will not go up (John 7:6-8). Yet afterward he also went up, not openly, but as it were in secret. From then therefore and thereafter until the coming of the Holy Spirit, by which the torpid hearts of the faithful grew warm again, as by the fire which the Lord sent into the earth for this very thing (Luke 12:49), it was winter. Will you then deny that it was winter then, when Peter was sitting at the coals, with a heart no less frozen than his body? Finally: It was cold, he says (John 18:18). Truly a great cold had constrained the heart of him who denied. Yet it is no wonder, when the fire had been taken away from him. For a little before he was bearing with no small zeal, being still near the fire, who with drawn sword, lest he lose the fire, cut off the ear of the servant. But it was not the time of pruning: and therefore he hears: Put thy sword back into its place. For it was the hour and the power of darkness: and whoever of the disciples then should raise the sword either of iron or of the word, either was to be cut off by iron, and would gain no one, nor bring forth any fruit; or certainly was to be compelled by the sword of fear unto denying; and so he himself would rather perish, according to the word of the Lord which he soon added, saying thus: Everyone who has taken the sword shall perish by the sword (Matt. 26:52). For who of the rest would stand fearless before the dreadful image of death, when the prince himself was trembling and yielding, even he who had been fortified by the comforting voice of his emperor, and forewarned to strengthen others? (Luke 22:32.)
58.6: But neither he nor they had yet put on power from on high; and for this reason it was not safe for them to go out into the vineyards, to put forth the hoe of the tongue, and with the sword of the Spirit to prune the vines, to purge the branches, that they might bring forth more fruit. Finally the Lord himself was silent in the passion, and asked in many things he was not answering (Matt. 27:12), made, according to the Prophet, as a man not hearing, and not having reproofs in his mouth (Ps. 38:14). But he was saying: If I tell you, you will not believe me; but if I also ask, you will not answer me (Luke 22:67-68): knowing that the time of pruning had not yet come, nor that his vineyard would answer at all to the labors expended, that is would return any fruit neither of faith nor of good work. Why? Because winter was in the hearts of the faithless, and certain winter rains of malice had occupied the earth, readier to choke the sown seeds of the word than to foster them; but also about to frustrate all labor to be expended on the cultivation of the vineyards.
58.7: Whom do you think me now to say are rains? those which we see turbulent spirit scatter through the air, clouds running over the earth? It is not so. But those which turbulent-spirited men carry up from earth into the air, setting their mouth in heaven, and their tongue passing upon the earth, as a most bitter rain, makes the earth itself marshy and sterile, and useless both for plants and for crops, not indeed for these visible and bodily ones given for our bodily uses, of which plainly God has no care, as neither of oxen. But for which? Surely those which the hand of God and not of man has sown and planted; which also could either germinate or take root in faith and charity, and bring forth the fruits of salvation, if they were watered with good and timely rains. Finally they are souls, for whom Christ died. Woe to the clouds raining rains of this sort upon them, which make mud, do not bring forth fruit! For as there are both good and bad trees, each bearing fruits differing according to their unlikeness, namely good ones good, and bad ones bad: so also I judge there are clouds both good, which rain good; and bad, which rain bad rains. And see lest perhaps he hinted to us this difference of clouds and rains, who was saying: I will command my clouds, that they rain not upon it (without doubt upon the vineyard) rain (Isa. 5:6). Why do you think he added significantly, my, except because there are also bad clouds, which are not his? Away, away, they say, crucify him (John 19:15). O violent and turbid clouds! O stormy rain, o torrent of iniquity, fit rather to overturn than to fertilize! Nor less bad nor less bitter, though rushing with lesser impetus, was that rain which followed: He saved others, himself he cannot make safe. Christ the king of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we believe him (Matt. 27:42). The windy loquacity of philosophers is not a good rain, which brought sterility upon the lands rather than fertility. Much more the wicked dogmas of heretics are bad rains, which produce thorns and thistles for fruits. Bad rains also are the traditions of the Pharisees, which the Savior reproved, and they themselves bad clouds. And lest you think me to do injury to Moses, for that is a good cloud, I will not yet say that all which even she herself rains is good, lest I contradict him who says: I gave them, that is the Jews, precepts that were not good (without doubt through Moses) and justifications, in which they shall not live (Ezek. 20:25). That literal observance, for example, of the Sabbath, sounding rest, not giving it; the enjoined rite of sacrifices, the forbidden eating of swine's flesh, and of some similar things which are judged unclean by Moses, all this is rain descending from that cloud, but I do not wish it sometime to descend into my field or garden. Let it have been good indeed in its time; if it comes after the time, I no longer judge it good. Every rain also gentle and descending lightly, if it be untimely, is troublesome.
58.8: Therefore while pestilent waters of this sort occupied the earth, and prevailed over it; the vineyards did not have their time, nor was there that for which the bride should be invited to pruning the vineyards. But when those were running off the earth appeared dry, and flowers appeared in it, signifying that the time of pruning was present. Do you ask when this was? when, think you, except when the flesh of Christ flowered again in the resurrection? And this is the first and greatest flower, which appeared in our land. For Christ is the firstfruits of them that sleep (1 Cor. 15:20). He himself, I say, is the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, Jesus (Song 2:1), as he was thought the son of Joseph of Nazareth (Luke 3:23), which is interpreted flower. That flower therefore appeared first, not alone. For many bodies also of the saints who had slept rose together, who as certain most bright flowers appeared together in our land. Finally they came into the holy city, and appeared to many (Matt. 27:52-53). Flowers also were those who first believed of the people, the firstfruits of the saints. Their flowers were miracles, producing after the manner of flowers the fruit of faith. For after that rain of unbelief had gone away and departed a little, or in part, there soon followed a voluntary rain, which God set apart for his inheritance, and flowers began to appear. The Lord gave kindness, and our land gave its flowers, so that in one day three thousand, in another five thousand of the people believed (Acts 2:41; 4:4): so greatly in a short time grew the number of flowers, that is the multitude of believers. And the frost of malice could not prevail against the flowers that were appearing, nor snatch away, as it is wont, the fruit of life which they were promising.
58.9: For when all who had believed were clothed with power from on high, there arose from them men who despised the threats of men, strong in faith. They suffered indeed very many contradictors; but they did not yield, nor flee away, from both doing and announcing the works of God. For according to that in the psalm spiritually indeed: And they sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and made fruit of birth (Ps. 107:37). In the course of time the tempest was calmed, and peace restored to the lands, the vineyards grew, and were propagated, and dilated, and multiplied beyond number. And then at last the bride is invited to the vineyards, not indeed to plant, but to prune what was already planted. Opportunely indeed: for that work required a time of peace. For when in a time of persecution would that be permitted? Otherwise to take into the hands two-edged swords, to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles; and to execute among them the written judgment (Ps. 149:6-9) (for this indeed is to prune vineyards): these, I say, all things scarcely even in a time of peace are practiced in peace. And of these enough.
58.10: The sermon could also be finished, if first according to my custom I had admonished each of you concerning his own vineyard. For who has so to the nail cut away all superfluities from himself, that he thinks he has nothing worthy of pruning? Believe me, even things pruned sprout again, and things put to flight return, and things extinguished are rekindled, and things lulled are stirred again. Therefore it is little to have pruned once; one must prune often, nay, if it can be done, always; because always you find what ought to be pruned, if you do not dissemble. However much you have advanced while remaining in this body, you err if you think vices dead, and not rather suppressed. Willing or unwilling, within your borders dwells the Jebusite (Judg. 1:21); he can be subdued, but not exterminated. I know, he says, that good does not dwell in me. It is little unless he confesses also that evil is within. For he says: Not what I will, that I do; but what I hate, that I do. But if what I hate, that I do, already it is not I that work it, but sin that dwells in me (Rom. 7:15-20). Either therefore, if you dare, prefer yourself to the Apostle (for this voice is his); or confess with him that you also are not without vices. Finally virtue holds the middle of vices; and therefore you need diligent not only pruning, but also circumcision. Otherwise it is to be feared that all around from vices licking, or rather gnawing, that virtue, while you know not, gradually grow faint; or, if they have overgrown, be choked. One counsel in so great a crisis is to observe diligently, and as soon as the heads of things being reborn appear, to cut them down with ready severity. Virtue cannot grow together with vices. Therefore that that may thrive, these must not be allowed to grow. Take away superfluities, and wholesome things rise. Whatever you subtract from cupidity accrues to utility. Let us give effort to pruning. Let cupidity be pruned, that virtue may be strengthened.
58.11: For us, brothers, there is always a time of pruning, as there is always need. For I trust that for us winter has already passed. Do you know what winter I mean? That fear which is not in charity, which though it initiates all unto wisdom, consummates no one; because charity coming upon drives it out, as summer winter. For summer is charity: which if it has already come, nay because it has come, as it is just for me to feel concerning you, must have dried every winter rain, namely every tear of anxiety which the bitter recollection of sin and fear of judgment formerly wrung out. Therefore (which I say not doubtfully, even if not of all of you, surely of many) this rain has already gone away and departed: for flowers also appear as signs of a sweeter rain. Summer also has its rains, sweet and abundant. What sweeter than the tears of charity? For charity weeps, but from love, not from sorrow; it weeps from desire, it weeps with them that weep. With such rain I do not doubt that the acts of your obedience have been more richly watered, which I look upon gladly, not foul with murmuring, not somewhat dark with sadness, but joyful and flowering with a certain spiritual joy. So they are, as if you always carry flowers in your hands.
58.12: Therefore if winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed; if at last flowers have appeared in our land, and presently a certain vernal temper of spiritual grace declares the time of pruning: what remains, except that for the rest we wholly apply ourselves to this work so holy, so necessary? Let us search, according to the prophet, our ways (Lam. 3:40) and our pursuits, and let each judge himself to have advanced in this, not when he has not found what to reprove, but when, what he has found, he will reprove. Then you have not searched yourself in vain, if you have noticed that there is need of scrutiny again: and so often your inquiry has not deceived you, as often as you have thought it must be repeated. But if you always do this, when there is need, you always do it. Always therefore remember that there is need for you of heavenly help, and of the mercy of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.
58.title: In what way the bridegroom exhorts the bride, that is, perfect men, to the governance of the imperfect. Likewise concerning the pruning of vices to be made in them, so that virtues may grow up.

59.1: The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land (Song 2:12). I can no longer at all dissemble, that behold a second time he who is from heaven speaks of the earth: so worthily indeed, so companionably, as one from the earth. This is the bridegroom: who when he sent before that flowers had appeared on the earth, added our; and now nonetheless: The voice, he says, of the turtledove is heard in our land. Will speech so unwonted for God, not to say unworthy, therefore lack reason? Nowhere, as I think, will you find him so speaking of heaven, nowhere elsewhere of earth. Mark therefore of how great sweetness it is for the God of heaven to say, in our land. And you earth-born and sons of men, hear; the Lord has magnified to do with us (Ps. 126:3). Much has he with the earth, much with the bride, whom it pleased him to take to himself from the lands. In our land, he says. This voice plainly does not sound principality, but companionship, but familiarity. As a bridegroom he says this, not as Lord. What? He is the Creator, and he reckons himself a consort! Love speaks, which knows not a lord. It is of course a song of love, nor ought it to be supported by other than amatory things. God also loves, nor has he this from elsewhere, but he himself is that whence he loves. And therefore more vehemently, because he does not so much have love, as he himself is this. But those whom he loves he has as friends, not servants. Finally a friend is made of a master: for he would not call the disciples friends, if they were not.
59.2: Do you see majesty itself also yield to love? So it is, brothers; love looks up to no one, but neither does it look down. It looks upon all equally who love it perfectly, and in itself temperates the lofty and the humble; and makes them not only equals, but one. You perhaps still think God excepted from this rule of love; but he who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). Why do you marvel at this? He himself has been made as one of us. I have said less: not as one, but one. It is little to be equal to men: he is man. Thence he claims our land for himself, but as a fatherland, not as a possession. Why should he not claim it? Thence for him the bride, thence the substance of the body; thence the bridegroom himself; thence two in one flesh. If one flesh, why not also one fatherland? The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, he says, but the earth he has given to the sons of men (Ps. 115:16). Therefore as son of man he inherits the earth, as lord he subjects it, as creator he administers it, as bridegroom he shares it. For by saying, in our land, he plainly renounces proprietorship, he does not reject society. And these things for that the bridegroom has used so kind a word, that he has deigned to say, in our land. Now let us see the rest.
59.3: The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. And this is a sign of winter finished, announcing nonetheless that the time of pruning is present. That according to the letter. Otherwise the voice of the turtledove does not sound very sweet, but it signifies sweet things. The little bird itself, if you buy it, is not of great; if you examine it, is not of small price. And the voice indeed more like to one groaning than to one singing admonishes us of our pilgrimage. Gladly I hear the voice of that teacher: who may move not applause for himself, but lament for me. Truly you exhibit a turtledove, if you teach to groan: and if you wish to persuade, you will need to study that more by groaning than by declaiming. Example indeed, both in many other things, and most of all in this business, is more efficacious than a word. You will give to your voice a voice of power, if what you persuade, you first know yourself to have persuaded to yourself. Stronger is the voice of work than of the mouth. Do as you speak, and not only do you more easily amend me, but you also free yourself from no light disgrace. It will no longer pertain to you, if anyone says: They bind heavy and unbearable burdens, and lay them on the shoulders of men, but with their finger they will not move them (Matt. 23:4). But neither need you fear that: You who teach others, you do not teach yourself (Rom. 2:21).
59.4: The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. While men for the worship of God received reward only on earth, and only earth, that namely flowing with milk and honey, they did not at all know themselves pilgrims upon the earth, nor after the manner of the turtledove did they groan as remembering the fatherland; but rather abusing exile for a fatherland, they gave themselves to eat fat things, and to drink honeyed wine. So for so long the voice of the turtledove was not heard in our land. When therefore the promise of the kingdom of heaven was made, then men understood that they have not here an abiding city, but began with all avidity to seek the one to come; and then first the voice of the turtledove sounded manifestly on the earth. For while every holy soul already was sighing for the presence of Christ, was bearing heavily the delay of the kingdom, was greeting the desired fatherland from afar with groans and sighs: does it not seem to you to perform the office of the groaning and most chaste turtledove, whatever soul on the earth had so done? From then therefore and thereafter the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. Why should the absence of Christ not move me to frequent tears and daily groans! Lord, before thee is all my desire, and my groan is not hidden from thee (Ps. 38:9). I have labored in my groan, thou knowest; but blessed is he who could say: I will wash my bed through each night, with my tears I will water my couch (Ps. 6:6). But not only to me, but also to all who love his coming, these groans are known. For this is what he himself was saying. Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn, he says, while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will mourn (Matt. 9:15); as if he were saying: And then the voice of the turtledove will be heard.
59.5: So it is, good Jesus, those days have come. For the creation itself groans and travails until now, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God. And not only it, but we ourselves also groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the sons of God, the redemption of our body (Rom. 8:22-23): knowing this, that while we are in this body, we are pilgrims from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6). Nor are the groans empty, to which from heaven it is so mercifully answered: For the misery of the needy and the groan of the poor now will I arise, says the Lord (Ps. 12:5). There was also in the time of the Fathers that voice of those groaning; but rare, and with each his own groan. Whence also one was saying: My secret to me, my secret to me (Isa. 24:16). But also he who was saying: My groan is not hidden from thee, surely was showing it to be hidden, which was not hidden to God alone. And therefore then it could not be said: The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land; because the secret still of a few had not then gone out to the multitude. But when it was cried openly: Seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1), that turtledove groan began already to pertain to all, and there was one reason of groaning for all, because all knew the Lord, according to what is read in Jeremiah: And all shall know me from the least unto the greatest, says the Lord (Jer. 31:34).
59.6: But if many are groaning, what does the expression of one mean for itself? The voice of the turtledove, he says. Why not of turtledoves? Perhaps the Apostle solves that, where he says that the Spirit himself asks for the saints with unutterable groans (Rom. 8:26). So it is. He himself is introduced groaning, who makes them groan. And however many they be whom you hear so groan, the voice of one sounds through the lips of all. Why not of him, who forms that very voice in the mouth of each for the necessities of each? Finally to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit unto utility (1 Cor. 12:7). His own voice makes each manifest, and indicates him present. And hear from the Gospel, that the Holy Spirit has a voice. The Spirit, he says, breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice; and you know not whence he comes, or whither he goes (John 3:8). Although he did not know, that dead master who was teaching the killing letter to the dead [namely Nicodemus]; let us know, who translated from death unto life by the life-giving Spirit, by certain and daily experience, he himself illuminating us, prove that our vows and groans come from him, and go to him, and there find mercy in the eyes of God. For when would God make void the voice of his Spirit? But he himself knows what the Spirit desires, because according to God he asks for the saints.
59.7: Nor do groans alone recommend the turtledove; chastity also recommends it. Finally by the merit of this it was worthy to be given as a victim for the virginal birth. For so you have: A pair of turtledoves, or two young of doves (Luke 2:24). And although elsewhere indeed the Holy Spirit is wont to be designated by the dove; yet because it is a libidinous bird, it was not fitting to offer it in sacrifice to the Lord, except surely at that age at which it would not know lust. But the age of the turtledove is not designated, because chastity is recognized at whatever age. Finally it is content with one mate; which lost, it admits another no longer, reproving the numerousness of marriages among men. For although perhaps the fault for incontinence is venial, yet so great an incontinence itself is base. It shames that reason cannot in man for the business of honesty what nature can in a bird. For one may see the turtledove in the time of its widowhood strenuously and indefatigably executing the work of holy widowhood. You may see it everywhere singular, everywhere hear it groaning; nor will you ever behold it sitting on a green branch, that you may learn from it to avoid the virulent greenness of pleasures. Add that on the ridges of mountains and on the summits of trees its converse is more frequent: that, which most of all becomes the purpose of purity, it may teach us to despise earthly things, and to love heavenly.
59.8: From which it is gathered that the voice of the turtledove is also the preaching of chastity. For neither from the beginning was this voice heard on the earth, but rather that: Increase, and multiply, and fill the earth (Gen. 1:28). In vain surely would that voice of purity have sounded, the fatherland of those rising not yet being disclosed: in which far more happily men neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven (Luke 20:35-36). Would you then say that there was a time for that voice then, when every barren woman in Israel lay under a curse, when the Patriarchs themselves had many wives at once, when a brother was compelled by law to raise up seed for a brother dead without children? But when from the mouth of the heavenly turtledove that commendation of eunuchs sounded, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God (Matt. 19:12); and again the counsel of another most chaste turtledove of the same kind concerning virgins prevailed everywhere (1 Cor. 7:25), then first it could truly be said that the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
59.9: Therefore, if in our land both flowers have appeared, and the voice of the turtledove is heard; surely truth also has been discovered by sight, and by hearing. For a voice is heard, a flower is discerned. A flower is a miracle, as our superior interpretation has it, which joining the voice brings forth the fruit of faith. Although faith is from hearing, yet confirmation is from sight. The voice sounded, the flower shone, and truth has sprung from the earth (Ps. 85:11) through the confession of the faithful, word and sign alike concurring unto the testimony of faith. These testimonies have been made exceedingly credible, while the flower attests to the voice, the eye to the ear. Things heard confirm things seen, that the testimony of two (I speak of ear and eye) may be ratified. Therefore the Lord was saying: Go, report to John (for he was speaking to his disciples) the things which you have heard and seen (Luke 7:22). Nor more briefly nor more plainly could the certainty of faith be intimated to them. The same persuasion indeed in a short time was also made to the whole earth, and by the same brevity of argument. The things which you have heard, he says, and seen. O abbreviated word, yet living and efficacious! Without doubt surely I assert what I have perceived with ears and eyes. The saving trumpet sounds, miracles flash, and the world believes. Quickly is that persuaded which is said, while that which is wondered at is shown. But you have that the apostles going forth preached everywhere, the Lord cooperating, and confirming the word with following signs (Mark 16:20). You have him on the mountain transfigured with stupendous brightness, and nonetheless testified by a heavenly voice (Matt. 17:2-5). You have at the Jordan similarly both the dove designating, and the voice testifying (Matt. 3:16-17). Thus these two everywhere alike, voice and sign, from the divine bounty concur unto introducing faith: that a broad entrance through both windows may lie open for truth unto the soul.
59.10: There follows: The fig tree has put forth its green figs. Let us not eat of them: for they are not fit for eating because of their unripeness. They have the appearance of good figs, but the likeness, not the savor, perhaps designating hypocrites. Yet let us not cast them away, elsewhere perhaps we shall have need of them. Otherwise they will fall lightly enough of themselves, and before the time, like the grass of housetops, which withered before it was plucked up (Ps. 129:6); which I think said of hypocrites. Yet not without cause has mention of them been made in the nuptial carmen. They will without doubt be, if not for eating, for some use whatsoever. Many things at weddings besides the feast are necessarily procured. But I so little think this should be passed over, that whatever that is, I am unwilling to discuss amid the straits of the extremities of this sermon; but I defer it to another day, and a freer hour. But whether necessarily, you will then be permitted to experience: only let your vows obtain for me opportunity and ability to bring forth what I feel, unto your own edification, unto the praise and glory of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ the Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.
59.title: Concerning the groans of the soul sighing for the heavenly homeland, and concerning the commendation of chastity and widowhood.

60.1: The fig tree has put forth its green figs (Song 2:13). The present place hangs upon what went before. For he had said that the time of pruning had come, asserting this as much from the flowers which were already appearing as from the turtledove's voice that had been heard. He still affirms the same from the putting forth of the green figs; because experience of the time is taken not only from the flowers and the turtledove's voice; it is taken also from the fig tree. For the air is not then other than milder, when the fig tree has put forth its green figs. The fig tree has no flowers, but in place of flowers it sends forth green figs at the time when the other trees flower. And as flowers appear and pass away, useful for nothing, except that they are certain forerunners of the fruit that is to follow; so also are the green figs. They arise, but fall unripe, and give place to those that are to be ripened, themselves by no means fit for eating. And hence also, therefore, as I have said, the bridegroom takes experience of the time, and an argument of persuasion, that the bride not be sluggish in going to the vineyards, because the work does not perish which comes in season. And the letter, indeed, thus.
60.2: But what of the spirit? that plainly in this place we look not upon a fig tree, but upon a people: for God's care is for men, not for trees. Truly a fig tree is the people, fragile in flesh, little in sense, humble in mind, whose first fruits, that for the moment we may play upon the name, are assuredly green figs and earthly. For it is not of popular zeal first to seek the kingdom of God and his justice (Matt. 6:33); but, as the Apostle says, to think the things that are of the world, how they may please their wives, or those their husbands. They of this sort will have tribulation of the flesh (1 Cor. 7:33, 28); but in the last things we do not deny that they will obtain the fruits of faith, if they shall have had a good last confession, and especially if they shall have redeemed the works of the flesh by alms. Therefore the first fruits of the peoples are not even fruits, no more than the green figs of fig trees. Finally if afterward they shall have done fruits worthy of repentance (for what is spiritual is not first, but what is animal (1 Cor. 15:46) it will be said to them: What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? (Rom. 6:21.)
60.3: I, however, do not think it free in this place to interpret any people whatever: one is signally expressed. For he did not say, They have put forth, as of many; but as of one, the fig tree, he says, has put forth its green figs; and, as I feel, it is the people of the Jews. How many things does the Savior seem to speak parabolically in the Gospel against this people? as is that: A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard (Luke 13:6) etc.; likewise: See the fig tree and all the trees (Luke 21:29): and to Nathanael it was said: When you were under the fig tree, I saw you (John 1:48). And again he curses the fig tree, for this reason, that he did not find fruit on it (Mark 11:13, 14). Well a fig tree, which although it came forth from a good root of the patriarchs, yet never wished to advance on high, never to lift itself from the soil, never to answer to the root by loftiness of branches, by nobility of flowers, by fecundity of fruits. Ill indeed do you agree with your root, little tree, twisted, knotted. For the root is holy. What appears in your branches worthy of it? The fig tree, he says, has put forth its green figs. You did not draw these from a noble root, wicked seed. What is in it is of the Holy Spirit; and through this, altogether subtle and sweet. Whence to you these green figs? And truly what is not green-fig-like in that race? Neither act, to be sure, nor affection, nor understanding, nor even the rite which it had in worshiping God. For the act was in wars, the affection wholly in gains, the understanding in the density of the letter, the worship in the blood of sheep and of herds.
60.4: But someone says: since that race has never at any time ceased to put forth green figs of this sort, therefore the time of pruning never at any time existed, because one time is asserted to exist for both things. It is not so. We say that women have begotten sons, not when they are in labor, but when they have already brought forth. We say also that trees have put forth their flowers, not when they have begun to flower, but rather when they have ceased. So here also it has been said that the fig tree has put forth its green figs, not when it put forth some, but when it put forth all, that is, when the putting forth came to an end. Do you ask at what time a completion of this sort happened to that people? When it killed Christ, then its malice was completed, according to what he himself had foretold to them: Fill up the measure of your fathers (Matt. 23:32). Whence on the gibbet, about already to give up the spirit: It is consummated, he says (John 19:30). O what a consummation this cursed fig tree gave to its green figs, and was thereupon condemned to eternal barrenness! O how are the last worse than the first! Beginning from the useless, it came to the pernicious and the poisoned. O green-fig-like and viperous affection, to hate the man who both heals the bodies of men and saves their souls! O no less a green-fig-like and surely bovine understanding, which did not understand God even in the works of God!
60.5: Perhaps the Jew may complain of me too much in his own aspersions, who call his understanding bovine. But let him read in Isaiah, and he will hear more than bovine. The ox, he says, has known his owner, and the ass his master's crib: Israel has not known me; my people has not understood (Isa. 1:3). You see me, O Jew, milder to you than your prophet. I have compared you to beasts of burden; he puts you beneath them. Although the prophet did not say this in his own person, but in God's, who proclaims himself God even by the very works: Even if you do not believe me, he says, believe the works: if I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe (John 10:38, 37); and yet even so they are not watchful to understand. Not the flight of demons, not the obedience of the elements, not the life of the dead, was able to drive away from them this bestial, and more than bestial, dullness: from which blindness, no less wonderful than miserable, it came about that they rushed into that so horrible and so enormously green-fig-like crime, laying sacrilegious hands upon the Lord of majesty. From then, therefore, it could be said that the fig tree has put forth its green figs, when already, namely, the lawful things of that people began to be as it were at the exit upon the summit: so that, according to the ancient prophecy, when new things came upon them, the old might be cast away (Lev. 26:10). Not otherwise, surely, than as green figs fall and yield to the good figs rising beneath. As long, he says, as the fig tree did not cease to produce its green figs, I did not call you, O bride, knowing that the best figs could not come forth together. But now, those having been produced which first had to be produced, I no longer invite you unseasonably, when good and salutary fruits are known to be near, about to blot out the useless ones.
60.6: For the flowering vineyards, he says, have given their odor; which nonetheless is an indication of approaching fruit. This odor puts serpents to flight. They say that when vineyards are flowering every venomous reptile yields the place, and by no means endures the odor of the new flowers. Let our novices attend to this, and act confidently, thinking what sort of spirit they have received, whose firstfruits the demons do not endure. If such is the novice's fervor, what will absolute perfection be? Let the fruit be weighed from the flower, and let the virtue of the taste be estimated from the force of the odor. The flowering vineyards have given their odor. And in the beginning indeed it was so. Upon the preaching of the new grace there followed newness of life in those who had believed, who having their conversation good among the nations. They were the good odor of Christ in every place (2 Cor. 2:14, 15). A good odor, a good testimony. This odor proceeds from a good work as from a flower. And since with such a flower and such an odor in the first beginnings of nascent faith faithful souls, as certain spiritual vineyards, appeared filled, having a good testimony even from those who were outside; not incongruously, as I think, we feel that it was said of them that the flowering vineyards have given their odor. To what end? that, provoked by that, even those who had not yet believed, considering them from their good works, might themselves also glorify God, and so the odor of life might begin to be to them unto life. Therefore they are not undeservedly related to have given an odor, who sought not their own glory, but the salvation of others from their good opinion. Otherwise they could after the manner of certain ones count piety a gain, for example, of ostentation, of hire. But that would be not to give an odor, but to sell it. Now truly because they did all their things in charity, they plainly did not sell the odor, but gave it.
60.7: But if the vineyards are souls, the flower a work, the odor opinion: what is the fruit? Martyrdom. And truly the fruit of the vine is the blood of the martyr. When he shall have given sleep to his beloved, he says, behold the inheritance of the Lord is children, the reward the fruit of the womb (Ps. 127:2, 3). I had almost said, the fruit of the vine. Why should I not call the blood of the grape most undiluted, the blood of the innocent, the blood of the Just One? Why not the must, red, proved, precious, plainly from the vineyard of Sorek, pressed out in the winepress of the passion? Finally precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. 116:15). These things for that which was said, that the flowering vineyards have given their odor.
60.8: So if we prefer to look upon this place with respect to the times of grace, or if it pleases more that it be referred to the Fathers (for the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa. 5:7), the sense will be: the prophets and patriarchs scented Christ about to be born in the flesh and to die, but they did not then give that same odor of theirs, because they did not exhibit in the flesh him whom they had fore-sensed in the spirit. They did not give their odor, nor publish their secret, waiting that it might be revealed in its time. Who indeed then would grasp wisdom hidden in mystery, not exhibited in a body? Thus the vineyards then indeed did not give their odor. But they gave it afterward, when through the successions of generations they brought forth to the ages by a virgin birth Christ born from themselves according to the flesh. Then plainly, I say, those spiritual vineyards gave their odor, when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared (Tit. 3:4); and the world began to have present him whom few as yet had fore-sensed absent. That man, for example, who touching Jacob and sensing Christ: Behold, he says, the odor of my son is as the odor of a full field, which the Lord has blessed (Gen. 27:27); when he said this, he had his delights for himself, nor did he communicate them to anyone. But when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4, 5); then utterly the odor which was in him scattered itself everywhere, so much so that from the ends of the earth the Church, sensing him, cried out: Your name is oil poured out: and the young maidens ran in the odor of this oil (Song 1:2, 3). Thus that vineyard gave its odor, and at that time the others also gave it, in which this same odor of life had existed. Why should they not have given it, from whom is Christ according to the flesh? It has been said, therefore, that the vineyards have given their odor, whether because faithful souls scatter a good opinion of themselves everywhere; or because the oracles and revelations of the Fathers have been made plain to the world, and their fragrance has gone out into all the earth, the Apostle saying: Manifestly great is the sacrament of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory (1 Tim. 3:16).
60.9: But it is marvelous if neither this fig tree nor these vineyards have anything that builds up morals. I judge this place to be moral also. And I say that by the grace of God which is in us we too have both fig trees and vineyards. Fig trees indeed, those who are sweeter in manners; but vineyards, those who are more fervent in spirit. Everyone among us who conducts himself commonly and socially, and not only converses among the brethren without complaint, but also with much sweetness offers himself to be enjoyed by all in every office of charity, why should I not most fittingly say that he plays the part of a fig tree? Who nonetheless must first have put forth and cast away his green figs, namely the fear of judgment, which perfect charity casts outside; and the bitterness of sins, which must needs yield to true confession and the infusion of grace and the pouring forth of frequent tears, and other such things, after the likeness of green figs going before the sweetness of fruits: which you too can think through for yourselves.
60.10: Yet that I may still add something of this sort that occurs, see lest perhaps even these can be counted among green figs: knowledge, prophecy, tongues, and the like. For these after the manner of green figs have to fail and yield to better things, the Apostle saying that knowledge also shall be destroyed, and prophecies shall be made void, and tongues shall cease. Understanding will also shut out faith itself, and vision must succeed to hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for it? Charity alone does not fall away (1 Cor. 13:8), but that by which God is loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, the whole strength (Luke 10:27). Therefore I would by no means have numbered this among green figs, nor would I even have said that it pertains to the fig tree, but to the vineyards. Now those who are vineyards show themselves to us more severe than sweeter, acting in a vehement spirit, zealous for discipline, most sharply reproving vices, fitting to themselves most congruously that voice: Have I not hated them, O Lord, who hated you, and wasted away over your enemies? (Ps. 139:21). Likewise: The zeal of your house has eaten me up (Ps. 69:9). And to me indeed those seem to excel in the love of neighbor, these in the love of God. But it is pleasant to pause under this vine and under this fig tree, where the love of God and of neighbor gives shade. I hold both when I love you, Lord Jesus Christ, who are my neighbor, because you are man, and have done mercy with me; and nonetheless you are God blessed above all things forever. Amen.
60.title: Concerning the unbelief of the Jews, by which they fulfilled the measure of their fathers in killing Christ.

61.1: Arise, my friend, my bride, and come (Song 2:13). The bridegroom commends his great love by repeating the voices of love. For repetition is an expression of affection: and that he again urges the beloved to the labor of the vineyards shows how solicitous he is for the salvation of souls. For that the vineyards are souls you have already heard. Let us not linger needlessly in the things that have been said. See what follows. Yet nowhere, as I remember, in this whole work had he openly named her bride as yet, except just now when one goes to the vineyards, when one draws near to the wine of charity. Which, when it has come and has been perfected, will make a spiritual marriage; and they will be two, not in one flesh, but in one spirit, the Apostle saying: He who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17).
61.2: There follows: My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall, show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears. He loves and goes on to speak amorous things. Again by caressing he calls her dove; he says she is his, and asserts her his own: and what he himself was wont more earnestly to be asked by her, he now in turn demands both her sight and her conversation. He acts as a bridegroom; but as a modest one, he blushes at the public, and determines to enjoy his delights in a sequestered place, namely in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the wall. Suppose then the bridegroom to say thus: Fear not, friend, as though this work of the vineyards, to which we exhort you, should have to impede or interrupt the business of love. There will certainly also be some use in it for that which we alike desire. Vineyards indeed have walls, and these are lodging places grateful to the modest. Here is the literal play. Why should I not call it play? For what serious thing does this series of the letter have? Not even worthy of hearing is what sounds outside, if the Spirit within does not help the weakness of our understanding. Therefore let us not remain outside, lest we seem also — which God forbid! — to be reviewing the allurements of base loves; bring chaste ears to the sermon which is in hand concerning love; and when you think of the lovers themselves, you must feel not man and woman, but the Word and the soul. And if I shall have said Christ and the Church, it is the same; except that by the name of Church not one soul, but the unity of many, or rather their unanimity, is designated. Nor indeed should you think the clefts of the rock, or the hollows of the wall, hiding places of those who work iniquity, lest any suspicion at all creep in concerning the works of darkness.
61.3: Another has so expounded this place, interpreting the clefts of the rock as the wounds of Christ. Altogether rightly; for the rock is Christ. Good clefts, which build up faith in the resurrection and the divinity of Christ. My Lord, he says, and my God (John 20:28). Whence was this oracle brought back, if not from the clefts of the rock? In these the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest, where she may lay her young (Ps. 84:3); in these the dove keeps herself safe, and fearlessly looks upon the hawk flying round about. And therefore he says: My dove in the clefts of the rock. The voice of the dove: He has exalted me upon a rock (Ps. 27:5); and likewise: He has set, he says, my feet upon a rock (Ps. 40:2). A wise man builds his house upon a rock, because there he fears neither the injuries of winds nor of floods (Matt. 7:24, 25). What good is not in the rock? Exalted upon the rock, secure upon the rock, upon the rock I stand firmly. Secure from the enemy, strong against a fall; and this because exalted from the earth. For everything earthly is doubtful and falling. Let our conversation be in the heavens, and we fear neither to fall nor to be cast down. In the heavens is the rock; in that is firmness and security. The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs (Ps. 104:18). And truly where is there safe and firm security and rest for the weak, if not in the wounds of the Savior? So much the more securely do I dwell there, the more powerful he is to save. The world roars, the body presses, the devil lies in wait: I do not fall; for I am founded upon a firm rock. I have sinned a great sin: conscience will be troubled, but will not be disturbed, because I will remember the wounds of the Lord. For he was wounded for our iniquities (Isa. 53:5). What is so unto death, that is not loosed by the death of Christ? If therefore so powerful and so effectual a medicine has come into mind, I can no longer be terrified by any malignity of disease.
61.4: And therefore it is clear that he erred who said: My iniquity is greater than that I should merit pardon (Gen. 4:13). Except that he was not of the members of Christ, nor did it pertain to him concerning the merit of Christ, that he should presume as his own, should call his own what was another's; as though a member the thing of the head. But I confidently usurp for myself from the bowels of the Lord what is lacking to me from myself, because they abound with mercy; nor are clefts lacking through which they may flow out. They dug his hands and feet, and pierced his side with a lance: and through these fissures it is allowed me to suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone; that is, to taste and see that the Lord is sweet. He was thinking thoughts of peace, and I did not know. For who has known the mind of the Lord? or who has been his counselor? But the key unlocking, the nail penetrating, has been made for me, that I may see the will of the Lord. Why should I not see through the cleft? The nail cries out, the wound cries out, that truly God is in Christ reconciling the world to himself. Iron has passed through his soul, and has drawn near to his heart, that he may no longer not know how to sympathize with my infirmities. The secret of the heart lies open through the clefts of the body; that great sacrament of piety lies open, the bowels of the mercy of our God lie open, in which the dayspring from on high has visited us. Why should not the bowels lie open through the wounds? For in what more clearly than in your wounds would it have shone forth that you, Lord, are sweet and mild, and of much mercy? For no one has greater compassion than that one should lay down his soul for those sentenced to death and condemned.
61.5: My merit, accordingly, is the compassion of the Lord. I am plainly not destitute of merit, as long as he shall not have been destitute of compassions. But if the mercies of the Lord are many, I nonetheless am much in merits. For what if I am conscious to myself of many offenses? For where offense has abounded, grace has also superabounded (Rom. 5:20). And if the mercies of the Lord are from eternity and unto eternity (Ps. 103:17), I also will sing the mercies of the Lord forever (Ps. 89:1). Do I sing my justices? Lord, I will remember your justice alone (Ps. 71:16). For that itself is also mine; for you have been made for me justice from God. Must I fear lest one not suffice for both? It is not a short cloak which, according to the prophet, cannot cover two (Isa. 28:20). Your justice is justice forever (Ps. 119:142). What is longer than eternity? And a large and eternal justice will cover both you and me abundantly. And in me indeed it covers a multitude of sins; but in you, Lord, what but treasures of piety, riches of goodness? These are laid up for me in the clefts of the rock. How great a multitude of your sweetness is in them, covered indeed, but for those who perish! For why should what is holy be given to dogs, or pearls to swine? But to us God has revealed through his Spirit, and even with the clefts opened has brought us into the holy places. How great in these a multitude of sweetness, a fullness of grace, and a perfection of virtues!
61.6: I will go for myself to those storehouses so filled, and at the prophet's admonition I will leave the cities, and will dwell in the rock (Jer. 48:28). I will be as a dove nesting in the very mouth of the cleft, that with Moses placed in the cleft of the rock, when the Lord passes by, I may merit at least to look upon his hinder parts (Exod. 33:22, 23). For who may see the face of him who stands, that is, the brightness of the unchangeable, except he who has already merited to be brought in, not into the holy places, but into the holy of holies? Yet neither is the contemplation of the hinder parts vile or to be despised. Let Herod despise; I so much the more do not despise, the more contemptible he shows himself to Herod. The hinder parts of the Lord also have something that it delights to see. Who knows if God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? There will be a time when he will show his face, and we shall be saved. But in the meantime let him go before us with the blessings of sweetness, namely those which he has been accustomed to leave behind him. Now let him show the hinder parts of his condescension, hereafter about to show his face in the glory of dignity. Sublime in the kingdom, but sweet on the cross. In this vision let him go before me, in that let him fill me. You will fill me, he says, with joy with your countenance (Ps. 16:11). Both visions are salutary, both sweet; but that in sublimity, this in humility; that in splendor, this in paleness.
61.7: Finally he says, And the hinder parts of his back in the paleness of gold (Ps. 68:13). How should he not grow pale in death? But pale gold is better than shining brass, and what is foolish of God is wiser than men. Gold is the Word, gold is Wisdom. This gold discolored itself, hiding the form of God, and putting forward the form of a servant. It discolored the Church also, which says: Do not consider me that I am dark, because the sun has discolored me (Song 1:5). Therefore also his hinder parts are in the paleness of gold, she who did not blush at the duskiness of the cross, did not shudder at the burning of the passion, did not flee the bruise of the wounds. She even takes pleasure in those, and wishes her last things to be like these. Therefore finally she hears: My dove in the clefts of the rock, because she is wholly occupied with devotion in the wounds of Christ, and by continual meditation dwells in them. Thence the endurance of martyrdom, thence for her great confidence with God most high. There is no reason why the martyr should fear to lift to him a bloodless and livid face, by whose bruise he has been healed, to present the glorious likeness of his death, namely in the paleness of gold. What should he fear to whom even by the Lord it is said: Show me your face? To what end? As it seems to me, he wishes rather to show himself. So it is: he wishes to be seen, not to see. For what does he not see? There is no need for him that anyone show himself, by whom nothing is not seen, even if one hide himself. He wishes therefore to be seen; the kindly leader wishes the face and eyes of the devoted soldier to be lifted to his wounds, that from this he may raise that one's courage, and by his own example render him stronger to endure.
61.8: For indeed he will not feel his own, while he looks upon that one's wounds. The martyr stands dancing and triumphing, though with body all torn; and while the iron searches his sides, not only bravely but even cheerfully he looks round upon the sacred blood boiling forth from his flesh. Where then is the martyr's soul? Surely in safety, surely in the rock, surely in the bowels of Jesus, the wounds of course lying open for entering. If he were in his own bowels, the iron searching them would assuredly make him feel; he would not bear the pain, he would succumb, and deny. But now dwelling in the rock, what wonder if he has hardened after the manner of a rock? But neither is this wonderful, if an exile from the body he does not feel the pains of the body. Nor does stupor do this, but love. For sense is submitted, not lost. Nor is pain lacking, but it is overcome, but it is despised. Therefore from the rock is the martyr's fortitude, thence plainly powerful to drink the cup of the Lord. And this inebriating cup, how excellent it is! (Ps. 23:5.) Excellent, I say, and joyful no less to the emperor looking on than to the soldier triumphing. For the joy of the Lord is our strength (Neh. 8:10). Why should he not rejoice at the voice of a most strong confession? Finally he also requires it with desire: Let your voice sound, he says, in my ears. Nor will he delay to repay in turn according to his promise: immediately when one shall have confessed him before men, he also will confess him before his Father (Matt. 10:32). Let us break off the sermon, for it cannot now be finished; lest it be without measure, if we wish to embrace in this one sermon all things that still remain from the proposed chapter. Therefore what remains let us keep for another beginning, that of our word and measure alike the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all things forever, may rejoice. Amen.
61.title: In what way the Church finds the riches of divine mercy in the openings of the wounds of Christ, and concerning the strength of the martyrs which they received from Christ.

62.1: My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall (Song 2:14). Not only in the clefts of the rock does the dove find a safe refuge; she finds it also in the hollows of the wall.
