But if we take the wall not as a heap of stones, but as the communion of saints, let us see lest perhaps he called the hollows of the wall the places of the angels who fell through pride, places left as it were empty: which indeed are to be filled from men, as ruins to be repaired with living stones. Whence the apostle Peter: Coming, he says, to the living stone, you also as living stones are built up into spiritual houses (1 Pet. 2:4, 5). Nor do I think it beside the point if we understand the guardianship of angels to perform the office of a wall in the vineyard of the Lord, which is the Church of the predestined, when Paul says: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who take hold of the inheritance of salvation? (Heb. 1:14.) and the Prophet: The angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him (Ps. 34:7). And if it so stands, the sense will be that two things console the Church in the time and place of her pilgrimage; from the past indeed, the memory of the passion of Christ; but from the future, that she thinks and trusts that she is to be received into the lot of the saints. Both these things, as it were eyed before and behind, she contemplates with insatiable desire; and each looking is altogether grateful to her, each is for her a refuge from the tribulation of evils and from pain. A complete consolation, when she knows not only what is to be expected, but also from what it is to be presumed. A glad expectation and not doubtful, which has been confirmed by the death of Christ. Why should she tremble at the greatness of the reward, who considers the dignity of the price? How gladly in mind she visits the clefts through which the price of the most holy blood flowed for her! How gladly she walks through the hollows, and the lodging places, and the mansions, which in the Father's house are many and diverse, in which he has to place his sons according to the diversity of each one's merits! And now indeed, which alone she can for the meantime, she rests in these by memory alone, already clothing the mind with the heavenly habitation which is from above. It will be when she will fill the ruins, when she will inhabit the hollows both with body and with mind; when she herself by the presence of her universality will illuminate the empty dwellings which the ancient inhabitants left, nor will any hollow further appear at all in the heavenly wall, rejoicing for the rest in the happy perfection and integrity of herself; or, if you prefer that more, we will say that these hollows are not found by studious and pious minds, but made. In what way, you ask? By thought and by eagerness. For a pious wall yields after the manner of a softer wall to the desire of the soul, yields to pure contemplation, yields to frequent prayer. Finally the prayer of the just penetrates the heavens (Sir. 35:21). Not indeed will it cleave the spacious heights of this bodily air, as with a certain oarage of its wings after the likeness of a flying bird, or as a sharp sword pierce the solid and lofty summit of the firmament itself: but there are holy, living, rational heavens, which declare the glory of God, which with a certain favorable piety gladly incline themselves to our vows, and with affections bent at the touch of our devotion receive us into their bowels, as often as we knock to them with a worthy intention. For to him who knocks it will be opened. It will therefore be allowed each one of us, even in this time of our mortality, to hollow out for himself, in whatever part he will, hollows of the heavenly wall; now indeed to revisit the patriarchs, now truly to salute the prophets, now to mingle with the senate of the apostles, now to be joined to the choirs of martyrs; but also, running through with all eagerness of mind, to survey the stations and mansions of the blessed powers from the least angel even to the cherubim and seraphim, according as each one's devotion shall bear him. Among those with whom he shall be more affected, the Spirit sending into him as he wills; if he shall have stood and knocked, immediately it will be opened to him, and a hollow having been made as it were in the mountains, or rather in holy minds, while of their own accord they bend themselves to piety, he will rest even a little with them. Of every soul so doing both the face and the voice are acceptable to God: the face, on account of purity; the voice, on account of confession. For confession and beauty are in his sight (Ps. 96:6). Whence also it is said to him who is of this sort: Show me your face, let your voice sound in your ears. The voice is admiration in the mind of one contemplating, the voice is thanksgiving. God is altogether delighted with hollows of this sort, from which there resonates for him a voice of thanksgiving, a voice of admiration and of praise.
62.3: Happy the mind which shall have been eager frequently to hollow out for itself in this wall; but happier that which in the rock. It is indeed allowed to hollow even in the rock; but for this there is need of a purer sharpness of mind, and of an altogether more vehement intention, and also of stronger merits of holiness. And who is sufficient for these things? Surely he who said: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning with God (John 1:1, 2). Does he not seem to you to have immersed himself in the very inner chambers of the Word; and from the hidden places of his breast to have drawn forth a certain most holy marrow of intimate wisdom? What of him who spoke wisdom among the perfect, wisdom hidden in mystery, which none of the princes of this world knew? (1 Cor. 2:6, 8). Did not the pious searcher, having bored through one and another heaven with a sharp but pious curiosity, at last bring this forth from the third? But he did not keep silent about it to us, faithfully intimating it in such words as he could to the faithful. But he heard ineffable words, which it was not allowed him to speak (2 Cor. 12:2, 4). Not indeed to man, for he was speaking those things to himself and to God; suppose then that God consoles Paul's as it were anxious charity in this way, and says: Why are you anxious that human hearing does not grasp what you have conceived? Let your voice sound in my ears; that is: If what you feel it is not allowed to reveal to mortals, yet be consoled that your voice can soothe the divine ears. Do you see the holy soul, now indeed sober with charity toward us, but now exceeding with purity unto God? (2 Cor. 5:13.) See also concerning holy David, lest perhaps he himself be that man of whom he speaks with God as of another: For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnants of thought shall keep a feast day to you (Ps. 76:10). Therefore what from prophetic thought could come into the open by the word and example of the Prophet, that the Prophet soon released into public confession, and from it confessed to the Lord among the peoples, keeping the rest for himself and for God, and together leading a festal day in joy and exultation. This then is what he wished to intimate to us by the mentioned little verse. Namely, whatever by that searching and eager thought of his he prevailed to draw forth from the secret of wisdom, the part which he could he imparted by solicitous preaching for the salvation of the peoples; the rest which the peoples could not grasp he expended in festal jubilation in the praises of God. You see that nothing perishes to holy contemplation, while what cannot be expended upon the edification of the peoples is itself most of all a joyful and becoming praise to God.
62.4: Which things being so, it is clear that there are two kinds of contemplation: one, concerning the state and happiness and glory of the city above, with which that huge multitude of heavenly citizens is occupied either in act or in leisure; the other, concerning the majesty, eternity, divinity of the king himself. That in the wall, this in the rock. But the more difficultly this is hollowed, the more sweetly tastes what you draw forth from it. Nor fear that which Scripture threatens against the searchers of majesty (Prov. 25:27). Only bring a pure and simple eye; you will not be oppressed by glory, but admitted, unless you have sought not God's glory but your own. Otherwise each one is oppressed by his own glory, not by God's, while inclined toward that, he is not allowed to lift the neck to this, a neck heavy of course with cupidity. This shaken off, let us securely search in the Rock, in which are the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3). If you still doubt, hear the Rock herself: Those who work in me, she says, shall not sin (Sir. 24:30). Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I will fly, and will rest? (Ps. 55:6.) There the meek and simple finds rest, where the deceitful is oppressed, or the proud, and the cupidinous of empty glory. The Church is a dove, and therefore she rests. A dove, because innocent, because mourning. A dove, I say, because in meekness she receives the implanted word. And she rests in the Word, that is in the rock: for the rock is the Word. The Church therefore is in the clefts of the rock, through which she looks in, and sees the glory of her bridegroom; nor yet is she oppressed by glory, because she does not usurp it for herself. She is not oppressed, because she is not a searcher of majesty, but of will. For as to what pertains to majesty, she sometimes indeed dares even to intend upon it, but as admiring, not as searching. But if at times it happens that she is caught up into it by excess, that is the finger of God, graciously lifting man, not the temerity of man insolently invading the heights of God. For when the Apostle recalls that he was caught up (2 Cor. 12), that he may excuse the daring; who else of mortals would presume to entangle himself by his own efforts in this dreadful scrutiny of the divine majesty, and as an importunate contemplator to break into the fearful secrets? Searchers of majesty, therefore, I think are to be called as it were breakers-in, not namely those who are caught up into it, but those who rush in. They therefore are oppressed by glory.
62.5: Therefore the searching of majesty is fearful: but of will, as safe as it is pious. Why should I not insist with all diligence in searching upon the sacrament of the glory of the will, which I know I must obey in all things? Sweet glory, which proceeds from nowhere else than from the contemplation of that sweetness itself, than from the looking upon the riches of goodness and of much compassion. Finally we have seen this glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father (John 1:14). For altogether kind and truly paternal was what appeared of glory in this part. That glory will not oppress me, though I intend upon it with all my strength: I rather will be impressed upon it. For we, beholding with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from clarity into clarity, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). We are transformed when we are conformed. But far be it that conformity of God by man be presumed in the glory of majesty, and not rather in the modesty of will! This is my glory, if ever I shall hear of myself: I have found a man according to my heart. The heart of the bridegroom, the heart of his Father. What is that itself like? Be merciful, he says, as your Father also is merciful (Luke 6:36). This is the form which he desires to see, when he says to the Church: Show me your face: the form of piety and of meekness. This with all confidence she lifts to the Rock; to whom she is like: Come to him, he says, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded (Ps. 34:5). By what pact shall the humble be confounded by the humble, the holy by the pious, and the modest by the meek? Plainly the pure face of the bride will not shrink from the purity of the rock, no more than virtue from virtue, light from light.
62.6: But because the Church cannot as yet in the meantime approach from every part to the rock that is to be bored (for it is not of all who are in the Church to look into the sacraments of the divine will, or by themselves to apprehend the deep things of God); therefore she is shown to dwell not only in the clefts of the rock, but also in the hollows of the wall. Therefore in the perfect indeed, who both dare by purity of conscience and are able by sharpness of understanding to search and penetrate the secrets of wisdom, she dwells in the clefts of the rock. For the rest in the hollows of the wall: so that those who by themselves either do not suffice, or do not presume, to dig in the rock may dig in the wall, content at least to look with the mind upon the glory of the saints. If even this is not possible for anyone, for him indeed he will set forth Jesus, and him crucified: that he too without his own labor may dwell in the clefts of the rock, in which he has not labored. The Jews labored in these, and he will enter into the labors of the unbelieving, that he may be faithful. Nor is it to be feared that he suffer a rebuff, who is also called that he may enter. Enter, he says, into the rock, hide yourself in the dug earth from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the glory of his majesty (Isa. 2:10). To the soul still weak and inert (which according to what in the Gospel a certain one confesses of himself, is not able to dig, and is ashamed to beg) (Luke 16:3.) dug earth is shown where she may hide, until she grows strong and advances, so that she too may be able by herself to hollow out clefts in the rock, through which she may enter into the inner things of the Word, namely by vigor and purity of mind.
62.7: And if we have understood the dug earth as that which says: They have dug my hands and my feet (Ps. 22:16); there will be no doubting concerning health to be obtained more quickly in it by the wounded soul which shall dwell in it. For what is so effectual for curing the wounds of conscience, and also for purging the sharpness of the mind, as diligent meditation on the wounds of Christ? But until she shall have been perfectly purged and healed, I do not see how that which is said can be fitted to her: Show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears. How finally should she dare to show her face, or to lift her voice, to whom it is also enjoined to hide? Hide yourself, he says, in the dug earth. Why? Because she is not beautiful of face, nor worthy to be seen. She will not be worthy to be seen, as long as she shall not be fit to see. But when through dwelling in the dug earth she shall have advanced so far in healing the interior eye that she herself also can with unveiled face behold the glory of God; then at last what she shall see she will already speak confidently, pleasing in voice and face. The face must please which can intend upon the brightness of God. For she could not do that, unless she herself also were bright and pure, transformed of course into the same image of brightness which she beholds. Otherwise she would rebound by the very dissimilitude, struck back by the unaccustomed splendor. Therefore when the pure shall have been able to look upon pure truth, then the bridegroom will desire to see her face, and consequently also to hear her voice.
62.8: For how greatly preaching of the truth with purity of mind indeed pleases him, he shows when he next adds: For your voice is sweet. Because why a voice should not please if the face displeases, he demonstrates when he immediately subjoins: And your face is comely. What is the beauty of the inward face, if not purity? In many this has pleased without the voice of preaching; that without this, in no one. To the impure Truth does not show herself, Wisdom does not entrust herself. What then do they speak which they have not seen? What we know, he says, we speak, and what we have seen we testify (John 3:11). Go then you, and dare to testify what you have not seen, and to speak what you are ignorant of. Do you ask whom I call impure? He who seeks human praises, who does not set forth the Gospel without a fee, who evangelizes that he may eat, who counts piety a gain, who seeks not the fruit but the gift. Such are impure; and when they have not whence they may see the truth because of impurity, they nonetheless have whence they may speak it. Why do you act prematurely? why do you not wait for the light; why do you presume the work of light before the light? It is vain for you to rise before the light. Light is purity, light is charity, which does not seek the things that are its own (1 Cor. 13:5). Let this go before, and the foot of the tongue is not set in uncertainty. Truth is not seen by a proud eye; it lies open to a sincere one. There is no reason why truth should refuse herself to be looked upon by a pure heart, and through this neither to be spoken. But to the sinner God says: Why do you declare my justices, and take up my testament through your mouth? (Ps. 50:16.) Many, purity neglected, have tried to speak before they see; and either have gravely erred, not knowing of what things they spoke, nor of what they affirmed; or have basely become vile, while those who would teach others had not taught themselves. From which twofold evil may the Bridegroom of the Church, entreated by you, always guard us, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all things forever. Amen.
62.title: What it is for the faithful soul to sojourn «in the openings of the rock;» and what in the caverns of the wall. Concerning the will of God rather than his majesty to be searched out. Finally concerning the purity of mind necessary for the preaching of the truth.

63.1: Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards: for our vineyard has flowered (Song 2:15). It is clear that it was not idly that they went to the vineyards, when there foxes were found destroying them. The letter indeed is that. But what of the spirit? Before all things surely, that from this explanation we utterly reject the common and accustomed sense of the letter, as inept and tasteless, and plainly unworthy to be received in a Scripture so holy, so authentic. Unless perhaps someone is so foolish and dull of mind as to count it a great thing to have learned from it, after the manner of the children of this world, to take care of earthly possessions, to guard and defend vineyards from beasts rushing in, lest it happen that one lose the fruit of wine, in which is luxury; and at the same time the labor and the expense perish. A great loss indeed, that for that reason we should read a holy book with so great zeal and so great veneration, because we are taught in it to guard vineyards from foxes, lest in cultivating them purses be emptied in vain, if we shall have been sluggish in guarding them! You are not so rude, nor so destitute of spiritual grace, as to savor things thus carnally. Therefore let us seek these things in the spirit. There indeed we find, with a sound understanding indeed, and a sense nonetheless worthy, both flowering vineyards and destroying foxes, in the catching or removing of which one labors both more honorably and more fruitfully. Or do you doubt that one must insist far more vigilantly upon keeping minds than crops; that one must watch far more carefully to beware spiritual wickednesses for the sake of those, than to catch fraudulent little foxes for the sake of these?
63.2: But now by me these spiritual vines as well as foxes are to be shown. It will be your concern, sons, for each to provide for his own vineyard, when, as I dispute, he shall have noticed in what things and from whom especially he must beware. For a wise man his life is a vineyard, his mind, his conscience. For the wise man will leave nothing untilled or deserted in himself. Not so the fool. You will find all things neglected with him, all things lying flat, all things untilled and filthy. There is no vineyard for the fool. How a vineyard, where nothing planted, nothing worked anywhere appears? The whole life of the fool grows wild with thorns and briers: and is it a vineyard? Even if it was, now it is not, reduced of course to a solitude. Where is the vine of virtue? where the cluster of good work? where the wine of spiritual joy? I passed through the field of the lazy man, he says, and through the vineyard of the foolish man: and behold nettles had filled the whole, and thorns had covered its surface, and the wall of stones was destroyed (Prov. 24:30, 31). You hear the wise man mocking the fool, because by neglecting he has reduced into a non-vineyard the goods of nature and the gifts of grace, which perhaps he had received through the bath of regeneration, like that first vineyard of his which God planted and not man. Finally there cannot be a vineyard where there is not life. For what the fool lives, I would judge rather death than life. How life with sterility? A dry tree and turned to sterility, is it not judged dead? And the twigs are dead. And he killed, he says, their vines with hail (Ps. 78:47); showing those deprived of life which have been condemned to sterility. So the fool, by the very fact that he lives uselessly, living is dead.
63.3: Therefore it befits the wise man alone to have, or rather to be, a vineyard, who has life. He is a fruit-bearing tree in the house of God, and through this a living tree. Since indeed wisdom itself, by which a wise man is called and is, is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it (Prov. 3:18). Why should not its layhold-er live? He lives, but by faith. For the just man is wise, and the just lives by faith (Heb. 10:38). And if the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom, as it is; assuredly he is wise who is just. He therefore, whether you name him just or wise, will never live without a vineyard, because he will never not live. For to him this is a vineyard which is life. And a good vineyard is the just man's, rather a good vineyard is the just man, whose virtue is the vine, whose action the branch, whose wine the testimony of conscience, whose tongue the winepress of expression. Finally: This is our glory, he says, the testimony of our conscience (2 Cor. 1:12). Do you see that with the wise man nothing is idle? Speech, thought, conversation, and if there is anything else from him, why is not the whole the agriculture of God, the building of God, and the vineyard of the Lord of hosts? What finally can perish for him of himself, when even his leaf shall not fall?
63.4: But for such a vineyard infestations, snares, will never be lacking. For where there are many riches, there are also many who eat them (Eccl. 5:10). The wise man will be solicitous to keep his vineyard no less than to cultivate it, nor will he suffer it to be devoured by foxes. The worst fox is the hidden detractor, but no less wicked the bland flatterer. The wise man will beware of these. He will take care, surely as far as in him lies, to catch those who do such things; but to catch them by benefits and services, and by salutary admonitions, and by prayers for them to God. He will not cease to heap coals of fire of this sort upon the head of the one who curses (Rom. 12:20), and likewise upon that of the flatterer, until, if it can be done, he takes away from that one envy, and from this one simulation, from the heart, doing the commandment of the bridegroom who says: Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards. Or does he not seem to you caught, who with face suffused with blush, blushing of course at his own judgment, is himself witness of his confusion and repentance; whether because he has hated a man most worthy of love; or because he has loved only in word and tongue him from whom he has even late experienced that he is loved in work and truth? Caught plainly, and caught for the Lord, according to what he himself expressly said by name: Catch, saying, for us. Would that I could so catch all who oppose me without cause, that I might either restore them to Christ, or acquire them! So, so let them be confounded and ashamed who seek my soul, let them be turned backward and blush who wish evils for me: that I too may be found obedient to the bridegroom, that I too may catch foxes, not for myself, but for him. But let the sermon be turned back to its beginning, that the series of the explanation may proceed in its order.
63.5: Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards. The place is moral; and according to the discipline of morals we have already shown that these spiritual vineyards are nothing other than spiritual men, whose when all the inward things are cultivated, and all germinating, all fructifying and bringing forth the spirit of salvation, as it has been said of the kingdom of God; so equally of these vineyards of the Lord of hosts we can say that they are within us (Luke 17:21). Finally, in the Gospel it is read that the kingdom of God is to be given to the nations doing its fruits (Matt. 21:43). These are those whom Paul enumerates, saying: But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, longsuffering, goodness, kindness, meekness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity (Gal. 5:22, 23). These fruits, our advances. These are accepted by the bridegroom, because he has a care for us. Is God's care for shrubs? The God-Man loves men, not trees, and counts our advances as his fruits. He diligently observes the time of these, smiles upon them appearing, and solicitously is busy lest they perish for us, when they have appeared; rather lest they perish for himself: for he counts himself as us. And therefore providing, he commands the little foxes that lie in wait to be caught for himself, lest they themselves snatch away the new fruits. Catch, he says, for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards. And as if someone should say: You fear prematurely, the time of fruits has not yet come: It is not so, he says: for our vineyard has flowered. After flowers there is no delay of fruits; while those are still falling these break forth at once, at once begin to appear.
63.6: This parable is of the present time. Do you see these novices? They have come lately, they have been converted lately. We cannot say of them that our vineyard has flowered: for it is flowering. Meanwhile, what you see appearing in them is flower: the time of fruits has not yet come. The flower is a new conversation, the flower is the fresh pattern of an amended life. They have put on for themselves a disciplined face, and a good composition of the whole body. The things that are on the face please, I confess: more negligent of course is that culture of bodies which appears outside as to garments, speech rarer, countenance more cheerful, look more modest, gait more mature. But because these have begun newly, by their very newness they are to be counted flowers, and the hope of fruits, rather than fruits. For you, little sons, we do not fear from the fraud of foxes, which are known to envy fruits more than flowers. Your peril is from elsewhere. I certainly fear burning for the flowers; not stealth, but burning from cold. The north wind is suspect to me, and the morning frosts, which are accustomed to destroy unseasonable flowers, to snatch away fruits. And so from the north your evil is spread. From the face of his cold who shall stand? (Ps. 147:17.) If this cold shall once have invaded the soul (the soul's, as usual, by neglect, the spirit drowsing) and then, which God forbid! with no one hindering shall have reached its inward parts, shall have descended into the bowels of the heart and the bosom of the mind, shall have shaken the affections, occupied the paths of counsel, disturbed the light of judgment, enslaved the liberty of the spirit: soon, as is wont to happen in the body to those in fever, a certain rigidity of mind comes on, and vigor grows soft, languor of powers is feigned, horror of austerity is intensified, fear of poverty troubles, the mind contracts, grace is withdrawn, the length of life is drawn out, reason is put to sleep, the spirit is extinguished, the novice's fervor cools, a fastidious lukewarmness grows heavy, fraternal charity grows cold, pleasure flatters, security deceives, habit calls back. What more? The law is dissembled, right is abdicated, the lawful is proscribed, the fear of the Lord is abandoned. At last hands are given to shamelessness; that rash, that shameful, that most foul leap is presumed, full of ignominy and confusion, from the height into the abyss, from the pavement into the dunghill, from the throne into the sewer, from heaven into the mire, from the cloister into the world, from paradise into hell. The beginning and origin of this pest, and either by what art it is avoided, or by what virtue it is overcome, it is not of this time to show: that will be another time; now let us follow what has been begun.
63.7: The sermon is to be turned back to those more advanced and stronger, to the vineyard which has already flowered, for which indeed, although there is nothing that the flowers should fear from cold, yet the fruits are not secure from foxes. It must be said more openly what these foxes are spiritually, why they are called little, why they are especially commanded to be caught, and not driven away, or killed: also diverse kinds of these beasts are to be introduced for the greater knowledge and caution of the hearers; not indeed in this sermon, that we may consult against weariness, and that the eagerness of our devotion may be perpetuated in the grace and confession of the glory of the great Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all things forever. Amen.
63.title: Concerning the vineyard seriously to be cultivated by a pious and wise man, that is, by each one his own life, or his mind and conscience; and concerning the two kinds of foxes, namely, flatterers and detractors; and concerning the temptations of novice monks.

64.1: I am present for my promise. Catch for us the little foxes that demolish the vines: for our vine has flowered (Song 2:15). Foxes are temptations. It is necessary that temptations come. For who will be crowned, except he who has contended lawfully? (2 Tim. 2:5) or how will they contend, if there is lacking one who attacks? You therefore, approaching the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation (Sir. 2:1), certain that all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). Further, temptations are diverse, according to the diversity of times. And in our beginnings indeed, as upon the tender flowers of young plantings, there presses openly a force of cold, of which we made mention in another sermon, and beginning from this plague we rendered the beginners cautious (Above, serm. 63, n. 6). But now, against the holier pursuits of those advancing, contrary virtues by no means dare openly to set themselves, but they are accustomed to lie in wait in secret, like certain fraudulent little foxes; in appearance indeed virtues, but in reality vices. How many, for example, who have entered the ways of life, progressed to better things, advancing and progressing well and securely upon the paths of justice, have I experienced foully tripped up by the fraud, for shame! of these foxes, and late lamenting in themselves the fruits of virtues smothered!
64.2: I have seen a man running well; and behold a thought: was it not a little fox? To how many, he says, could I share the good which I alone enjoy, if I were in my homeland, with brothers and kinsmen, acquaintances and friends? They love me, and would easily assent to one persuading. Why this waste? I go there, and I save many of them, and myself likewise. Nor is there to be fear in a change of place. For, while I do good, what does it matter where? except that there without doubt it is better, where I may live more fruitfully. What more? He goes, and the wretched man perishes, not so much an exile to his homeland, as returned to the vomit of the flesh. And the unhappy man has lost himself, and has acquired none of his own. Behold one little fox, namely that frustratory hope which he had in the acquisition of his own. You too can by yourself in yourself find or notice other and still other ones like this, if you are not negligent.
64.3: Do you wish, however, that I still show you one more? I will make even a third, and I will show a fourth also, if I find you watchful to catch those which by chance from these you notice in your vineyard. Sometimes, of someone progressing well, when he has felt some more abundant dew of heavenly grace sprinkled upon himself, there enters the mind a desire of preaching, not indeed to parents and relatives, according to that: Immediately I did not consent to flesh and blood (Gal. 1:16); but as if more purely, more fruitfully, and more strongly, everywhere to strangers and to all. Cautiously altogether. Indeed he fears to incur the prophetic curse, if he hides among the peoples the wheat which he has received in secret (Prov. 11:26): and to act against the Gospel, unless what he has heard in the ear he has preached upon the housetops (Matt. 10:27). It is a fox, and more harmful than the former by as much as it comes more hidden. But I catch it for you. First Moses says: You shall not plow with the firstborn of the ox (Deut. 15:19). Paul interpreting this: Not a neophyte, he says, lest being lifted up into pride he fall into the judgment of the devil (1 Tim. 3:6): and again, Nor does anyone, he says, take honor to himself, but he who is called by God as Aaron (Heb. 5:4); likewise he himself: How shall they preach, he says, unless they are sent? (Rom. 10:15.) And we know that the office of a monk is not to teach, but to mourn. From these and like things collected I weave for myself a net, and I catch the fox, lest it demolish the vineyard. From these indeed it is clear and certain that to preach publicly neither befits a monk, nor is expedient for a novice, nor is it lawful for one not sent. Further, to go against these three, how great a demolition of conscience is it? Therefore whatever of this sort is suggested to the mind, whether it be your thought, or an injection through an evil angel, recognize as a deceitful little fox, that is, evil under the appearance of good.
64.4: But look at another. How many, fervent in spirit, has the solitude of the desert received from the monasteries, and either cast forth cooled, or held against the law of the desert, not only remiss, but even dissolute? And thus it appeared that a little fox had been present, where so great a devastation of the vineyard was made, that is, the detriment of the life and conscience of a man. He was thinking that if he lived alone, he would receive much more abundant fruits of the spirit, inasmuch as in the common life he had experienced so much spiritual grace. And his thought seemed good to him; but the outcome of the matter showed that that same thought had rather been for him a demolishing fox.
64.5: What of that which so often and so gravely also disturbs us in this house — I speak of the notable and superstitious abstinence of certain ones who are among us, from which they render themselves troublesome to all, and all to themselves? How is this very discord, so general, not both a dissipation of his own conscience, and, as far as in him lies, also a demolition of this great vineyard which the right hand of the Lord has planted, namely of the unanimity of you all? Woe to the man through whom scandal comes? (Matt. 18:7.) He who shall scandalize, he says, one of these little ones (Mark 9:42): hard is what follows. How much harder things does he deserve, who scandalizes so great and so holy a multitude? A most hard judgment indeed will he bear, whoever he is. But these things elsewhere.
64.6: But now let us attend to those things which are said by the Bridegroom concerning these little and cunning animals that demolish the vines. Little I would say, not in malice, but in subtlety. For this kind of animal is by nature cunning, and very ready to harm in secret: and it seems to me to designate most fittingly certain most subtle vices cloaked under the appearance of virtues, the form of which, at least, I have already for some time expressed to notice by the examples set forth, though few. For they cannot otherwise harm, except that they feign themselves virtues by a certain likeness of virtues. And they are either vain thoughts of men, or injections made through evil angels, angels of Satan, who transform themselves into angels of light (2 Cor. 11:14), preparing their arrows in the quiver, that is, in secret, that they may shoot in the dark the upright of heart (Ps. 11:2). Whence I also think they are called little for this reason, that whereas other vices by a certain as it were corpulence of themselves offer themselves openly, this kind, by reason of its subtlety, can hardly easily be recognized, and therefore neither guarded against, except only by the perfect and exercised, and who have the eyes of the heart illuminated unto the discernment of good and evil, and especially unto the discernment of spirits, who with the Apostle can say that we are not ignorant of the crafts of Satan, nor of his thoughts (2 Cor. 2:11). And see lest perhaps for this reason they are commanded by the bridegroom not indeed to be exterminated, or driven away, or killed, but to be caught: namely because spiritual and deceitful little beasts of this sort ought to be observed and examined with all vigilance and caution, and so caught, that is, comprehended, in their craftiness. Therefore, when the deceit is betrayed, when the fraud is opened, when the falsehood is convicted; then most rightly is the little fox said to be caught, which was demolishing the vineyard. Finally, we say that a man is caught in speech, as you have in the Gospel, that the Pharisees came together into one, that they might catch Jesus in speech (Matt. 22:15).
64.7: Thus therefore the bridegroom commands the little foxes that demolish the vines to be caught, that is, to be detected, convicted, betrayed. This kind of malignity alone has this as proper to it, that once known it no longer harms, so that to be recognized is for it to be overcome. For who, unless mad, having discovered a snare, knowingly and wisely puts his foot into it? It is enough therefore if those of this sort are caught, that is, if you betray and lead them into the midst; inasmuch as for them to appear is to perish. Not so the other vices. For they come openly, they harm openly; they captivate the knowing, they overcome those resisting, as acting by force, not by deceit. Therefore against beasts of this sort raging openly there is need not of investigation, but of restraint. These little foxes alone, greatest dissemblers, because once betrayed they no longer harm, it is enough that they be brought into the light, and caught in their cunning. For they have dens. For such a reason therefore these foxes are both commanded to be caught, and described as little. Or little for this reason, that watching vigilantly the nascent vices in their very rising, while at any rate they are little, you may immediately comprehend them, lest growing they harm more and be caught with more difficulty.
64.8: And if according to the allegory we understand the vines as Churches, the foxes as heresies, or rather the heretics themselves: the sense is simple, that heretics be caught rather than put to flight. Let them be caught, I say, not with arms, but with arguments, by which their errors may be refuted; but they themselves, if it can be done, reconciled to the Catholic [Church], recalled to the true faith. For this is the will of him who wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4). This finally he declares that he wills, who not simply [says], catch the foxes, but, catch, he says, for us the foxes. For himself therefore and for his bride, that is, the Catholic [Church], he commands these foxes to be acquired, when he says, Catch them for us. And so a man of the Church, exercised and learned, if he undertakes to dispute with a heretical man, ought to direct his intention to this, that he so convict the one erring that he also convert him, thinking of that of the apostle James: That he who has caused a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, will save his soul from death, and covers a multitude of sins (Jas. 5:20). But if he has been unwilling to return, nor convicted after a first and already a second admonition, inasmuch as he is altogether subverted; he will be according to the Apostle to be avoided (Tit. 3:10). From this point already it is better, as indeed I judge, that he be put to flight, or even bound, than that he be allowed to demolish the vines.
64.9: Nor for that reason indeed let him think he has done nothing, who has conquered and convicted a heretic, confuted heresies, clearly and openly distinguished the probable from the true; has shown by plain and irrefragable reason that perverse dogmas are perverse; has finally reduced to captivity the perverse understanding that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. For he has nonetheless caught, who has wrought such things, a fox, even if not unto salvation for that one; and he has caught it for the bridegroom and the bride, though otherwise. For, even if the heretic has not risen from the dregs, yet the Church is confirmed in the faith: and indeed the bridegroom without doubt congratulates the advances of the bride. For the joy of the Lord is our strength (Neh. 8:10). Finally he does not think our gains alien from himself, who so graciously associates himself with us, while he commands the foxes to be caught, not for himself, but for us with himself. Catch, saying, for us. For it is to be noted what he says, for us. What more social than this voice? Does it not seem to you that he says this, like a certain head of a household, who of himself has nothing, but all things in common with wife and children and household? And he who speaks is God — yet not at all as God does he say it, but as bridegroom.
64.10: Catch for us the foxes. Do you see how socially he speaks, who has no companion? He could have said: For me, but he preferred, for us, delighted with fellowship. O sweetness! o grace! o force of love! Has then the highest of all been made one of all? Who has done this? Love, ignorant of dignity, rich in condescension, powerful in affection, efficacious in persuasion. What more violent? Love triumphs over God. Yet what so not violent? It is love. What is this force, I ask, so violent unto victory, so conquered unto violence? Finally he emptied himself (Phil. 2:7), that you may know it was of love, that fullness was poured out, that height was leveled, that singularity was associated. With whom for you, O admirable bridegroom, so familiar a fellowship? For us, you say, catch. With whom with you? or the Church from the Gentiles? It has been gathered from mortals and sinners. We know who she is. But who are you, so devoted, so ambitious a lover of this Ethiopian woman? Not indeed another Moses, but more than Moses (Num. 12:1). Are you that one fair of form above the sons of men? (Ps. 45:2.) I have said too little; you are the brightness of eternal life, the splendor and figure of the substance of God (Heb. 1:3); finally God above all things blessed throughout the ages. Amen (Rom. 9:5). ADMONITION CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING SERMONS. We have assigned a more fitting place among the letters of various persons to Bernard for the letter of Everwinus, hitherto edited here among the sermons. See Opp. tom. I col. 676. EDIT.
64.title: Concerning the temptations of advanced monks, which the foxes, or temptations more hostile to them, suffer. Likewise concerning the heretics, foxes of the Church, to be caught.

65.1: I have disputed two sermons to you upon one chapter: I prepare a third, if it does not weary you to hear. And I judge it necessary. For as to what pertains indeed to our domestic vineyard, which you are, I think I have done enough in two sermons for its fortification against the snares of a threefold kind of foxes, who are flatterers, detractors, and certain seducing spirits, skilled and accustomed to bring in evils under the appearance of good. But not so of the Lord's vineyard. I speak of that which has filled the earth, of which we also are a portion: a vineyard exceedingly great, planted by the hand of the Lord, redeemed by blood, watered by the word, propagated by grace, made fruitful by the Spirit. Therefore, taking more care of what is my own, I have profited less for the common. But I am moved for it by the multitude of those demolishing it, the fewness of defenders, the difficulty of defense. Concealment makes the difficulty. For although the Church from her beginning has always had foxes, all were quickly discovered and caught. The heretic contended openly (for thence was he most of all a heretic, that he desired to conquer openly), and he succumbed. Thus therefore those foxes were easily caught. For what if, the truth having been set in the light, the heretic remaining in the darkness of his pertinacity, alone bound outside, dried up? — nonetheless the fox was reckoned caught, the impiety condemned, and the impious cast forth, already for show to those who would live, not for fruit. From this, according to the prophet, they had withered breasts, and a sterile womb (Hos. 9:14); because an error publicly confuted does not sprout again, and an opened falsehood does not germinate.
65.2: What shall we do with these most malignant foxes, that they may be able to be caught, who prefer to harm rather than to conquer, and do not even wish to appear, but to creep? All heretics have always had one intention: to snatch glory from singularity of knowledge. This alone, more malignant and more crafty than the other heresies, feeds on others' losses, negligent of its own glory. Taught, I believe, by the examples of the ancients, which when betrayed could not escape, but were immediately caught, it is cautious to work the mystery of iniquity by a new kind of crime, the more freely the more secretly. Finally they have appointed for themselves, as it is said, hiding places, they have established for themselves a wicked speech. Swear, forswear; do not betray the secret. For otherwise they by no means assent even thinly to swear in any way, on account of that from the Gospel: Not to swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth (Matt. 5:34, 35), etc. O foolish and slow of heart, filled plainly with the Pharisaic spirit, straining out the gnat, and swallowing the camel! (Matt. 23:24). Is it not lawful to swear, and is it lawful to forswear? Or in this alone is both lawful? From what place of the Gospels do you produce for me that exception, who do not pass over even an iota, as you falsely boast? It is plain that you both superstitiously observe concerning the oath, and flagitiously presume concerning perjury. O perversity! What was counseled for caution, namely, not to swear; this they observe so contentiously in place of a command: and what has been sanctioned by immovable right, namely that one must not forswear, this as if indifferent they dispense according to their will. Not, they say, but lest we publish the mystery. As if it were not the glory of God to reveal a word. Or do they envy the glory of God? But I rather believe that they blush to open it, knowing it inglorious. For they are said to do unspeakable and obscene things in secret, since indeed the hind parts of foxes also stink.
65.3: But I am silent about what they would deny: let them answer to the manifest. Or according to the Gospel do they beware of giving the holy to dogs, and pearls to swine (Matt. 7:6)? But that is openly to confess that they are not of the Church, who judge all who are of the Church to be dogs and swine. For without exception they think that that thing of theirs, whatever it is, is to be withheld from all who are not of their sect. For the rest, even if they feel this, they will not answer, lest they become manifest, which indeed they flee in every way, but they will not escape. Answer me, O man, who know more than is fitting, and are foolish beyond what can be said. Is the mystery which you hide God's, or not? If it is, why do you not open it to his glory? For the glory of God is to reveal a word. If not, why do you have faith in that which is not of God, unless because you are a heretic? Either therefore let them betray the secret of God to the glory of God; or let them deny the mystery of God, and by no means deny that they are heretics; or certainly nonetheless let them confess themselves manifest enemies of the glory of God; who are unwilling that that become manifest, which they know will be for his glory. For the truth of Scripture stands: The glory of kings is to conceal a word, the glory of God to reveal a speech (Prov. 25:2). Are you unwilling to reveal? Therefore you are unwilling to glorify God. But perhaps you do not receive this Scripture. So it is: they profess themselves emulators of the Gospel alone, and alone. Let them answer therefore to the Gospel. What I say, he says, in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops (Matt. 10:27). Now it is not lawful to be silent. How long is that held hidden, which God commands to be made openly? How long is your Gospel covered? I suspect; yours is not Paul's: for he confesses that his is not covered. And if, he says, our Gospel is covered, it is covered in those who perish (2 Cor. 4:3). See lest he were speaking of you, among whom the Gospel is found covered. What more open than that you perish? Or perhaps you do not receive Paul either? Of certain ones I have so heard. For not among you all do you agree in all things, although you all dissent from us.
65.4: But indeed the words and writings and traditions of those who were bodily with the Savior, you all, unless I am mistaken, receive indifferently with equal authority of the Gospel. Did they hold their Gospel covered? Did they keep silent concerning the weak things of God in the flesh, the horrors of death, the ignominy of the cross? And indeed their sound has gone out into all the earth (Ps. 19:4). Where is the apostolic form and life of which you boast? They cry out, you whisper; they in public, you in a corner; they fly as clouds (Isa. 60:8), you lurk in darkness and in underground houses. What like to them do you show in yourselves? Or that you do not lead about little women with you, but shut them in? Companionship is not equally open to suspicion as cohabitation. But who would suspect anything sinister of those who raised the dead? Do you likewise, and I will think the woman reclining with you a man. Otherwise you rashly usurp for yourself the dispensation of those whose holiness you do not have. To be always with a woman, and not to know a woman, is it not more than to raise a dead man? What is less you cannot; and what is greater you wish me to believe of you? Daily your side is to the side of a young woman at table; your bed to her bed in the chamber, your eyes to her eyes in conversation, your hands to her hands in work: and you wish to be thought continent? Be it that you are: but I am not without suspicion. You are a scandal to me: take away the cause of scandal, by which you may prove yourself a true emulator of the Gospel, as you boast. Does not the Gospel condemn him who shall have scandalized one of the Church? You scandalize the Church. You are a fox demolishing the vineyard. Help me, companions, that she may be caught; or rather catch her for us yourselves, O holy angels. She is very crafty, covered with her iniquity and impiety. Plainly so little and subtle, that she may easily indeed frustrate human gazes. And yours also? Therefore that voice is to you, as comrades of the bridegroom: Catch for us the little foxes (Song 2:15). Therefore do what you are commanded; catch for us this so versatile little fox, which behold for a long time now we pursue in vain. Teach and suggest how the fraud may be detected. For this is to have caught the fox; because a false Catholic harms far more than if a true heretic appeared. But it is not of man to know what is in man, unless perhaps someone for this very thing has been either illuminated by the Spirit of God, or informed by angelic industry. What sign will you give, that this worst heresy may become open, taught to lie not with the tongue only, but with the life?
65.5: And indeed a recent devastation of the vineyard indicates that a fox has been present: but by I know not what art of feigning this most cunning animal so confounds its tracks, that by what way it either enters or exits can hardly easily be detected by man. And though the work is open, the author does not appear; so through those things which are on the face it dissembles all. Finally if you ask about faith, nothing more Christian; if about conversation, nothing more irreprehensible: and what it speaks, it proves by deeds. You may see a man in testimony of his faith frequent the church, honor the priests, offer his gift, make confession, communicate in the sacraments. What more faithful? Now as to what pertains to life and manners, he circumventes no one, surpasses no one, shakes no one. Moreover the mouth is pale with fasts, he does not eat bread idle, he works with his hands whence he sustains life. Where now is the fox? We were holding her: how has she slipped from our hands? How has she disappeared so suddenly? Let us press on, let us investigate: by her fruits we shall know her. And certainly the demolition of vineyards testifies to the fox. Women, having left their husbands, and likewise men, having dismissed their wives, betake themselves to these. Clerics and priests, having left peoples and churches, unshorn and bearded, have often been found among them among weavers and weaving-women. Is this not a grave demolition? are these not the works of foxes?
65.6: But perhaps among all these things are not so manifestly detected: and if they are, there is nothing whence they may be proved. In what way do we catch them? Let us return to the consortium and companionship of women: for among them there is no one who lacks this. I ask some one of these. Ho you, good man! what woman is this, and whence is she to you? Is she your wife? No, he says, for that does not agree with my vow. A daughter then? It is not. What then? Not a sister, not a niece, not belonging to you at least by some degree of kinship or affinity? By none at all. And how is your continence safe for you with this one? Indeed this is not even lawful for you. Cohabitation, if you do not know, of men and women among those who have vowed continence, the Church forbids. If you are unwilling to scandalize the Church, cast out the woman. Otherwise from this one thing the rest, which are not so manifest, without doubt become credible.
65.7: But in what place of the Gospel, he says, do you show me that this is forbidden? You have called upon the Gospel; you will go to the Gospel. If you obey the Gospel, you will not make a scandal: for the Gospel plainly forbids a scandal to be made. But you make one, by not removing this woman according to the constitution of the Church. You were suspect, but now you will openly be judged both a despiser of the Gospel, and an adversary of the Church. What do you judge, brethren? If he has been obstinate so as neither to obey the Gospel, nor to acquiesce to the Church, what can he still tergiversate? Does it not openly seem to you that the fraud has been detected, and the fox comprehended? If he does not remove the woman, he does not remove the scandal; if he does not remove the scandal when he can remove it, he is held a transgressor of the Gospel. What is the Church to do, except that she remove him who is unwilling to remove the scandal, lest she be like him disobedient? For she has a command from this in the Gospel, not to spare the eye scandalizing her, not the hand, not the foot; to pluck it out, to cut these off, and to cast them from herself. If, he says, he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as the heathen and the publican (Matt. 18:6-9, 17).
65.8: Have we done something? I think that we have done. We have caught the fox, because we have perceived the fraud. Manifest are those who were lurking, false Catholics, true plunderers of the Catholic [Church]. For while with me you took sweet foods (I mean the body and blood of Christ), while we walked in the house of God with consent, there was a place for persuading, nay an opportunity of seducing, according to that of Wisdom: The simulator with his mouth deceives his friend (Prov. 11:9). But now easily, according to the wisdom of Paul, after a first and second admonition I will avoid a heretical man, knowing that he is subverted who is of this sort (Tit. 3:10, 11); and therefore cautious to provide, lest he now be also a subverter. And so it is something, according to the word of the Wise Man, that the wicked have been caught in their snares (Prov. 11:6), those wicked especially who are cautious to use snares for arms. For conflict and defense have altogether perished from these. For this kind is base and rustic, and without letters, and altogether unwarlike. Finally they are foxes, and little ones; but neither are those things in which they are said to think badly defensible; nor so subtle as suasible, and that only to rustic little women and idiots, and such indeed as all are, as many as I have still experienced to be of this sect. For in all their assertions, for they are many, I do not recall that I have heard anything new or unheard of, but what is trite, and long ventilated among the ancient heretics, but by ours ground down and winnowed out. Yet it must be said, and I will say, what those ineptitudes are; partly which they themselves, answering less cautiously to Catholics questioning them, have confessed; partly which, divided from one another and litigating, have betrayed concerning one another; partly also which some of them returning to the Church have uncovered: not that I may answer to all, for it is not necessary, but only that they may become known. But that will be the work of another sermon, to the praise and glory of the name of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
65.title: Concerning the clandestine heretics, whose preposterous religion and zeal for concealing their mysteries, and also the scandalous living together with women, he censures.

66.1: Catch for us the little foxes that demolish the vines (Song 2:15). Behold, I am at those foxes. They themselves are they who pass by the way, and strip the vineyard. They are not content to desert the way, unless they can also lay waste the vineyard, adding prevarication. It is not enough that they be heretics, unless they be hypocrites also, that sin may be exceeding sinful. These are they who come in sheep's clothing to strip the sheep and to spoil the rams. Does not both seem to you fulfilled, where both the peoples are found plundered of faith, and the priests of the peoples? Who are these robbers? These are sheep in habit, foxes in craft, wolves in act and cruelty. These are they who wish to seem good, not to be; not to seem evil, but to be. They are evil, and wish to seem good, lest they alone be evil; they fear to seem evil, lest they be too little evil. For malice has always harmed less openly, nor has a good man ever been deceived except by the simulation of good. Thus therefore unto the harm of the good they strive to appear good; they are unwilling to appear evil, that they may be permitted to malign more. For it is not with them to cultivate virtues, but to color vices with a certain as it were vermilion of virtues. Finally they title the impiety of superstition with the name of religion. They define innocence as only not to harm openly, claiming for themselves therefore only the color of innocence. For a covering of turpitude they have marked themselves with a vow of continence. Further they judge turpitude to be reckoned in wives alone: when even that alone which is with a wife is the cause that excuses turpitude in coition. They are rustic men and idiots, and altogether contemptible: but there is not, I tell you, to be dealt with them negligently. For they advance much unto impiety, and their speech creeps as a cancer (2 Tim. 2:16, 17).
66.2: Finally the Holy Spirit has not neglected, who once prophesied of these so manifestly, the Apostle saying: But the Spirit manifestly says that in the last times certain ones will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error, and doctrines of demons, speaking a lie in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding to marry, to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4:1-3). These precisely, these he was saying. These forbid to marry, these abstain from foods which God created, of which we shall see afterward. But now see whether this is not properly a mockery of demons and not of men, according to what the Spirit had foretold. Ask of them the author of their sect; they will give none. What heresy has not had from men its own heresiarch? The Manichaeans had Manes as prince and teacher, the Sabellians Sabellius, the Arians Arius, the Eunomians Eunomius, the Nestorians Nestorius. Thus all the other plagues of this sort are known each to have had single masters, men, from whom they drew origin and name together. By what name or title will you reckon these? By none; because their heresy is not from man, nor have they received it through man. Yet far be it that it be through the revelation of Jesus Christ, but rather and without doubt, as the Holy Spirit foretold, through the injection and fraud of demons, speaking a lie in hypocrisy, forbidding to marry!
66.3: In hypocrisy plainly and with vulpine deceitfulness they speak this, feigning that they say from love of chastity that which they have rather invented for the sake of fostering and multiplying turpitude. Yet the matter is so open, that I wonder how it could ever have been persuaded to a Christian man, unless that these are either so bestial that they do not notice how he who condemns marriage loosens the reins to every uncleanness; or certainly so full of wickedness, and absorbed by diabolical malignity, that noticing they dissemble, and rejoice in the perdition of men. Take from the Church honorable marriage and the undefiled bed (Heb. 13:4); do you not fill her with concubinaries, the incestuous, those who emit seed, soft ones, those who lie with males, and finally with every kind of the unclean? Choose therefore whichever you will, either that all these monsters of men be saved, or that the number of those to be saved be reduced to the fewness of the continent. How sparing in the one! how lavish in the other! Neither of these befits the Savior. What? shall turpitude be crowned? Nothing less becomes the author of honesty. Shall the universality be damned except a few continent ones? This is not to be a Savior. Continence is rare on earth, nor for so small a gain did that fullness empty itself unto the lands. And how have we all received of that, if it granted participation of itself to the continent alone? There is not what they may answer to this. But neither, I believe, to that. If there is a place for honesty in the heavens, but there be no consortium of the honest and the base, as there is no fellowship of light with darkness: surely no place remains for any of the unclean in the place of salvation. If anyone thinks otherwise, the apostolic voice will refute him, asserting without any ambiguity: That they who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God (Gal. 5:21). By what way now will this insidious little fox go out from the cavern? I think her caught in the pit, in which she has made for herself two as it were openings, one by which she may enter, another by which she may exit. For she has been accustomed so. See therefore how on both sides exit has been shut off from her. If she places the continent alone in the heavenly places, salvation perishes for the greatest part; if she places every filth equally with the continent, the honest perishes. But more justly she herself perishes, about to go out neither this way nor that, shut in perpetually, and caught in the pit which she made.
66.4: Certain ones nevertheless, dissenting from the others, confess that marriage can be contracted among virgins alone. But what of reason they can bring in this distinction, I do not see: except that each according to his own pleasure strives in rivalry to tear asunder with a viperous tooth the sacraments of the Church, as the bowels of a mother. For as to what they are said to allege of the first spouses, that they were virgins; what prejudice, I ask, does that hold against the liberty of marriage, that it may not be lawful to be contracted also among non-virgins? But they whisper that they have found I know not what in the Gospel, which they vainly think to favor their ineptitude. That, I believe, which when the Lord had first set forth the testimony from Genesis: And God created man unto his image and likeness, male and female he created them; afterward he brought in: Therefore what God has joined, let man not separate (Gen. 1:27; Matt. 19:4, 6). These, they say, God joined, because both were virgins, and now it was not lawful to be separated: but a coupling presumed otherwise will not be from God. Who told you that they were for that reason joined by God, because they were virgins? For Scripture does not say this. Were they not virgins, he says? They were; but it is not the same thing, joined as virgins, and joined because virgins. Although not even this will you find said by name, that they were virgins, although they were. The diversity of sexes indeed is expressed, not virginity, when it was said: Male and female he created them. Deservedly indeed. For the marital coupling of bodies does not require integrity, but aptitude of sexes. Well therefore the Holy Spirit, instituting it, expressed sex, and was silent about virginity, nor gave occasion of hunting a word to the insidious little foxes. Which indeed they would gladly have done; although that also in vain. For what if he had said: He created them virgins? Would you for that reason at once have obtained that virgins alone are permitted to be joined? And yet how would you have exulted from the sole occasion of a word? how would you have blown away second and third marriages? how would you have insulted the Catholic [Church], joining harlots and panders to one another the more gladly, by as much as she does not doubt that they thereby pass from the base to the honest? Perhaps you would also rebuke God commanding the prophet to take a fornicating woman (Hos. 1:2): but now both occasion is lacking, and it pleases to be a heretic for nothing. For the testimony which you have usurped to build up your error has been found to avail more for destroying it; to do nothing for you, very much against you.
66.5: But now hear what either confounds you altogether, or corrects you, and wholly crushes and shatters your heresy. A woman for as long a time as her husband lives is bound to the husband; but if her husband shall have slept, she is loosed from the law of the husband; let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:39). It is Paul who grants to the widow that she may marry whom she will: and you on the contrary command: Let none marry except a virgin, and this only to a virgin, so that not even she herself may marry whom she will. Why do you shorten the hand of God? why do you restrict the ample blessing of nuptials? why do you claim as proper to the virgin what has been granted to the sex? Paul would not grant this, unless it were lawful. But I say too little, he grants: he also wills. I will, he says, that the younger women marry (1 Tim. 5:14): nor is it doubtful that he means widows. What more manifest? Therefore what he grants, because it is lawful; he also wills, because it is expedient. What is lawful and expedient, does the heretic forbid? From this prohibition he will persuade nothing, except that he is a heretic.
66.6: It remains that we also somewhat agitate these concerning the rest of the apostolic prophecy. For these abstain, as that one foretold, from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4:3): proving themselves heretics from this also, not indeed because they abstain, but because they abstain heretically. For I also sometimes abstain; but my abstinence is satisfaction for sins, not superstition for impiety. Do we refute Paul, that he chastises his body, and brings it into servitude? (1 Cor. 9:27.) I will abstain from wine, because in wine is luxury (Eph. 5:18); or if I am infirm, I will use a little, according to the counsel of Paul (1 Tim. 5:23). I will abstain from meats, lest while they nourish the flesh too much, they nourish at the same time also the vices of the flesh. The bread itself I will strive to take with measure, lest with a burdened belly it weary me to stand for praying, and lest the prophet also upbraid me, that I have eaten my bread in satiety (Ezek. 16:49). But neither with simple water even will I be accustomed to gorge myself, lest the distension of the belly reach even unto the titillation of lust. The heretic otherwise. For he abhors milk, and whatever is made from it: finally everything that is created from coition. Rightly and Christianly, if not for this reason because from coition, but lest they provoke unto coition.
66.7: For the rest, what does it mean, that so generally everything which is generated from coition is avoided? That observance of foods so signally expressed generates suspicion for me. Nevertheless if you bring this to us from the rule of physicians, we do not reprehend care of the flesh, which no one has ever held in hatred, if nonetheless it has not been excessive. If from the discipline of those who abstain, that is, the school of spiritual physicians; we also approve the virtue by which you tame the flesh, bridle lust. But if from the insanity of Manes you prescribe against the beneficence of God, so that what he created and gave to be received with thanksgiving, you not only ungrateful, but also a rash censor decree unclean, and abstain as from an evil; I will not at all praise the abstinence, but I will execrate the blasphemy: I would rather say you unclean, who think something unclean. All things are clean to the clean, says that best estimator of things: and nothing unclean, except to him who thinks something unclean: But to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but their mind and conscience is polluted (Tit. 1:15). Woe to you who reject the foods which God created, judging them unclean and unworthy to be passed into your bodies: when for that reason the body of Christ, which is the Church, has spit you out as polluted and unclean.
66.8: I am not unaware that they boast that they alone are the body of Christ: but let those persuade themselves of this who have also been persuaded of that, that they have power daily at their table to consecrate the body and blood of Christ unto nourishing themselves into the body of Christ and members. For they boast that they are successors of the apostles, and name themselves apostolics, yet able to show no sign of their apostleship. How long is the lamp under a bushel? You are the light of the world, was said to the apostles: and therefore the apostles upon a candlestick, that they may shine to the whole world. Let it shame successors of the apostles not to be the light of the world, but of the bushel, but darkness of the world. Let us say to them: You are the darkness of the world: and let us pass to other things. They say they are the Church. But they contradict him who says: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt. 5:14-16). Do you so believe the stone cut from the mountain without hands, made a mountain, and filling the world (Dan. 2:34, 35), shut up in your caves? And not even here must one linger. The opinion itself flees being published, content with its own whispering. Christ has, and always will have, his inheritance entire, and his possession the ends of the earth. Rather they withdraw themselves from this great inheritance, who try to snatch it from Christ.
66.9: See the detractors, see the dogs. They mock us, that we baptize infants; that we pray for the dead; that we seek the suffrages of the saints. In every kind of men and in either sex they hasten to proscribe Christ, in adults and little ones, in the living and the dead; here indeed prescribing to infants from the impossibility of nature, there to adults from the difficulty of continence. Further defrauding the dead of the helps of the living, spoiling the living nonetheless of the suffrages of the saints who have departed. Far be it! The Lord will not leave his people, which is as the sand of the sea, nor will he be content with the fewness of heretics, who has redeemed all. For with him redemption is not small, but plainly copious. But what is the number of these to the greatness of the price? Rather they defraud themselves of the price, who try to empty it. For what if the infant cannot speak for himself, for whom the voice of the blood of his brother, and of such a brother, cries to God from the earth? Mother Church also stands and cries nonetheless. Yet what of the infant? Does he not also seem to you somehow to gape at the fountains of the Savior, to cry out to God, and with his wailings to clamor: Lord, I suffer violence, answer for me? (Isa. 38:14.) He demands the help of grace, because he suffers violence from nature. The innocence of the wretched cries, the ignorance of the little one cries, the infirmity of the condemned cries. Thus therefore all these cry, the blood of the brother, the faith of the mother, the destitution of the wretched, and the misery of the destitute: and it is cried to the Father. Further the Father cannot deny himself: for he is a father.
66.10: Let no one tell me that he has not faith, to whom the mother imparts her own, wrapping it for him in the Sacrament, until he become fit by his own, not only sense, but also assent, to perceive it unwrapped and pure. Is it a short cloak, that it cannot cover both? Great is the faith of the Church. Is it less than the faith of the Canaanite woman, which is established to have been able to suffice both for the daughter and for herself? Therefore she heard: O woman, great is your faith! be it to you as you have asked (Matt. 15:28). Is it less than the faith of those who, letting down the paralytic through the tiles, obtained for him salvation of soul and of body together? Finally you have: Whose faith when he saw, he said to the paralytic: Have confidence, son, your sins are forgiven you; and a little after: Take up your bed, and walk (Matt. 9:2, 5, 6). He who believes these things will easily be persuaded that the Church rightly presumes not only salvation for little ones baptized in her faith, but also the crown of martyrdom for infants slain for Christ. Which things being so, the regenerated will suffer no prejudice from that which was said: Without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6), since they are not without faith, who have received the grace of baptism in testimony of faith. But neither from that which was likewise said: But he who has not believed will be condemned (Mark 16:16). For what is it to believe, except to have faith? And so both the woman will be saved through the generation of children, if she shall have persevered in faith with mildness (1 Tim. 2:15); and help will be given to infants through the washing of regeneration; and adults who will not have been able to contain themselves will redeem themselves by the thirtyfold fruit of marriage; the dead also who will have need, and will be worthy, will receive the prayers and sacrifices of the living, mediating angels; and of those who have already arrived, consolations will by no means be lacking to those still living through God who is everywhere, and in God by the affection of charity of those nowhere absent. For Christ also for this died and rose again, that he might be Lord of the living and of the dead (Rom. 14:9). For this also an infant was born, and through each of the grades of ages advanced unto a man, that he might be lacking to no age.
66.11: They do not believe that a purgatorial fire remains after death; but that the soul at once loosed from the body passes either unto rest, or unto damnation. Let them ask therefore of him who said that there is a certain sin, which would be forgiven neither in this world nor in the future (Matt. 12:32), why he said this, if no remission or purgation of sin remains in the future. Now indeed those who do not acknowledge the Church, it is no wonder if they detract from the orders of the Church, if they do not receive the institutions, if they despise the Sacraments, if they do not obey the commands. Sinners, they say, are the apostolics, archbishops, bishops, priests: and through this fit neither for giving nor for receiving the sacraments. Shall these two never agree, to be a bishop and a sinner? It is false. Caiaphas was a bishop: and yet how great a sinner, who was dictating against the Lord a sentence of death? If you deny him a bishop, the testimony of John will refute you, who reports that he even prophesied in testimony of his pontificate (John 11:51). Judas was an apostle: and although avaricious and wicked, yet chosen by the Lord. Or do you doubt of the apostleship of him whom the Lord chose? Have not I, he says, chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil? (John 6:71.) You hear the same one chosen an apostle, and to have been a devil; and do you deny that one can be a bishop who is a sinner? Upon the chair of Moses sat the Scribes and Pharisees, and they who did not obey them as bishops were guilty of disobedience, even against the Lord himself commanding, and saying: What they say, do (Matt. 23:2, 3). It is plain therefore that although Scribes, although Pharisees, although namely the greatest sinners; yet because of the chair of Moses, to them also nonetheless pertains what he likewise said: He who hears you, hears me; and he who despises you, despises me (Luke 10:16).
66.12: Many other evils indeed have been persuaded to this foolish and unwise people by spirits of error, speaking a lie in hypocrisy: but it is not to answer to all. For who knows all things? Further the labor would be infinite, by no means necessary. For as to these, they are neither convicted by reasons, because they do not understand; nor corrected by authorities, because they do not receive them; nor bent by persuasions, because they are subverted. It has been proved: they choose rather to die than to be converted. Their end is destruction, their last things fire awaits. For of these indeed in the deed of Samson from the kindled tails of foxes a figure went before (Judg. 15:4, 5). Often the faithful, laying hands on them, have dragged some of them into the midst. Asked concerning the faith, when concerning the things of which they seemed suspect they denied all things altogether after their manner; examined by the judgment of water, they were found liars. And when now they could not deny, inasmuch as detected, the water not receiving them; having seized, as it is said, the bit with their teeth, as wretchedly as freely they have not confessed but professed impiety, openly asserting piety, and ready to undergo death for it.
