Nor less ready to inflict it were those who stood by. And so the people rushing upon them gave to the heretics new martyrs of their own perfidy. We approve the zeal, but we do not counsel the deed; because faith is to be persuaded, not imposed. Although without doubt they are better coerced by the sword, namely of him who does not bear the sword without cause, than permitted to transfer many into their error. For he is the minister of God, an avenger unto wrath for him who does evil (Rom. 13:4).
66.13: Some wonder that they were led to death not only patiently, but even gladly, as it seemed; but they who less notice how great is the power of the devil, not only in the bodies of men, but also in the hearts, which once permitted he has possessed. Is it not more that a man lay hands upon himself than that he willingly sustain it from another? But this we have frequently experienced the devil to have been able in many, who have either drowned or hanged themselves. Finally Judas hanged himself (Matt. 27:5), the devil without doubt injecting. Yet I judge it greater, and more do I marvel, that he could have injected into his heart that he should betray the Lord (John 13:2), than that he should hang himself. Nothing therefore similar have the constancy of martyrs and the pertinacity of these; because contempt of death in those piety works, in these hardness of heart. And therefore the Prophet was saying perhaps in the voice of a martyr: Their heart is curdled like milk, but I have meditated on your law (Ps. 119:70): namely for this reason that although the punishment seemed the same, the intention was far diverse; that one hardening the heart against the Lord, this one meditating in the law of the Lord.
66.14: Which things being so, there is no need, as I have said, to say many things in vain against most foolish and most obstinate men: it is enough that they have become known that they may be avoided. Wherefore that they may be detected, they must be compelled either to cast out the women, or to go out from the Church, inasmuch as scandalizing the Church in the living-together and companionship of women. It is greatly to be lamented that not only lay princes, but also certain ones, as it is said, of the clergy, and even of the order of bishops who ought rather to have persecuted them, sustain them for gain, receiving gifts from them. And how, they say, shall we condemn those neither convicted nor confessed? Frivolous enough, not a reason, but an occasion. By this alone, even if there were nothing else, you easily detect them, if, as I have said, you separate from one another the men and women who call themselves continent: and compel the women indeed to live with others of their sex and vow; the men equally with men of the same purpose. For by this provision will be made at once for the vow and the fame of both, when they will have both witnesses and guardians of their continence. But if they do not sustain it, they will most justly be eliminated from the Church, which they scandalize, not only by notable, but also by illicit cohabitation. Therefore let these things suffice for detecting the deceits of these foxes, unto giving knowledge and caution to the beloved and glorious bride of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is above all things God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
66.title: Concerning the errors of heretics about marriage, the baptism of children, purgatory, prayers for the dead, and the invocation of the saints.

67.1: My beloved is mine, and I am his (Song 2:16). Thus far the words of the bridegroom. May he himself be present, that we may be able worthily to investigate the words of his bride, to his glory and to our own salvation. For they are not such as can be considered and discussed by us, as is fitting, unless he himself has been the guide of the word. For they are as sweet to grace as they are fruitful to the senses, and as profound too to mysteries. To what shall I compare them? For the present, to some one of the dishes, which stands out by a certain threefold grace; delicious to the taste, solid to nourishment, effective to medicine. Thus, I say, thus does each single word of the bride both soothe the affection from that which sounds sweetly, and fatten and nourish the mind by the abundance of the senses; and by the depth of its mysteries, while it exercises the intellect the more, it frightens it the more, in a wonderful way it heals the swelling of puffed-up knowledge. For if some one of those who seem to themselves to know should give himself more curiously to the scrutiny of these words, when he has seen the powers of his own ability give way, and has perceived every understanding led into captivity, will he not, humbled, be driven to that voice, so as to say: Your knowledge has become wonderful to me; it is strengthened, and I shall not be able to reach it? (Ps. 139:6.) And now indeed what a mark of sweetness does the beginning of her words put forward? For see what a beginning she has given. My beloved, she says, is mine, and I am his. It seems a simple voice, because it sounds sweetly; but concerning this it will be seen afterwards.
67.2: But now she begins from love, she proceeds concerning the beloved, showing that she knows nothing else but the beloved. It is clear of whom the speech is: not so with whom. For it is not permitted to feel that she is with him himself, since he himself is no longer present. Nor is that doubtful: for soon she seems to recall him, and as it were to cry after his back: Return, she says, my beloved. From which we are led to conjecture nothing else for certain, but that when his words were finished, he again absented himself in his own manner, and she remained nonetheless speaking of him who is never absent to himself. So it is: she kept in her mouth him who did not depart from her heart, not even when he was departing. What goes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Luke 6:45). Therefore she speaks of her beloved, as one truly beloved and truly to be loved, because she loves much. We seek with whom: for of whom, we know. And nothing occurs, unless perhaps with the young maidens, who cannot be absent from the mother, when the bridegroom has departed. But better, as I think, do we feel that she has spoken thus with herself rather than with another, especially since that speech is found truncated and little self-contained, plainly insufficient to give understanding to the hearer, on account of which especially we speak with one another. My beloved is mine, she says, and I am his. Nothing more? The speech hangs suspended; rather, it does not hang, but fails. The hearer is suspended, and is not cut short, but is lifted up.
67.3: What is this that she says, he is mine, and I am his? We do not know what she says, because we do not feel what she feels. O holy soul, what is your beloved to you, what are you to him? What, I ask, is this so familiar and so favorable an interchange and requital running between you? He to you, and you in turn to him. But what? The very same to him, which he is to you, or something else? If you speak to us, if you speak to our understanding, declare plainly what you feel: How long do you lift up our souls? Or, according to the prophet, is your secret yours? (Isa. 24:16.) So it is: affection has spoken, not understanding, and therefore not to the understanding. To what then? To nothing, except that, wonderfully delighted and vehemently moved toward the longed-for utterances, with him making the end she could not at all keep wholly silent, nor yet express what she felt. For she did not speak thus in order to express, but in order not to be silent. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth has spoken, but not in proportion to the abundance. Affections have their own utterances, through which they betray themselves even when they do not wish: fear, for example, fearful ones, grief groaning ones, love joyful ones. Do the lamentations of the grieving, or the sobs and groans of the mourning, the sudden and frenzied cries of the stricken, and likewise of the trembling, or indeed the belches of the satiated, does use produce, or reason arouse, or deliberation order, or premeditation form? It is certain that things of this sort do not come forth by the nod of the mind, but burst forth by its movement. Thus burning and vehement love, especially divine love, when it cannot contain itself within itself, does not attend to with what order, by what law, or with what series or fewness of words it bubbles forth, provided only that it feels no loss to itself from this. Sometimes it requires no words, sometimes no utterances at all, content for this with sighs alone. From this it is that the bride, burning with holy love, and that in an incredible way, certainly for the sake of capturing some small escape of the ardor she suffers, does not consider what or how she utters: but whatever comes to her mouth, driven by love she does not enunciate but belches forth. Why should she not belch forth, thus refreshed and thus filled?
67.4: Run through the text of this epithalamium from its very beginning up to this point, and see if so great an abundance was ever granted her anywhere, as on this occasion in all the visitations and addresses of the bridegroom; and if she ever received from his mouth not only so many, but also so pleasant words. She, therefore, who had filled her desire with good things, what wonder if she made a belch rather than a word? And if she seems to you to have made a word, think that it was belched out, and not adorned or preordained. For the bride does not think it a robbery to fit to herself the saying of the Prophet: My heart has belched out a good word (Ps. 45:2), since she is filled with the same spirit. My beloved is mine, and I am his. It has nothing of consequence; something is lacking to the speech. What of it? It is a belch. Why do you seek in a belch the joinings of orations, the formalities of words? What laws or rules do you impose upon your belch? It does not receive your moderation, does not expect composition from you, does not require convenience or opportunity. By itself, out of the inmost parts, not only when you do not wish, but even when you do not know, it bursts forth, torn out rather than emitted. Nevertheless the belch carries an odor, sometimes good, sometimes bad, according to the contrary qualities of the vessels from which it ascends. In short, the good man out of his good treasure brings forth good things, and the evil man evil (Matt. 12:35). The bride of my Lord is a good vessel, and there is a good odor to me from her.
67.5: I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, who have deigned to admit me at least to smelling. Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from the table of their masters (Matt. 15:27). To me, I confess, the belch of your beloved smells well, and from her fullness, however little, I gladly receive. She belches out to me the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, and I have smelled something ineffable of your condescension and love in this voice: My beloved is mine, and I am his. Let her, as is fitting, feast and exult in your sight, and delight in gladness: yet let her exceed for you in such a way that she may be sober for us. Let her therefore be filled with the good things of your house, and be given to drink from the torrent of your pleasure: but, I ask, let there reach me, a poor man, even a thin odor as she belches forth, when she has been satiated. Moses belched well for me, and there is a good odor in his belch, of creating power: In the beginning, he says, God created heaven and earth (Gen. 1:1). Isaiah well: for he gave the most sweet odor of redeeming mercy, belching thus: He delivered his soul to death, and was reckoned with the wicked, and he himself bore the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors (Isa. 53:12), that they might not perish. What smells equally of mercy? There is also a good belch from the mouth of Jeremiah; a good one from David, who said: My heart has belched out a good word. All were filled with the Holy Spirit, and belching forth they filled all things with goodness. Do you seek the belch of Jeremiah? I have not forgotten; I was already preparing it. It is good to await in silence the salvation of the Lord (Lam. 3:26). It is his, I am not mistaken; bring it to your nostrils: the sweetness of rewarding justice, which it brings, surpasses balsam. He wills that I, patient for justice, await the reward in the future, not receive it in the present, because the reward of justice, salvation, is not of the world, but of the Lord. If he has delayed, he says, wait for him (Hab. 2:3); and do not murmur, because it is good to wait with silence. Therefore I will do what he urges; I will wait for the Lord my Savior.
67.6: But I am a sinner, and a great way still remains for me, because salvation is far from sinners. Yet I will not murmur: in the mean time I will comfort myself in the odor. The just man will rejoice in the Lord, by taste experiencing what I feel by smell. Whom the just man beholds, the sinner awaits; and expectation is an odor. For the expectation, it says, of the creature awaits the revelation of the sons of God (Rom. 8:19). Moreover, to behold is to taste, and to see that the Lord is sweet. Or rather, is he blessed who both awaits and already holds? In short, the expectation of the just is gladness (Prov. 10:28). For the sinner awaits nothing. And he is a sinner for this very reason, that, detained and even content with present goods, he awaits nothing in the future, deaf to that voice: Wait for me, says the Lord, in the day of my resurrection, in the future (Zeph. 3:8). And therefore Simeon was just, because he awaited and already smelled Christ in spirit, whom he did not yet adore in the flesh. And blessed in his expectation, because by the odor of expectation he came to the taste of contemplation. In short he says: And my eyes have seen your salvation (Luke 2:25). The just Abraham also, who himself likewise waited to see the day of the Lord, and was not confounded in his expectation; for he saw and rejoiced (John 8:56). The just apostles, when they heard: And you be like men awaiting their lord (Luke 12:36, 30).
67.7: Why should not David also be just, when he was saying: Waiting I waited for the Lord? (Ps. 40:2.) He himself is the fourth of the number of my above-named belchers, whom I had almost passed over. It is not expedient, indeed. This man opened his mouth and drew in the spirit (Ps. 119:131), and being satiated not only belched, but also sang. Good Jesus! how much sweetness has this man poured into my nostrils and ears in his belch and song concerning the oil of gladness with which God, your God, anointed you above your companions: from myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments, from the ivory palaces, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor! (Ps. 45:8-10.) Would that you deign me the encounter of so great a seer and friend of yours in the day of solemnity and gladness, when he goes forth from your chamber, singing his epithalamium on the pleasant psaltery with the cithara, abounding in delights, sprinkled and sprinkling all things with this sort of perfumed powder! In that day, or rather in that hour: for it is an hour if ever it is, and perhaps not even an hour, but half an hour, according to that saying of Scripture: There was made silence in heaven as it were for half an hour (Rev. 8:1): therefore in that hour my mouth will be filled with joy, and my tongue with exultation, while I feel each one of the single verses, I do not say psalms, to be a belch, and indeed odoriferous above all spices. What is more fragrant than the belch of John, who smells to me of the eternity, the generation, the divinity of the Word? What shall I say of the belches of Paul, with how great sweetness they have filled the world? In short, he was a good odor of Christ in every place (2 Cor. 2:14, 15). He certainly offers words unutterable, though not that I may hear, yet that I may long for them, and that it may please me to smell what it is not lawful to hear (2 Cor. 12:4). For I do not know in what manner, the more they lie hidden, the more they please, and we gape more eagerly after things denied. But now consider a like thing in the bride: how, like Paul, in the present chapter she neither opens her secret, nor yet passes it by untouched, granting something as it were to our sense of smell, which perhaps she has judged for the time not to befit our taste, whether on account of our unworthiness, or on account of our incapacity.
67.8: My beloved is mine, and I am his. Concerning which there is no doubt: in this place indeed the mutual love of the two burns; but in the love the supreme happiness of the one is certain, the wonderful condescension of the other. For this agreement or embrace is not between equals. But that she should glory from this prerogative of love that so much has been spent on her and repaid in turn by her, who may presume to know clearly, except he who by pre-eminent purity of mind and sanctity of body has merited to experience something of the sort in himself? It is a matter of the affections; nor is it reached by reason, but by conformity. How few, truly, there are who say: But we, beholding with uncovered face the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).
67.9: But in order that what is read may be reduced to some form, however slight, of understanding: saving indeed the bride's own singular secret, to which for the present it is not given to approach, especially to such as we are; something ought certainly to be set before us, so much the more adapted to the common sense as it is more customary, which may give both sequence to the words and understanding to the little ones. And to me indeed it seems enough for our gross and, as it were, popular understanding, if, in saying: My beloved is mine, we understand in addition: He attends; so that the sense may be: My beloved attends to me, and I to him. Although yet neither have I alone felt this, nor am I the first, since the Prophet said before me: Waiting I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me. You have openly the attention of the Lord to the Prophet; and you have the attention of the Prophet to the Lord in that which he says: Waiting I waited. For he who waits attends, and to wait is to attend. The very same sense, almost the same words are in the Prophet as in the bride, but transposed by the Prophet. For he placed first that which she placed later, and conversely.
67.10: But the bride has spoken more rightly, not setting forth her merit first, but putting the benefit first, and confessing that she has been anticipated by the grace of her beloved. Rightly altogether. For who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him? (Rom. 11:35.) In short, hear John, what he felt concerning this in his Epistle. In this is love, he says, not as it were that we have loved God, but that he first loved us (1 John 4:10). The Prophet, however, although he kept silent about the prevention of grace, did not deny the following; plainly he did not keep silent. But receive also in another place his more certain confession concerning this matter. And your mercy, he says (he was speaking to the Lord), will follow me all the days of my life (Ps. 23:6). Hear also his no less certain and manifest knowledge concerning the prevention itself. My God, he says, his mercy will prevent me (Ps. 59:11); likewise to the Lord: Quickly, he says, let your mercies anticipate us, because we have been made exceedingly poor (Ps. 79:8). Beautifully the bride, unless I am mistaken, places these same words later, not in the same order, but follows the order of the Prophet as well, speaking in this way: I to my beloved, and my beloved to me. Why so? Surely that then she may prove herself more full of grace, when she shall have given all to grace, ascribing to it both the first and the last parts. Otherwise how is she full of grace, if she has anything which is not of grace? There is no place by which grace may enter, where merit has already taken possession. Therefore the full confession of grace already signifies the fullness of grace itself in the soul of the one confessing. For if anything of her own is in her, in so far as it is, grace must needs yield to it. Whatever you ascribe to merits is lacking to grace. I do not wish a merit which excludes grace. I shrink from whatever is of my own, so that I may be my own, unless what is perhaps more mine is that which makes me mine. Grace restores me to myself, freely justified, and thus freed from the servitude of sin. In short, where the Spirit is, there is liberty.
67.11: O foolish bride, the Synagogue, which, despising the justice of God, that is, the grace of her bridegroom, and wishing to establish her own, has not been subject to the justice of God! On account of this the wretched one was put away, and she is no longer a bride, but the Church, to whom it is said: I have espoused you to me in faith; I have espoused you to me in judgment and in justice; I have espoused you to me in mercy and in mercies (Hos. 2:19, 20). Nor did you choose me, but I chose you; nor, that I might choose you, did I find merits of yours, but I anticipated them. Thus therefore in faith I espoused you to me, and not in the works of the law; and I espoused you in justice, but the justice which is of faith, not of the law. It remains that you judge a right judgment between me and you, the judgment in which I espoused you, where it is established that not your merit but my good pleasure intervened. This, however, is the judgment, that you not extol your merits, not prefer the works of the law, not boast of the weight of the day and the heat, since you are known to be espoused rather in faith and in the justice which is of faith, and also in mercy and in mercies.
67.12: She who is truly a bride acknowledges these things, and confesses both graces: first indeed that which is first, by which she was anticipated; afterwards, however, also the subsequent one. She says therefore now: My beloved is mine, and I am his; giving the beginning to the beloved. In what follows: I, she says, to my beloved, and my beloved to me; equally conceding to him the consummation. Now let us see what she says: My beloved is mine. For if this is received, that we understand in addition, he attends, as we have already said, and as the Prophet says: Waiting I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me: in this word I feel something not quite small, nor of middling prerogative. But a matter worthy of all eagerness is not to be thrust upon weary ears and minds. If it does not burden, let it be put off, and not for long; tomorrow's sermon will begin from there. Only pray that in the mean time the grace and mercy of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever, may guard us from the crowding occupations. Amen.
67.title: Concerning the wonderful affection of the bride's love, which she pours forth on account of the love of Christ the bridegroom.

68.1: Hear now what we put off yesterday; hear the joy which I felt. And it is yours: hear, rejoicing. In one word of the bride I felt this, and as one who had smelled it I hid it, to be set before you today the more festively, the more seasonably. The bride has spoken, and has said that the bridegroom attends to her. Who is the bride, and who is the bridegroom? This one is our God: and she, if I dare to say it, we ourselves are, with the rest of that great multitude of captives whom he himself knows. Let us rejoice: this is our glory; we are those upon whom God attends. Yet how great the disparity. What are the earth-born and the sons of men before him? According to the prophet, they are as if they were not, and are counted before him as nothing and vanity (Isa. 40:17). What then does this comparison, between such unequal parties, intend for itself? Either she glories immeasurably, or he loves immeasurably. How admirable it is, that she claims his attention for herself as it were her own, saying: My beloved is mine? Nor, however, content with that, she proceeds to glory further, that she responds to him as it were on equal terms, complies with him, repays him in turn. For it follows: And I am his (Song 2:16). An insolent word, and I am his. Nor is my beloved is mine less insolent: except that both together are more insolent than either.
68.2: O what a pure heart dares, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith! On me, she says, he attends. Is that majesty, upon which rests equally the governance and the administration of the universe, so intent upon her; and is the care of the ages transferred to the sole business, nay, leisure, of this love and desire? Indeed plainly so. For she is the Church of the elect, of whom the Apostle: All things, he says, for the elect (2 Tim. 2:10). And to whom is it doubtful, that the grace and mercy of God is upon his saints, and his regard upon his elect? (Wis. 4:15.) Therefore we do not deny providence to the other creatures: but the bride claims the care for herself. Is God concerned about oxen? (1 Cor. 9:9.) Nor is there doubt that we can say the same of horses, of camels, of elephants, and of all the beasts of the earth: likewise of the fishes of the sea, and the birds of the air; finally of everything which is upon the earth, those alone being excepted, to whom it is said: Casting all your care upon him, because he has care of you (1 Pet. 5:7). Does it not seem to you that it is said as it were in these words: Attend to him, because he attends to you? And observe the apostle Peter (for these are his words), whether he also has not observed the order of the words of the bride. For indeed he does not say: Casting all your care upon him, that he may have care of you; but, because he has care of you: thereby openly showing that the Church of the saints is not only beloved, but that she was first loved.
68.3: It is established that that word does not pertain to her, which the Apostle said about oxen: for he who loved her has care of her, and gave himself for her. Is not this that erring sheep, the care of which was even preferred to the care of the heavenly flocks? In short, having laid those aside, the shepherd came down to this one, sought her diligently, and having found her did not lead her back, but carried her back: with her and about her he brought into the heavens new feasts of joys, the peoples of the angels being invited to the solemnity (Luke 15:4-7, 10). What then? he deigned to carry her back on his own shoulders; and will he not have care of her? Therefore she is not confounded to say: The Lord is solicitous for me (Ps. 40:18). Nor does she think she errs, when she likewise says: The Lord will repay for me (Ps. 138:8); and if there is anything else, which seems to signify the care of God about her. From this it is that she calls the Lord of hosts her beloved, and glories that he who judges all things with tranquillity (Wis. 12:18) attends to her. Why should she not glory? She has heard him saying to her: Can a mother forget, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? And if she has forgotten, I yet will not forget you (Isa. 49:15). In short, the eyes of the Lord are upon the just (Ps. 34:16). And what is the bride, but the congregation of the just? What is she, but the generation of those seeking the Lord, of those seeking the face of the bridegroom? For he does not attend to her, and she not to him. Therefore she sets down both, saying: He is mine, and I am his. He is mine, because he is kind and merciful; I am his, because I am not ungrateful. He gives me grace from grace, I give him grace for grace; he to my liberation, I to his honor; he to my salvation, I to his will; he to me, and not to another, because I am his one dove; I to him, and not to another: for I do not hear the voice of strangers; nor do I assent to those saying to me: Behold, here is Christ; or: Behold, there he is (Mark 13:21). This is the Church.
68.4: What of each single one of us? do we think that there is anyone among us to whom what is said can be fitted? What did I say, among us? But I, indeed, if anyone should seek this of anyone established within the Church, should not judge him altogether to be reprehended. For the account of one is not the same as that of many. In short, not for one soul, but for many to be gathered into one Church, to be bound into one bride, did God do and bear so many and such great things, when he wrought salvation in the midst of the earth. That most dear one is one to one, not cleaving to another bridegroom, not yielding to another bride. What would she not dare before so ambitious a lover? What would she not hope from him, who sought her from heaven, called her from the ends of the earth? Nor did he only seek, but he acquired. Add also, concerning the manner of the acquisition, in the blood of the acquirer. At other times, however, as is customary, she presumes the more on this account, because, looking ahead to the future, she does not ignore that the Lord himself has need. Do you ask for what? To see in the goodness of his elect, to rejoice in the gladness of his people, that he may be praised with his inheritance (Ps. 106:5). Nor do you think this work a small one: no work, I tell you, will remain perfect, if this one falters. Does not the end of all things hang upon the state and consummation of the Church? Take her away, and this lower creature in vain awaits the revelation of the sons of God. Take her away, and neither the patriarchs nor the prophets will be consummated, since Paul affirms that God has so provided for us, that without us they should not be consummated (Heb. 11:40). Take her away, and the very glory of the holy angels, on account of the imperfection of their number, will go lame, nor will the city of God rejoice in its integrity.
68.5: From where then will the purpose of God be fulfilled, and the mystery of his will, and that great sacrament of piety? From where, in the end, will you give me infants and sucklings, out of whose mouth God may perfect his praise? (Ps. 8:3.) Heaven has no infants; the Church has them, to whom indeed it says: I gave you milk to drink, not food (1 Cor. 3:2). And these are invited by the Prophet, as to the completing, as it were, of the praise, who says: Praise the Lord, you children (Ps. 113:1). Do you think our God will have the whole praise of his glory, until those come who sing to him in the sight of the angels: We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we have seen evils? (Ps. 90:15.) The heavens have not known this kind of gladness, except through the sons of the Church; no one ever rejoices in this, who never is not rejoicing. Seasonably does joy come after sadness, rest after labor, port after shipwreck. Security pleases all, but him the more who was afraid. Light is pleasant to all, but more pleasant to him escaping from the power of darkness. To have passed from death to life doubles the grace of life. This is my portion in the heavenly banquet, and apart from the blessed spirits themselves. I dare to say that the blessed life itself is without my beatitude, unless it deign to confess that through love it enjoys her in me, and through me. Something indeed seems to have accrued even to that perfection from me, and that not little. In short, the angels rejoice at the repentance of a sinner. But if my tears are the delights of the angels, what delights? Their whole work is to praise God: but praise is lacking, if those are wanting who say: We have passed through fire and water, and you have brought us out into a refreshing place (Ps. 66:12).
68.6: Happy therefore in her universality is the Church, all whose glory is unequal to its cause, not only for those things which have already been done for her, but also for those things which yet ought to be done for her. For why should she be solicitous about merits, to whom, from the purpose of God, a firmer and more secure reason of glorying is available? God cannot deny himself, nor fail to do what he has already done, as it is written, who has made the things which are to be (Isa. 46:10). He will do it, he will do it, nor will God fail his purpose. Thus there is nothing now for you to seek by what merits we may hope for good things, especially since you hear at the prophet: Not for you, but for myself, I will do it, says the Lord (Ezek. 36:22). It suffices for merit to know that merits do not suffice. But, as it is enough for merit not to presume of merits, so to lack merits is enough for judgment. Moreover, of the renewed infants, none lack merits, but have the merits of Christ. Yet they render themselves unworthy of them, if they have not been able, but have neglected, to join their own. Which indeed is the peril of the already-adult age. Therefore take care to have merits; having them, know that they are given; for the fruit you will hope for, the mercy of God: and you have escaped every peril of poverty, of ingratitude, of presumption. Pernicious poverty is the want of merits; but presumption of spirit is deceitful riches. And therefore: Give me not riches and poverty, Lord, says the Wise Man (Prov. 30:8). Happy is the Church, to which neither are merits without presumption lacking, nor presumption without merits. She has whence to presume, but not merits: she has merits, but for deserving, not for presuming. Is not the very not-presuming itself a deserving? Therefore she presumes the more securely, the more she does not presume: and there is nothing in which she is confounded in the word of glory, who has so much matter of glorying. The mercies of the Lord are many, and his truth endures forever.
68.7: Why should she not glory securely, in whose testimony of glory mercy and truth have met together? (Ps. 85:11.) Whether she says: My beloved is mine; or then again says: Waiting I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me; or even: The Lord is solicitous for me (Ps. 40:2, 18); or whatever other and other voices there are of this sort, which seem likewise to express some divine affection and singular favor toward something: she will think nothing of these alien to herself, whose reason of presuming is the constitution of the Lord, especially since she does not see another bride, nor another Church, to which those things could be done which cannot but be done. Therefore it is plain concerning the Church, that she will in no respect fear to fit all these things to herself. It is also asked concerning a single soul, if she be spiritual and holy, whether it be lawful for her to dare in such things in any way. For she will not arrogate to herself all the prerogatives of that one catholic multitude, on account of whom all things are done, the one from the multitude, however much she may stand out in sanctity. And therefore, as I feel, it will be found with more difficulty, if indeed it is found at all, how it can be lawful. From which I think it necessary that this be attempted in another sermon, and that I not now enter the ways of a scrupulous disputation, whose exit we do not yet know, unless first over the hidden word there has been prayed to him who opens, and no one closes, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
68.title: In what way the bridegroom Christ attends to the bride the Church, and she to him; and concerning the care which God has for the elect. Likewise concerning the merit and confidence of the Church.

69.1: My beloved is mine, and I am his (Song 2:16). The preceding sermon assigned this voice to the universal Church, on account of the promises made to her by God of her life, both that which now is, and likewise that which is future; but concerning the soul the question is proposed, because one cannot arrogate to herself what the whole universality dares, nor in any way draw that to herself. If it is not lawful, we ought therefore to refer it to the Church in such a way that we by no means refer it to a person; and not only this one, but also the other voices like to this, speaking great things, for example: Waiting I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me (Ps. 40:2); and whatever others the preceding sermon touched upon. But if anyone thinks it lawful, I do not refuse; but it matters to whom: for not to just anyone. Truly the Church of God has her spiritual ones, who act not only faithfully, but also with confidence toward him, speaking with God as with a friend, the conscience of his glory bearing testimony to them. Who those are, that indeed is with God; but you hear what sort you ought to be, if you wish to be such. Which yet I would say, not as one who has experienced it, but as one desiring to experience it. Give me a soul loving nothing but God, and that which is to be loved for the sake of God; for whom to live is Christ not only, but has already long been; whose study and leisure it is to keep the Lord always in her sight; for whom to walk carefully with the Lord her God, I do not say greatly, but is one will, and the ability is not lacking: give, I say, such a soul, and I do not deny her worthy of the care of the bridegroom, of the regard of the majesty, of the favor of the ruler, of the solicitude of the governor: and if she wills to glory, she will not be unwise; only let him who glories glory in the Lord. Thus in that in which many dare, one also dares, but for another reason.
69.2: For the above-mentioned causes make the holy multitude confident; a certain double reason makes the holy soul. First indeed, that in the most simple nature of the bridegroom the divinity has as it were one regard for many, and as it were for many as one. Nor will it be enlarged to the multitude, nor rare to the few; nor divided to diversity, nor restricted to one; nor anxious to cares, nor disturbed or turbulent to solicitudes. Thus indeed intent on one, so as not to be detained; thus on many, so as not to be stretched out. Then, that which as it is most sweet to prove, so it is most rare to have proved; so great is the condescension of the Word, so great the benevolence of the Father of the Word toward a well-affected and well-composed soul (which indeed is itself the gift of the Father, and the work of the Word), that the soul whom they have prevented and prepared for themselves by such their blessing, they deign also to honor with their presence, and so, that not only they come to her, but also make their abode with her (John 14:23). For it is not enough to show themselves, unless they also afford the abundance of themselves. What is it for the Word to come to the soul? To instruct her in wisdom. What is it for the Father to come? To move her to the love of wisdom, so that she may be able to say, that I have been made a lover of her beauty (Wis. 8:2). To love is the Father's: and therefore the coming of the Father is proved by the infused love. What would instruction do without love? It would puff up. What would love do, without instruction? It would err. In short, they erred, of whom it was said: I bear them witness that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10:2). It is not fitting that the bride of the Word be foolish: moreover the Father does not endure one who is puffed up. For the Father loves the Son, and always has at hand to cast down and destroy every height exalting itself against the knowledge of the Word, whether by sending zeal, or by attending; of which the one is of mercy, the other of judgment. Would that in me he might compress every exaltation, nay cast it down, and reduce it to nothing, not by kindled fury, but by infused love! Would that I might learn not to be proud, but rather with unction, than with vengeance, as mistress! Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, as the angel exalting himself in heaven: nor chasten me in your anger, as the man in paradise. Both meditated iniquity, affecting height; he, of power; this one, of knowledge. In short, the foolish woman believed the one promising, but seducing: You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil (Gen. 3:5). He had already before seduced himself, to whom he had persuaded that he would be like the Most High? (Isa. 14:14.) For he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, seduces himself (Gal. 6:3).
69.3: But truly both heights were cast down, but in man more mildly, he who does all things in weight and measure so judging. For the angel being punished, nay condemned, in fury, man felt only anger, and not fury. For when he was angry, he remembered mercy. On this account his seed are children of wrath, and not of fury, unto this day. If I were not born a child of wrath, there would be no need to be born again; if I were born a child of fury, being born again would either not have befallen, or would not have profited. Do you wish to see a child of fury? If you have seen Satan falling as lightning from heaven, which was cast headlong in the rush of fury; and you have known of the fury of God that in short he did not remember his mercy, because he will remember mercy when he has been angry, not when he has already burned to the point of fury. Woe to the children of distrust! and to those too who are from Adam, who, being born children of wrath, convert wrath for themselves into fury, the rod into a staff, nay into a hammer, by diabolical obstinacy. In short, they treasure up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). But wrath heaped up, what but fury? They have sinned the sin of the devil, and are struck down by the sentence of the devil. Woe also, although more mildly, to certain children of wrath, who, born in wrath, have not waited to be born again in grace! For, dead in that in which they were also born, they will remain children of wrath. I would say of wrath, not of fury; because, as is most piously believed, and most humanely lamented, most mild are the punishments of those who draw whole whatever they are addicted to from elsewhere.
69.4: Therefore the devil was judged in fury, because his iniquity was found unto hatred; but man's unto wrath, and therefore he is chastised in anger. Thus every height has been broken, both that which puffs up, and that which precipitates, the Father surely being jealous for the Son. For on either side it is the injury of the Son, both concerning the usurped power against the virtue of God, which he himself is; and concerning the presumed knowledge from elsewhere than from the wisdom of God, which is nonetheless himself. Lord, who is like to you? Who, but the splendor and figure of your substance? who, but your image? Alone in your form, alone has the most high Son of the Most High thought it not robbery to be equal to you (Phil. 2:6). How not equal? Indeed you and he are one. The seat is to him at your right hand, not under your feet. By what means does anyone dare to invade the place of your Only-begotten? let him be cast headlong. He sets himself a seat on high; let the chair of pestilence be overturned. Again, who teaches man knowledge? Is it not you, O key of David, opening to whom you will, and closing to whom you will? And how, without the key, was the entry, nay a breaking in, to the treasures of wisdom and knowledge being attempted? He who does not enter by the door, he is a thief and a robber. Peter therefore will enter, who received the keys. Not however alone: for he will bring in me too, if he wills, and will shut out another whom perhaps he wills, in the knowledge and power given to him from above.
69.5: And these keys, what are they? The power of opening, and of closing, and the discretion between those to be excluded and those to be admitted. And the treasures are not in the serpent, but in Christ. And therefore the serpent could not give the knowledge which he did not have; but he who had it, gave it. For neither could he himself have the power which he did not receive; but he who received it, had it. Christ gave (Matt. 16:19), Peter received, neither puffed up because of knowledge, nor to be cast headlong because of power. Why? Because in neither does he exalt himself against the knowledge of God, who sought nothing of these apart from the knowledge of God, like that one who acted deceitfully in his sight, that his iniquity might be found unto hatred (Ps. 36:3). How, in the end, apart from the knowledge of God, he who writes himself an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the foreknowledge of God the Father? (1 Pet. 1:1, 2.) And let these things have been said on account of that which fell in concerning the zeal of God, which he brought to bear upon the transgressing angel and man (for in both he found perversity); how, namely, in his anger and in his fury he destroyed every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God.
69.6: Now we must return to the zeal of mercy, that is, to that which is not brought to bear, but which is sent; since that which is brought to bear, as we have already said, is of judgment, and has sufficiently terrified us from the remembered examples of those so gravely punished. Therefore I will go for myself to the place of refuge from the face of the fury of the Lord, to that zeal of piety, certainly, gently burning, efficaciously expiating. Does not love expiate? And powerfully. I have read that it covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8). But I say: is it not fit or sufficient to cast down and humble every exaltation of the eyes and of the heart? And especially: for it is not exalted, it is not puffed up. If therefore the Lord Jesus deigns to come to me, or rather into me, not in the zeal of fury, nor indeed in anger, but in love and the spirit of gentleness, being jealous over me with the jealousy of God: for what is so of God as love? For indeed he is God: if, I say, he comes in that, in this I shall know that he is not alone, but that his Father also has come with him. For what is equally paternal? For on this account indeed, he has been called not only the Father of the Word, but also the Father of mercies (2 Cor. 1:3), because he has it innate always to show mercy and to spare. If I feel the understanding, so as to understand the Scriptures, being opened to me, or a word of wisdom as it were bubbling up from my inmost parts, or mysteries being revealed to me by the light infused from above, or certainly some most ample bosom of heaven being spread open to me; and more abundant rains of meditations flowing into my mind from above; I do not doubt that the bridegroom is present. For these are the riches of the Word, and from his fullness we receive these things. But if a certain humble, but rich, devotion of inward sprinkling has poured itself in likewise, so that the love of the known truth generates in me a certain necessary hatred and contempt of vanity, lest perhaps either knowledge puff me up, or the frequency of visitations exalt me: then truly I feel that I am dealt with paternally, and I do not doubt that the Father is present. But if I shall have persevered in always responding to this condescension with the affections and acts worthy of it, so far as in me lies, and the grace of God shall not have been void in me: then the Father, nourishing, and the Word, instructing, will make their abode with me.
69.7: How great a grace of familiarity do you think arises from this abode between the soul and the Word, how great a confidence follows from the familiarity? There is nothing, as I think, that such a soul now fears to say: My beloved is mine; which, from the fact that she feels herself to love, and to love vehemently, does not doubt that she is likewise vehemently loved, and from her own singular intention, solicitude, care, work, diligence, and zeal, with which she unceasingly and ardently watches, how she may please God, equally recognizes all these things in him without doubt, remembering his promise: In what measure you have measured, it will be measured again to you (Matt. 7:2); except that the prudent bride is more cautious to draw the repayment of grace to her own part, knowing that she was rather anticipated by the beloved. From this it is that she prefers his work: My beloved, she says, is mine, and I am his. Therefore from his own things which are with God she recognizes; nor does she doubt that she is loved, who loves. So it is. The love of God begets the love of the soul, and his preceding attention makes the soul attentive, and his solicitude makes her solicitous. For I do not know by what nearness of nature, when the soul will be able once with unveiled face to contemplate the glory of God, she must presently be conformed to him, and be transformed into the same image. Therefore, of what sort you shall have prepared yourself for God, of such a sort God ought to appear to you. With the holy he will be holy, and with the innocent man he will be innocent (Ps. 18:26). Why not equally with the loving one loving, and with the vacant one vacant, and with the attentive one attentive, and solicitous with the solicitous?
69.8: In short he says: I love those who love me, and those who shall have kept watch in the morning for me will find me (Prov. 8:17). You see how he makes you certain not only of his love, if indeed you love him: but also of his solicitude, which he bears for you, if he shall have felt you solicitous of him. Do you keep watch? he also keeps watch. Arise in the night in the beginning of your watches, hasten however much even to anticipate the watches themselves; you will find him, you will not prevent him. In such a business you rashly attribute to yourself either something first, or something more; and he loves more, and before. If this soul knows, nay because she knows, do you wonder that she glories that that majesty, as it were not caring for the rest, attends to her alone, to whom she alone, all cares being set aside, keeps herself with all devotion? The sermon desires an end; but I say one thing to the spiritual ones who are among you, wonderful indeed, but true: a soul seeing God sees him no otherwise than as if she alone were seen by God. With that confidence, therefore, she says that he attends to her, and she to him, seeing nothing besides herself and him. You are good, Lord, to the soul seeking you! you run to meet her, you embrace her, you show yourself a bridegroom, who are the Lord, nay who are above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
69.title: In what way every height raising itself up against the knowledge of God is cast down. Concerning the coming and the abiding of the Father and the Word with the soul that loves, and concerning the familiarity which is contracted from this between God and the soul.

70.1: My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies (Song 2:16). Who will now impute to her presumption or insolence, if she says she has entered into fellowship with him who feeds among the lilies? Even if he fed among the stars, by the sole fact that he fed, I do not know what great thing it might seem to have friendships or familiarity of that sort with him. Something altogether ignoble and humble does feeding sound. But now, since he is also reported to feed among the lilies, the addition of the lowering removes and drives further away the mark of rashness. For what are the lilies? According to the word of the Lord, grass, which is today, and tomorrow is cast into the furnace (Matt. 6:28-30). How great is he who feeds on grass, like one of the lambs or calves? And plainly a lamb, and a fatted calf. But you perhaps have observed more vigilantly, that not the pasture is signified in this place, but the place: for it is not said, feeding on lilies; but, among the lilies. Be it so. He does not eat grass as an ox; yet to move about in the grass, and to recline upon the grass like one of the crowd, what eminence can it have? But what glory is it to her, to have as her beloved him who has done this? And according to the letter indeed the modesty of the bride and the caution of her prudence in speaking sufficiently appears, setting out her words in judgment, as she does, and tempering the glory of the things with the modesty of the words.
70.2: But at other times she does not ignore that he is one, both he who is fed, and he who feeds; abiding among the lilies, and reigning over the stars. But she more gladly recalls the humble things of the beloved, on account of humility indeed, as I have said; but more because from that he began to be the beloved, from which also to be fed. Nor only from that point, but from that. For he who is the Lord in the highest, is the beloved in the lowest; reigning over the stars, and loving among the lilies. He loved even above the stars, because nowhere and never could he not love, because he is love; but until he came down to the lilies, and was found to feed among the lilies, he was neither loved, nor made the beloved. What? was he not loved by the patriarchs and prophets? He was: but not before he was seen by them also to feed among the lilies. For they did not fail to see him whom they foresaw; unless one be so without spirit, as to think that one who sees in spirit sees nothing. From where, then, the Seers, for so the prophets were called (1 Sam. 9:9), if they saw nothing? From this it is, that they wished to see him whom they did not see. For neither could they wish to see in the body him whom they had not seen in spirit. But I say: what, all the prophets? As if all wished to see, or the faith of all had been such. But indeed those who saw, were either prophets, or those assenting to the prophets. For to have believed is to have seen. For not only he who sees through the spirit of prophecy, but also he who sees through faith, if anyone should say that he too sees in spirit, does not seem to me to err.
70.3: Thus therefore the fact that he who feeds all deigned to descend to the lilies, and to feed among the lilies, made him the beloved, because he could not be loved before he was known. And by this, when mention was made of the beloved, that also was beautifully recalled, which was the cause of the love and of the knowledge. This refreshment among the lilies is to be sought in spirit: for to think of a bodily one is ridiculous. Nay, the lilies themselves must be shown by us as spiritual, if indeed we shall be able. I think we shall also have to say this, from what the beloved feeds among the lilies, whether on the lilies themselves, or on other herbs or flowers hidden among the lilies? And in these, that appears to me the more difficult, that he is reported to be fed, not to feed. For that he feeds is not doubtful, for it is not unworthy of him: but to be fed sounds of need, and not even spiritually does it seem that it can easily be assigned to him without injury of the majesty. Nor indeed do I remember having noticed up to now that he is anywhere reported fed in this song, while, I think, you remember with me that he feeds. In short, she once asked to be shown where he fed and rested at midday (Song 1:6). And now indeed, that which she had not yet said, she reports that he is fed, but she does not likewise ask that the place be shown to her; but she herself shows it, assigning it, among the lilies. She knows this, she does not know that; because that which is lofty and in the height, and that which is humble and upon the earth, cannot equally be at hand. Sublime is the work, sublime also the place: nor is the access to it even yet to the bride herself.
70.4: And therefore he emptied himself even to this, that he himself, the shepherd of all, should be fed; and he was found among the lilies, and was seen by the Church, was loved by the poor, being poor, made the beloved on account of the likeness. Not only, however, but also on account of truth, and gentleness, and justice: because through him, namely, the promises were fulfilled, because iniquities were remitted, because the proud demons together with their prince were judged. Such therefore he appeared, who with merit might be loved, truthful for himself, gentle to men, just for men. O truly to be loved, and with all the marrow of the heart to be embraced, bridegroom! Why should the Church now delay to commit herself wholly with entire devotion to so faithful a repayer, so pious a sparer, so just a defender? Moreover the Prophet had sent before, saying: In your beauty and in your comeliness attend, go prosperously. From where this beauty and comeliness? I think, from the lilies. What is more beautiful than a lily? Thus nothing is more comely than the bridegroom. What therefore are those lilies, from which is the beauty of his comeliness? Go forth, he says, and reign for truth, and gentleness, and justice (Ps. 45:5). They are lilies, lilies, I say, sprung from the earth, shining upon the earth, eminent among the flowers of the earth, fragrant above the odor of spices. Therefore among these lilies is the bridegroom, and altogether beautiful and comely from these. For otherwise (which indeed looks to the infirmities of the flesh) he had no form nor comeliness (Isa. 53:2).
70.5: But truth is a good lily, conspicuous in whiteness, pre-eminent in odor; in short it is the candor of eternal light, the splendor and figure of the substance of God (Wis. 7:26). Plainly a lily, which our earth produced for a new blessing, and prepared before the face of all peoples, a light to the revelation of the nations (Luke 2:31, 32). While the earth was under the curse, it brought forth thorns and thistles. But now Truth has arisen from the earth, the Lord blessing (Ps. 85:12, 13, 2), altogether a beautiful flower of the field, and a lily of the valleys. Recognize the lily by its whiteness, which soon at the very rising of the flower shone out to the shepherds by night, the Gospel saying that the angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the brightness of God shone around them (Luke 2:9). Well of God, because the whiteness was not of an angel, but of a lily. He was present, but that shone from as far as Bethlehem. Recognize the lily also by its odor, by which it became known even to those placed far away, the Magi. And indeed a star appeared; but the grave men would by no means have followed it, unless they were drawn by some inmost sweetness of the arisen lily. And truly is truth a lily, whose odor gives life to faith, whose splendor illuminates the understanding. Lift up your eyes even now to the very person of the Lord, who speaks in the Gospel: I am the truth (John 14:6). And see how competently truth is compared to a lily. If you have not observed, observe as it were golden rods coming forth from the middle of this flower, and girt with a most white flower, beautifully and fitly disposed into a crown: and recognize in Christ the golden divinity, crowned with the purity of the human nature, that is, Christ in the diadem with which his mother crowned him. For in that in which his Father crowned him, he inhabits inaccessible light, nor could you see him in it as yet for the time. But of this elsewhere.
70.6: But now truth is a lily; gentleness also is one. And well is gentleness a lily, having the whiteness of innocence, and the odor of hope, because there are remnants, it says, for the peaceable man (Ps. 37:37). The gentle man is of good hope, nor is he less even in the present a certain shining example of social life. Is it not a lily, which shines by duty, and is fragrant with hope? Add that as truth arose from the earth, so also gentleness. Unless one doubt that the Lamb, the lord of the earth, arose from the earth (Isa. 16:1), that lamb who was led to the slaughter, and opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7). Nor only gentleness or truth arose from the earth, but also justice, the prophet saying: Distill, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the just; let the earth open, and bring forth the Savior, and let justice arise at once (Isa. 45:8). But that justice is a lily, remember from Scripture, because the just shall sprout like the lily, and shall bloom forever before the Lord (Hos. 14:6). This lily is by no means today, and tomorrow cast into the furnace, because it will bloom forever. And it will bloom before the Lord, in whose eternal memory the just man will be, and he will not fear the evil hearing (Ps. 112:7), that hearing, namely, by which sinners are commanded to go into the furnace of fire. Moreover, to whom does the whiteness of this lily not shine, unless to him to whom it does not please? In short, it is the sun, but not that which rises over the good and the evil. For neither have those who are to say: The sun of justice has not risen to us (Wis. 5:6) ever seen its light. But all those have seen it who heard: To you who fear God, the sun of justice will rise (Mal. 4:2). Therefore the whiteness of this lily is with the just; its fragrance spreads even to the wicked, although not for their good. In short, we have heard the just saying that we are the good odor of Christ in every place; but to some indeed an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death (2 Cor. 2:15, 16). Who, even the most wicked, would not approve the reputation of a just man, although he does not love his work? And blessed, if he does not judge himself in that which he approves. But he judges himself, approving the good and not loving it: and therefore not blessed at all, but miserable, condemned by his own judgment. What is more miserable than him, to whom the odor of life is the messenger, not of life, but of death? Nay, not even a messenger, but a bearer.
70.7: There are with the bridegroom many other lilies besides these, which have come to us from the Prophet; I speak of truth, and gentleness, and justice; nor will it be difficult for any of you now to find similar ones by himself in the garden of so delicious a bridegroom. He abounds and superabounds in such: who would enumerate them? For as many virtues, so many lilies. What is the end of the virtues in the Lord of virtues? But if the fullness of virtues is in Christ, so also of lilies. And perhaps therefore he himself called himself a lily, because he is wholly engaged among the lilies, and all the things which are his are lilies; his conception, birth, conversation, words, miracles, sacraments, passion, death, resurrection, ascension. What of these is not white, and not most sweetly fragrant? In short, in the conception such a brightness of the heavenly light shone from the abundance of the surpassing Spirit, that not even the holy Virgin herself would have sustained it, if she had not been overshadowed by the power of the Most High. Moreover, the incorrupt virginity of the mother made white the birth; the innocence of life, the conversation; truth, the words; the purity of heart, the miracles; the secret of piety, the sacraments; the will of suffering, the passion; the freedom of not dying, the death; the courage of the martyrs, the resurrection; the performance of the promises, the ascension. How good is the odor of faith in each of these, surely filling our times and inmost parts, who have not seen the whiteness! And blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed (John 20:29). My portion in these is the odor of life, which proceeds from them. This, poured into my nostrils by a certain fit instrument of faith, and indeed the more abundantly according to the multitude of the lilies, truly both lightens the exile, and continually renews in my inmost parts the desire of the homeland.
70.8: Some of the companions of the bridegroom also have lilies, but not in abundance. For all received the Spirit by measure, the virtues and gifts by measure; he alone who has the whole has not a limit (John 3:34). It is one thing to have lilies, another to have nothing but lilies. Whom will you give me of the sons of captivity so innocent and holy, who has been able to cover all his land with flowers, and with flowers of this sort? Certainly not even an infant of one day is without stain upon the earth (Job 14:4, 5, according to the LXX). Great is he who has been able to build three or four lilies in his land, in so great a thickness of thorns and thistles, which are the inveterate sprouts of the ancient curse. But it goes well with me, who am poor, if I shall ever suffice to reclaim, by rooting out and cultivating, so much of my land from this worst crop, namely of iniquities and vices, from which I could produce at least one lily, if perhaps he who feeds among the lilies deigns sometimes to feed even at my side.
70.9: But I said too little, one: out of the poverty of my heart my mouth has spoken. One is altogether not enough; two at least are necessary. I mean continence, and innocence: of which neither the one without the other will save. In short, I will in vain invite the bridegroom to any one of these, who is reported to feed not at a lily, but among the lilies. I will therefore take pains to have lilies, lest he, who will not feed except among the lilies, complain of the singleness of the lily, and so turn away in anger from his servant. I set therefore above all innocence as the first: and if I shall have been able to join continence to it, I shall think myself rich in the possession of lilies. But I am a king, if I shall be able to add to these a third, patience. And indeed those can suffice; but because they can also fail in temptations, since the life of man upon the earth is a temptation (Job 7:1), truly patience is needed, which may be as it were a certain guardian and keeper of both. I think, if that lover of the lilies comes, and finds it so, he will not disdain to feed among us, and to keep the Passover among us: where there will be to him much sweetness in the two, and great security on account of the third. But by what means he who feeds all may be said to be fed, will be seen afterwards. But now it appears that the bridegroom not only appears among the lilies, but can by no means ever be found outside the lilies, since everything which is of him, and he himself, is a lily, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
70.title: Whence the bridegroom is called beloved; and concerning the truth, meekness, and justice, and the other virtues, which are the lilies among which he feeds.

71.1: The end of the preceding sermon is the beginning of this one. The bridegroom, therefore, is a lily, but not a lily among thorns, since he who committed no sin has no thorns. In short, he declared the bride to be a lily among thorns; since if even she should say that she has no thorns, she deceives herself, and the truth is not in her. But he professed himself indeed a flower and a lily, not however among thorns. More than that: I, he says, am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys (Song 2:1, 2). And there is no mention of thorns, because he alone among men is he who has no need to say: I am turned in my affliction, whilst the thorn is fastened upon me (Ps. 32:4). Him who is always without vices, therefore, is never without lilies; because he is wholly and always white, comely in form above the sons of men (Ps. 45:3). You, therefore, who hear or read these things, take care to have lilies with you, if you wish to have this inhabitant of the lilies dwelling in you. Your work, your study, your desire: let a certain moral whiteness of the things themselves, and their odor, testify that they are lilies. Morals too have their colors, they have their odors also. For in spirits color and odor are not the same thing, no more than in bodies. Therefore let the conscience be consulted concerning the color, and fame concerning the odor. You have made our odor to stink before Pharaoh and his servants, they say (Exod. 5:21), speaking concerning reputation. Moreover, the attention of the heart gives color to your work, and the judgment of the conscience. Vices are black; virtue is white. Between this and those, the consulted conscience discerns. The sentence of the Lord concerning the evil and the clear eye stands (Matt. 6:22, 23), because he set fixed limits between the white and the black, and divided the light from the darkness. What therefore goes out from a pure heart and a good conscience is white, and is virtue; but if good fame also has followed, it is also a lily, since indeed neither the whiteness of the lily is wanting to it, nor the odor.
71.2: Moreover, virtue, although not therefore greater, is yet made more beautiful and more illustrious. But if there has been a spot in the conscience, neither will what has come forth from it be without a spot. For if the root is in a vice, so is the branch. And by this, whatever it be that the corrupted root produces from itself not without the shoot of the vice, for example, speech, action, prayer, even if fame seems to applaud, it is not what should be called a lily; because although the odor seems to connive, the color does not. For how a lily with a spot of impurity? Nor indeed will fame avail to vindicate to virtue that which the conscience has convicted to be a vice. Virtue will indeed be content with the whiteness of the conscience, where the odor of fame cannot follow: but the odor of fame will not suffice to excuse the vice of a discolored conscience. The man of virtue will nevertheless always provide, so far as in him lies, for good things, not only before God, but also before men (Rom. 12:17), that he may truly be a lily.
71.3: But there is also a whiteness of the soul, the indulgence of God, he himself saying through the prophet: If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow, and if they are red as crimson, they shall be as white wool (Isa. 1:18). And there is a whiteness, which he puts on who shows mercy with cheerfulness. For if you look upon him, whom the Prophet paints, the pleasant man, who shows mercy and lends (Ps. 112:5), will he not seem to you, from the very cheerfulness of the mind, to have put on a certain whiteness of kindness alike upon his face and upon his work? Just as, on the other hand, if one gives from sadness and as it were from necessity, he puts forward plainly not a white, but a foul color in hand and brow. And therefore God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). What, even a sad one? Truly, he who looked upon Abel because of the whiteness of his alacrity, turned his face away from Cain, because his countenance had fallen (Gen. 4:4, 5), namely from sadness and envy. Observe of what sort is the color of sadness or envy, which turns away from itself the look of God. Beautifully and elegantly, in the coloring of a kindness, has the whiteness of cheerfulness been praised by that voice of the poet: Above all things the looks of the good have been added (Ovid, Metam. lib. VIII). Nor only the cheerful giver, but also he who gives in simplicity (Rom. 12:8), is loved by God. And simplicity is a whiteness. We prove it from the contrary: for the spot is duplicity. I said too little; it is a stain. What is duplicity but deceit? But indeed, he who acted deceitfully in the sight of God, his iniquity was found unto hatred (Ps. 36:3). And therefore blessed is he to whom the Lord will not impute sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit (Ps. 32:2). Beautifully the Lord with few words marked both stains, deceit and sadness: Do not, he says, be like the hypocrites, sad (Matt. 6:16). The bridegroom, therefore, although he is virtue, takes pleasure in virtues; and although he is a lily, he gladly dwells among lilies; and although he is whiteness, he delights in white things.
71.4: And perhaps this is what is said, to feed among the lilies, to be delighted with the whiteness and odor of the virtues. And indeed he once fed corporeally at the house of Mary and Martha, reclining even in body among lilies (I speak of those women, for they were lilies), and nonetheless refreshed his spirit with the devotion and virtues of the women. But if at that hour a prophet, or an angel, or any other spiritual person had entered, not at all ignorant what majesty was reclining; would he not, struck with wonder at the condescension and familiarity which he would see him to have with pure souls and chaste bodies, yet earthly ones and of the weaker sex, justly testify: That I have seen him not only abiding, but also feeding among the lilies? Thus therefore according to both, I mean the flesh and the spirit, the bridegroom was found to feed among the lilies. But I think that he also in turn fed them, but in spirit. By this very fact that he was being fed, how did he feed? How, I say, did he strengthen the timidity of the women, gladden their humility, fatten their devotion? But if you have seen that to be fed is for him to feed; see also now, lest perhaps, conversely, to feed be for him to be fed. Lord, who feed me from my youth, says the holy patriarch Jacob (Gen. 48:15). A good father of a family, who bears the care of his household, especially in evil days, to feed them in famine, feeding them with the bread of life and understanding, and so nourishing them to eternal life. But while feeding, I think he is nonetheless himself fed, and indeed with the foods of which he gladly partakes, our progresses. For the joy of the Lord is our strength.
71.5: Thus therefore both when he feeds he is fed, and when he is fed he feeds, at once refreshing us with his spiritual joy, and rejoicing over our equally spiritual progress. His food is my penitence, his food is my salvation, his food is I myself. Does he not eat ashes as it were bread? But because I am a sinner, I am ashes, that I may be eaten by him. I am chewed when I am rebuked, I am swallowed when I am instructed, I am digested when I am changed, I am assimilated when I am transformed, I am united when I am conformed. Do not wonder at this: he eats us, and is eaten by us, that we may be bound to him the more closely. Not indeed otherwise are we perfectly united to him. For if I eat and am not eaten, he will seem to be in me, but not yet I in him. But if I am indeed eaten, and do not eat, he will seem to have me in himself, but not also to be in me; nor will the union be perfect in either one of these. But let him eat me, that he may have me in himself; and let him in turn be eaten by me, that he may be in me: so that the joining may be whole and firm, when I am in him and he will nonetheless be in me himself.
71.6: Do you wish me to show you by a likeness what is said? Lift up your eyes now to a certain more sublime, though similar, agreement. If the bridegroom himself were so in the Father, that the Father were not, however, in him; or the Father were so in him, that he himself were not in the Father: I dare to say that even their unity would remain short of perfect, if nevertheless it were unity. But now, since both he is in the Father, and the Father in him, there is nothing by which the unity might go lame, but truly and perfectly are he and the Father one. Thus therefore let the soul, for whom to cleave to God is good (Ps. 73:28), not think herself perfectly united to him, until she has perceived both him abiding in her, and herself in him. Not because even then she is called one with God, as the Father and the Son are one: although he who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). I have read this, but I have not read that. I do not speak of myself, who am nothing, but plainly no one; except a madman, whether from earth or from heaven, will usurp to himself that voice of the Only-begotten: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). And yet I, though dust and ashes, relying indeed on the authority of Scripture, would by no means fear to say this very thing, that I am one spirit with God: if ever, however, I shall be persuaded by sure experiences that I cleave to God in the manner of one of those who abide in love, and by this abide in God, and God in them, eating God, and being eaten by God. For concerning such a cleaving I think it was said: He who cleaves to God is one spirit. What then? The Son says: I am in the Father, and the Father is in me (John 14:11), and we are one (John 10:30); the man says: I am in God, and God is in me, and we are one spirit.
71.7: But do the Father and the Son, in order that they may be in each other, and hence one, eat each other, as God and man mutually pass over into each other by a certain mutual eating, certainly by this, although not one, yet existing as one spirit? Far be it! for not in one way are these and those in each other, nor is there one unity of the two. one and one: since neither can one befit the Father and the Son, nor one befit man and God. You, if you are wise, having taken the occasion will be the wiser, prudently observing, that there indeed by one is signified the unity of substance or nature; here however by one alike a unity, but therefore far different, because between the substances and natures, namely of man and God, each has its own nature and substance, while it is established that the Father's and the Son's is wholly one. You see that that is not even unity, if indeed it is compared to this singular and supreme unity. For how is it unity, where there is a number of natures, a diversity of substances? And yet the soul cleaving to God is called and is one spirit with God; nor does the plurality of things prejudice this unity, which is made not by the confusion of natures, but by the consent of wills. On account of this also many hearts are said to be one, and many souls one, as it is written: Of the multitude of believers there was one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). And this, therefore, is a unity.
71.8: But what is this to that unity, which consists not by uniting, but stands forth by eternity? Plainly some mutual eating, in the manner of this, does not make that, because it is not made. For it is. But neither a conjunction, or as it were a composition, or anything of the sort, which is not of one. But to the Father and the Son, the nature, essence, will is not only one, but one thing. For that is to them their being, which is to be the nature; this their willing, which is their being, or their being the nature. There is nothing, therefore, for which the unity, by which the Father and the Son are one, should be said to be made of natures or essences or wills, because they are not: there is nothing for which it should be said to be made, because it is. For it is not made, but innate. The Father and the Son are in themselves, not only in an ineffable, but also in an incomprehensible way, equally capable and containing of themselves: but surely so capable as not to be divisible; so containing as not to be partaking. For as the Church sings in the hymn: the whole Son is in the Father, and the whole Father is in the Word (Hymn for Tuesday at Matins). The Father is in the Son, in whom he has always taken good pleasure in himself; and the Son is in the Father, from whom, as he is never not begotten, so he is never separated. Moreover by love man is in God, and God in man, John saying, because he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him (1 John 4:16). one and one, the difference also of the unities themselves is intimated; since indeed neither can one befit the Father and the Son, nor one befit man and God. The Father and the Son cannot be called one person, because the one is the Father, and the other is the Son: yet they are said and are one thing, because their substance is altogether one, and not each its own. On the contrary, man and God, because they are not of one substance or nature, cannot indeed be called one thing; yet they are called one spirit with certain and absolute truth, if they cleave to each other with the glue of love.
