Which unity indeed is made not so much by the coherence of essences, as by the consent of wills.
71.9: It is plain, if I am not mistaken, enough, not only the diversity, but also the disparity of the unities, the one existing in one essence, the other in diverse ones. What is so far from itself, as the unity of many and the unity of one? Thus among the unities, as I said, one and one mark off the difference, because by one indeed in the Father and the Son the unity of essence is signified, by one however between God and man, not this, but a certain agreeing piety of affections is signified. With the addition, however, the Father and the Son are also most soundly called one; for example, one God, one Lord, and whatever else is said of each in himself, and not of the other. Since indeed their divinity or majesty is not diverse, no more than their substance, or essence, or nature. For indeed all these very things, if you consider piously, are in them not diverse or divided, but one. I said too little: they are one also with them. What of that unity, by which many hearts are read as one, and many souls as one? Nor is it to be esteemed, as I think, under the name of unity, compared to this, which does not unite many, but singularly signifies one. Therefore that is the singular and supreme unity, which consists not by uniting, but stands forth by eternity. Nor indeed does that aforesaid spiritual eating make this, because it is not made. For it is. Much less is any conjunction of essences, or consent of wills, to be thought to make it, because they are not. For one, as has been said, is to them both the essence and the will; but to one there is no consent, no composition, no copulation, or anything of the sort. There must needs be at least two wills, that there may be a consent; likewise two essences, that there may be a conjunction or union through consent. None of these is in the Father and the Son, since indeed they have neither two essences, nor two wills. The two things are one to them; or rather, as I remember having said before, those two are one in them, and are one also with them; and by this they themselves, as they abide in each other incomprehensibly, so incommutably, are truly and singularly one. If anyone, however, says there is a consent between the Father and the Son, I do not contend, provided he understand not a union of wills, but a unity of will.
71.10: But we feel that God and man, because they stand forth and are distant in their own wills and substances, abide in each other far differently, that is, not confounded in substances, but consenting in wills. And this is the union to them, the communion of wills, and the consent in love. A happy union, if you experience it; none, if you compare it. The voice of one who has experienced: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps. 73:28). Plainly good, if you have cleaved on every side. Who is he who perfectly cleaves to God, unless he who, abiding in God, as one loved by God, has nonetheless drawn God into himself by loving in return? Therefore when man and God cleave to each other on every side (and they cleave on every side, being mutually made one within the other by inmost and mutual love), by this I would without hesitation say that God is in man, and man in God. But man indeed is in God from eternity, as one loved from eternity, if he be of those who say that he loved us and graced us in his beloved Son before the constitution of the world (Eph. 1:6, 4); God however is in man, from the time when he was loved by man. And if it is so, man indeed is in God even when God is not in man; but God is not in man who is not in God. For he cannot abide in love, although perhaps for a time he who is not loved may love; but even one who is loved can as yet not love. Otherwise how will this stand, that he first loved us? (1 John 4:10.) Moreover, when he who was before loved now also loves, both man is in God, and God is in man. But he who never loves, it is certain that he was never loved; and by this neither is he in God, nor God in him. Let these things have been said to give the difference between that joining, by which the Father and the Son are one, and that by which a soul cleaving to God is one spirit, lest perhaps, because it is read of man abiding in love, that he abides in God, and God in him; and likewise of the Son, that he is nonetheless in the Father, and the Father in him; an equal prerogative should be thought of the adopted, and of the Only-begotten.
71.11: These things being therefore settled, we must return to him who feeds among the lilies, because from there this excursion has been made up to this point: whether not idly, you will judge. And I had already set down two understandings of the place itself, either that he feeds on the virtues of the white ones, who is virtue and whiteness; or that he receives sinners to penitence in his body, which is the Church, for the sake of incorporating which to himself he made himself sin, who committed no sin, that the body of sin might be destroyed, to which sinners had at some time been engrafted, and they would be justice in him, justified freely.
71.12: I set down still a third opinion, which occurs to me; and I think it will suffice not only for the explanation of the place, but also for the end of the sermon. The word of God is truth, and he himself is the bridegroom. You know this; hear the rest. When he is heard, and he is by no means obeyed, he remains in the mean time as it were empty and fasting, altogether sad and querulous, that he has been brought forth into emptiness. But if he has been obeyed, will not the word seem to you to have grown into a certain corpulence, because the work has been added to the word, as being refreshed with certain fruits of obedience, the crops of justice? From this it is that he speaks in the Apocalypse: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any one hears my voice, and opens to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me (Rev. 3:20). This sense seems also to be approved by the sentence of the Lord at the prophet, where he says that his word will not return to him empty, but will prosper, and will do that for which he sent it (Isa. 55:12). It will not return, he says, to me empty or fasting, but as one prospering in all things, it will be satiated with the good deeds of those who shall rest in him in love. In short, by the manner of speaking, a word is said to be fulfilled when it has been consigned to its effect: because, of course, it is so long empty and lean, and, as it were, famished, until it is completed by the work.
71.13: But hear of what food he says he is nourished. My food, he says, is to do the will of my Father (John 4:34). This is the word of the Word openly indicating that a good deed is his food; if, however, he finds it among the lilies, that is, among the virtues. Otherwise, if he finds it outside, although it seems good food, so far as it is in itself, he who feeds among the lilies will not touch it. For example, he does not receive alms from the hand of a plunderer or a usurer; but not even from a hypocrite, who, when he does alms, causes a trumpet to be sounded before him, that he may be glorified by men. But neither will he in any way hear the prayer of him who loves to pray in the corners of the streets, that he may be seen by men (Matt. 6:2, 5). For the prayer of a sinner will be abominable (Prov. 28:9). In vain also does he offer his gift at the altar, who is conscious to himself that his brother has something against him (Matt. 5:23, 24). In short, he did not look upon the gifts of Cain (Gen. 4:5), because he did not walk aright with his brother. Witness the holy prophet, he even abominated the sabbaths, and the new moons, and the sacrifices of the Jews, so as openly to declare that his soul hated them, and he said: When you come before my face, who sought these things from your hands? I believe those hands did not smell of lilies, and therefore he rejected the gift from those who is wont to feed among the lilies, and not among thorns. Why should not those hands have been thorny, to whom he said: Your hands are full of blood (Isa. 1:13-15). And the hands of Esau were hairy, like thorns; and therefore they were not admitted, to minister to the Holy One.
71.14: I fear that there are even some among us, whose gifts the bridegroom does not accept, because they do not smell of lilies. For if my own will is found in the day of my fast, such a fast the bridegroom has not chosen, nor does my fast savor to him, which savors not of the lily of obedience, but of the vice of my own will. But I feel the same, not only concerning the fast, but concerning silence, vigils, prayer, reading, the work of the hands, finally concerning every observance of a monk, where his own will is found in it, and not the obedience of his master. By no means, truly, would I judge those observances, although good in themselves, to be reckoned among the lilies, that is, among the virtues; but he who is of that sort will hear from the prophet: Is such the obedience which I have chosen, says the Lord? and he will add: In the day of your good things your wills are found (Isa. 58:3-5). A great evil is one's own will, by which it comes about that your good things are not good to you. It is fitting, therefore, that those which are of this sort become lilies, because nothing at all, which is defiled by one's own will, will he taste who feeds among the lilies. It is a wisdom reaching everywhere on account of its cleanness, and nothing defiled runs into it (Wis. 7:24, 25). Thus therefore the bridegroom loves to feed among the lilies, that is, at clean and bright hearts. But until when? Until the day breathe upon us, and the shadows be inclined. This is a shady and dense place: let us not enter this forest of a deep sacrament, except with the clear light of day. For already, as I dispute at greater length, the day is inclined; while we are dragged unwillingly away from these lilies. Nor am I overcome by the length, from whom the odor of the flowers would remove all loathing. A little seems to remain of the present chapter. But that little is too hidden, as also all the rest of this song are. But he who reveals mysteries will be present, as I trust, when we have begun to knock: and he will not close the mouths of those speaking of him, to whom it is more familiar to open what is closed, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
71.title: Concerning the spiritual lilies, that is, good works, whose odor is a right conscience, their color fame: and in what way the bridegroom both feeds us, and is fed by us. Likewise concerning the unity of God the Father with the Son, and of the holy soul with God.

72.1: My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies: until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined (Song 2:16, 17). Only the last part of this chapter is to be treated, and I doubt at the very entry, to which of the two preceding parts I should chiefly join it: for I can indifferently to either. For whether you say: My beloved is mine, and I am his until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined, with only, who feeds among the lilies, interposed; or, according to the order of the letter, who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined: you assign it not inconveniently to either. This certainly matters, that if you join until to the first, you must understand it as inclusive; if to the middle, you must feel it as exclusive. Grant, indeed, that the bridegroom signifies that he already feeds among the lilies when the day has breathed: will he likewise cease to attend to the bride, or she to him? Far be it! They will persevere to each other forever, except that then the more happily, the more vehemently; then the more vehemently, the more speedily. Let this until, therefore, be such as that in Matthew, where it is narrated that Joseph did not know Mary, until she brought forth her firstborn Son (Matt. 1:25): for not afterwards did he know her. Or certainly such as that in the psalm: Our eyes are to the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us (Ps. 123:2): for they will not be turned away when he has begun to have mercy. Or likewise such as that of the Lord to the apostles: Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the world (Matt. 28:20): for not afterwards will he not be with them. But this is so, if you refer until to my beloved is mine, and I am his. But if you prefer to look to who feeds among the lilies, it must be taken in another sense. Moreover, it will be shown more elaborately how then the beloved will cease to be fed, when the day has breathed. For if that is the day of the resurrection, why should it not much more delight him to feed there among the lilies, where there will be a far greater abundance of them? And for fitting the consequence of the letter indeed, let these things have been said.
72.2: Now observe with me, that although the whole kingdom shines with lilies, and the bridegroom is in the midst, delighting, there is yet not that which should be said, and be fed, according to indeed that which he had been accustomed to before. For where now are the sinners, whom Christ incorporates to himself, chewed and bitten as it were with certain teeth of a severer discipline, namely the affliction of the flesh, and the contrition of the heart? But neither will the bridegroom Word now exact for himself food from any deeds or works of obedience, where all business will be leisure, and the matter will be only in the beholding and the affection. And indeed his food is to do the will of his Father; but here, not there. For what should he do to a will already done? And it is certain that it will then be perfect. In short, it will then be for all the saints to prove what is the will of God, good, and acceptable, and perfect. And certainly after the perfect, nothing remains to be done. It remains henceforth to enjoy, not to be done; to experience, not to work; to live it, not to be exercised in it. Is it not this, which, taught indeed by the Lord, we ask with most pressing prayer to be perfected as in heaven, so also on earth (Matt. 6:10), that its fruit may then delight, not its act fatigue? Therefore the food of the bridegroom Word will not be of work, because all work must needs cease, where wisdom is more fully perceived by all. For they who are lessened in act, perceive it (Sir. 38:25).
72.3: But let us now see whether what we say can stand, also according to that opinion, by which some interpret to feed among the lilies as to be delighted with the whiteness of the virtues; for we too have not passed that opinion by among the others. Shall we say, either that they will not be, or that the virtues will by no means savor to the bridegroom then? And indeed to feel either is madness. But see, lest perhaps he be delighted with them otherwise; for it is certain that he is delighted, but perhaps by drink more than by food. Indeed, in this time and body, no virtue of ours will be so clarified to the pure, none so sweet and unmixed, that it may be fit for the bridegroom to drink. But he who wills all men to be saved dissembles many things, and that which in the mean time he cannot swallow with the ease of drinking, he takes care by some art and certain labor of chewing to elicit from it something savory. There will be a time when virtue will be drinkable, and will neither be pressed by the tooth, nor be wearied by the eater, or rather will not weary the eater, which, as plainly a drink, not food, will delight the one drinking without work. In short, you have him promising in the Gospel, that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine, he says, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father (Matt. 26:29). And of food there is no mention. But it is also read at the Prophet: As one mighty who is stupefied with wine (Ps. 78:65); but of food nothing at all is found there. The bride, therefore, conscious of this mystery, when she had discovered and reported that the beloved feeds among the lilies, set a limit until he should deign it, nay she recognized the limit as set and reported it, saying: Until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined. For she knew that afterwards he was to be drunk with the virtues rather than fed. The custom also seems to connive, by which a drink is wont to be taken after food. Therefore he who eats here, will drink there, then the more sweetly as the more securely, about to swallow even those very things, which he now more scrupulously, and in some way more laboriously, melts as it were by chewing.
72.4: Now let us set ourselves to consider of that day and its shadows, who he, what these are: he by what reason breathing, these in what power they have to be inclined. It was said altogether significantly, until the day breathe, nay singularly. For only in this place, if I am not mistaken, will you find the day breathing. For breezes, not times, are said to breathe. Man breathes, the other animals breathe, for whom the reciprocated air unceasingly continues life. And what is this but wind? The Holy Spirit also breathes, and from there the spirit. By what means, therefore, a day breathing, which is neither wind, nor spirit, nor animal? Although he is called not indeed breathing, but, which sounds more significative, aspiring. Nor is it less said contrary to custom, and the shadows be inclined. In short, at the rising of this corporeal and visible light, the shadows are not inclined, but are annihilated. Therefore these things are to be sought outside bodies. And if indeed we find the day and the shadows spiritual, then perhaps both the inclination of these, and the aspiration of that, will shine forth more easily. He who thinks that day corporeal, of which the Prophet says: One day in your courts is better above thousands (Ps. 84:11), let him think I know not what as not corporeal. There is also a day in an evil signification, which the prophets cursed (Job 3:3; Jer. 20:14). But far be it that it be of these visible ones, which the Lord made! Therefore it is spiritual.
72.5: Who now doubts that that is a spiritual shadow, by which Mary was overshadowed conceiving (Luke 1:35); and likewise that which is so remembered in the prophet: The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord, under his shadow we will live among the nations (Lam. 4:20)? I nevertheless think that in this place the contrary powers are rather signified by the name of the shadows, which are reported by the Apostle not only shadows, or darkness, but also the princes of these darknesses (Eph. 6:12), and together with them those cleaving to them of our race, certainly the children of night, and not of light, nor of day. For these shadows will not plainly, when the day has breathed, return to nothing, as we see corporeal shadows at the face of this corporeal light not only disappear, but also utterly perish. They will therefore be, indeed not more extremely than nothing, but yet more miserably. They will be, but inclined and subjected. In short: He will incline himself, it says, and fall (there is no doubt that it is the prince of the shadows), when he shall have ruled over the poor (Ps. 9:10). Therefore it will not be destroyed in nature, but stripped in power; the substance will not perish, but the hour and the power of the darkness will pass. They are taken away, lest they see the glory of God; they are not annihilated, that they may always be burned. Why should not the shadows be inclined, when the mighty will be deposed from their seat, and will be made the footstool of the feet? (Rom. 13:12.) Which indeed must needs be done soon. It is the last hour; the night has gone before, but the day has drawn near. The day will breathe in, and the night will breathe out. The night is the devil, the night is the angel of Satan, although he transforms himself into an angel of light. The night is also Antichrist, whom the Lord will slay with the spirit of his mouth and will destroy with the brightness of his coming (2 Thess. 2:8). Is not the Lord the day? Plainly a day illuminating and breathing, who with the spirit of his mouth puts to flight the shadows, and destroys the phantoms with the brightness of his coming. Or if it pleases you more to take the word of inclination simply, and to think that to be inclined is nothing other than to be annihilated: that we may not fail this sense also, we say the shadows are the figures and enigmas of the Scriptures, and also the sophistical locutions, the cavillations of words and the entangled arguments, which in the mean time obscure the light of the truth. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But the day breathing in, the shadows will be inclined, because, the fullness of light occupying all things, no part of the darkness will be able to remain. In short, when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away (1 Cor. 13:9, 10).
72.6: Thus far could suffice concerning these things, if that day had been called breathing, and not aspiring. But now, for so small an addition, I think something is still to be added, namely for investigating the reason of this diversity. For I, to confess the truth, have long since persuaded myself that in the text of the sacred and precious eloquence not even a small particle is idle. But we are wont to use this word, when we vehemently desire something; as, for example, when we say: He aspires to that honor, or that dignity. There is designated, therefore, by this word the wonderful abounding and vehemence of the spirit that is to come on that day, when not only the hearts, but also the bodies, in their own kind, will be spiritual; and those who will be found worthy will be inebriated with the abundance of the house of the Lord, and will be given to drink from the torrent of his pleasure.
72.7: Or in another way. Already to the holy angels a sanctified day has shone forth, breathing to them with a continual rush of perpetual course the honey-flowing secrets of the everlasting divinity. In short: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps. 46:5); but the city, to which it is said: As the habitation of all rejoicing is in you (Ps. 87:7). But when he shall have deigned to breathe also to us who inhabit the earth, it will be not only breathing, but also aspiring, because with an opened bosom he admits us also. Or (that we may take it up a little higher, and treat at greater length) man being formed from the mud of the earth, the former, as the truthful history narrates, breathed into his face the breath of life (Gen. 2:7), and consequently was made to him an inspiring day: and behold, envious night cunningly impinged upon this day, certainly with a feigned light. For while it promises as it were a more splendid light of knowledge, it poured over the new light the unexpected darkness of a wicked counsel, and brought into the first beginnings of our origin the foul darkness of the ruinous transgression. Woe, woe! they have not known, nor have they understood; they walk in the darkness unknowing, putting darkness for light, and light for darkness. In short, the woman ate of the tree, which the serpent had given her, God had forbidden: and she gave to her husband, and it began as it were anew to grow day to them. For immediately the eyes of both were opened, and there was made a conspiring day, beating out the inspiring one, and substituting the expiring one. For they conspired and came together as one against the Lord, and against his Christ, the cunning of the serpent, the blandishments of the woman, the softness of the man. From where also they spoke mutually to each other, namely the Lord and his Christ: Behold, Adam is become as one of us (Gen. 3), because he had acquiesced to the sinners boasting themselves, to the injury of both.
72.8: In this day we are all born. In short, we all bear the brand of the ancient conspiracy impressed upon us, with Eve indeed living in our flesh, whose consent the serpent, through hereditary concupiscence, carefully strives to claim for his own faction. Therefore, as I said, the saints cursed this day, wishing it short, and quickly turned into darkness (Job 3:3; Jer. 20:14), because it is a day of contention and contradiction, while in it the flesh does not cease to desire against the spirit, and the law of the members continually contradicts, with untiring rebellion, the law of the mind. And so it was made an expiring day. For from then on and henceforth, who is the man who will live, and will not see death? (Ps. 89:49.) If someone would speak for anger, I would think no less for mercy, lest, namely, the elect, on account of whom all things are done, be long wearied by the troublesome contradiction, by which they too are led captive in the law of sin, which is in their members. They shrink, of course, from, and bear with the utmost difficulty, the foul captivity and the sad contention.
72.9: Let us therefore hasten to breathe away from the ancient and iniquitous conspiracy, since the days of man are short (Job 14:5). Rather let a breathing day receive us, before a sighing night swallow us up, to be wrapped in the exterior darkness of the eternal gloom. Do you ask in what that breathing consists? In this, if the spirit begins in turn to desire against the flesh. If you fight against this, you breathe; if in spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you have breathed; if you crucify this with its vices and concupiscences, you have breathed. I chasten my body, he says, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself be made reprobate (1 Cor. 9:27). It is the voice of one breathing, nay of one who had already breathed. Go, and do you likewise (Luke 10:37), that you may prove that you have breathed, that you may know a day again inspiring has shone for you. Nor will the night of death prevail against this revived day; but rather it shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. So much do I think that not even with departing life does the light of life give way, that I judge that voice fitting to no one more suitably than to one so dead: And the night is my illumination in my delights (Ps. 139:11). Why should he not see more clearly, released from the cloud, or rather the dregs, of the body? He will without doubt, loosed from the bodily bonds, be free among the dead, and seeing among the blind. For just as once, every eye being darkened throughout all Egypt, alone in the midst of the darkness saw clearly the people seeing God, that is, the people of Israel, the Scripture saying that wherever Israel was, there was light (Exod. 10:23): so among the children of the darkness, in the foul darkness of death, will the just shine, and will see, indeed the more clearly, the more they are stripped of the shadows of the bodies. For those too who before have not breathed: for they did not seek the light of the inspiring day, and the sun of justice has not risen to them: these, I say, will go from darkness into denser darkness, that they who are in darkness may grow darker still; and those who see, may see the more.
72.10: Where, perhaps not inconveniently, will also be brought forward the word of the Lord, which he spoke, that to him who has it will be given, and he will abound; but from him who has not, even that which he seems to have will be taken away from him (Luke 19:26). So it is: and in death it is added to the seeing, and taken from the not-seeing. For the more these see less and less, the more those see more and more, until the sighing night receives these, and the aspiring day those; which are the last things of both, namely extreme blindness, and supreme brightness. From this there is now nothing to be taken from the wholly empty, and nothing to be added to the full, except that these presume that they will receive I know not what more than the full, according to the promise made to them. And the word of the promise indeed is such: A good measure, and pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, will they give into your bosom (Luke 6:38). Does not that which runs over seem to you to be in some manner more than full? Moreover you will peaceably hear full and fuller, if you remember that you have read: For ever and beyond (Exod. 15:18). Therefore this heap will be of the aspiring day. It, I say, will add to the measure of the inspired fullness, to the abundance of the inspiring day, working above measure into an exalted weight of glory, so that the running-over addition of the clarification may overflow upon the bodies. For this cause indeed it has been called not breathing, but aspiring, because it adds to the inspiring, the Holy Spirit signifying this by the added preposition ad, to; because those whom that one illuminates within, this one adorns without, and clothes them with the robe of glory.
72.11: And that suffices for giving the reason of the word, which is Aspiring. And if you wish to know, the aspiring day is he himself, the Savior whom we await, who will reform the body of our humility, configured to the body of his brightness (Phil. 3:20, 21). For he himself is likewise none the less the inspiring one, according to the operation by which he first makes us breathe in the light which he inspires, that we may be also ourselves a breathing day in him, according to which our inner man is renewed from day to day, and is renewed in the spirit of his mind to the image of him who created him, and is consequently made day from day, and light from light. Since therefore two days go before in us, one indeed inspiring for the life of the body, the other however breathing in the grace of sanctification, and moreover a third remains aspiring in the glory of the resurrection: it is clearly evident that there will at some time be fulfilled in the body that which went before in the head, indeed the great sacrament of piety, and the testimony of the prophet, who says: He will give us life after two days, on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight; we will know, and follow, that we may know the Lord (Hos. 6:3). He is he into whom the angels desire to look, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
72.title: What the day breathing forth, and the shadows inclined, are. Then the various days of men are explained. And that a clearer day awaits the just, as living in light; but the impious, busied in the works of darkness, an eternal night.

73.1: Return; be like, my beloved, to a roe and to the fawn of the harts (Song 2:17). What? just now he goes, and now you call him back? What sudden thing has arisen in so short a time? Has she forgotten something? Indeed, she has forgotten everything which is not he himself, and herself too. In short, although she is not without reason, yet now, as it seems, she is not in possession of her reason. But neither in her feeling does there appear to be left in her any sense of shame, which perhaps she has in her morals. Intemperate love does this. For it is this which, triumphing over and enslaving in itself every sense of shame, the measure of what is fitting, the counsel of deliberation, begets a certain neglect and a certain carelessness of all modesty and opportunity. For see now how she demands that he, almost still beginning to go, already return. She even asks him to hasten, and indeed to run like some one of the beasts of the woods running swiftly, for example, a roe, or the fawn of the harts. This is the tenor of the letter, and this is the portion of the Jews.
73.2: But I, as I have received from the Lord, will search out for myself spirit and life in the deep bosom of the sacred eloquence; and this is my portion, I who believe in Christ. Why should I not dig out the sweet and wholesome feast of the spirit from the barren and tasteless letter, as the grain from the chaff, the kernel from the shell, the marrow from the bone? I have nothing to do with this letter, which, tasted, savors of flesh, swallowed, brings death; but indeed that which is hidden in it is of the Holy Spirit. But the Spirit speaks mysteries, as the Apostle testifies (1 Cor. 14:2); but Israel, for the veiled mystery, holds the very veil of the mystery. Why, except because a veil is still placed over his heart? Thus what the letter sounds is his; what it signifies is mine; and by this, to him is the ministry of death in the letter, to me life in the spirit. For it is the Spirit who gives life (John 6:64): for he gives understanding. Is not understanding life? Give me understanding, and I will live, says the Prophet to the Lord. Understanding does not remain outside, does not cling to the surface, does not like a blind man feel at external things; but it searches out the depths, accustomed from there to snatch and take to itself, with all eagerness, the most precious spoils of the truth, and to say with the Prophet to the Lord: I will rejoice over your words, as one who has found much spoil (Ps. 119:144, 162). For thus the kingdom of truth suffers violence, and the violent carry it off (Matt. 11:12). But that elder brother, who, coming from the field, held the form of the old and earthly people, who, taught to love the threshing for an earthly inheritance, groans anxious with a worn brow under the heavy yoke of the law, and bears the weight of the day and the heat. He, I say, because he had not understanding, stands outside even now, and is not willing, even invited by the father, to enter the house of the feast, defrauding himself even up to now of the partaking of the music, and the choir, and the fatted calf (Luke 15:25-30). Wretched he who refuses to experience how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in one. And let these things have been said for the distinction of the part of the Church and the part of the Synagogue, that both the blindness of this one may be made more manifest from the prudence of that one, and the happiness of that one may stand out above the piteous folly of this one.
73.3: Now let us search out the words of the bride, and so try to set forth the chaste affections of holy love, that nothing lacking reason, nothing unseemly or importunate, may appear to have stayed in the sacred eloquence. And if that hour comes to mind, when the Lord Jesus (for he is the bridegroom) passed out of this world to the Father (John 13:1), and at the same time what her own domestic Church was then feeling at heart, certainly a new bride, when she would see herself deserted as it were a widow desolate of her only hope: I speak of the apostles, who, having left all, had followed him, and had remained with him in his temptations; if we have thought on these things, I say, not undeservedly nor incongruously, I think, it will seem how much she was as sad at his departure as solicitous for his return, especially being so affected, and so left behind. Therefore to one loving and in need, this very double reason was for admonishing the beloved, that, since he could not be persuaded but that he should go and ascend where he had been before, at least he should hasten anew the promised coming. For that she wishes and demands him to be like wild beasts, and such wild beasts, which seem to be more agile in the course, is a sign of a longing mind, for whom nothing is hastened enough. Does she not ask this daily, when she says in prayer: Your kingdom come (Matt. 6:10)?
73.4: I nevertheless think that besides the agility, the infirmity is expressed no less significantly, and indeed of sex in the roe, of age in the fawn. She wills him, therefore, as it seems to me, although to come with power, yet not to appear in judgment in the form of God; but certainly in that in which he was not only born, but was born a little child for us, and that only of the weaker female sex. Why this? Surely, that admonished by either infirmity he may grow mild in the day of wrath, and may remember in judgment to make mercy exalt over judgment. For if he has observed iniquities, even of the elect, who will endure? (Ps. 130:3.) The stars are not clean in his sight, and in his angels he finds perversity (Job 4:18). Hear in short what the holy and elect man says to God: You, he says, have forgiven the wickedness of my sin. For this every saint will pray to you in the seasonable time (Ps. 32:5, 6). The saints therefore have need also to pray for sins, that they may be saved by mercy, not trusting in their own justice. For all have sinned, and all stand in need of mercy. That, therefore, when he has been angry he may remember mercy, he is asked by her to appear in the habit of mercy, that of which the Apostle: And in habit, he says, he was found as a man (Phil. 2:7).
73.5: Necessarily indeed. For if along with this mitigation there will be so great severity in the judgment, so great harshness in the judge, so great sublimity in the majesty, so great novelty in the very face of things, that according to the prophet the day of his coming cannot be conceived (Mal. 3:2): what, think you, would it be, if that consuming fire (I speak of the omnipotent God) had come in that magnitude, fortitude, purity of his divinity, about to show his power against the leaf which is carried by the wind, and to persecute the dry stubble? (Job 13:25.) And he is a man, it says, and who will see him? And who will stand to see him (Mal. 3:2). How much more would none of men bear God presenting himself to us without the man, as inaccessible in brightness, unattainable in height, incomprehensible in majesty? But now, when his anger burns out in a little (Ps. 2:13), how grateful for the sons of grace will appear a certain bland vision of a man, indeed the firmament of faith, the strength of hope, the increase of confidence: that, namely, grace and mercy are upon his saints, and his regard upon his elect (Wis. 4:15). In short, God the Father himself gave the Son power of judgment, and not because he is his Son, but because he is the Son of man (John 5:27). O truly the Father of mercies! he wills men to be judged by a man, that in so great trembling and perturbation of the evil, the likeness of nature may give confidence to the elect. The holy David had once foretold this, praying and prophesying alike: God, he says, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king's son (Ps. 72:2). But neither does the promise made through the angels disagree with this, who, he being taken up, spoke thus to the apostles: This Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, will so come, as you have seen him going into heaven (Acts 1:11), that is, in this very form and substance of body.
73.6: It is clear from all these things that the bride has in herself a divine counsel, and by no means ignores the mystery of the heavenly will, she who under the shadow of unwarlike and weak animals declares, both with the affection of one praying and the spirit of one prophesying, that a weaker, or rather a lower, nature (because it will no longer be infirm) is to be exhibited in judgment; so that he who will move heaven and earth in his power, girt with strength against the senseless, may nonetheless appear sweet and mild, and as it were wholly unarmed, on account of the elect. Where this also can be added, that to distinguish the one from the other, he will in a manner have need, with the leaps indeed of the fawn, and the eyes of the roe; in order that in so great a multitude and in so great a turbation he may be able to see and discern on whom he ought to leap, and whom to leap over, lest perhaps it happen that the just be trodden under foot for the impious, when in anger he breaks the peoples. For as to the impious, it is necessary that the prophecy of David be fulfilled, rather the word of the Lord speaking through his mouth, because I will break them as dust before the face of the wind, I will destroy them like the mud of the streets (Ps. 18:43); and likewise another word, which he had foretold through another prophet, will be known to be fulfilled none the less then, when, returning to the angels, he will say: I trod them down in my fury, and I trampled them in my wrath (Isa. 63:3).
73.7: But if it seems to someone better to be understood in this way, that our fawn ought rather to leap over the evil, and to leap upon the good, I do not contend: only let him think the leap will be ordered into a discrimination of the good and the evil. For I also, if I remember well, spoke thus in another sermon, where the same chapter, set down elsewhere above both by the author, and expounded by me likewise, is found (Above, serm. 54). But there, according to the dispensation indeed of grace, which in the present life is given to some, is not given to others, by God's judgment indeed just but hidden, this fawn was said to leap and to leap over; but here, according to the final and varied retribution of merits. And perhaps the end of this chapter will seem to agree with this sense, which indeed I had almost forgotten. For saying: Be like, my beloved, to a roe and to the fawn of the harts, he adds, upon the mountains of Bethel. For in the house of God, which Bethel sounds, there are not evil mountains. Wherefore the fawn leaping upon them does not tread them down, but gladdens them, that the Scripture be fulfilled which says: The mountains and the hills will sing praises before God (Isa. 55:12). And indeed there are mountains, which according to the Gospel faith, compared to a grain of mustard seed, removes (Matt. 17:19), but they are not mountains of Bethel. For as many as are of Bethel, faith by no means removes them, but reveres them.
73.8: But if the principalities and powers, and likewise also the other ranks of the blessed Spirits, and the virtues of the heavens, are mountains of Bethel, so that we understand it said of them: Its foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps. 87:1), that fawn is certainly not base and contemptible, who has appeared above such excellent mountains, made so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they (Heb. 1:4). For what, if in the psalm we read that he was made a little lower than the angels? (Ps. 8:6.) For neither is he therefore not better, because lower; nor did the Apostle and the Prophet speak contrary things, since indeed they have the same Spirit. For if it was of condescension that he was made lower, not of necessity; nothing plainly is prescribed to goodness in this, but is ascribed to it. In short, the Prophet reported him made lower, not lower, raising up grace, and thrusting away injury. For nature refuses the inferiority, and the cause excuses the making-lower. For he was made lower, because he himself willed: he was made lower by his own will, and by our necessity. Thus to be made lower was to have mercy. What kind of loss is this? Truly, whatever seemed to have perished from the majesty, accrued to the piety. Although neither did the Apostle keep silent this great secret of great piety, but said: But him who was made a little lower than the angels, we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honor for the passion of death (Heb. 2:9).
73.9: And let these have been said for the name and likeness of the fawn, that we may fit it to the bridegroom, according to the word of the bride, without injury of the majesty. Why do I say, without injury of the majesty, when not even the infirmity has remained unhonored? He is a fawn, he is a little one; he is also reported like to a roe, as one made of a woman: yet above the mountains of Bethel, yet made higher than the heavens (Heb. 7:26). He does not say: higher than the heavens being or existing; but, made higher than the heavens: lest anyone think it said of that nature, in which is he who is. But also where he is preferred to the angels, he is nevertheless reported made better, and is not said to be remaining or existing better. From which it appears, that not only in that which he is from eternity, but also in that which he was made in time, he claims for himself all eminence above every principality and power, above every creature finally, as the firstborn of every creature. And so the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:25). This indeed the Apostle. But it does not seem to me that he errs, if anyone say that the same foolishness and weakness of God is to be preferred even to the wisdom and strength of the angels. Thus therefore the present place will be fitly adapted to the universal Church.
73.10: But now, as to what looks to one soul singularly (for even one, if it loves God sweetly, wisely, vehemently, is a bride), each spiritual man can perceive in himself what peculiar experience answers to this for him. But I will not fear to speak plainly whatever that is, which of such things has been given to me to experience. For although it has perhaps been heard as vile, and may seem despicable, it is not my concern; because he who is spiritual will not despise me; he who is less, will not understand me. Yet if I keep this for another sermon, perhaps there will not be lacking those who are edified in those things, which in the mean time the Lord being entreated will inspire, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever. Amen.
73.title: In what way Christ will come to judge in human form, so that he may appear sweet to the elect; and in what way less than the angels, and more sublime than the same.

74.1: Return, he says (Song 2:17). It is clear that he whom she calls back is not present; yet that he has been present, and that not long before: since, while he was still going away, he seems to be called back. An unseasonable calling back is a sign of a great love in the one, and of a great loveliness in the other. Who are these devotees of charity, and followers so unwearied of the business of loving, of whom so restless a love attends the one and presses the other? And upon me indeed, as I remember my promise, it lies to assign this place to the Word and to the soul; but that this may be done worthily, or even for a little, I confess that I stand in need of the help of the Word himself. And surely this discourse would have better befitted one more experienced, and more inwardly aware of a holy and secret love; but I cannot fail my office, nor your desires at all. I see my danger, and I do not guard against it; you compel me. You compel me altogether to walk in things great and in wonders above me. Alas! how I fear lest presently I hear: Why do you tell of my delights, and take up my mystery by your mouth? Hear me nonetheless, a man who trembles to speak and cannot keep silence. Perhaps my very trembling will excuse the boldness; but more so your upbuilding, if it comes about. And perhaps these tears will be seen together with it. Return, she says. Well. He was going away; he is called back. Who will open for me the mystery of this changeableness? Who will worthily explain to me the going and the returning of the Word? Does the bridegroom deal in lightness? Whence, or whither, can he come, or go again, who fills all things? Finally, what local motion can he have, who is spirit? Or what motion, last of all, even of any kind whatever, do you attribute to him who is God? For he is altogether unchangeable.
74.2: But let him who can take these things take them. We, however, walking warily and simply in the expounding of the sacred and mystic speech, let us conform to the manner of Scripture, which in our words speaks wisdom hidden in a mystery; which, while it figures God, conveys him to our affections; and in known likenesses of things that can be sensed, as in certain cups of a meaner material, offers to human minds the things that are precious, the unknown and invisible things of God. Let us follow, then, we also, the custom of chaste speech, and let us say that the Word of God, God the bridegroom of the soul, both comes to the soul as he wills, and again lets her go: only so that we understand these things to happen by the feeling of the soul, not by a movement of the Word. For example, when she feels grace, she acknowledges his presence: when she does not, she complains of his absence, and again seeks his presence, saying with the Prophet: My face has sought you out; your face, Lord, I will seek (Ps. 27:8). Why should she not seek it? For, so sweet a bridegroom having been withdrawn from her, it will not please her meanwhile, I do not say to desire, but not even to think, anything else. It remains, therefore, that she earnestly seek him absent, and call back him who is departing. Thus, then, the Word is called back, and he is called back by the desire of the soul, but of that soul to which he has once granted the sweetness of himself. Is not desire a voice? And a strong one. Finally: The desire of the poor, he says, the Lord has heard (Ps. 10:17). The Word, therefore, going away, the one voice of the soul meanwhile, and a continuous one, is her continuous desire, as it were one continuous Return, until he come.
74.3: And now give me a soul whom the Word, the bridegroom, is wont often to visit, to whom familiarity has given boldness, taste has given hunger, and contempt of all things has given leisure: and to her I unhesitatingly assign both the voice and the name of bride; nor would I judge the passage now in hand wholly foreign to her. For such a one is introduced here as speaking. For he whom she calls back, of him she proves without doubt that she has merited the presence, though not the fullness. Otherwise she would not have called him back, but have called him. Further, the word of calling back is Return. And perhaps for this reason he withdrew himself, that he might be called back more eagerly, and held more firmly. For once also he made as if he would go farther, not because he willed this, but he willed to hear: Stay with us, Lord, because it is toward evening (Luke 24:28, 29). And again, another time, walking upon the sea, when the apostles were sailing and toiling at the oars, as if wishing to pass them by, not even then did he will that, but rather to prove their faith and to draw out a prayer. Finally, as the evangelist says: They were troubled, and cried out, thinking that it was a phantom (Mark 6:48, 49). Therefore a loving feigning of this sort, or rather a saving dispensation, which the Word made flesh then from time to time showed in the body, the Word who is spirit does not cease, in his own spiritual way, to practice again and again with the soul devoted to him. Passing by, he wishes to be held; going away, to be called back. For this word is not one that cannot be called back. He goes and he returns according to his good pleasure, as one visiting in the early morning and proving of a sudden. And his going is in a manner a matter of dispensation; but his returning is always voluntary: and both are full of judgment. But the reason of these things lies with him.
74.4: But now it is certain that changes of this kind, of the Word going and returning, take place in the soul, as he says: I go, and I come to you (John 14:28); likewise: A little while, and you shall not see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me (John 16:16). O little while, and little while! o long little while! O kind Lord, do you call it a little while, that we shall not see you? Let the word of my Lord stand: it is long, and far too long indeed. Yet both are true: a little while as to merits, and long as to desires. You have both in the prophet: If he delay, he says, wait for him, because coming he will come, and will not be late (Hab. 2:3). How will he not be late, if he delay, unless because what suffices for merit does not suffice for desire? Further, the loving soul is carried by her wishes, drawn by her desires, makes little of merits, shuts her eyes to the majesty, opens them to delight, setting them upon the one who saves, and dealing trustfully in him. Fearless at last, and unabashed, she calls the Word back, and with confidence asks again for her delights, calling, with her accustomed liberty, not Lord but beloved: Return, my beloved: and she adds: Be like the roe, and the young of the harts, upon the mountains of Bether. But that later.
74.5: But now bear with a little of my foolishness. I wish to say, for this too I promised, how it goes with me in such things. It is not expedient, indeed. But I shall be exposed, surely, that I may be of use: and if you have profited, I shall console my foolishness; if not, I shall confess my foolishness. I confess that the Word has come even to me, I say it in foolishness, and many times. And though he has entered into me quite often, sometimes I did not feel it when he entered. I have felt him present, I remember that he has been present; sometimes I have even been able to anticipate his entrance, never to feel it, nor even his departure. For whence he came into my soul, or whither he went when he left her again; but also by what way he either entered or went out; even now I confess that I do not know, according to that word: You do not know whence he comes, or whither he goes (John 3:8). Nor is it wonderful, however, because he it is to whom it was said: And your footsteps shall not be known (Ps. 77:19). Surely he did not enter through the eyes, because he is not colored; nor yet through the ears, because he did not sound; nor yet through the nostrils, because he is not mixed with the air, but with the mind; nor did he taint the air, but made it; nor yet through the throat, because he is not chewed or drunk; nor did I discover him by touch, because he cannot be handled. By what way, then, did he enter? Or perhaps he did not enter at all, because he did not come from outside? For neither is he any one of those things which are outside. Further, neither did he come from within me, since he is good, and I know that there is no good in me. I went up also into what is above me: and behold, the Word standing out above this. To what is below me also I went down, a curious searcher: and nonetheless he was found below. If I looked outside, I found him to be beyond everything external to me; but if within, he himself was more inward still. And I knew that what I had read is true, that in him we live, and move, and are (Acts 17:28): but blessed is he in whom he himself is, who lives to him, who is moved by him.
74.6: You ask, then, since his ways are altogether past searching out, whence I know that he is present? He is living and effectual: and as soon as he has come within, he has wakened my sleeping soul; he has moved, and softened, and wounded my heart, because it was hard and stony, and badly whole. He began also to pluck up and to destroy, to build and to plant, to water the dry places, to enlighten the dark, to open what was shut, to set on fire what was cold, and also to make the crooked into straight, and the rough into smooth ways; so that my soul blessed the Lord, and all that is within me his holy name. Thus, then, the Word the bridegroom, entering into me at times, never made his entrance known by any signs, not by voice, not by appearance, not by step. By none of his movements, finally, was he discovered to me, nor did he slip into my inmost parts by any of my senses: only from the movement of the heart, as I have said before, did I understand his presence; and from the flight of vices, and the checking of carnal affections, I perceived the power of his virtue; and from the searching, or the reproof, of my hidden things I wondered at the depth of his wisdom; and from some little amendment of my manners I experienced the goodness of his gentleness; and from the renewing and reforming of the spirit of my mind, that is, of my inward man, I perceived in some measure the beauty of his comeliness; and from the beholding of all these things together I was struck with fear at the multitude of his greatness.
74.7: But because all these things, when the Word has withdrawn, just as if you should take the fire from under a boiling pot, at once begin to lie sluggish with a kind of languor, and cold; and this, for me, must be a sad sign of his departure, until he return again, and my heart grow warm again within me in its wonted way; and let that be the sign of his return. Having, surely, such an experience of the Word, what wonder if I also take to myself the voice of the bride in calling him back, when he has absented himself, I who am carried by a desire, if not equal, yet like it, or like it in part? It will be familiar to me, as long as I live, to use for the calling back of the Word the word of calling back, which is Return. And as often as he slips away, so often shall it be repeated by me; nor shall I cease to cry out, as it were behind the back of one departing, with the burning desire of the heart, that he return, and give me back the joy of his salvation, give me back himself. I confess to you, sons, that meanwhile nothing else pleases, while that which alone pleases is not at hand. And this I pray, that he come not empty, but full of grace and truth (John 1:14): after his own manner, surely, as yesterday and the day before. In which it seems to me that the likeness of the roe and of the fawn can be shown, since truth has the eyes of the roe, and grace the gladness of the fawn.
74.8: Both things are necessary to me: truth, indeed, from whom I cannot be hidden; but grace, from whom I would not wish to be. Otherwise the visit will not be full without one or the other, since the severity of the former without the latter can seem burdensome, and the gladness of the latter without the former can seem loose. Truth is bitter without the seasoning of grace; just as, without the bridle of truth, devotion itself is light and knows no measure, and very often insolent. How many have gained nothing by having received grace, because they did not equally receive temperance from the truth? For from this they were pleased with themselves in it more than they ought, while they did not fear the looks of truth, while they did not look to the gravity of the roe, but rather gave themselves wholly to the lightness and the gladness of the fawn. Hence it came about that they were deprived of the grace in which they had wished to exult privately, they to whom it could be said, even late: Go, therefore, and learn what this is: Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice unto him with trembling (Ps. 2:11). A certain holy soul, finally, had said in her abundance, I shall not be moved forever: when suddenly she felt the face of the Word turned away from her, and herself not only moved, but also troubled (Ps. 30:6, 7); and so in sadness she learned that she had needed, together with the gift indeed of devotion, the weight also of truth. Therefore the fullness of grace is not in grace alone, nor yet in truth alone. What does it profit to know what you ought to do, if the will to do it is not also given? What, if you should indeed will, but be quite unable? How many have I known made sadder by the truth once known, and the more so because they might no longer flee to the excuse of ignorance, knowing, and not doing, what the Truth urged?
74.9: Since these things are so, neither without the other suffices. I have said too little: it is not expedient, either. Whence do we know this? To him who knows the good, he says, and does not do it, it is sin to him (Jas. 4:17); likewise: The servant who knows the will of his lord, and does not do it, shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47). But that is on the side of truth. What on the side of grace? It is written: And after the morsel Satan entered into him (John 13:27). He speaks of Judas, who, having received the gift of grace, because he did not walk in the truth with the Master of truth, or rather with Truth the mistress, gave place in himself to the devil. Hear yet further: He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey out of the rock. Whom? The enemies of the Lord have lied to him (Ps. 81:16, 15). Those whom he fed with honey and with fat, these have lied to him and become enemies; because they did not join truth to grace. Of whom elsewhere you have: The children of strangers have lied to me; the children of strangers have grown old, and have halted from their paths (Ps. 18:45). Why should they not halt, content with the one foot of grace, and not adding truth? Their time, therefore, shall be forever (Ps. 81:15), as also that of their prince, who himself also did not stand in the truth, but was a liar from the beginning (John 8:44), and therefore heard: You have lost wisdom in your beauty (Ezek. 28:17). I do not want a beauty that takes wisdom from me.
74.10: Do you ask what that beauty is, so harmful and so ruinous? Yours. Are you perhaps still without understanding? Hear more plainly. Private, one's own. We do not blame the gift, but the use. Finally, if you have noticed, he is said to have lost wisdom not in beauty, but in his own beauty. And, unless I am mistaken, the beauty of the angel and of the soul is one and the same. For what is either she or he without wisdom, except a rough and misshapen material? By it, therefore, he was not only formed, but also beautiful. But he lost it when he made it his own: so that to have lost wisdom in his own beauty is nothing other than to have lost it in his own wisdom. Ownership is the cause. That he was wise for himself, that he did not give the glory to God, that he did not return grace for grace, that he did not walk in it according to truth, but twisted it back to his own will: that is why he lost it; rather, that is what lost it. For to have it thus is to lose it. And if Abraham, he says, was justified by works, he has glory, but not with God (Rom. 4:2). And I: I am not in safety, I say. I have lost whatever I have that is not with God. For what is so lost as that which is in exile outside God? What is death, if not the privation of life? So nothing is perdition, if not estrangement from God. Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight! (Isa. 5:21) of you it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor. 1:19). They have lost wisdom, because their own wisdom has lost them. What have they not lost, who are themselves lost? Or are they not lost, whom God does not know?
74.11: Further, the foolish virgins, whom indeed I think foolish for no other reason than that, saying they were wise, they became fools; these, I say, are to hear from God: I do not know you (Matt. 25:12). And likewise those who have taken the grace of miracles to their own glory are nonetheless going to hear: I never knew you (Matt. 7:23): that it may be clearly plain from these things that grace does not profit where truth is not in the intention; but rather does harm. And indeed both things are with the bridegroom. Finally: Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, says John the Baptist (John 1:17). If, therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ (for he is the Word of God, the bridegroom of the soul) shall have knocked at my door with any one of these without the other, he will indeed enter, not as a bridegroom, but as a judge. Far be it, let this by no means happen! Let him not enter into judgment with his servant. Let him enter peaceable, let him enter pleasant and glad: yet let him enter ripe and grave, who with a somewhat sterner countenance of truth may, while he checks insolence in me, purify gladness. Let him enter like a fawn leaping, like a roe looking about, who by dissembling may leap over the fault, and by pitying may look upon the penalty. Let him enter as one coming down from the mountains of Bethel, festive and splendid, and as one proceeding from the Father, sweet and gentle, who does not disdain to be called, and to become, the bridegroom of the soul that seeks him, though he is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
74.title: Concerning the visitations of the Word the bridegroom, how hiddenly they are made to the holy soul, and that Bernard by his own example declares this humbly and modestly for the edification of his own.

75.1: In my little bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves (Song 3:1). The bridegroom has not returned at the voice and the wish of her who calls him back. Why? That desire may grow, that affection may be proved, that the business of love may be exercised. It is a dissembling, then, surely, not indignation. But it remains that he be sought, if perhaps he may be found when sought, who did not come when called, the Lord saying: Everyone who seeks, finds (Matt. 7:8). Further, the word of calling back is this: Return; make yourself like, my beloved, to a roe and to the young of the harts (Song 2:17). While at that voice he has not returned, on account, surely, of those causes which have been said: hence she who loves, made the more eager, soon gave herself with all avidity to seeking. And first, indeed, she seeks him in the little bed, but does not find him at all. She rises from there, she goes about the city, she goes and returns through the broad ways and the streets, and he does not meet her, nor does he appear. Whoever may by chance have met her are asked, and nothing certain is brought back. Nor is this seeking, and this frustration, of one street, or of one night, since she says that she sought through the nights. What desire is this, and what ardor, that rising by night she is not ashamed of a public place, runs through the city, inquires openly and on every side about the beloved, and can be turned by no reason from searching out his paths, hindered by no difficulty, held back neither by love of a timely rest, nor by a bride's modesty, nor even by fear of the night? And yet in all these things she has until now been frustrated of her desire. Seek what this obstinate and long cheating means, nurse of weariness, kindling of suspicions, torch of impatience, stepmother of love, mother of despair? If it is still dissembling, it is too troublesome.
75.2: Grant that it was meanwhile dissembled lovingly and usefully, as long as the matter was still in calling only, or in calling back. But now, when he is sought, and sought in this way, what will dissembling any longer be able to confer? If the question is of carnal spouses and of shameful loves, as the surface of the letter seems to have played beforehand; and if such things can happen among them, it is no business of mine, let them see to it. But if I ought to answer and satisfy, according to what little power I have, the minds and affections of souls seeking the Lord, something vital must surely be drawn out of holy Scripture, in which they trust that they have life, something by which they may be spiritual; that the poor may eat and be filled, and their hearts may live. And what is so much the life of hearts as my Lord Jesus Christ, of whom he who lived by him was saying, that when Christ your life shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory? (Col. 3:4.) Let him come, then, into the midst, whereby it may truly be said to us also: But in the midst of you stands one whom you do not know (John 1:26). Though I do not know how the bridegroom who is Spirit is not known by spiritual persons, who nonetheless have so advanced in the spirit that they can say with the prophet: The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord (Lam. 4:20); and with the Apostle: And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer (2 Cor. 5:16). Is not he the one whom the bride was seeking? He truly is the bridegroom, both loving and lovable. He, I say, is truly the bridegroom; as his flesh truly is food, and his blood truly is drink (John 6:55): and all that is of him truly is, since he himself is nothing other, surely, than Truth itself.
75.3: But this bridegroom, how is it that he is not found when sought, though he is sought so earnestly and so actively, now indeed in the little bed, but now in the city, or even in the broad ways or the streets; while he himself says: Seek, and you shall find; and: He who seeks, finds? (Matt. 7:7, 8.) The prophet also may say to him: You are good, Lord, to the soul that seeks you (Lam. 3:25); and likewise holy Isaiah: Seek the Lord, while he can be found? (Isa. 55:6.) How, then, shall the Scriptures be fulfilled? For she who is brought in here seeking is not one of those to whom he himself says: You shall seek me, and shall not find me (John 7:34). But notice that there are three causes which occur meanwhile, and are wont to frustrate those who seek: when, namely, they either do not seek at the right time, or not as they ought, or not where they ought. For if every time is fit for seeking, why then does the prophet say, as I have already recalled: Seek the Lord, while he can be found? There will be, without doubt, a time when he will not be able to be found; and therefore he adds that he be called upon while he is near; because it is going to be that he will no longer be near. For by whom will he not then be sought? To me, he says, every knee shall bow (Isa. 45:23), and the rest, yet he shall not be found by the wicked, whom avenging angels will surely keep away, and will take them off lest they see the glory of God. In vain shall the foolish virgins also cry out; he now goes out to them not at all, the door being shut (Matt. 25:10). Let those women, therefore, think that it was said to them: You shall seek me, and shall not find me.
75.4: But now is the acceptable time, now are the days of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2); a time plainly both of seeking and of calling upon, when for the most part he is felt to be present even before he is called upon. Hear, finally, what he promises. Before you call upon me, he says, I will say: Behold, I am here (Isa. 65:24). Nor did this kindness and this easiness of the time that now is lie hidden from him who speaks in the psalm: The Lord has heard the desire of the poor, your ear has heard the preparation of their heart (Ps. 10:17). But if God is sought by good works, then while we have time let us work good toward all (Gal. 6:10): especially because the Lord openly foretells that the night is coming, when no one can work (John 9:4). Will you then find for yourself, in the ages to come, another time for seeking God, for working what is good, besides this which God has appointed for you, in which he may remember you? And therefore they are days of salvation, because in them God himself, our king before the ages, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 74:12).
75.5: Go, then, you, and in the midst of hell await the salvation which has already been wrought in the midst of the earth. What power of meriting pardon do you dream will come to you amid everlasting burnings, when the time of pitying has already passed? No victim for sins is left to you, if you have died in your sins. The Son of God is not crucified again; he died once, and now dies no more (Rom. 6:9). The blood which was poured out upon the earth does not go down to the lower regions. All the sinners of the earth have drunk: there is nothing of it that the demons may claim for themselves, to quench their fires; nor yet men, the companions of demons. Once he went down there, not the blood, but the soul; and this was the portion of those who were in prison: that one visitation, which was then made by the presence of the soul, while the body hung lifeless upon the earth. The blood watered the dry ground, the blood poured into the earth and made it drunk; the blood pacified the things that are on earth and the things that are in heaven, but not also the things that are in the lower world: except that once, as I said, his soul ran out there, and wrought a redemption in part, lest the work of charity should be idle even for that moment; but he will not add to it further. Now, therefore, is the acceptable time, and a time fit for seeking, in which plainly he who seeks finds: if nonetheless he seeks where, and as, he ought. And this is the one cause which can hinder the bridegroom from being found by those who seek him, when they do not seek at the opportune time. But it does not hinder the bride, for she calls upon him and seeks him at the opportune time. But neither does she seek him tepidly, or negligently, or as a mere form: for she seeks with a burning heart and altogether untiringly, plainly as is fitting.
75.6: It remains that we look at the third, lest, namely, she seek where it is not fitting. In my little bed I sought him whom my soul loves. Or perhaps he was not to be sought in a little bed, but in a bed; for to him the world is narrow? But I do not shudder at a little bed, I who know a little one. For a little one has been born to us (Isa. 9:6). Exult, you, and praise, O habitation of Zion, because great in the midst of you is the Holy One of Israel (Isa. 12:6). But the same Lord, great in Zion, has been found little among us, weak among us; from the one having to lie down, from the other having to lie in a little bed also. Is the little bed not the tomb? is the little bed not the manger? is the little bed not the womb of the Virgin? For the womb of the great Father is not a little bed, but a great bed, of which it is said to the Son: From the womb, he says, before the daystar I begot you (Ps. 110:3). Though perhaps that womb ought not even to be reckoned worthily a bed, since it is the place of one who reigns, rather than of one who lies down. For remaining in the Father he reigns with the Father over all things. Finally, an undoubted faith holds that the Son does not lie, but sits, at the right hand of the Father; and he himself declares that heaven is a seat for him, not a bed (Isa. 66:1): that you may know that he, in his own things, that is, in the things above, by no means has the comforts of weakness, but the insignia of power.
75.7: Rightly, therefore, the bride, in setting down the little bed, calls it hers, because everything that is weak of God is manifestly in him not from what is his own, but from what is ours. From us he took up the things which he endured for us: to be born, to be nursed, to die, to be buried. Mine is the mortality of him born, mine the weakness of the little one, mine the breathing out of him crucified, mine the sleep of him buried. The former things have passed, and behold, all things are new. In my little bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves. What? were you seeking in yours him who had already withdrawn himself into his own? Had you not seen the Son of man ascending where he was before? He has already exchanged the tomb and the stable for heaven, and do you still seek him in your little bed? He has risen, he is not here. Why do you seek in a little bed one who is strong, in a little bed one who is great, one glorified, in a stable? He has entered into the powers of the Lord, he has put on comeliness and strength: and behold, he sits above the cherubim, he who lay under the stone. From now on he no longer lies, but sits: and do you prepare supports, as for one lying down? Or, that the truth may be more complete, either he sits judging, or he stands helping.
75.8: So you, O good women, for whom, I ask, do you keep watch? for whom do you prepare spices, make ready ointments? If you knew how great he is, and how free among the dead is this dead man whom you are going to anoint, you would perhaps rather have asked to be anointed by him. Is not this he whom his God has anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows? (Ps. 45:7.) You will be blessed if you shall be able to glory as you return, and to say that of his fullness we also have received (John 1:16). Indeed it has come about so. For truly they return anointed, who had come to anoint. Why should they not be anointed by so glad a message of a new and fragrant resurrection? How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, of those who preach good things! (Rom. 10:15.) Sent by the angel, they do the work of evangelists; and, made apostles of the apostles, while they hasten to announce in the morning the mercy of the Lord, they say: In the odor of your ointments we run. From then on, therefore, and thereafter, the bridegroom has been sought in the little bed in vain; because even if the Church had known him according to the flesh, that is, according to the weakness of the flesh, yet now she knows him no longer. Finally he was sought afterward by Peter and John, again and again, in the sepulcher, but was not found at all. See, you, whether each of them could then fittingly and suitably have said: In my little bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought, and did not find. For the flesh which was not of the Father, being about to go to the Father, first by the glory of the resurrection put off from itself everything weak, girded itself with power, put on light as a garment: in which glory, surely, and array it befitted her to be presented to the Father's looks.
75.9: But beautifully the bride: not he whom I love, she says, but he whom my soul loves: because that love by which she loves something spiritually, for example God, an angel, a soul, truly and properly belongs to the soul alone. But to love justice, truth, piety, wisdom, and the other virtues, is of this sort. For when the soul loves, or rather desires, something according to the flesh, for example food, clothing, dominion, and bodily or earthly things of this kind, it is to be called the love of the flesh rather than of the soul. And this is why the bride, less usually, but no less properly, says that her soul loves the bridegroom, showing thereby that the bridegroom is spirit, and that he is loved by her not with a carnal but with a spiritual love. And well does she say that she sought him through the nights. For if, according to Paul, they who sleep, sleep in the night, and they who are drunk, are drunk in the night (1 Thess. 5:7): so, not absurdly, as I think, it can be said that they who are ignorant, are ignorant in the night; and therefore they who seek, seek in the night. For who would seek what he has in the open? Further, the day makes open what the night hides, so that you may find by day what you had sought in the night. It is night, therefore, as long as the bridegroom is sought; since if it were day, he would be out in the open, and would not be sought at all. And of this, enough: unless perhaps this number of nights still signifies something to be sought, because she put not night, but nights.
75.10: And it seems to me, if you have nothing better, that such a reason can be given. This world has its nights, and not a few. Why do I say that the world has nights, when almost the whole of it is itself night, and the whole is always turning about in darkness? The perfidy of the Jews is night, the ignorance of the pagans is night, heretical depravity is night, the carnal or animal way of life even of Catholics is night. Is it not night, where the things that are of the Spirit of God are not perceived? But also among heretics or schismatics, as many sects, so many nights. In vain do you seek through these nights the sun of justice and the light of truth, that is, the bridegroom; because there is no fellowship of light with darkness. But someone says that the bride is not so foolish, or so blind, as to seek light in the darkness, to seek the beloved among the ignorant, and among those who do not love him. As if indeed she says that she now seeks him through the nights, and not rather that she has sought him; she does not say: I seek; but, I sought through the nights him whom my soul loves.
