And the sense is, that when she was a little one, she thought as a little one, and understood as a little one, and sought the truth where it was not, wandering and not finding, according to that in the psalm: I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost (Ps. 119:176). Finally she recalls that she was then still in the little bed, as one weak in age and a little one in sense.
75.11: If, however, you construe it thus: In my little bed, you understand, being or lying, I sought him whom my soul loves; I did not seek in the little bed, but, being in the little bed, I sought, that is: While I was still weak and without strength, and altogether less fit to follow the bridegroom wherever he went, to follow him to the hard and high places of that loftiness of his, I fell in with many who, knowing my desire, said to me: Behold, here is Christ, behold, he is there (Mark 13:21): and he was neither here nor there. But I fell in with them, and not unto folly for me. For the nearer I approached, and the more diligently I searched, the sooner and the more certainly I knew that the truth was by no means with them. For I sought, and did not find; and I caught the nights, which were feigning themselves to be days.
75.12: And I said: I will arise, and go about the city; through the streets and the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loves. See, even now, that she lies who says: I will arise. Altogether beautifully. Why should she not arise, once the resurrection of the beloved was known? But, O blessed one, if you have risen with Christ, you ought to mind the things that are above; and you must seek Christ not below, but above, where he sits at the right hand of the Father (Col. 3:1, 2). But I will go about, you say, the city. To what end? The wicked walk in a circuit. Leave that to the Jews, to whom their own prophet foretold this, that they shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go about the city (Ps. 59:6). And if you enter into the city, according to another prophet, behold, they are wasted with hunger (Jer. 14:18): which surely would not be, if the bread of life had been in it. He has risen from the heart of the earth, but he has not remained upon the earth. But he has ascended where he was before. For he who descended, he is also he who ascended, the living bread who came down from heaven, the same bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
75.title: God is to be sought at the due time, manner, and place. And that now is the acceptable time, in which each one by good works can find God for himself, and work out his own salvation.

76.1: By the streets and the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loves (Song 3:2). She still thinks as a little one. I think she supposed that, having gone out from the tomb, he had soon sought the public place, so that he might teach the peoples as he used to, and heal the sick, and so that he might manifest his glory in Israel, if perhaps they would receive him rising from death, who were promising that they would receive him coming down from the cross. But he had finished the work which the Father had given him to do: which she surely ought to have understood even from the voice of him as he hung, that voice, namely, by which, about to breathe his last at once, he says: It is consummated (John 19:30). There was now no cause for which he should commit himself again to the crowds, which perhaps were not going to believe in him even so. And he was hastening to the Father, who would say to him: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 110:1). More strongly indeed, and more divinely, when he has been lifted up from the earth, he will draw all things to himself. But she thought he was to be sought through the streets and the broad ways, eager to enjoy, but ignorant of the mystery. Frustrated again, therefore, she repeats, saying: I sought him, and I did not find him; that the word might be fulfilled which he said: Because I go to the Father, and now you shall not see me (John 16:16).
76.2: Perhaps she may say: How then shall they believe in him, whom they will not see? As if faith were from sight, and not rather from hearing. What great thing is it to believe what you see? and what praise does it deserve not to deny faith to your own eyes? But if we hope for that which we do not see, through patience we wait for it; and patience is merit. Blessed, finally, are they who have not seen, and have believed (John 20:29). Accordingly, that the merit of faith be not made void, let him withdraw himself from sight, giving place to virtue. It is time also that he now retire into his own. You ask, into which own of his? To the right hand of the Father. For he will not think it robbery to be equal to God, since he is in the form of God (Phil. 2:6). Let that, then, be the place of the Only-begotten; in which every injury of his may be seen driven off. Let him sit, surely, beside, not beneath, that all may honor the Son, as they honor the Father. In this the equality of majesty will appear, if you look up to him as neither lower than the Father, nor later. But she meanwhile notices none of these things: but as if drunk for love, running this way and that, she seeks with the eyes him whom the eye no longer reaches, but faith. For she does not think that Christ ought otherwise to enter into his glory, unless first, the glory of the resurrection becoming publicly known to the world, impiety be confounded, the faithful exult, the disciples glory, the peoples be converted, and at last he himself be glorified by all, when from the presence of him rising the truth of him preaching has become clear to all. You are mistaken, O bride. These things must indeed come to pass, but in their time.
76.3: Now indeed, meanwhile, see whether perhaps this be more worthy, and more agreeable to heavenly justice; if what is holy be not given to dogs, and pearls to swine: if rather, according to Scripture, the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory of God (Isa. 26:10); if faith be not cheated of its merit, which is then surely recognized as the more approved, when that which is not seen is believed; if with her there be kept for the worthy that which is hidden from the unworthy, so that they who are in filth may be filthy still, and the just may be justified the more (Rev. 22:11), if they do not grow drowsy from weariness. Let the heavens and the heavens of heavens waste away and be confounded from their expectation, if the almighty Father himself be not now cheated longer of the desire of his heart; if finally the Only-begotten be not delayed somewhat further from the entrance of his glory, which even alone is most unworthy. Of how great account do you think any glory whatever of mortals is to be esteemed, that it ought to hold him back even for a little from that which has been prepared for him by his Father from eternity? Add that by no reason ought the petition of the Son himself to be drawn out longer. Which petition do I mean, you ask? That one, surely, by which he says: Father, glorify your Son. Which nonetheless I would take him to have asked, not as a suppliant, but as one who knows beforehand. Freely is that asked which it is in the power of the one who asks to receive. The petition of the Son, therefore, is dispensational, not necessary, since with the Father he gives whatever he has received from the Father.
76.4: Where this too is to be said, that not only does the Father glorify the Son, but the Son also glorifies the Father: lest anyone say the Son is less than the Father, as one who is glorified by the Father, when he himself also glorifies the Father, the Son saying: Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you. But perhaps you may still think the Son is to be set lower, because he seems, as if without glory, to receive from the Father a brightness which at last he pours back upon the Father. Hear that it is not so: Glorify me, he says, Father, with the brightness which I had, before the world was made, with you (John 17:1, 5). If, then, the brightness of the Son is not later, inasmuch as it is from eternity, the Father and the Son glorify one another as equals. And if it is so, where is the primacy of the Father? It is equality, surely, where there is coeternity. And equality to such a degree that there is one brightness of both, just as they themselves are one. Whence it seems to me that, by saying again: Father, glorify your name, he asks, surely, nothing other than that he himself be glorified, in whom, and through whom, the name of the Father would without doubt be glorified: and he received an answer from the Father: I have both glorified it, and I will glorify it again (John 12:28). Which very answer of the Father was no small glorification of the Son. But more abundantly at the streams of the Jordan, and more augustly, he is recognized to have been glorified, both by the testimony of John, and by the pointing of the dove, and by the voice of the Father saying: This is my beloved Son (Matt. 3:14, 16, 17). But on the mountain also, before three disciples, he was nonetheless glorified most magnificently, both by the same voice coming down upon him again from heaven, and by that wonderful and excellent transfiguration of his body, and also by the attestation of the two prophets, who appeared there speaking with him (Matt. 17:2, 5).
76.5: It remains, therefore, that according to the promise of the Father he be glorified once more, and that will be the fullness of glory, to which nothing further can be added. But where shall that blessing be given? For not, as she suspected, in the broad ways, or the streets, unless perhaps in those of which it is said: Your streets, O Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold, and through all your lanes alleluia shall be sung (Tob. 13:22). In these, truly, the Son received from the Father that brightness, to which a like one will not be able to be found, not even among the heavenly things. For to which of the angels was it ever said: Sit at my right hand? (Heb. 1:13.) But not only from the number of the angels, but not even from the higher remaining orders of the blessed has anyone at all been found fit to take up this supereminent glory. To none whatsoever of them was that voice of singular glory made, to none was it given to experience in himself the working of the voice. Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers, they surely desire to look into him; they do not presume to compare themselves to him. Therefore to my Lord singularly it has both been said by the Lord, and given, to sit at the right hand of his glory, as being in a coequal glory, in a consubstantial essence, by a like generation, in a majesty not unequal, in an eternity not later. There, there shall he who seeks him find him, and shall see his glory: not a glory as of one of the rest, but plainly a glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father (John 1:14).
76.6: What will you do, O bride? Do you think you can follow him there? or do you dare, or are you able, to thrust yourself into this sanctuary so holy, and this holy place so secret, that you may look upon the Son in the Father, and the Father in the Son? Not at all. Where he is, you cannot come now, but you shall come afterward. Come nonetheless, follow, seek; nor let that inaccessible brightness or loftiness frighten you from seeking, or make you despair of finding. If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes (Mark 9:23). The word is near, he says, in your mouth and in your heart (Rom. 10:8). Believe, and you have found. For to believe is to have found. The faithful know that Christ dwells by faith in their hearts (Eph. 3:17). What is nearer? Seek, therefore, without fear; seek devoutly. The Lord is good to the soul that seeks him (Lam. 3:25). Seek by vows, follow by deeds, find by faith. What shall faith not find? It touches the unapproached, it catches the unknown, it comprehends the measureless, it lays hold of the last things; finally, eternity itself it in a certain way encloses in that most vast bosom of its own. I would confidently say: the eternal and blessed Trinity, which I do not understand, I believe; and by faith I hold what I do not grasp with the mind.
76.7: But someone says: How shall he believe without one who preaches, since faith is from hearing, and hearing is through the word of preaching? (Rom. 10:14, 17.) God will provide this. And behold, already at hand are those who may instruct and form the new bride, about to be wed to the heavenly bridegroom, in the things in which it is needful, may teach the faith, and may hand on the form of piety and of religion. For hear what she adds: The watchmen found me, who keep the city. For who are these watchmen? Those, surely, whom the Savior in the Gospel pronounces blessed, if, when he comes, he finds them watching (Luke 12:37). How good the watchmen, who, while we sleep, themselves keep watch, as about to render an account for our souls! How good the keepers, who, watchful in spirit and passing the night in prayers, shrewdly search out the ambushes of enemies, anticipate the counsels of the malignant, catch the snares, elude the traps, scatter the nets, and frustrate the devices? These are lovers of the brethren and of the Christian people, who pray much for the people and for the whole holy city. These are they who, greatly solicitous for the Lord's sheep committed to them, give their heart to watching toward the dawn unto the Lord who made them, and make supplication in the sight of the Most High. And they watch, and they make supplication, knowing their own insufficiency in keeping the city, and that unless the Lord keep the city, in vain does he watch who keeps it (Ps. 127:1).
76.8: Further, since the Lord so commands: Watch, and pray, that you enter not into temptation (Mark 14:38); it is clear that without this twofold exercise of the faithful, and the zeal of the keepers, the city cannot be secure, nor the bride, nor the sheep. Do you ask the difference of these? They are one. A city on account of the gathering, a bride on account of the love, sheep on account of the meekness. Do you wish to know that she is a bride, which is to be a city? I saw, he says, the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 21:2). In the same way this will appear clearly to you also concerning the sheep, if you recall how attentively that first keeper (I speak of Peter), when the sheep were first committed to him, was at the same time admonished about love. Which, surely, so wise a creditor would not have done with such care, unless he felt himself to be the bridegroom, conscience answering him this, surely, from within. Hear these things, friends of the bridegroom, if friends indeed. But I have said too little, friends: they must be the dearest friends, who are granted the privilege of so great a familiarity. Not idly was it so often repeated: Peter, do you love me? (John 21:15-17). in the commissioning of the sheep. And I indeed think this was signified just as if Jesus had said to him: Unless, with conscience bearing witness to you that you love me, and love me greatly and perfectly, that is, more than your own things, more than your own people, more even than yourself, so that the number of this repetition of mine be fulfilled, you by no means take up this care, nor thrust yourself in among my sheep, for whom my blood has surely been poured out. A terrible word, and one that could shake even the fearless hearts of any tyrants whatever.
76.9: For this reason take heed to yourselves, whoever you are that have obtained by lot the work of this ministry; take heed, I say, to yourselves, and to the precious deposit which has been entrusted to you. It is a city: watch unto its keeping, and unto concord. It is a bride: be zealous for her adornment. They are sheep: attend to their pasture. And these three will perhaps not unfittingly be said to pertain to that threefold inquiry of the Lord. Further, that the keeping of the city may be sufficient, it will be threefold: from the violence of tyrants, from the fraud of heretics, from the temptations of demons. But the adornment of the bride is in good works, and in manners, and in orders. And the pasture of the sheep is indeed in common in the pastures of the Scriptures, as in the inheritance of the Lord; but there is a distinction among them. For there are commandments, which are laid upon hard and carnal minds out of the law of life and of discipline: and there are the herbs of dispensations, which out of regard for mercy are set before the weak and those small of heart: and there are the solid and strong things of the counsels, which out of the inmost parts of wisdom are set before the sound, and those who have their senses exercised unto the discernment of good and evil. For to the little ones, as to lambs, the milk of exhortation is given for drink, not solid food. Besides this, good and solicitous shepherds do not cease to fatten the flock with good and glad examples, and with their own rather than with those of others. For if with those of others and not with their own; it is a disgrace to them, and the flock thus does not profit. For if, for example, I who seem among you to bear the care of a shepherd shall have set before you the meekness of Moses, the patience of Job, the mercy of Samuel, the holiness of David, and whatever examples there are of this sort of good men, while I myself am harsh and impatient, and unmerciful and by no means holy: the word, as I fear, will turn out less savory, and you will take it in less eagerly. But this I leave to heavenly piety, that what comes to you less from us, she herself may supply; and what is amiss, she herself may correct. But now the good shepherd will take care of this also, that according to the Gospel he be found to have salt in himself (Mark 9:50); knowing that a word seasoned with salt, by as much as it shall have pleased unto grace, by so much will it profit unto salvation. Let these things meanwhile have been said concerning the keeping of the city, and the adornment of the bride, and also the pasture of the sheep.
76.10: I wish nonetheless still to mark out the same things a little more expressly, on account of those who, while they gape too eagerly after honors, less providently put themselves under heavy burdens and expose themselves to dangers: that they may know to what they have come, as it is written: Friend, for what have you come? (Matt. 26:50.) Unless I am mistaken, for the keeping of the city alone, that it may be provided for as much as is enough, there is need of a man strong, spiritual, faithful: strong to drive back injuries, spiritual to detect ambushes, faithful, who does not seek the things that are his own. Further, moreover, for making manners honorable, or for correcting them, which surely pertains to the beauty of the bride, who does not clearly recognize that the censure of discipline will be most necessary, together with much diligence indeed? For that reason everyone on whom this work lies ought to burn with that zeal, kindled with which that foremost emulator of the bride of the Lord was saying: I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor. 11:2). Now how shall an untaught shepherd lead out the Lord's flocks into the pastures of the divine utterances? But even if he shall indeed have been learned, yet is not good, it is to be feared that he may not so much nourish with a rich teaching as harm with a barren life. Rashly, therefore, in this part also is this burden undergone without knowledge equally and a praiseworthy life. But behold, an end is imposed, which we do not praise, where there was no end. They are called away into another matter, and one to which it is unworthy that this should yield. I am distressed on every side, and I do not know which I shall bear more hardly, to be torn away from this, or to be stretched out into that: except that either way both together are more troublesome. O slavery! o necessity! what I will, that I do not, but what I hate, that I do. Note nonetheless where we leave off, so that, as soon as it shall be free to return to this, we may at once begin from there, in the name of the bridegroom. Of the Church, of Jesus Christ our Lord, who above all things is God blessed unto the ages, Amen.
76.title: Concerning the brightness of the bridegroom, in which he sits equal to the Father at the right hand of his glory: and in what way good pastors ought to be solicitous, watchful, and discerning about feeding the souls committed to them.

77.1: Well then, we are unburdened! We said in yesterday's sermon what sort of guides we would wish to have on this way on which we walk, not of what sort we have. We find them far unlike. Not all are friends of the bridegroom whom you see today standing by the bride on this side and on that, and who, as men commonly say, seem as it were to escort her at the right hand. Very few there are who do not seek the things that are their own, out of all her dear ones. They love gifts, and they cannot at the same time love Christ; because they have given their hands to mammon. Look how they step along, sleek and adorned, clothed about with many colors, like a bride coming forth from her chamber. If you should suddenly catch sight of any such one coming forward from afar, will you not think him the bride rather than a keeper of the bride? But whence do you think this abundance of things overflows upon them, the splendor of garments, the luxury of tables, the heap of vessels of silver and of gold, if not from the goods of the bride? Hence it is that she is left poor, and needy, and naked, her face pitiable, unkempt, rough, bloodless. For this reason, at this time, it is not to adorn the bride, but to strip her; it is not to keep her, but to lose her; it is not to defend her, but to expose her; it is not to instruct her, but to prostitute her; it is not to feed the flock, but to slaughter and devour it, the Lord saying of them: They who devour my people as the food of bread (Ps. 14:4; 53:4); and: Because they have eaten up Jacob, and have laid waste his place (Ps. 79:7), and in another prophet: They shall eat the sins of my people (Hos. 4:8); as if he should say: They exact the prices of sins, and they do not spend upon sinners the care that is owed. Whom will you give me, from the number of those set over others, who does not watch more to empty the purses of his subjects than to root out vices? where is he who by prayer may bend wrath; who may preach the acceptable year of the Lord? We speak of lighter things; a heavier judgment awaits the heavier.
77.2: Yet we linger without cause either upon these or upon those, because they do not hear us. But even if these things which we say should perhaps be committed to letters, they will disdain to read; or if by chance they shall have read, they will be angry at me, although they would more rightly do this to themselves. For this reason let us leave these, not finders of the bride but sellers of her; and let us rather seek out those by whom the bride says that she was found. And indeed these have obtained the place of the ministry of those, but not the zeal. All desire to be successors, few to be imitators. O that they were found as watchful for the care as they run eager to the chair! They would surely keep watch, carefully preserving her whom those found, and who has been entrusted to them. Or rather they would wake for themselves, nor would they allow it to be said of them: My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood (Ps. 38:11). An altogether just complaint, nor one to be referred to any age more justly than to our own. It is too little for our watchmen that they do not keep us, unless they also destroy us. For, sunk deep in a sleep of forgetfulness, they are not wakened at any thunder of the Lord's threatening, so as even to grow terrified at their own peril. Hence it is that they do not spare their own, who do not spare themselves, destroying and perishing alike.
77.3: But who indeed are those watchmen by whom the bride declares that she was found? The apostles, surely, and apostolic men. Truly these are they who keep the city, that is, that very city which they found. The Church, and the more watchfully, the more gravely they behold her at this time in peril, from an evil domestic and inward, surely, as it is written: And a man's enemies are they of his household (Mic. 7:6). For her, for whom they stood firm even unto blood, they do not leave destitute of their protection, but they protect and keep her by day and by night, that is, in their life and in their death. And if precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. 116:15), I myself do not doubt that they do this even so much more powerfully in death, by as much as in death itself their principality has been strengthened the more (Ps. 139:17).
77.4: You assert these things thus, someone says, as if you had seen them with your eyes; but they are shut away from human sights. To whom I reply: If you think the witness of your own eyes faithful, the witness of God is greater. But he says: Upon your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen: all the day and all the night they shall not be silent forever (Isa. 62:6). But this, you say, was said of the angels. I do not deny it: they are all ministering spirits (Heb. 1:14). But who may forbid me to think the same also of these, who in power are now by no means unequal to the angels themselves, but in affection and in mercy are perhaps the nearer kin to us, the more closely they are joined by nature? Join also the endurance of those same passions and miseries in which we for the time still move about. Will nothing more of pity for us, or of solicitude, be worked in holy minds by this, that they remember without doubt that they themselves also passed through them? Is not that their own voice: We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment? (Ps. 66:12.) What? have they themselves passed through, and will they leave us behind in the midst of the fires or the waves, and not deign even to stretch out a hand to children in peril? It is not so. It is well with you, O mother Church, it is well with you in the place of your pilgrimage: help comes to you from heaven and from earth. They who keep you do not slumber, nor do they sleep. Your keepers are the holy angels, your watchmen the spirits and the souls of the just. They are not mistaken who have perceived that you were found by both spirits, and are kept by both alike. And of this solicitude there is a reason of its own for each: for these indeed, that without you they shall not be made complete; but for those, that except from you they are by no means restored to the fullness of their own. For who does not know that, when Satan fell from heaven, and his companions with him, the number of the multitude above was lessened by no small part? From you, therefore, all await a completion, some of their number, others of their desire. Recognize, accordingly, the voice in the psalm: The just wait for me, until you repay me (Ps. 142:7).
77.5: And it is to be noticed that not she is reported to have found them, but they rather to have found her, and, as I suspect, appointed to this very thing by design. For how shall they preach, unless they are sent? Finally you have one speaking in the Gospels: Go, behold I send you (Luke 10:3); and: Go, preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16:15). So it is. She was seeking the bridegroom, and it did not lie hidden from the bridegroom. For he who had stirred her up to this very thing, that she should seek him, had also given her a heart for the precepts, and a law of life and of discipline, provided there should be one who would instruct her and teach the way of prudence. And he sent planters and waterers to meet her, who might nourish her and confirm her in all certainty of the truth, that is, might point out to her, and render certain, the things concerning the beloved; because it is the truth which she seeks, and which her soul truly loves. And truly, what faithful or true love of a soul is there, except surely that by which the truth is loved? I am master of reason, I am capable of truth; but would that I were not, if love of what is true were wanting. Of these branches, surely, that is the fruit, and I am the root. I am not safe from the axe, if I am found without it. In that gift of nature, surely, there is no doubt that the mark of the divine image shines out, by which she stands before the other living beings. Hence it is that my soul dares to rise to the sweet and chaste embraces of the truth, and so to rest in the love of it with entire security and sweetness, if nonetheless she finds grace in the eyes of so great a bridegroom, that he may account her worthy to reach this glory; or rather, that he himself may present her to himself having neither spot nor wrinkle, nor anything of the kind. Of how great a difference do you think it is, or worthy of what punishment, to hold idle so great a gift of God? But this at another time.
77.6: But now the bride by no means found him whom she was seeking; and by those whom she was not seeking, she herself was found. Let them hear this, who do not fear to enter upon the ways of life without a guide and a teacher; being to themselves, in the spiritual art, both disciples and masters together. This does not suffice: they even heap up disciples to themselves, blind guides of the blind. How many from this cause have been found to have strayed most dangerously from the straight path! Surely, ignorant of the cunning of Satan and of his thoughts, it has come about that they who had begun in the spirit were brought to completion in the flesh, led away shamefully, fallen to their damnation. Let them see, accordingly, who are of this sort, how cautiously they walk, and let them take example from the bride, who was not able in any way to come to him whom she desired, before there met her those whose teaching she might use, to know about the beloved, certainly to learn the fear of the Lord. He gives his hand to the seducer, who neglects to give it to a teacher. And he who sends the sheep into the pastures without a keeper is a shepherd not of the sheep, but of the wolves.
77.7: Now let us see already, concerning the bride, how she says that she was found. For to me she seems to have set down the word of finding quite unusually. For she says this in such a way as if the Church had come from one place. But she comes from the East and from the West, according to the word of the Lord (Matt. 8:11), and from all the ends of the earth. Nor was she at any time gathered into one place, where she might be found by the apostles or by the angels, to be led or directed to him whom her soul loves. Was she found before she was gathered? Not so; because she did not even exist. For which reason, if she had said that she was collected, if assembled, if certainly, which fits the name of Church better, called together by the preachers, I would have passed on simply, hesitating in nothing at all. For they are fellow workers with God, and they heard him saying: He who does not gather with me scatters (Matt. 12:30). But neither will this seem to me beside the matter, if someone shall say that she was founded or built by them. Since they did this together with him who speaks in the Gospels: And upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. 16:18); and: Because it was founded upon the firm rock (Matt. 7:25). But now, saying none of these things, but declaring herself found, beyond what is usual indeed, she makes us hesitate a little, and leads us to suspect that something lies hidden in the wording, which is to be looked at more carefully.
77.8: I was wishing, I confess, to pass it by, and to withdraw myself from this search, to which I did not feel that I would be equal. But remembering in how many things equally doubtful and obscure, you indeed lifting up your hearts, I have felt myself helped even beyond my hope, I am ashamed of my want of trust: and, rebuking my fear, I set upon, yet not rashly, what I was timidly shunning. The accustomed help will be at hand, as I trust: but if it is less, still, among hearers of good will, what I have wished will not be idle. But the following sermon shall have this for a beginning; for we close the present one here. But may he himself grant you not only to hold in memory the things that are said, but also to love them ardently and to fulfill them effectually, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
77.title: Concerning the evil pastors of the Church; likewise in what way the blessed in heaven together with the angels are a help to the elect still sojourning.

78.1: At the word of finding, if I remember well, we stood there and stuck, hearing more scrupulously, namely, that the bride said she had been found by her preachers. Further, the causes of our delay and of our doubt were set out by us, and it seemed that there was something to be sought; but not at the heel of the sermon, by which we were already pressed, could what was sought be unfolded. What remains, except that we now pay what is owed? In the unfolding of a great sacrament: I speak of that which the Doctor of the Gentiles has interpreted as, in Christ and in the Church, a holy and chaste wedlock (Eph. 5:32); this itself is the work of our salvation: in it, I say, three work together with one another; God, an angel, and a man. And why should God not work, and take care of the nuptials of his beloved Son? He himself, truly, and with his whole will. And surely by himself he would have sufficed, even without the help of these; but these without him can do nothing. Therefore, that he took of them into the work of this ministry, he sought not a comfort for himself, but an advancement for them. For to men indeed he has placed merits in the work, according to that word: The workman is worthy of his wages (Luke 10:7): and because each shall receive according to his own labor (1 Cor. 3:8), whether he who plants in faith, or he who waters what has been planted. But when he uses the ministry of angels unto the salvation of the human race, does he not bring it about that angels are loved by men? For that men are loved by angels can be noticed from this above all, that the angels are not ignorant that the ancient losses of their city are going to be repaired from men. Nor surely did it befit the kingdom of charity to be ruled by other laws than by the loving and mutual loves of those who are alike to reign, and by pure affections toward one another and toward God.
78.2: But there is a great difference in the manner of working, according, surely, to the dignity of each worker. For God does what he wills by the very ease of willing alone, without heat, without motion, without prejudice of place or of time, or of cause, or of person. For he is the Lord of hosts, who judges all things with tranquillity (Wis. 12:18). He is also Wisdom, disposing all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). Further, an angel does not work without motion, as well of place as of time, yet without heat. But a man, in working, is free neither from the heat of the mind nor from the motion of body and of mind. Finally, he himself is bidden to work out his own salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12), and in the sweat of his face to eat his bread (Gen. 3:19).
78.3: These things thus unfolded, look now with me, in this so magnificent work of our salvation, at three things which God the author claims for himself, and in them goes before all his helpers and fellow workers: predestination, creation, inspiration. Of these, predestination had a beginning, I do not say from the rising of the Church, but not even from the beginning of the world, nor finally from this time or from that: it is before the times. Further, creation is with time; inspiration now comes to pass in time, where and when God wills. Surely, according to predestination, the Church of the elect was never not with God. If an unbeliever wonders at this, let him hear what he may wonder at more: she never stood forth not pleasing, she was never not beloved. Why should I not boldly speak a secret which that ready bearer of the counsels of those above opened to me from the heart of God? I speak of Paul, who, as of many other things, so of this secret also of the riches of his goodness did not fear to publish it abroad: He blessed us, he says, with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and unspotted in his sight in charity; and he adds: Who predestined us unto the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the purpose of his will, unto the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he has graced us in his beloved Son (Eph. 1:3-6). Nor is there doubt that these things are said with the voice of all the elect: and they themselves are the Church. In that so deep bosom of eternity, therefore, before she came forth into the light and the work of this creation, who, even of the blessed spirits, could in any way have found her, unless to someone God, eternity itself, had willed to reveal her?
78.4: But even when, at the nod of the one creating, she was seen to have come forth into these made and visible kinds and forms, she was not for all that found at once by any man or angel, because she was not recognized, shadowed by the image of the earthly man, and covered with the mist of death. Without which veil, surely, of a general confusion, none of the sons of men has entered this life, one only excepted, surely, who enters without spot. He is Emmanuel, who nonetheless, himself also one of us, for us put on the likeness of our curse and of our sin, not the reality. For so you have it, that he appeared in the likeness of the flesh of sin, that out of sin he might condemn sin in the flesh (Rom. 8:3). For the rest, there is one entrance for all, through all things, for the elect, I say, and for the reprobate. For there is no distinction. All have sinned, and all wear the hood of their shame. For this reason, therefore, even though the Church already existed created among the things that were made, not even so could she be found or recognized by any creature, hidden meanwhile in both ways wonderfully, both within the bosom of a blessed predestination and within the mass of a wretched damnation.
78.5: But her whom Wisdom, predestining, had hidden from eternity, and whom Power, creating, had likewise by no means brought forth from the beginning, visiting grace indeed revealed in her own time, according to an operation which for this reason I named inspiration above, because something was poured from the spirit of the bridegroom into human spirits unto the preparation of the gospel of peace, that is, to prepare the way of the Lord, and of the gospel of his glory, unto the hearts of all, as many as had been predestined to life. In vain would the watchmen have labored in preaching, if this grace had not gone before. But now, seeing the word run swiftly, and the peoples of the nations turned to the Lord with all readiness, tribes and tongues running together into the unity of faith, and the ends of the earth gathered into one catholic mother, they knew her from the riches of grace which from of old were kept hidden in the secret place of eternal predestination, and they rejoiced that they had found her whom before the ages the Lord had chosen to himself for a bride.
78.6: From which, as I think, it becomes clear that it is not idle that the bride has borne witness that she was found by these; but for this reason, that she recognized herself as gathered by them, not as chosen; as discovered, not as converted. For the conversion of each one is to be ascribed to him to whom all must of necessity say that word from the psalm: Turn us, O God our savior (Ps. 85:4). But perhaps I would not fit the word of finding to him as aptly as the word of conversion. Or rather, so it is. It belongs not to the Lord to find, but to go before, and his going before shuts out finding. Finally, what shall he find, who has never not known anything? The Lord knows who are his, someone says (2 Tim. 2:19). But what of him himself? I know, he says, whom I have chosen from the beginning (John 13:18). Plainly, her whom from eternity he foreknew, whom he chose, whom he loved, whom he made, it was not according to reason that she should be declared found by the same. Prepared by him nonetheless, that she might be found, I would say with confidence. For he who saw has borne witness: and we know that his witness is true (John 19:35). I saw, he says, the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 21:2): and he is one of the watchmen who keep the city. But hear her preparer himself, as if pointing her out to the watchmen with his finger, yet under another figure. Lift up your eyes, he says, and see the regions, for they are white already, that is, prepared, unto the harvest (John 4:35). Hence the householder invites workmen to the work, when he has already perceived all things so prepared that, without much labor of their own, they can glory and say that we are God's fellow workers (1 Cor. 3:9). For what are they about to do? To seek the bride, surely, and, when she has been found, to make known to her the things concerning the beloved. For they will seek not their own glory, but the bridegroom's, since they are friends of the bridegroom. And for this they will not labor much with her: she is present, and already she seeks him with her whole devotion; so greatly has her will been prepared by the Lord.
78.7: Finally, while they are not yet saying anything, she asks about the beloved, and, herself gone before, she goes before her preachers, inquiring and saying: Have you seen him whom my soul loves? (Song 3:3.) Well, accordingly, did she declare herself found by these who keep the city, she who already knew herself foreknown and gone before by the Lord of the city, so that they might find her such, not make her such. Thus Cornelius was found by Peter, and Paul by Ananias, for both had been gone before by the Lord, and prepared. What was readier than Saul, who with mind and voice already suppliant had cried: Lord, what do you will that I do? (Acts 9:6.) Nor less Cornelius, who by his alms and his prayers, the Lord indeed breathing them into him, merited to arrive at faith (Acts 10:4). Philip also found Nathanael; but the Lord had already seen him before, when he was under the fig tree: and that vision of the Lord, was it not a preparation? And Andrew likewise is reported to have found Simon his brother, but equally foreseen by the Lord and foreknown, that he should be called Cephas, that is, strong in faith (John 1:45, 48, 41, 42).
78.8: We read of Mary that she was found to have in the womb from the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:18). But I think that in this part the bride of the Lord has something like her, to his own mother. For unless she also had been found having from the Holy Spirit, she would by no means have inquired so familiarly of those who found her concerning him whose Spirit he is. She did not bear that they should speak out to what end they had come; she herself spoke, and indeed out of the abundance of the heart: Have you seen him whom my soul loves? She knew that blessed are the eyes that had seen, and, wondering at those who had seen, she was saying: Are you they to whom it was granted to see him whom so many kings and prophets wished to see, and did not see? Are you they who have merited to look upon Wisdom in the flesh, Truth in a body, God in a man? Many say, Behold, he is here, and behold, he is there: but I think it safer for myself to grant belief to you, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. And let this have been said of that about which the bride inquired of the watchmen. If it is anything less, it will be supplied in another sermon. But now from this it is clear above all that she had been gone before by the Holy Spirit, but found and discovered by these who keep the city, because truly she herself is the one whom God foreknew and predestined before the ages, and prepared for his beloved Son as everlasting delights unto the eternal ages, that she may be holy and unspotted in his sight, sprouting like a lily, and flowering forever before the Lord, the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
78.title: That the bride, that is, the Church of the elect, was predestined by God before the ages, and prevented by him, so that she would seek him, and be converted.

79.1: Have you seen him whom my soul loves? (Song 3:3.) O love headlong, vehement, burning, impetuous, who allow nothing besides yourself to be thought, you scorn the rest, you despise all things besides yourself, content with yourself! You confound ranks, you set customary use aside, you know no measure; everything that seems to belong to fitness, to reason, to shame, to counsel or to judgment, you triumph over within yourself and lead captive. Behold, everything she thinks, and everything she speaks, sounds of you, breathes of you, and of nothing else: so have you claimed for yourself both her heart and her tongue. She says: Have you seen him whom my soul loves? As if indeed these know what she herself is thinking. Him whom your soul loves, about him do you inquire? And has he no name? But who, truly, are you, and who is he? And these things I would have said thus on account of the singularity of the speech, and the remarkable carelessness of the words, by which the present writing appears unlike enough the rest. Whence, in this wedding song, not words are to be weighed, but affection. Why so, if not because holy love, which is agreed to be the one matter of this whole volume, is not to be measured by word or by tongue, but by work and by truth? Love speaks everywhere: and if anyone desires to gain knowledge of these things that are read, let him love. Otherwise, he who does not love draws near in vain to hear or to read the song of love: since a cold breast cannot at all take in a fiery speech. For as he who does not know Greek does not understand one speaking Greek, nor he who is not Latin one speaking Latin, and so of the rest; so the tongue of love will be barbarous to him who does not love, and it will be as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal (1 Cor. 13:1). But these (I speak of the watchmen), since they also have received of the Spirit that they may love, know what the Spirit speaks, and, the voices of love being best known to them, they have it ready to answer in a like tongue, that is, by the pursuits of love and the offices of piety.
79.2: Finally, they send her away taught in so short a space about that which she seeks, so that she says: When I had passed a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves. Well, a little, because they made for her an abbreviated word, handing on the Symbol of the faith. And what follows is of this sort. It was needful indeed that the bride pass through those through whom she might come to know the truth; but nonetheless also that she pass beyond. For unless she had passed beyond even them, she would not have found him whom she was seeking. And do not doubt that this very thing was urged upon her by them. For they were not preaching themselves, but the Lord Jesus, who without doubt is both above them and beyond them. Whence he also says: Pass over to me, all you who desire me (Sir. 24:19). Nor did it suffice to pass through, but she is taught also to pass beyond. Since he whom she was tracking had passed beyond. For not only had he passed from death to life, but he had passed beyond into glory. Why ought she not also to have passed beyond equally? Otherwise she could not lay hold of him whom she would not follow by the same footsteps wherever he had gone.
79.3: And that what I say may be clearer: if my Lord Jesus had indeed risen from the dead, but had not at all ascended into the heavens, it could not have been said of him that he had passed beyond, but only that he had passed through; and for this reason the bride seeking him would have needed only to pass through, not to pass beyond. But now, since by rising he had already passed through, and had added a passing beyond, by ascending, surely; rightly did she also declare that she had not passed through, but had passed beyond, she who followed him indeed by faith and devotion even unto the heavens. To believe the resurrection, therefore, is to pass through; to believe the ascension also is to pass beyond. And perhaps (which I remember I said one day, when I was treating it [Serm. 1 for the feast of Easter]) she knew the former, she did not know the latter. Therefore, instructed by them in what she lacked, namely that he who had risen had also ascended, she also ascended equally, that is, she passed beyond, and she found. Why should she not have found, reaching with the mind where he is in the body? When I had passed a little beyond them. And well, beyond them: for our head went before, and passed beyond, both them and his other members which are upon the earth, by two points, by the resurrection, as we have already said, and by the ascension. For Christ is the firstfruits. But if he went before; our faith also. For where would she not follow him? If he shall go up into heaven, she is there; if he shall go down into hell, she is present; and if he shall take his wings at the dawn and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, there, he says, your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me (Ps. 139:8-10). Has not, finally, according to this faith, the almighty and supremely good Father of the bridegroom raised us up together, and made us sit together at his right hand? And this for that which the Church said, that I passed beyond them; since she has also passed beyond herself, standing by faith where she has not yet arrived in the thing itself. I think this also is plain, why she preferred to say that she had passed beyond, rather than that she had passed through. And let us pass on to the things that follow.
79.4: I held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who bore me. So it is: from then on, and thereafter, the Christian race does not fail, nor faith from the earth, nor charity from the Church. The floods came, the winds blew, and they beat upon her, and she did not fall, because she had been founded upon the rock (Matt. 7:25). And the rock is Christ. And so, neither by the wordiness of philosophers, nor by the cavils of heretics, nor by the swords of persecutors, could she, or shall she ever be able, to be separated from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:39): so strongly does she hold him whom her soul loves, so good is it for her to cling to God. The solder is good, says Isaiah (Isa. 41:7). What is more tenacious than this solder, which is neither washed away by waters, nor loosened by winds, nor cut by swords? Finally, many waters shall not be able to quench charity (Song 8:7). I held him, and I will not let him go. And the holy patriarch: I will not let you go, he says, unless you bless me (Gen. 32:26). So she is unwilling to let him go, and perhaps more unwilling than the patriarch, because not even for a blessing: since he, once the blessing had been received, let him go, but she not so. I do not want, she says, your blessing, but you. For what is there for me in heaven, and besides you what have I desired upon earth? (Ps. 73:25.) I will not let you go, not even if you bless me.
79.5: I held him, and I will not let him go. Nor perhaps is he less willing to be held, when he declares, saying: My delights are to be with the sons of men (Prov. 8:31): and when, promising, he says: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20). What is stronger than this bond, which has been made firm by the one so vehement will of the two? I held him, she says. But nonetheless she in turn is held by him whom she holds, to whom she says elsewhere: You have held my right hand (Ps. 73:23). She who is held and who holds, how can she now fall? She holds by the firmness of faith, she holds by the affection of devotion. But she would by no means hold long, if she were not held. But she is held by the power and the mercy of the Lord. I held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who bore me. Great is the charity of the Church, which does not begrudge her delights even to the rival Synagogue. What is kinder than that she should be ready to share, even with an enemy, him whom her soul loves? Nor is it wonderful, however, because salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Let the Savior return to the place from which he had gone out, that the remnant of Israel may be saved. Let not the branches be ungrateful to the root, nor the children to their mother. Let not the branches begrudge the root that which they took from her: nor the children their mother, that which they sucked from her breasts. Let the Church, therefore, hold firmly the salvation which Judea lost and which she herself has laid hold of, until the fullness of the nations comes in, and so all Israel may be saved. Let her will the common salvation to come into the common possession, a salvation which is so received by all that nothing is lessened for each. Surely she does this, and more. What more? That she desires for her both the name of bride and the grace. Altogether this is above salvation.
79.6: An unbelievable charity, if the word which she herself spoke had not made it credible. For she said, if you noticed, that she wishes to bring him whom she was holding not only into the house of her mother, but also into the chamber, which is a mark of prerogative. It would have sufficed for salvation, if he entered the house: but the secrecy of the chamber signifies grace. Today, he says, salvation has been made for this house (Luke 19:9). Why should there not be salvation for the household, when the Savior has entered the house? But she who merits to receive him into the chamber has her secret apart for herself. Salvation is made for the house; delights are stored up for the bridal chamber. Into the house of my mother I will bring him, she says. Into which house, if not that of which he once foretold to the Jews: Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate? (Luke 13:35.) He did what he said, as you have his witness of this also in the prophet: I have left, he says, my house, I have forsaken my inheritance (Jer. 12:7): and now she promises to lead him back, and to restore to the house of her mother the salvation that was lost. And if this seems too little, hear what good thing she adds: And into the chamber of her who bore me. He who enters the bridal chamber is the bridegroom. Great is the power of love! The Savior had gone out indignant from his house and from his inheritance: and now, softened at her grace, he is so bent that he returns not only as Savior, but also as bridegroom. Blessed are you by the Lord, O daughter, who both check his indignation and have restored the inheritance. Blessed are you to your mother, by whose kindness wrath is turned aside, salvation returns, and he returns who may say to her: I am your salvation (Ps. 35:3). This does not suffice; let him add and say: I will betroth you to me in faith, I will betroth you to me in judgment and in justice, I will betroth you to me in mercy and in compassions (Hos. 2:19, 20). But remember that she who gains these friendships is the bride. How, then, does she yield the bridegroom, and this bridegroom, to another, not to say desire it? It is not so. The good daughter does indeed desire him for her mother, yet not that she may yield him to her, but that she may share him. One suffices for two, except that now they were not two, but one in him. For he himself is our peace, who makes both one, that there may be one bride, and one bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
79.title: Concerning the tenacious and indissoluble love, by which the soul holds the bridegroom: likewise concerning the return of the bridegroom at the end of the age to save the Synagogue of the Jews.

80.1: Some of you, as I have learned, bear it with less than a fair mind, that now for several days, while it pleases us to cling to wonder and admiration of the mysteries, the sermon we serve has been seasoned either with none, or with very little, of the salt of moral things. That indeed is beyond what is usual. But may one not look again at the things that have been said? I do not go on, unless I first turn all of them over. Come, tell me, if you remember, from what place of Scripture this withholding began, so that from there I may take it up again. It is mine to repair the losses, or rather the Lord's, on whom we presume for the whole. From what beginning, then, is it to be taken up again? From there, perhaps: In my little bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves? (Song 3:1.) Unless I am mistaken, from there. From then on, and thereafter, my one care has been, the thick mist of these allegories having been discussed, to set in the light the secret delights of Christ and of the Church. Let us return, therefore, to searching out the moral senses. For that cannot be irksome to me which will have been profitable to you. And this will be done fittingly in this way, if the things that have been said in Christ and in the Church we nonetheless assign, the same, to the Word and to the soul.
80.2: But someone says to me: Why do you join these two? for what has the soul to do with the Word? Much, in every way. First, indeed, because the kinship of the natures is so great that this one is the image, and that one is according to the image. Next, because likeness bears witness to the kinship. For she was made not only according to the image, but according to the likeness. In what she is like, you ask? Hear first concerning the image. The Word is truth, is wisdom, is justice: and this is the image. Of what? Of justice, of wisdom, and of truth. For this image is justice from justice, wisdom from wisdom, truth from truth, as light from light, God from God. The soul is none of these things, since she is not the image. She is nonetheless capable of them, and desirous of them, and from that, perhaps, according to the image. A lofty creature, bearing a mark, in capacity indeed of majesty, but in desire of uprightness. We read that God made man upright (Eccl. 7:29), which greatness also, as has been said, the capacity proves. For that which is according to the image must agree with the image, and not share the name of image in vain, just as the image itself is not called image by a name alone or an empty one. But you have it of him who is the image, that, being in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2:6). Where, surely, both his uprightness in the form of God is hinted to you, and his majesty in the equality: so that, while uprightness is compared with uprightness, and greatness with greatness, that which is according to the image, and the image, may appear to answer one another in harmony from either side; just as the image also nonetheless answers in both to him whose image it is. For he it is of whom you have heard holy David singing in the psalms, now indeed: Great is our Lord, and great is his power (Ps. 147:5); but now: Upright is the Lord our God, and there is no iniquity in him (Ps. 92:15). From that upright and great God his image has it that she also is upright, and great: the soul has it, which is according to the image.
80.3: But I say: Does the image, then, have nothing more than the soul which is according to the image, because to this one also we assign what is great and upright? And very much. This one received them to a measure, that one to an equality. Is this not more? Notice also another thing. To this one, either creation or favor conferred both; to that one, generation. And that this is more magnificent is not doubtful. But neither would anyone deny that this too is more eminent, that, whereas for this one both are from God, for that one both are also of God, that is, of the substance of God. For his image is consubstantial with God, and everything that seems to be imparted to that image of his is, for both, substantial, not accidental. Attend yet to one thing in which the image stands out not a little. Great and upright (who does not know that these two differ by nature from one another?) in the image they are one. Nor this only: they are one also with the image. For to the image, not only is to be upright the same as to be great, but also to be great and upright is the same as to be. Not so for the soul. Both her greatness, and her uprightness, are diverse from her, and diverse from one another. For if, as I taught above, the soul is great in that she is capable of eternal things, and upright in that she desires the things above: she who neither seeks nor savors the things that are above, but the things that are upon the earth, is plainly not upright, but bent, while nonetheless she does not cease, on account of this sort of thing, to be great, remaining capable of eternity even so. For she will not at any time be incapable of it, even if she shall never have been one who grasps it, so that it may be as it is written: Surely man passes as an image (Ps. 39:6); in part, however, that the eminence of the Word may appear from that very wholeness. For how should the Word fall away from what is great or upright, which possesses them in such a way as to be what it possesses? Or for this reason in part, lest, if he were deprived of the whole, no hope of salvation should remain. For if she cease to be great, she ceases also to be capable. Since, as I said, the greatness of the soul is reckoned from her capacity. But what could he hope, of which he would not be capable.
80.4: And so, through the greatness which he retains even when uprightness has been lost, man passes in the image, limping as it were on one foot, and made a stranger's son. For of such I think it was said: The children of strangers have lied to me, the children of strangers have grown old, and have halted from their paths (Ps. 18:45). Beautifully have they been called children of strangers: for children, on account of the greatness retained; strangers, on account of the uprightness lost. Nor would he have said, they halted, but: They fell, or something like it, if men had put off the image wholly. But now, according to greatness indeed, man passes in the image; but as regards uprightness, as one limping, he is troubled and cast down from the image, Scripture saying thus: Surely man passes as an image; but he is troubled in vain. Altogether in vain: for it follows: He heaps up treasure, and does not know for whom he shall gather it (Ps. 39:6). Why does he not know, if not because, bending himself to these lowest and earthly things, he heaps up earth for himself? He is altogether ignorant, concerning the things he commits to the earth, for whom he shall gather them, whether for the moth that destroys, or for the thief that digs through; for the enemy that plunders, or for the fire that devours. And hence, for the wretched man bending himself down and lying upon the things that are on the earth, that tearful voice from the psalm: I have been made wretched, and I have been bowed down to the end; all the day I went sorrowful (Ps. 38:6). In himself, surely, he experiences the truth of that sentence of the Wise Man: God made man upright, but he has entangled himself with many sorrows (Eccl. 7:29). And at once a voice of mockery to him: Bow down, that we may go over (Isa. 51:23).
80.5: But whence have we come here? From there, surely, when we wished to teach that what is upright and what is great (by which twin good we had defined the image) are neither one in the soul, nor one with the soul, in the same way that we taught, by an assertion equally to be believed, that they are one in the Word and with the Word. And concerning uprightness, indeed, from the things that have been said it is clear that it is diverse both from the soul and from the greatness of the soul: since, even when it does not exist, both the soul remains, and remains great. But whence shall the diversity of greatness and of the soul be taught? For it cannot be from there whence the diversity of uprightness and of the soul was shown, since the soul cannot be deprived of her greatness as she can of her uprightness. Yet her greatness is not the soul. For although the soul is not found without her greatness, that greatness itself is nonetheless found also outside the soul. You ask where? In the angels. For from there the angels are great, from where the greatness of the soul is proved, namely from the grasp of eternity. But if the soul was established to differ from her uprightness in this, that she can lack it: why should it not be equally clear that she is diverse also from her greatness, which she cannot claim as proper to herself? Since, therefore, neither the former is in every soul, nor the latter in the soul alone, it is plain that both differ from her indifferently. Likewise, no form is that of which it is the form. But greatness is a form of the soul. For it is not for that reason not a form, because it is inseparable from her. For all substantial differences are this, this not only what is properly proper, but also certain properties, this also other innumerable forms. Her greatness, therefore, is not the soul, no more than his blackness is the raven, than her whiteness the snow, than his ability to laugh or his rationality the man: though nonetheless you never find a raven without blackness, nor snow without whiteness, nor a man who is not both able to laugh and rational. So also the soul, and the greatness of the soul, though inseparable, are nonetheless diverse from one another. How are they not diverse, when this is in a subject, and that is the subject and the substance? The supreme and uncreated nature alone, which is the Trinity, God, claims for herself this pure and singular simplicity of her essence, so that not one thing and another, nor in one place and another, nor even in one manner and another, is found in her. For remaining in herself, she is what she has, and what she is, she always is, and in one manner. In her both many things are brought back into one, and diverse things into the same, so that she takes plurality neither from the number of things, nor feels alteration from variety. She contains all places, and orders each in its own places, herself contained by the places nowhere. Times pass under her, not for her. She does not wait for things to come, she does not think back on things past, she does not experience things present.
80.6: Let them depart from us, most dear ones, let them depart, the new men, not dialecticians but heretics, who most impiously dispute that the greatness by which God is great, and likewise the goodness by which he is good, and also the wisdom by which he is wise and the justice by which he is just, and lastly the divinity by which he is God, are not God. By divinity, they say, God is, but divinity is not God. Perhaps that which is so great as to make God does not deign to be God. But if it is not God, what is it? For either it is God, or something which is not God, or nothing. You do not grant, indeed, that it is God, but neither, as I think, will you grant that it is nothing, which you confess to be so necessary to God that not only can God not be without it, but that by it he is. But if it is something which is not God: it will be either less than God, or greater, or equal. But how less, by which God is? It remains that you confess it either greater or equal. But if greater, it itself is the supreme good, not God; if equal, there are two supreme goods, not one: both of which the catholic sense shuns. Now concerning greatness, goodness, justice, and wisdom, we think throughout the same as concerning divinity: they are one in God, and with God. For he is not good from anywhere else than from where he is great, nor just or wise from anywhere else than from where he is great and good, nor finally is he all these things together from anywhere else than from where he is God, and this too only by himself.
80.7: But the heretic says: What? Do you deny that God is by divinity? Not so, but I assert that the same divinity by which he is, is nonetheless God, lest I agree that anything is more excellent than God. For by greatness also I say that he is great, but by a greatness which he himself is, lest I set anything greater than God; and by goodness I confess that he is good, but by no other than he himself is, lest I seem to myself to have found anything better than him; and of the rest in this manner. Secure and willing, I go on with unstumbling foot, as they say, into the opinion of him who was saying: God is great by no greatness except that which is what he himself is. Otherwise that greatness will be greater than God. This is Augustine, the most mighty hammer of heretics. If, therefore, anything can be said of God properly, it will be said more rightly and more fittingly: God is greatness, goodness, justice, wisdom, than: God is great, good, just, or wise.
80.8: Whence, not undeservedly, lately in the council which Pope Eugenius held at Rheims, that exposition seemed perverse, and altogether suspect, both to him and to the other bishops, in the book of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, in which, upon the words of Boethius on the Trinity, most sound indeed and catholic, he was commenting in this manner: The Father is truth, that is, true; the Son is truth, that is, true; the Holy Spirit is truth, that is, true. And these three together are not three truths, but one truth, that is, one true. O dark and perverse explanation! How much more truly and more soundly he would have said it the other way about, thus: The Father is true, that is, truth; the Son is true, that is, truth; the Holy Spirit is true, that is, truth. And these three are one true, that is, one truth. Which indeed he would have done, if he had deigned to imitate the holy Fulgentius, who says: For the one truth of the one God, or rather, the one truth, the one God, does not suffer the service and worship of the creator and of the creature to be joined. A good corrector, who would speak most truly of the truth, who would think piously and in a catholic way of the true and pure simplicity of the divine substance, in which there can be nothing which itself is not, and itself God. Though more manifestly, in several other places, that book of the aforesaid bishop has seemed to depart from the rightness of the faith; of which, for example, I still set down one. For while the author was saying, When it is said, God, God, God, it pertains to the substance: our commentator added, Not that which he is, but that by which he is. Far be it that the catholic Church assent to this, namely that there is a substance, or any thing at all, by which God is, and which is not God!
80.9: But these things we now say by no means against him himself; for he, in that same assembly, humbly acquiescing in the sentence of the bishops, condemned with his own mouth both these things and the rest that were found worthy of rebuke; but on account of those who are still reported to copy out and to read that book, against the apostolic interdict certainly promulgated there, persisting rather contentiously to follow the bishop where he himself did not stand, and preferring to have as master the error rather than the correction. But not only so, but also on account of you, the occasion being taken from the difference of the image and of the soul which was made according to the image, I believed it worth the labor to make this digression: so that if any have perhaps at some time drunk something of the stolen waters, which seem sweeter (Prov. 9:17), they may, the antidote having been taken, vomit it out, and, the stomach of the mind having been purged, approaching what, according to our promise, remains to be said concerning the likeness, may now in joy draw purer things, not from our own, but from the fountains of the Savior, the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
80.title: Concerning the image or Word of God, and the soul which is made after the image, a subtle disputation: and concerning the error of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers.

81.1: Inquiry was made before concerning the kinship of the soul to the Word, and that indeed of necessity. For what agreement is there between so great a majesty and so great a poverty, that that loftiness and that lowliness are said to embrace one another, after the manner and the love of spouses, as if on equal terms? For if we say this truly, the confidence is very glad; if falsely, the boldness is very much to be punished. For this reason, therefore, inquiry had to be made concerning the fitness of these two: which has indeed already been found to be great, but not the whole of it. For who, even if exceedingly dull, does not see how near at hand image and that which is according to the image look upon one another? Of which, surely, yesterday's sermon, if you recall, assigned the one to the one and the other to the other. Nor was the nearness shown there from the image only, but also from the likeness, except that it has not yet been declared by us in what, or in what things above all, that likeness itself consists. Come, let us now give heed to this declaration, so that the more fully the soul recognizes her origin, the more she may blush to have a degenerate life; or rather, what she finds vitiated by sin in her nature, let her study to reform by diligence; so that, guiding herself worthily of her kind, by the gift of God indeed, she may confidently approach the embraces of the Word.
81.2: Let her notice, therefore, that from this divine nobility of likeness there is in her that natural simplicity of her substance, by which for her to be is the same as to live, though not the same as to live well, or to live blessedly, so that there is likeness, not equality. A step that is near, yet a step. For they are not of one excellence or of an equal height, to have being the same as living, and likewise to have this being the same as living blessedly. If, then, the former belongs to the Word by reason of sublimity, and the latter to the soul by reason of likeness, the eminence of the Word being indeed kept safe, the kinship of the natures is plain, the prerogative of the soul is plain. And that what is said may be plainer: for God alone, to be is the same as to be blessed; and this is the first and purest simple. But the second is like to this, namely to have being the same as living; and this belongs to the soul. From this, though from a lower step, one can ascend not only to living well, but even to living blessedly: not that even then, for him who has arrived there, to be will be the same as to be blessed; so that he may thus glory on account of the likeness, yet on account of the disparity always have that whereby all his bones may say: Lord, who is like you? (Ps. 35:10). A good step of the soul nonetheless, from which, and from which alone, one ascends to the blessed life.
81.3: For there are living things, and two kinds of them: those which feel, and those which do not feel. Further, things that feel are preferred to things that do not feel, and to both is preferred the life by which one lives and feels. Life and a living thing will not stand together on one step; much less life, and the things which are without life. The soul is a life, living indeed, but from nowhere else than from herself; and for this reason not so much a living thing as a life, that we may speak of her properly. Hence it is that, poured into the body, she makes it live, so that from the presence of life the body is not a life, but a living thing. From which it is clear that not even for a living body is to live the same as to be, since it can be and not live at all. Much less will the things which are without experience of life rise to this step. But neither will everything which is called life, or is life, straightway be able to reach this far. There is a life of cattle, and there is also a life of trees, the one vigorous with sense, the other lacking it. But for neither, nonetheless, is to be the same as to live: since, as indeed is the opinion of many, they existed in the elements before either the former existed in the members or the latter in the branches; but according to this, when they cease to give life, they cease at the same time to live, but not also to be. They are loosed together and dissolved, as though not only bound, but bound up together. For neither of these is one simple thing; but each consists of several. And for that reason it is not reduced to nothing, but flies apart into parts, so that each also runs back to its own beginning; for example, air to air, fire to fire, and the rest in this manner. By no means, therefore, is to be and to live the same for such a life, which also is when it does not live.
81.4: Further, none of those things for which to be is not the same as to live will ever advance or emerge to living well and blessedly: since indeed it could not even arrive at this lower step. The soul of man alone, which is known to stand on that very step, was created in this dignity, a life from life, simple from the simple, immortal from the immortal, so that she might not be far from the highest step, where namely to be is the same as to live blessedly, on which he alone stands who is blessed, and he alone who is powerful, the King of kings and the Lord of lords. The soul received, therefore, in her creation, if not to be blessed, yet to be able to be blessed; drawing near, accordingly, to the highest step as far as is permitted, yet not reaching it. For not even for her, as we said above, will to be ever be the same as to be blessed, not even when she shall be blessed. We confess a likeness; we refuse an equality. For example, God is life, and the soul also is life; like indeed, but unequal. Like, further, in that she is life, in that she lives by herself, in that she is not only living but also life-giving, just as he also is all these things. Unequal, truly, by as much as the created is unequal to the creating. Unequal, because, as she would not be unless created by him, so she would not live unless made alive by him. I say she would not live, but with the spiritual life, not the natural. For with the natural life, indeed, even she who does not live spiritually must of necessity live immortally. But what a life, in which it would be better not to be born than not to die out of it! It is rather a death: and the heavier for this, that it is of sin, not of nature; finally, the death of sinners is the worst (Ps. 34:21). So, then, the soul which lives according to the flesh is dead while living; for to her it was good not to live at all, rather than to live thus. From which, surely, a certain vital death, she will by no means ever rise again, except through the word of life, or rather through the Word who is life, living indeed and making alive.
