81.5: But in another respect the soul is immortal, and in this nonetheless like to the Word indeed, but not equal. For the immortality of the Godhead so far excels, that the Apostle says of God: Who alone has immortality (1 Tim. 6:16). Which I think was said for this reason, that God alone is unchangeable by nature, he who says: I am the Lord, and I am not changed (Mal. 3:6). For true and entire immortality no more admits change than it admits an end, because every change is a kind of imitation of death. For everything that is changed, while it passes from one being to another, must in a certain way die to what it is, that it may begin to be what it is not. But if there are as many deaths as there are changes, where is immortality? And to this vanity the creature herself has been made subject, not willingly, but on account of him who subjected her in hope (Rom. 8:20). Nevertheless the soul is immortal; since, as she is life to herself, just as there is nowhere she may fall from herself, so there is nowhere she may fall from life. But since it is established that she is changed by her affections, let her acknowledge that she is like God in immortality in such a way that she knows no small part of immortality is lacking to her, yielding to him alone an absolute and perfect immortality, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration. No mean dignity of the soul, nonetheless, has been found by the present discussion, which by a certain twofold nearness of nature seems to draw near to the Word, by simplicity of essence and by perpetuity of life.
81.6: But still one thing occurs, which I shall by no means pass over: for it makes the soul no less marked, and no less like the Word, and perhaps even more. This is freedom of choice, plainly something divine shining out in the soul, like a gem in gold. From this, surely, there is in her, between good and evil indeed, and also between life and death, but nonetheless also between light and darkness, both the knowledge of judgment and the choice of choosing; and whatever other things there are which likewise seem to look upon one another from opposite sides in the disposition of the mind. Nonetheless, among these very things a certain censor as judge (this is the eye of the soul) judges and discerns, as a judge in discerning, so free in choosing. Whence it is also named free choice, because it is permitted to move among these things according to the decision of the will. Hence man is able to merit. For everything you have done, good or evil, which indeed it was free not to do, is rightly reckoned toward merit. And, as he is rightly praised, not only who was able to do evil things and did not, but also who was able not to do good things and did them; so he does not lack the merit of evil, as much the one who was able not to do evil things and did them, as the one who was able to do good things and did not. But where there is no liberty, there is also no merit. For this reason the animals which lack reason merit nothing; because, as they lack deliberation, so also they lack liberty. They are driven by sense, they are carried by impulse, they are seized by appetite. For they do not have a judgment by which they may judge or rule themselves, nor even the instrument of judgment, that is, reason. Hence it is that they are not judged, because they do not judge. For by what reason should an account be required of those who have not received reason?
81.7: This force man alone does not suffer from nature, and therefore he alone among living beings is free. And yet, with sin intervening, he too suffers a certain force, but from the will, not from nature, so that not even thus is he deprived of his inborn liberty. For what is voluntary is also free. And indeed by sin it has come about that the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul; but by love, not by mass. For that the soul can no longer rise by herself, she who was able to fall by herself, the will is the cause, which, languishing and lying under the vitiated and vicious love of the corrupted body, does not likewise admit the love of justice. Thus, in some perverse and wonderful way, the will itself, changed indeed by sin for the worse, makes a necessity: so that neither can the necessity, since it is voluntary, avail to excuse the will; nor the will, since it has been enticed, avail to shut out the necessity. For this necessity is in a certain way voluntary. It is a certain favorable force, coaxing by pressing and pressing by coaxing: from which the guilty will, once it has consented to sin, can neither now of itself shake itself free, nor yet in any way excuse itself on the ground of reason. Hence that complaining voice, as of one groaning under the burden of this necessity: Lord, he says, I suffer violence, answer for me. But again, knowing that he would not justly plead a cause against the Lord, since his own will was rather the cause, mark what he went on to add: What shall I say, or what will he answer me, when I myself have done it? (Isa. 38:14, 15.) He was pressed by a yoke, yet by no other than that of a certain voluntary slavery; and he was indeed pitiable on account of the slavery, but inexcusable on account of the will. For it is the will which, when it was free, made itself the slave of sin, by assenting to sin: it is nonetheless the will which holds itself under sin, by serving voluntarily.
81.8: See what you are saying, someone says to me. Do you call voluntary that which is already established to be necessary? It is true indeed that the will has given herself over: but she does not hold herself; rather she is held, and that unwilling. You grant this at least well, that she is held. But carefully hold to this, that it is a will which you confess is held. And so you speak of a will that is unwilling? By no means is a will held if she is not willing. For a will belongs to one who wills, not to one who is unwilling. But if she is held while willing, she holds herself. What then shall she say, or what shall she answer him, when she herself has done it? What has she done? She has made herself a slave: whence it is said: He who commits sin is the slave of sin (John 8:34). Therefore, when she sinned (and she sinned when she determined to obey sin), she made herself a slave. But she becomes free, if she does not still do it. But she does do it, holding herself in the same slavery. For a will is not held if she is not willing: for she is a will. Therefore, because she is willing, she has not only made herself a slave, but also makes herself one. Rightly, therefore, a thing often to be remembered, what shall she answer him, when she herself has done it, and herself also does it?
81.9: But you will not, you say, make me disbelieve the necessity which I suffer, which I experience in my very self, and against which I also struggle continually. Where, I ask, do you feel this necessity? Is it not in the will? You do not, therefore, will with too little firmness that which you also will necessarily. You will much that which you are unable not to will, not even by struggling much. Further, where there is will, there is also liberty. Yet what I say I say of the natural liberty, not of the spiritual, by which liberty, as the Apostle says, Christ has set us free (Gal. 5:1). For of that same liberty he says: Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (2 Cor. 3:17). Thus the soul, in a certain wonderful and evil way, under this necessity, voluntary in a way and evilly free, is held both a handmaid and free: a handmaid, on account of the necessity; free, on account of the will: and, what is more wonderful and more wretched, guilty in the degree that she is free, and a handmaid in the degree that she is guilty, and therefore a handmaid in the degree that she is free. Wretched man that I am, who will set me free from the charge of this shameful slavery? Wretched, but free. Free, because a man; wretched, because a slave. Free, because like God; wretched, because contrary to God. O keeper of men, why have you set me contrary to you? For you have set me so, in that you did not forbid it. Otherwise I have set myself, and I am become a burden to myself (Job 7:20). Most justly indeed, that your enemy should be my enemy also, and that he who fights against you should fight against me also. But I, who have been made contrary to you, I who have been made contrary to myself, and find in my members what contradicts both my mind and your law: who will set me free from my own hands? For I do not do that which I will, but, with no other forbidding me, that which I hate, that I do (Rom. 7:15), but with no other compelling me. And would that this forbidding, and this compelling, were so violent that it were not voluntary; for perhaps thus I could be excused: or at least so voluntary that it were not violent; for surely thus I could be corrected. But now nowhere does a way out lie open for the wretch, whom, as I have said, the will makes inexcusable, and the necessity incorrigible. Who will snatch me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the one who acts against the law and is unjust? (Ps. 71:4.)
81.10: Someone asks, of whom I complain? Of myself. I am that sinner, that man without law, that unjust man. A sinner, because I have sinned; without law, because I persist by will in acting against the law. For my will itself is the law in my members, kicking against the divine law. And since the law of the Lord is the law of my mind, as it is written: The law of his God is in his heart (Ps. 37:31); for this reason my own will is found contrary also to myself, which is the greatest iniquity. For to whom is he not unjust, who is so to myself? He who is worthless to himself, he says, to whom is he good? (Sir. 14:5) I confess I am not good, because there is no good in me. I shall console myself nonetheless, because this voice is also that of the saints: I know, he says, that there is no good in me. He nonetheless distinguishes what he says: In himself. Explaining it as in his flesh, on account of the contradicting law which is in it. For he has a law also in the mind, and a better one. Is not the law of God good? But if he is evil on account of the evil law, how is he not good on account of the good one? Or is the law his which is in his flesh, and therefore he is evil from the evil law; and not at all good from the good one? It is not so. The law of his God is in his mind, and so in the mind that it also belongs to the mind. Witness is he himself who says: I find another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind. Is what is of his flesh his, and what is of his mind not his? I say even more. Why should I not say what the same teacher himself says? For serving the law of God indeed with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin, he shows plainly what he confesses to be more his own, when he judges the evil which is in the flesh so foreign to himself that he says: And so it is no longer I who work it, but the sin that dwells in me. And for that reason perhaps he said that another law was found in his members, because he reckoned this one foreign, and as it were come in from outside. Whence I also still dare something further, yet by no means rashly: namely, that Paul is not now evil, on account of the evil which he has in the flesh; but rather good, on account of the good which he has in the mind. Is he not good, who consents to the law of God, since it is good? For although he likewise confesses that he serves the law of sin, he does this with the flesh, not with the mind. But when with the mind indeed he serves the law of God, and with the flesh the law of sin, which of these you think is chiefly to be imputed to Paul, you yourself must see. For I confess that I am easily persuaded that what is of the mind is of more account than what is of the flesh, not only to me, but also to Paul himself, as has already been said, who says: But if what I do not will, that I do, it is no longer I who work it, but the sin that dwells in me (Rom. 7:18, 23, 25, 20).
81.11: But let these things suffice concerning that liberty. In the little book which I wrote on Grace and Free Choice, things perhaps different concerning the image and the likeness are read to have been discussed; but, as I judge, not things opposed. You have read those; you have heard these: which of them you approve more, I leave to your judgment; or if you taste something better than both, in this I rejoice and shall rejoice. But however those things stand, you hold three things in particular commended at present: simplicity, immortality, liberty. And this I now judge appears clearly to you, that the soul, on account of the inborn and noble likeness, which shines out so eminently in these, has no small kinship with the Word, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
81.title: Concerning the agreement and likeness of the soul with the Word, according to the identity of essence, and the immortality of life, and the liberty of the will.

82.1: What seems to you? can we now go back to the order of expounding from which we digressed, since the nearness of the Word and the soul is plain, for the demonstrating of which, surely, the digression itself was made? We could, as it seems to me, unless I felt that a little something of doubt still remains in the things which have been said. I wish to steal nothing away. I do not gladly pass over what I think useful to you. And how should I dare it, especially concerning these things which I receive for you? I know a man who once, in the midst of speaking, held back and reserved to himself something of the things which the Spirit was suggesting, with a mind not unfaithful, yet less confident, so that he might have what to say when he was to treat the matter again; and behold, a voice to him, as indeed it seemed to him: As long as you hold that, you will not receive anything else. What if he had held it back, not providing for his own poverty, but envying the progress of the brethren? would not that very thing also, which he seemed to have, rightly be taken away from him? Which indeed may God always keep far from his servant, as he has also always done. So may that unfailing fountain of saving wisdom deign to abound to me continually, in the same way as without envy I have shared with you, and poured back, whatever he himself has hitherto deigned to pour into me. If I defraud you, by whom should I not now fear to be defrauded myself? Not even by God.
82.2: There is, therefore, in the things which have been said, something which, as I fear, can give an occasion of stumbling, if it is not made smooth. And, unless I am mistaken, there are some of those standing here for whom what I mean to say has moved a scruple. That threefold likeness of the Word, which we assigned to the soul, or rather with which we noticed that she is marked: do you recall that it also seemed to us to be in her inseparably? That indeed may seem to some to run against the testimonies of the Scriptures, as, for example, there is that in the psalms: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to the senseless beasts, and made like them (Ps. 49:12, 20); and likewise that: They changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay (Ps. 106:20), but also what was said openly in the person of God: You thought unjustly that I shall be like you (Ps. 50:21): and several other things, which seem with one accord to assert that the likeness of God in man was blotted out after sin. What, then, shall we say to these things? That those three are by no means in God, and so others must be sought, in which we may assign the likeness? or that they are indeed in God, but not in the soul, and that not even so is the likeness found in these? or that they are also in the soul, but can also not be in her, and for this reason are not inseparable? Far be it! They are both in God and in the soul, and they are always in them; nor is there cause that we should repent of having said any of these things, so wholly is the whole supported by undoubted and most absolute truth. But what Scripture says concerning an unlikeness that has been made, it says not because that likeness has been blotted out, but because another has been drawn over it. The soul has plainly not put off her native form, but has put on a foreign one. That has been added, this has not been lost: and what has come upon her was able to darken the inborn form, but not to destroy it. Finally: Their foolish heart has been darkened, says the Apostle (Rom. 1:21); and the prophet: How is the gold become dim, the finest color changed? (Lam. 4:1.) He laments gold that has been darkened, but gold nonetheless; a finest color changed, but not the foundation of the color torn out. Simplicity remains in the foundation altogether unshaken, but it by no means appears, covered by the duplicity of human deceit, pretense, and hypocrisy.
82.3: How unfittingly is duplicity mixed with simplicity! how unworthily is such a structure entrusted to such a foundation! The serpent had put on a cunning of this sort for himself, when, in order to deceive, he showed himself a counselor and pretended to be a friend. Those also who were seduced by him, the inhabitants of paradise, had put on for themselves a covering of this sort, when they tried to cover their now shameful nakedness, both with the shade of a leafy tree, and with girdles of leaves, and with words of excuse (Gen. 3). How widely from then on, and thereafter, has the hereditary poison of hypocrisy infected all posterity! Whom will you give of the sons of Adam who is willing, I do not say, or even who suffers himself, to be seen as what he is? But nonetheless, in every soul, together with the original duplicity, the general simplicity perseveres, so that confusion may be increased by the comparison: immortality perseveres equally, but dusky and foul, as the dark mist of bodily death rushes in. For although she is not deprived of life, she no longer suffices to claim for her own body the benefit of life. What of this, that she does not even keep for herself her own life, the spiritual one at least? For the soul that has sinned, the same shall die (Ezek. 18:4). Does not that immortality, of whatever sort, which she still holds, become dark enough and wretched, as this double death rushes in? Add that the appetite for earthly things, all of which indeed are unto destruction, thickens the darkness, so that in a soul living thus, in no part at all is anything seen to appear except a pale face and a certain image of death. For why does she who is immortal not desire immortal and eternal things like herself, so that she may appear what she is, and live what she was made? But she savors and seeks the contrary, and, conforming herself to mortality by a degenerate manner of life, she blackens the brightness of immortality with a certain pitch-like color of a death-dealing habit. Why will not an appetite for mortal things make the immortal like the mortal, and unlike the immortal? He who touches pitch, says the Wise Man, shall be defiled by it (Sir. 13:1). By enjoying mortal things she has put mortality on herself, and, with the likeness of death falling upon it, has discolored the garment of immortality, not put it off.
82.4: Look at Eve, how her immortal soul brought in upon the glory of her immortality the paint of mortality, by reaching, surely, after mortal things. For why, when she was immortal, did she not despise mortal and passing things, content with things like herself, immortal and eternal? She saw, it says, that the tree was beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in look, and sweet to eat (Gen. 3:6). That sweetness is not yours, O woman, nor that delight, nor that beauty: or if it is yours as regards the part of clay, it is not yours alone, but common to all the living things of the earth. Yours, that which is truly yours, is from elsewhere, and is another: for it is eternal, from eternity. Why do you impress upon your soul another form, or rather a foreign deformity? Indeed, what one delights to have, that one also fears to lose: and fear is a color. This, while it dyes liberty, covers it, and nonetheless renders it unlike itself. How much more worthily of her origin would she desire nothing, where she would fear nothing, and thereby defend from this servile fear the liberty inborn in her, remaining in its vigor and its grace! Alas! it is not so! the finest color is changed. You flee, and you hide: you hear the voice of the Lord God, and you hide yourself. Why this, unless because you fear him whom you loved, and a servile form has shut out the appearance of liberty?
82.5: But that voluntary necessity also, and the contrary law inflicted on the members, of which I discoursed in the last sermon, broods over the same liberty, and, while it entices, subjects to slavery the creature free by nature, through her own will, filling her face with ignominy, so that she even serves the law of sin with the flesh, and that not willingly. Because, therefore, she neglected to defend the nobleness of nature by uprightness of conduct, it has come about by the just judgment of the Author, not indeed that she should be stripped of her own liberty, but that she should nonetheless have her own confusion put on over her, as a double cloak (Ps. 109:29). And well as a double cloak, where, as with a garment doubled, liberty remaining on account of the will, a servile manner of life nonetheless proves the necessity. This is to be noticed concerning the simplicity, this concerning the immortality of the soul: and nothing will appear to you in her, if you consider well, which is not covered with a double cloak of this sort, of likeness and unlikeness together. Is it not a double cloak, where, not inborn but fastened on, and as it were sewn with the needle of sin, fraud is joined to simplicity, death to immortality, necessity to liberty? For duplicity of heart does not prescribe against the simplicity of essence; neither the death of sin, which is voluntary, nor the death of the body, which is necessary, against the immortality of nature; nor the necessity of voluntary slavery against the liberty of choice. Thus the evils that have come in from outside, while they do not succeed the goods of nature but accede to them, surely disgrace them, they do not destroy them; they trouble them, they do not cast them down. Hence the soul is unlike God, hence she is unlike herself also; hence she has been compared to the senseless beasts, and made like them; hence what is read, that she changed her glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay; hence men, like foxes, have the holes of duplicity and fraud, and because they have made themselves the equals of foxes, they shall be a portion for foxes; hence, according to Solomon, there is one end for man and for the beast (Eccl. 3:19). Why should he not go out in like manner, who has lived in like manner? He has lain upon earthly things after the manner of a beast; he will depart from the earth by the death of a beast. Hear another thing. What wonder if we obtain a like going out, who also have a like coming in? For whence comes to men, if not from a beastlike likeness, that ardor so intemperate in intercourse, that pain so immoderate in childbirth? Thus man, in conception and in birth, in life and in death, has been compared to the senseless beasts, and made like them.
82.6: What of this, that the free creature does not rule as mistress the appetite subjected to her, but follows and complies with it as a handmaid? Does she not in this also make herself like, and number herself with, the other living beings, which nature did not call into liberty, but established in slavery, to serve their own belly, to obey appetite? Is not God, by such a merit, confounded to be said, or thought, like her? And therefore he says: You thought unjustly that I shall be like you; and he adds: I will reprove you, and set it against your face (Ps. 50:21). It does not belong to a soul that sees herself to think God like herself, a soul, that is, such as mine is, sinful and unjust. For one of this sort is reproved: You thought unjustly, he says; and he does not say: You thought, O soul; or, you thought, O man, that I shall be like you. But if the unjust man is set before his own face, and is made to stand against a certain sickly and stinking countenance of his inner man, so that he cannot dissemble or turn aside the impurity of his conscience, but sees even unwilling the filth of his sins, and inspects the deformity of his vices; he will now by no means be able to think that God will be like himself, but, as though distrusting on account of so great an unlikeness as he will see, I think he will cry out and say: Lord, who is like you? (Ps. 35:10), which saying indeed is on account of that voluntary and recent unlikeness. For the first likeness remains: and for that reason the other displeases the more, because this one remains. O how great a good is this, and how great an evil that! Yet from their mutual comparison each thing stands out the more in its own kind.
82.7: When, therefore, the soul discerns in herself, one and the same, so great a distance of things, why should she not cry out, set surely between hope and despair: Lord, who is like you? She is drawn into despair on account of so great an evil; but she is called back into hope by so great a good. Hence it is that the more she displeases herself in the evil which she sees in herself, the more ardently she draws herself to the good which she equally beholds in herself, and desires to become what she was made, simple and upright, and fearing God, and departing from evil. Why should she not be able to depart from that to which she was able to approach? why should she not be able to approach that from which she was able to depart? Yet both of these I would say are to be presumed of grace, not of nature, nor even of industry. For wisdom overcomes malice (Wis. 7:30), not industry, or nature. Nor is the occasion of presuming lacking: her conversion is to the Word. The noble kinship of the soul is not idle with the Word, of which we have now been treating for three days, nor the likeness which perseveres, the witness of the kinship. He graciously admits into the fellowship of the Spirit one who is like in nature. And surely, by the reason of nature, like seeks like. The voice of the one who seeks: Return, O Shunammite; return, that we may look upon you (Song 6:12). He will look upon the one who is like, he who did not see the one who was unlike; but he will also offer himself to be looked upon. We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Think, therefore, that that question comes from the difficulty rather than from the impossibility: Lord, who is like you?
82.8: Or, if you approve this more, it is the voice of one who wonders. Altogether to be wondered at and to be amazed at is that likeness which the vision of God accompanies, or rather which is the vision of God; but I say, in charity. That charity is that vision, that likeness. Who would not be amazed at the charity of God scorned and calling back? Rightly is that unjust man reproved, who was brought in above, usurping to himself the likeness of God, since, by loving iniquity, he can neither love himself nor God: for so you have it: He who loves iniquity hates his own soul (Ps. 11:5). Iniquity, therefore, having been taken out of the way, which makes that unlikeness which is in part, there will be a union of spirit, there will be a mutual vision and a mutual love. For when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away; and there will be toward one another a chaste and consummate love, a full knowledge, a manifest vision, a firm joining, an undivided fellowship, a perfect likeness. Then the soul shall know, as she has been known (1 Cor. 13:10, 12); then she shall love, as she has been loved; and the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, knowing and known, loving and loved, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
82.title: In what way the soul, remaining like God, by sin nevertheless is made unlike in simplicity, immortality, and liberty.

83.1: As far indeed as the regular hour allowed, which we have set for ourselves for speaking, these three days have been spent in showing the kinship of the Word and the soul. What profit is there in all this labor? Surely this. We have taught that every soul, although burdened with sins, ensnared by vices, captured by allurements, a captive in exile, imprisoned in the body, clinging to the mud, stuck fast in the mire, fastened to her members, pinned through the calves, stretched by affairs, drawn tight by fears, afflicted with pains, wandering in errors, anxious with cares, restless with suspicions, and last of all a stranger in the land of enemies, according to the word of the prophet, defiled with the dead, reckoned with those who are in hell (Bar. 3:11); although, I say, thus condemned and thus despaired of, we have taught nonetheless that she can notice in herself not only that from which she may breathe again into a hope of pardon and a hope of mercy, but also that from which she may dare to aspire to the nuptials of the Word, may not tremble to enter a covenant of fellowship with God, and may not fear to draw the sweet yoke of love with the King of the angels. For what would she not safely dare with him, whose image she sees herself marked with, whose likeness she knows herself bright with? what, I say, should she fear from the majesty, she to whom confidence is given from her origin? Only let her take care to keep the nobleness of her nature by the honorableness of her life; rather, let her study to beautify and adorn with certain worthy colors of conduct and of affection the heavenly grace which is in her from the beginning.
83.2: For why should diligence sleep? Great indeed in us is the very gift of nature: and if it carries out its own part too little, will not what nature has remaining in us be wholly disturbed, wholly covered as with a certain rust of age? That indeed is an injury to the Author. And surely for this the Author himself, God, willed the mark of the divine nobility to be kept forever in the soul, that she might always have this in herself from the Word, by which she might always be reminded either to stand with the Word, or to return, if she has been moved. Not moved as though migrating from place to place, or walking on foot, but moved (as a spiritual substance is moved, namely, when she is moved with her affections, or rather her failings) she goes in a manner from herself toward the worse, when by crookedness of life and of conduct she makes herself unlike herself and renders herself degenerate: which unlikeness, however, is not the abolition of nature, but a vice, raising the very good of nature by comparison with itself as much as it fouls it by being joined to it. Now the return of the soul is her conversion to the Word, that she may be reformed by him and conformed to him. In what? In charity. For he says: Be imitators of God, as most dear sons; and walk in love, as Christ also has loved you (Eph. 5:1, 2).
83.3: Such a conformity marries the soul to the Word, when, namely, she who is like him by nature shows herself nonetheless like him by the will, loving as she has been loved. If, then, she loves perfectly, she has married. What is more joyful than this conformity? what more to be wished than the charity by which it comes about that, not content with human teaching, you, O soul, confidently approach the Word through yourself, cling constantly to the Word, question the Word familiarly, and consult him about everything, as bold in desire as you are capable in understanding? Truly this is the contract of a spiritual and holy marriage. I have said too little, a contract: it is an embrace. An embrace, plainly, in which to will the same thing and to refuse the same thing makes one spirit out of two. Nor is it to be feared that inequality of persons should make the agreement of wills limp in any point, because love knows no reverence. For love takes its name from loving, not from honoring. Let him honor, certainly, who shudders, who is stunned, who fears, who wonders: all these are idle in the case of one who loves. Love abounds to itself; love, when it has come, draws all the other affections over into itself and takes them captive. Therefore she who loves, loves, and knows nothing else. He who is rightly a matter for honor, rightly for amazement and wonder: yet he loves rather to be loved. They are bridegroom and bride. What other kinship or bond do you seek between spouses, besides being loved and loving? This bond conquers even that which nature has bound more tightly, the bond of parents to their children. For on this account, he says, a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his bride (Matt. 19:5). You see how this affection in spouses is more powerful not only than the other affections, but even than itself.
83.4: Add that this bridegroom is not only loving, but is love. Is he honor? Let someone contend that he is: I have not read it. But I have read that God is charity (1 John 4:16); and I have not read that he is honor, or dignity. Not that God does not want honor, he who says: If I am a father, where is my honor? But that is the Father. Yet if he shows himself a bridegroom, I think he will change his voice, and will say: If I am a bridegroom, where is my love? For he has also spoken thus before: If I am the Lord, where is my fear? (Mal. 1:6.) God therefore requires to be feared as Lord, to be honored as Father, and, as bridegroom, to be loved. What among these stands first, what stands out? Surely love. Without this, fear has torment, and honor has no grace. Fear is servile, so long as it is not set free by love. And honor which does not come from love is not honor, but flattery. And indeed to God alone be honor and glory: but God will accept neither of these, if they have not been seasoned with the honey of love. Love by itself is enough; it by itself pleases, and for its own sake. It is itself its merit; it is itself its reward to itself. Love requires no cause beyond itself, no fruit. Its fruit is its enjoyment. I love because I love; I love that I may love. Love is a great thing, if only it runs back to its own beginning, if, returned to its origin, if, poured back into its fountain, it always takes from that fountain that by which it may flow without ceasing. Love alone, of all the motions, senses, and affections of the soul, is that in which the creature, though not on equal terms, can answer the Author, or pay back a mutual return of like kind. For example, if God should be angry with me, shall I in like manner be angry back at him? By no means, but I shall be in dread, I shall tremble, I shall beg for pardon. So if he accuses me, he will not be accused in return by me, but will rather be justified out of me. Nor, if he shall judge me, shall I judge him, but I shall adore him: and he who saves me does not himself seek to be saved by me, nor in turn does he who sets all free need to be set free by anyone. If he is lord, I must serve; if he commands, I must obey, and not in turn exact from the Lord either service or compliance. Now see how it is otherwise with love. For when God loves, he wills nothing else than to be loved: for he loves to no other end than that he may be loved, knowing that they are blessed by love itself who shall have loved him.
83.5: Love is a great thing; but there are degrees in it. The bride stands at the summit. For sons also love, but they think of the inheritance: and while they fear to lose it in any way, they reverence more, and love less, him from whom the inheritance is expected. I suspect a love which the hope of obtaining something else seems to support. It is weak, which, the hope perhaps taken away, is either put out or made less. It is impure, which desires something else as well. Pure love is not a hireling. Pure love does not take its strength from hope, nor yet does it feel the losses of distrust. This love is the bride's, because by this, whoever she is, she is the bride. For the bride, the substance and the hope are one love. In this the bride abounds; with this the bridegroom also is content. He seeks nothing else, and she has nothing else. Hence he is the bridegroom, and she is the bride. This love is proper to spouses, and no other attains it, not even a son. Finally he cries out to the sons: Where is my honor? and not. Where is my love, he says, reserving the prerogative for the bride. But a man is also bidden to honor his father and his mother (Deut. 5:16), and of love there is silence: not because parents are not to be loved by their children, but because many of their children are more disposed to honor their parents than to love them. Grant that the honor of a king loves judgment: but the love of the bridegroom, or rather the Bridegroom who is Love, requires only love in return, and faith. Let the beloved, then, be permitted to love in return. Why should the bride not love, and she the bride of Love? Why should Love not be loved?
83.6: Rightly, renouncing all other affections, she gives herself, alone and whole, to love, she who has it in her to answer love itself by paying love back. For even when she has poured herself out wholly into love, how much is this to the unfailing outflow of that fountain? Not at all with equal abundance do the lover and Love flow, the soul and the Word, the bride and the bridegroom, the Creator and the creature, no more than the one who thirsts and the fountain. What then? shall the vow of her who is about to marry perish for this cause, and be wholly emptied out, the longing of her who sighs, the ardor of her who loves, the confidence of her who presumes, because she cannot run on equal terms with a giant, vie in sweetness with honey, in gentleness with the lamb, in whiteness with the lily, in brightness with the sun, in charity with him who is charity? Not so. For although the creature loves less, because she is less, yet if she loves out of her whole self, nothing is wanting where the whole is there. For this reason, as I said, to love thus is to have married: since she cannot love thus and be loved too little, so that in the consent of the two the marriage stands whole and perfect. Unless someone doubts that the soul is loved by the Word both first and more. She is altogether both anticipated in the loving, and surpassed. Happy she who has merited to be anticipated in the blessing of so great a sweetness! Happy she to whom it has been granted to experience an embrace of so great a pleasantness! Which is nothing other than a holy and chaste love, a love sweet and pleasant; a love of as great a serenity as of sincerity; a mutual love, inward and strong, which joins two not in one flesh but plainly in one spirit, and makes two now not two but one, Paul saying thus: He who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). And now let us rather hear her upon these things, her whom both the anointing, as teacher, and frequent experience have easily made a teacher concerning all things. Unless perhaps we keep that better for another beginning of a sermon, lest we press a good thing into the straits of this one, already nearly to be ended. And if you approve, I make an end even before the end, so that we who are hungry may come together in good time tomorrow for the delights of the holy soul, which she is blessed to enjoy with the Word and from the Word, her bridegroom surely, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
83.title: In what way the soul, however much corrupted by vices, can still by chaste and holy love return to the likeness of the bridegroom, that is, of Christ.

84.1: In my bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves (Song 3:1). It is a great good to seek God. I judge this second to none among the goods of the soul. It is the first among the gifts, the last among the advances. To none of the virtues is it added; to none does it yield. To which should it be added, seeing that none goes before it? to which should it yield, seeing that it is rather the consummation of all? For what virtue can be ascribed to one who does not seek God? or what limit is there for one who seeks God? Seek, he says, his face always (Ps. 105:4). I judge that not even when he has been found will there be a ceasing from seeking. God is sought not by steps of the feet, but by desires. And a happy finding surely does not beat out a holy desire, but stretches it further. Is the completion of joy the using up of desire? It is rather oil to that desire: for the desire itself is a flame. So it is. Joy shall be filled; but of desire there shall be no end, and therefore none of the seeking either. But do you consider, if you can, this zeal of seeking without want, and desire without anxiety. Presence, surely, shuts out the one; abundance the other.
84.2: Now see why I set these things down first. Surely, that every soul among you which seeks God, lest she twist a great good into a great evil for herself, may know that she has been anticipated in it, and sought before she was a seeker. For so, out of great goods, evils that are not the least are wont to arise, when, made outstanding by the goods of the Lord, we use the gifts as though they had not been given, and do not give the glory to God. So, surely, they who seemed the greatest for the grace received are accounted the least before God for the grace not paid back. But I spare you. I have used the milder words, greatest and least; but what I feel I have not expressed. I wrapped the difference up; I myself will lay it bare: I ought to have said the best and the worst. For truly, and without doubt, each one is the worst in the very degree in which he is the best, if he ascribes to himself this very thing by which he is the best. This, surely, is the worst thing. But if someone says, Far be it, I acknowledge that by the grace of God I am what I am, and yet studies to catch a little glory for the grace which he has received: is he not a thief and a robber? Let him who is of this sort hear: Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant (Luke 19:22). What is more wicked than a servant who takes to himself the glory of his lord?
84.3: In my bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves. The soul seeks the Word, but a soul which has first been sought by the Word. Otherwise, once gone out or cast out from the face of the Word, her eye will not return that she may see good things, if she is not sought again by the Word. As if our soul were anything else than a spirit that goes and does not return, if she has been left to herself. Hear the fugitive and the wanderer, what she laments, and what she asks. I have strayed, she says, like a sheep that is lost: seek your servant (Ps. 119:176). O man, do you wish to return? But if the thing rests in the will, why do you beg for help? why do you go begging elsewhere for that in which you yourself abound to yourself? It is plain that she wills, and cannot: for she is a spirit that goes and does not return, though he is one who ranges still farther, who does not even will. Yet I would not say that that soul has been altogether exposed or abandoned, which longs to return and asks to be sought. For whence does this will come to her? From this, unless I am mistaken, that she has already been visited by the Word, and sought. Nor was the seeking idle, since it worked the will, without which there could have been no return. But it does not suffice to be sought once: so great is the soul's languor, and so great the difficulty in returning. For what if she wills? The will lies helpless where the power does not answer. For to will, he says, is present with me; but to accomplish the good I do not find (Rom. 7:18). What, then, does he seek, the man whom we brought in from the psalm? Plainly nothing else than to be sought: which he would not be seeking unless he had been sought; and again he would not be seeking it if he had been sought enough. And this is what he asks: Seek, he says, your servant; that he who gave the willing may also give the accomplishing, for the sake of the good will.
84.4: To me, however, the present place does not seem able to fit a soul of this kind, which has not yet received the second grace, willing indeed, but not able, to go to him whom her soul loves. For how can what follows there suit her — to rise and go about the city, and even through the lanes and the squares to seek the beloved (Song 3:2) — she who herself needs to be sought? Let her do this who can: only let her remember that she was sought first, even as she was loved first; and that from that it comes, both that she seeks and that she loves. Let us also pray, most dear, that these mercies may quickly come before us, because we have been made exceedingly poor: which I do not say of all of you. For I know very many of you walking in the love with which Christ has loved us, and seeking him in simplicity of heart. But there are some, which I say with sorrow, who have as yet given us no sign in themselves of this so saving anticipation, and therefore none of their salvation: men who love themselves, not the Lord; and who seek the things that are their own, not the things that are the Lord's.
84.5: I have sought, she says, him whom my soul loves. Surely the kindness of him who comes before you stirs you to this, who both sought you first and loved you first. You would not seek at all unless you had first been sought, just as neither would you love unless first loved. You have been come before not in one blessing only, but in two, in love and in the seeking. Love is the cause of the seeking; the seeking is the fruit of the love, and its assurance. You have been loved, lest you suspect that you were sought rather for punishment; you have been sought, lest you complain that you were loved to no purpose. Each sweetness, found so friendly, both gave boldness and drove shame away, and persuaded the return, and stirred the affection. Hence the zeal, hence this ardor of seeking him whom your soul loves; because surely, not having been sought, you could not seek, and, having been sought, you cannot now refrain from seeking.
84.6: But do not forget from whence you have come to this point. And that I may rather shift onto myself the things that are said, for that is safer: are you, O my soul, she who, having left your former husband, with whom it had been well for you, made your first faith void, going after your lovers? And now, having played the harlot with them as long as it pleased you, and perhaps scorned by them too, do you dare, shameless and bold of face, to wish to return to him whom in pride you scorned? What? worthy of hiding-places, do you seek the light, and run to the bridegroom, more worthy of stripes than of kisses? It would be strange if you did not meet a judge in place of a bridegroom. Happy the man who shall have heard his soul answering to these things: I do not fear, because I love; which I would by no means do, were I not loved. Love, therefore, as well. One who is loved has nothing to fear. Let those be afraid who do not love. Why should they not be always suspecting enmities? But I, because I love, cannot doubt that I am loved, any more than that I love. Nor can I fear the countenance whose affection I have felt. In what? In this, that he not only sought one such as I am, but also touched her with affection, and thereby made her sure of the seeking. Why should I not answer in the seeking him to whom I answer in affection? Will he be angry at being sought, he who dissembled even when he was scorned? Nay, he will not thrust away one who seeks him, who even seeks one who scorns him. Kind is the Spirit of the Word, and he reports kind things to me, making known and urging the zeal and the desire of the Word, which surely cannot be hidden from that Spirit. He searches the deep things of God, privy to the thoughts which he thinks, thoughts of peace and not of affliction. Why should I not take heart to seek, having experienced clemency and been persuaded of peace?
84.7: Brethren, to have this urged upon one is to be sought by the Word; to be persuaded of it is to be found. But not all take this saying. What shall we do for our little ones, those I mean who are still beginners among us, yet not without wisdom, since they hold the beginning of wisdom, subject to one another in the fear of Christ. From whence, I say, shall we give them assurance that these things are so in the case of the bride, when they themselves have not yet felt such things being done in their own case? But I send them to one whom they ought not to disbelieve. Let them read in the book that which, because they do not see it in another's heart, they do not believe. It is written in the prophets: If a husband shall have put away his wife, and she, going away, shall have married another man, shall he return to her any more? shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have played the harlot with many lovers: and yet return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you (Jer. 3:1). They are the words of the Lord: it is not lawful to hold belief in suspense. Let them believe what they do not experience, that by the merit of faith they may some day come to the fruit of experience. I judge it has been set out clearly enough what it is to be sought by the Word, and of what sort this necessity is, a necessity not of the Word but of the soul; save that she who has experienced it knows these things both more fully and more happily. It remains that in the following discourse we teach thirsting souls to seek him by whom they have been sought, or rather that we learn this from her who is brought in, in this place, seeking him whom her soul loves, the Bridegroom of the soul, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God blessed unto the ages. Amen.
84.title: That the soul seeking God is prevented by him: and what that seeking is, in which she has already been prevented by him.

85.1: In my bed I sought him whom my soul loves (Song 3:1). To what end? It has been said, and to repeat it is superfluous: yet for the sake of certain ones who were not present when it was treated, I say something briefly, and something which perhaps even those who were present will not be sorry to hear. For the whole could not be said then. The soul seeks the Word, to whom she may consent for correction, by whom she may be enlightened unto knowledge, on whom she may lean for virtue, by whom she may be reformed unto wisdom, to whom she may be conformed unto beauty, to whom she may be married unto fruitfulness, whom she may enjoy unto delight. On account of all these causes the soul seeks the Word. I do not doubt that there are very many others besides: but these, for the present, occur. Anyone, however, to whom it is a matter of the heart, will easily be able to notice still others, and others again, in himself. For many are our turnings aside, many also and without end are the needs of the soul, and of anxieties there is no number. But the Word abounds more richly and more fully in good things, inasmuch as he is Wisdom overcoming malice, overcoming evils amid goods. And now take the account of these which I have set down. And first, since it is first, see in what way there is consent unto correction. We read the Word speaking in the Gospels: Be consenting, he says, to your adversary, while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps he deliver you to the judge, and the judge to the torturer (Matt. 5:25). What is more advisable? It is the counsel of the Word, unless I am mistaken, of one who professes himself an adversary, because he is opposed to our carnal desires while he says: These always err in the heart (Ps. 95:10). You therefore who hear these things, if in fear you begin to wish to flee from the wrath to come, I believe you will be anxious how you may consent to this adversary, who seems to hold out that wrath against you so terribly. But that is impossible, unless you dissent from yourself, unless you set yourself against yourself, unless with a heavy and watchful struggle you yourself fight untiringly against your very self; and lastly, unless you bid farewell to an inveterate custom and to an inborn affection. That indeed is hard. If you attempt it with your own strength, it will be as if, with one of your fingers, you should try to stop the rush of a torrent, or to turn the Jordan itself back again. What will you do? Seek the Word, to whom you may consent, he himself bringing it about that you consent. Flee to him who opposes you, through whom you may become such that he no longer opposes you, so that he who was threatening may caress, and grace poured in may be more effectual unto the changing than wrath drawn tight.
85.2: This, as I think, is the first necessity, on account of which the soul begins to seek the Word. But if you do not know what he wills, to whom you already consent with the will, will it not be said of you also, that you have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge? (Rom. 10:2.) And lest you reckon this a light thing, remember that it is written, that the ignorant man shall be ignored (1 Cor. 14:38). Do you wish to know what I counsel in this necessity also? The same as in the first. By my counsel you will now go to the Word this time also, and he will teach you his ways, lest, while indeed you will the good but do not know it, it happen that as you run you run beyond, and wander in a pathless place, and not in the way. For the Word is light. The declaration of the words, finally, gives light, and gives understanding to the little ones. Blessed are you, if you also say: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths (Ps. 119:130, 105). Nor has your soul advanced a little, whose will has been changed, whose reason has been enlightened, so that she both wills the good and knows it. In the one she has received life, in the other sight. For by willing evil she had been dead, and by being ignorant of the good she had been blind.
85.3: Now she lives, now she sees, now she stands in the good, but by the help and the working of the Word. She stands, raised by the hand of the Word as though upon two feet, devotion and recognition. She stands, I say, but let her think it said to herself: Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12). Do you think she can stand by herself, who was not able to rise by herself? I do not think so. Why, indeed? By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm (Ps. 33:6), and shall the earth stand without the Word? Why then, if she was able to stand by herself, did the man from the earth pray, saying: Strengthen me in your words? (Ps. 119:28.) And finally he had proved it. That voice was his very own: I was pushed and overthrown that I might fall, and the Lord upheld me (Ps. 118:13). Do you ask who that one is who pushes? There is not one. The devil is one who pushes, the world is one who pushes, man is one who pushes. Do you ask who this man is? Each man is his own. Do not wonder. So far is a man one who pushes himself, and one who hurls himself down, that there is nothing you need fear from another who pushes, if you yourself keep your own hands off yourself. For who, he says, will be able to harm you, if you have been zealous for what is good? (1 Pet. 3:13.) Your hand is your consent. If, the devil suggesting, or the world persuading, what ought not to be, you have held your assent, and have not given your members as weapons to iniquity, nor permitted sin to reign in your mortal body; you have proved yourself zealous for what is good, whom malice has harmed not at all: take care lest it have rather done you good. For it is written: Do what is good, and you shall have praise from her (Rom. 13:3). They have been confounded who were seeking your soul, but you shall sing: If they have not lorded it over me, then I shall be without spot (Ps. 19:13). You have plainly given the mark of one zealous for what is good, if by the counsel of the Wise Man you have pity on your own soul (Sir. 30:24), if with all watchfulness you keep your heart (Prov. 4:23), if according to the Apostle you keep yourself chaste (1 Tim. 5:22). Otherwise, even if you should gain the whole world, but suffer loss to your soul, we plainly do not judge you zealous for what is good, since neither does the Savior (Matt. 16:26).
85.4: Since, therefore, there are three pressing upon one who stands; of these the devil pushes by the spite of malice, the world by the wind of vanity, the man himself by the weight of his own corruption. The devil pushes, but does not overthrow, if indeed you have refused him your help, or even your assent. Finally you have it: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (Jas. 4:7). This is he who, full of envy, pushed those who were standing in paradise, and overthrew them, but as ones who consented, not as ones who resisted. This is he who, proud, with no one pushing, cast himself headlong from heaven: that you may know a man stands in much greater danger of his own fall, weighed down as he is by the weight of his own substance. The world also is one who pushes, because he is set in the evil one. He pushes all, but overthrows only his friends, that is, those who consent with him. I am unwilling to be a friend of the world, lest I fall. For he who wills to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God (Jas. 4:4), than which fall, surely, none is heavier. From which things it is clear enough how man is the chief one who pushes himself, who can fall by his own impulse without another's, and cannot fall by another's without his own. Which of these is chiefly to be resisted? Surely this one, who is the more troublesome as he is the more inward, who alone suffices to cast down, while without him the others can do nothing. Not without cause did the Wise Man set above the stormer of cities the man who rules his own spirit (Prov. 16:32). This is much for you: you have need of virtue, and not of just any virtue, but of that with which you may be clothed from on high. For that, if it be perfect, easily makes the mind a conqueror of itself, and so renders it unconquered toward all things. For it is a vigor of the mind that knows not how to yield, for the guarding of reason. Or, if you approve this more: a vigor of the mind standing unmoved with reason, or for reason. Or thus: a vigor of the mind which, so far as lies in it, compels or directs all things to reason.
85.5: Who shall go up onto the mountain of the Lord? Whoever sets out to press on to the summit of this mountain, that is, to the perfection of virtue, will surely know how steep the ascent is, and how vain the attempt apart from the help of the Word. Happy the soul which, the angels looking on, gave them joy and at the same time wonder at herself, so as to hear them speaking of her: Who is this that comes up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? (Song 8:5.) Otherwise she strives in vain, if she does not lean. Surely even pressing against herself she will grow strong, and, made stronger than her very self, will compel all things for reason's sake: anger, fear, desire, and joy she will govern, like a good charioteer, as a kind of chariot of the mind; and she will bring into captivity every carnal affection, and the sense of the flesh, at the nod of reason, into the service of virtue. Why should not all things be possible to one who leans upon him who can do all things? How great a voice of confidence: I can do all things in him who strengthens me! (Phil. 4:13.) Nothing renders the omnipotence of the Word more clear than that he makes all who hope in him omnipotent. Finally, all things are possible to him who believes (Mark 9:23). Is he not the Almighty, for whom all things are possible? So the mind, if it does not presume upon itself, but if it is strengthened by the Word, will surely be able to be lord of itself, so that every injustice does not lord it over the mind. So, I say, one who leans upon the Word, and is clothed with power from on high: no force, no deceit, no enticement will any longer be able either to cast down one who stands, or to put under one who rules.
85.6: Do you wish not to fear the one who pushes? Let not the foot of pride come upon you, and the hand of him who pushes will not move you. There have they fallen who work iniquity (Ps. 36:12). There the devil and his angels rushed down, who, though not pushed from without, were yet cast out, nor could they stand. Finally he did not stand in the truth, he who did not lean upon the Word, he who trusted in his own power. And for that reason, perhaps, he wished to sit, because he was not able to stand. For he was saying: I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant (Isa. 14:13). But God judging otherwise, he neither stood nor sat, but fell, the Lord saying: I saw Satan falling as lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). He therefore who stands, if he does not wish to fall, let him not trust himself, but let him lean upon the Word. The Word speaks: Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). So it is: neither to rise up to the good, nor to stand in the good, can we do without the Word. You therefore who stand, give the glory to the Word, and say: He has set my feet upon a rock, and has directed my steps (Ps. 40:2). By whose hand you are raised, by his power you must be held. These things for that which I said, that we have need of the Word, upon whom we may lean unto virtue.
85.7: Now at last we must look at that which I likewise recalled, namely that through the Word we are nonetheless also reformed unto wisdom. The Word is power, the Word is wisdom. Let the soul therefore take virtue out of virtue, and wisdom out of wisdom, and ascribe both gifts to the one Word. Otherwise, if from some other source she claims for herself either both, or one or the other, let her at the same time deny also that a stream comes from a spring, or wine from the vine, or that light arises from light. Faithful is the saying: If anyone, he says, lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, who gives to all men abundantly and does not upbraid; and it shall be given him (Jas. 1:5). So much for him. But I, for my part, would think no otherwise of virtue. Virtue is kin to wisdom. Virtue is a gift of God, to be counted among the best gifts, she also coming down from above, from the Father of the Word. And if anyone judges that she is in every respect the same thing as wisdom, I do not deny it, but in the Word, not in the soul. For the things which in the Word, on account of the singular simplicity of his divine nature, are one, do not nonetheless have one effect in the soul, but fit themselves to be shared, as though they were diverse, to her various and different needs. According to which account, surely, it is one thing for the mind to be moved by virtue, and another to be ruled by wisdom; one thing to bear rule in power, another to delight oneself in sweetness. For although wisdom also stands as powerful, and virtue as sweet; yet, that we may restore to the words the meanings proper to each, vigor shows virtue, and a calmness of mind, together with a certain spiritual sweetness, shows wisdom. This, I think, was marked by the Apostle where, after many exhortations belonging to virtue, he added what belongs to wisdom: in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit (2 Cor. 6:6). To stand, therefore, to resist, to drive back force with force, things which are surely reckoned to the part of virtue, is indeed an honor, but it is labor. For it is not the same thing to defend your honor with labor, and to possess it in quiet. It is not the same to be moved by virtue, and to enjoy virtue. Whatever virtue works out, wisdom enjoys; and what wisdom orders, weighs, and measures, virtue carries into effect.
85.8: Write wisdom in leisure, says the Wise Man (Sir. 38:25). The leisures of wisdom, therefore, are occupations, and the more unoccupied wisdom is, the more she is exercised in her own kind. On the other side, an exercised virtue is the more bright, and the more approved, the more full of duties she is. And if anyone shall define wisdom as the love of virtue, he does not seem to me to turn aside from the truth. But where love is, there is not labor, but savor. And perhaps wisdom is named from savor, in that, coming to virtue like a kind of seasoning, it makes savory what of itself was felt as in a way tasteless and harsh. Nor should I think it a thing to be blamed, if anyone defines wisdom as the savor of the good. This savor we lost almost from the very rising of our race. From the time that the poison of the ancient serpent, the sense of the flesh prevailing, infected the palate of the heart, the soul began not to savor the good, and a noxious savor began to creep in. For the thoughts and devices of man are prone to evil from his youth (Gen. 8:21), that is, from the folly of the first woman. Thus the folly of the woman shut out the savor of the good, because the malice of the serpent got round the folly of the woman. But from the side on which malice seemed to have conquered for a time, on that side she grieves to have been conquered forever. For see, the wisdom of a woman has filled heart and body once again, so that we who through a woman were misshapen into folly may through a woman be reshaped unto wisdom. And now wisdom unceasingly conquers malice in the minds into which she has entered, driving out, by a better savor, the savor of evil which that other brought in. Wisdom, as she enters, while she makes the sense of the flesh foolish, cleanses the understanding, and heals and repairs the palate of the heart. To the healed palate the good now has savor, wisdom herself has savor, than whom among good things there is nothing better.
85.9: How many good things are done, and have no savor for those who do them! since they are driven to them not by the savor of the good, but either by a consideration, or by some occasion or other, or by necessity: and on the contrary, for many the evils which they do have no savor, but they are drawn to them either by fear, or by desire of some object, rather than by the savor of evil. But those who have passed over into an affection of the heart are either wise, and are delighted with the very savor of the good; or they are malignant, and please themselves in malice itself, even when no hope of any other advantage coaxes them. But what is malice, if not the savor of evil? Blessed the mind which the savor of the good, and hatred of evil, has claimed wholly for itself. This is to be reformed unto wisdom; this is to experience, with happiness, the victory of wisdom. For in what is wisdom more evidently proved to conquer malice, than when, the savor of evil shut out, which is nothing other than malice itself, a certain inward savor of the good is felt, with an entire sweetness, to take possession of the inmost parts of the mind? And so, to bear tribulations with courage belongs to virtue; to rejoice in tribulations belongs to wisdom. To strengthen your heart, and to wait for the Lord, is of virtue; to taste and see that the Lord is sweet, is of wisdom. And that each good may stand out the more from the good of its own nature: modesty of mind proves a man wise, constancy shows a man of virtue. And rightly does wisdom come after virtue, because virtue is a kind of firm foundation, upon which wisdom may build herself a house. But knowledge of the good had to go before, because there is no fellowship between the light of wisdom and the darkness of ignorance. A good will had also to be there, because into a malevolent soul wisdom will not enter (Wis. 1:4).
85.10: Now if, in the change of the will, life has been given back and made known to the soul, in instruction soundness, in virtue steadiness, and last of all in wisdom ripeness; it remains that we find for her a beauty, without which she cannot please him who is fair of form beyond the sons of men. For she hears that the king shall desire your beauty (Ps. 45:2, 11). How many goods of the soul have we counted up, gifts of the Word — a good will, knowledge, virtue, wisdom — and the Word, the king, is read to desire none of these, but only this: The king, he says, shall desire your beauty. The Prophet says: The Lord has reigned, he has put on beauty (Ps. 93:1). Why should he not desire a like clothing for his image, and for his bride as well? By so much, surely, will she be dearer to him, by how much she shall be more like him. In what, then, does the beauty of the soul consist? Is it perhaps in that which is called the honorable? Let us hold this for the time, if nothing better comes to mind. But as to the honorable, let the outward manner of life be questioned: not that the honorable comes out of it, but through it. For in the conscience is both its dwelling and its origin. Its brightness, indeed, is the testimony of the conscience. Nothing is brighter than this light, nothing more glorious than this testimony, when the truth shines in the mind, and the mind sees herself in the truth. But as what sort of mind? As chaste, modest, timid, circumspect, admitting inwardly nothing at all that would empty the glory of the conscience which bears witness: conscious to herself of nothing for which she should blush at the presence of truth, for which she should be forced to turn her face away, as one confounded and beaten back by the light of God. This, plainly, this is that seemliness which, above all the goods of the soul, delights the eyes of God; and we name it, and we define it, the honorable.
85.11: But when love of this beauty has more abundantly filled the inmost heart, it must needs come forth abroad, like a lamp hidden under a bushel, or rather a light shining in the darkness, that cannot lie hid. Further, the body receives the likeness of the mind as it shines out, and as it breaks forth by certain rays of its own, and spreads it through the members and the senses, so that from it every action shines, every word, look, step, and laugh (if laugh there be), mixed with gravity and full of what is honorable. When the motions, gestures, and uses of these and of the other members and senses shall have appeared grave, pure, modest, void of all insolence and wantonness, a stranger both to levity and to sloth, but fitted to equity and serviceable to piety; the beauty of the soul will be in the open, provided there is no deceit in her spirit. For it can come about that all these things are feigned, and are not so moved out of the abundance of the heart. And that this beauty of the soul may shine out the more, let that honorable itself, if you please, in which we judged that this beauty is to be placed, be defined: an inborn nobleness of mind, careful to keep, along with a good conscience, an unspoiled reputation. Or, according to the Apostle: to provide things honest, not only before God, but also before men (2 Cor. 8:21). Blessed the mind which puts on this adornment of purity, and a kind of white robe, as it were, of heavenly innocence, through which she may claim for herself a glorious likeness, not to the world, but to the Word, of whom it is read that he is the brightness of eternal life (Wis. 7:26), the brightness and the figure of the substance of God (Heb. 1:3).
85.12: From this step now, she who is of this sort dares to think of marriage. Why should she not dare, seeing herself marriageable in the same degree in which she sees herself like him? His height does not frighten one whom likeness makes a companion, love reconciles, and a profession marries. This is the form of the profession: I have sworn, and am determined, to keep the judgments of your justice (Ps. 119:106). The apostles, following this, were saying. Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you (Matt. 19:27). Like to this is that which, spoken indeed of a bodily marriage, signified the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church: For this cause a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they two shall be in one flesh (Eph. 5:31, 32): and, in the Prophet, the glorying of a soul that is married, But it is good for me to cleave to God, to put my hope in the Lord God (Ps. 73:28). She, therefore, whom you see, having left all things, cleaving to the Word with every vow, living to the Word, ruling herself by the Word, conceiving of the Word that which she may bring forth to the Word; who is able to say, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil. 1:21): count her a wife, and married to the Word. The heart of her husband trusts in her, knowing her faithful, who has scorned all things for his sake, and counts all things as dung, that she may gain him himself. Such a one he knew, of whom he was saying: This man is a vessel of election unto me (Acts 9:15). Altogether a loving mother, and faithful to her husband, was the soul of Paul, when he said: My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you (Gal. 4:19).
85.13: But mark that in a spiritual marriage there are two kinds of bringing forth, and in consequence diverse offspring also, yet not at variance with one another, since holy mothers bring forth spiritual children either by preaching, in the case of souls, or by meditating, in the case of understandings. In this latter kind one is sometimes carried out of oneself, and withdrawn even from the bodily senses, so that she who feels the Word does not feel herself. This comes about when the mind, allured by the sweetness of the Word that cannot be spoken, in a manner steals herself away from herself, or rather is caught up and glides away from herself, that she may enjoy the Word. In one way, surely, is a mind affected which bears fruit to the Word; in another, a mind which enjoys the Word. In the one the need of the neighbor keeps her anxious; in the other the sweetness of the Word invites her. And a mother is glad indeed in her offspring; but a bride is gladder in the embraces. Dear are the pledges that children are; but kisses delight more. It is a good thing to save many; but to pass out of oneself, and to be with the Word, is far more joyful. But when does this happen, or for how long? A sweet exchange, but a brief moment, and an experience rarely had. This is what, above, after the other things, I remember that I said: namely, that the soul seeks the Word in order that she may enjoy him unto delight.
85.14: Someone may perhaps go on to ask of me this also: what is it to enjoy the Word? I answer: let him rather seek out one who has experienced it, of whom to ask it. Or, if it were granted to me also to experience it, do you think that I could utter what cannot be uttered? Hear one who has experienced it: Whether we are beside ourselves, he says, it is to God; or whether we are sober, it is for you (2 Cor. 5:13). That is: one thing I have with God, God alone the witness; another thing I have with you. That former thing I was permitted to experience, but not at all to speak of it: this latter I so come down to you, that I am able to say it, and you to take it in. O you, whoever you are, who are curious to know what this is, to enjoy the Word: prepare for it not the ear, but the mind. The tongue does not teach this; grace teaches it. It is hidden from the wise and the prudent, and it is revealed to little ones. Great, brethren, great and lofty is the virtue of humility, which earns what is not taught, which is worthy to obtain what cannot be learned, worthy to conceive from the Word, and of the Word, that which she cannot herself set forth in her own words. Why is this? Not because merit is of this sort, but because the good pleasure is of this sort before the Father of the Word, the Bridegroom of the soul, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God, blessed unto the ages. Amen.
85.title: Concerning the seven necessities, on account of which the soul seeks the Word: which at length reformed approaches his sweetness to contemplate and enjoy.

86.1: There is no cause why it should any longer be asked of me why the soul seeks the Word: that has been made known enough, and more than enough, above. Come, let us follow out what remains of the present chapter, those things at least which look to conduct. Mark now, first, the modesty of the bride, than which I know not whether anything more gracious can be marked in the manners of men. This, before all things, it is pleasant in a way to take up into the hands, and, as though it were some beautiful flower, to pluck from its place and set before our young men. Not that it is not to be retained with all zeal in a more advanced age also, since it is surely the ornament of every age; but because the grace of a tender modesty shines out more amply, and more beautifully, in the more tender age. What is more lovable than a modest youth? How fair is this, and how bright a jewel of manners, in the life and on the countenance of a young man! how true, and not at all doubtful, a messenger of a good hope, a token of a good disposition! For him it is a rod of discipline, which, bent over shameful affections, checks the motions of a slippery age and its light doings, and presses down such as are insolent. What so shrinks from foul speech, and in consequence from every foulness? She is the sister of continence. Of the simplicity of the dove there is no sign equally plain: and therefore she is a witness of innocence also. She is a lamp of a chaste mind, shining without pause, so that nothing base or unseemly attempts to settle in that mind which she does not straightway betray. So she is a pricker-out of evils, and a champion of inborn purity, the special glory of the conscience, the keeper of good name, the grace of life, the seat of virtue, the firstfruits of the virtues, the praise of nature, and the badge of all that is honorable. The very blush of the cheeks, which shame happens to bring on: how much grace and comeliness is it wont to lend to the face over which it is spread?
86.2: Modesty is to such a degree a native good of the mind, that even those who are not afraid to do ill are nonetheless ashamed to be seen doing it, the Lord saying: Everyone who does evil hates the light (John 3:20). But they also who sleep, sleep in the night; and they who are drunk, are drunk in the night (1 Thess. 5:7): hiding, of course, the works of darkness, things worthy of lurking-places, in the dark. Yet there is this difference, that the hidden shames which the modesty of these men blushes not to possess, but to have brought to light, the modesty of the bride does not cover at all, but spits them out, but drives them off. For this reason the Wise Man says: There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory (Sir. 4:25). The bride seeks the Word modestly indeed, because upon the bed, because through the nights; but this modesty has glory, not sin. She seeks this unto the cleansing of the conscience; she seeks it unto testimony, that she may be able to say: This is my glory, the testimony of my conscience (2 Cor. 1:12). Upon my bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves (Song 3:1). Modesty, if you take note, is signed for you both by the place and by the time. What is so friendly to a modest mind as secrecy? Secrecy, moreover, both the night and the bed possess. We are bidden, finally, when we wish to pray, to go into our chamber (Matt. 6:6), for the sake of secrecy, of course.
