That, indeed, is for a precaution, lest human praise, in the sight of those who pray, steal away the fruit of the prayer, and cheat it of its effect. But by this sentence you are taught modesty none the less. What is so proper to modesty as to shun praises of one's own, to shun vainglory? It is plain that the Son, who is also the teacher of modesty, has pointedly charged those who pray to seek secrecy, and that unto modesty. What is so unbecoming, above all in a youth, as a display of holiness? And yet it is from this age most of all that a beginning of the religious life, fit indeed and timely, is taken, Jeremiah saying: It is good for a man if he has borne the yoke from his youth (Lam. 3:27). It is a good commendation of the prayer that is to follow, if you send modesty before it, saying: I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your justifications (Ps. 119:141).
86.3: And not the place only, but the time also, ought he to observe who shall have willed to pray for himself. A time that is free from work is the more convenient and the more fit; but most of all, when the deep sleep of night enjoins silence, then plainly prayer goes out the more free and the more pure. Rise in the night, he says, at the beginning of your watches, and pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord your God (Lam. 2:19). How safe is the ascent of prayer by night, with God alone for witness, and the holy angel, who takes it up to present it at the altar on high! How welcome and bright it is, colored with the blush of modesty! How calm and peaceable, disturbed by no shout or din! How clean, finally, and sincere, sprinkled with no dust of earthly worry, tried by no praise or flattery of one who looks on! For this cause, therefore, the bride was seeking the secrecy of the bed and of the night, no less modestly than warily, wishing to pray, that is, wishing to seek the Word. For the two are one. Otherwise you do not pray aright, if in praying you seek anything apart from the Word, or anything which you do not seek for the Word's sake, since in him are all things. There are the remedies of wounds, there the supplies of needs, there the mending of failings, there store of progress, there, finally, whatever it profits men to receive or to possess, whatever is fitting, whatever is required. To no purpose, therefore, is anything else sought from the Word, when he himself is all things. For even if, when need requires, we seem to ask for these temporal things, if the Word is the cause, as indeed is worthy, it is surely not those things, but rather him, that we seek, for whose sake we ask the rest. They know this, who have made it their way to turn every use of these things toward deserving the Word.
86.4: Let it not weary us, however, to search still further the secrets of this bed and of this time, to see whether perhaps something spiritual lies hid in them, which it would profit to bring into the midst. And if it pleases us to take it that by the name of the bed human weakness is figured, and by the darkness of night an ignorance equally human; it follows, and it is fitting enough, that the Word, the power of God and the wisdom of God, should be sought the more urgently against either original evil. For what is more fitting than that power should be set over against weakness, and wisdom against ignorance? And lest any doubt about this interpretation linger in the hearts of the more simple, let them hear what the holy Prophet says concerning these: May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his sorrow; you have turned his whole couch in his weakness (Ps. 41:3). And that, indeed, as to the bed. Now as to the night of ignorance, what is plainer than what, in another psalm, he says over and over: They have not known, nor understood; in darkness they walk? (Ps. 82:5), expressing for certain that very ignorance of the whole human race in which they were born. This, as I think, is the ignorance to which the blessed Apostle both confesses that he was born, and boasts that he was snatched away, saying: Who has delivered us from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13). Whence he said also: We are not sons of the night, nor of darkness (1 Thess. 5:5); and likewise, to all the elect: Walk, he says, as sons of the light (Eph. 5:8).
86.title: Concerning the caution and modesty of the bride seeking the Word; and concerning the commendation of modesty.
